Eternal destiny. One of the charms of our Lord Jesus Christ is that he tells you the truth, gives it to you straight, and often cuts to the chase. Last time we saw Jesus on a mountain appointing twelve of his disciples as his special envoys or apostles. Afterwards, he descended with them to the rest of the followers, and a great multitude of people from nearby regions. This could have looked like some outdoor mega church Sunday worship, but Jesus completely goes against modern man-made church growth models. With a sermon about suffering, loving enemies, and moral living He is going to tell them plainly what it means to be a disciple of Jesus This speech, this passage for today, is often entitled Sermon on the Plain, or Level Place, as verse 17 puts it in chapter 6. You will see that the contents here look very similar to the Sermon on the Mount in Matthew chapter 5-7, but without the Jewish portions from the Old Testament. J. Carl Laney notes other important differences. Matthew's sermon is found after the call of the first four disciples. While Luke's sermon takes place after the appointment of the twelve, about a year later. Jesus sat down to preach in Matthew 5. 1, but stood in Luke 6. 17. The Sermon on the Mount contains 107 verses, while the Sermon on the Plain contains 30 verses. Same truths are expressed with different language and phrases. Jesus, like any good teacher or college professor, had a body of teaching material such as Matthew 5 to 7 that he would reuse and repeat during his ministry. So I think that's what's going on here The sermon is relevant to all kinds of people throughout every age, for all who are following Jesus or considering following him. Commentator C. Marvin Pate writes, quote, It may be surmised that the sermon served as a two-fold function. to encourage faithfulness among Jesus' disciples and to challenge non-disciples to follow him. End quote Now with such a demanding message, certain disciples may quit, and those on the fringe may be scared off. Nevertheless, we appreciate Jesus for not putting the cost of discipleship in fine print. Let's read the passage for today from Luke chapter 6, verses 20 to 49 Luke chapter 6, verse 20 to 49. The passage is also in the insert inside the bulletin. Luke six, twenty to forty nine, the end of the chapter Then he lifted up his eyes toward his disciples and said, Blessed are you poor, for yours is the kingdom of God. Blessed are you who hunger now, for you shall be filled. Blessed are you who weep now, for you shall laugh. Blessed are you when men hate you, and when they exclude you, and revile you, and cast out your name as evil, for the Son of Man's sake. Rejoice in that day and leave for joy, for indeed your reward is great in heaven, for in like manner their fathers did to the prophets. But woe to you who are rich, for you have received your consolation. Woe to you who are full, for you shall hunger. Woe to you who laugh now, for you shall mourn and weep. Woe to you when all men speak well of you, for so did their fathers to the false prophets. But I say to you who hear, love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, bless those who curse you, and pray for those who spitefully use you. To him who strikes you on the one sheep, offer the other also. And from him who takes away your cloak, do not withhold your tunic either Give to everyone who asks of you, and from him who takes away your goods, do not ask them back. And just as you want men to do to you, you also do to them likewise. But if you love those who love you, what credit is that to you? For even sinners love those who love them. And if you do good to those who do good to you, what credit is that to you? For even sinners do the same. And if you lend to those from whom you hope to receive back, what credit is that to you? For even sinners lend to sinners to receive as much back. But love your enemies, do good, and lend, hoping for nothing in return, and your reward will be great, and you will be sons of the Most High. Forgive, and you will be forgiven. Give and it will be given to you. And why do you look at the speck in your brother's eye, but do not perceive the plank in your own eye? Or how can you say to your brother, brother, let me remove the speck that is in your eye when you yourself do not see the plank that is in your own eye? Hypocrite. First remove the plank from your own eye, and then you will see clearly to remove the speck that is in your brother's eye. For a good tree does not bear bad fruit, nor does a bad tree bear good fruit. For every tree is known by its own fruit. For men do not gather figs from thorns, nor do they gather grapes from a bramble bush. A good man out of the good treasure of his heart brings forth good, and an evil man out of the evil treasure of his heart Brings forth evil. For out of the abundance of the heart his mouth speaks. But why do you call me Lord, Lord, and not do the things which I say? Whoever comes to me and hears my sayings and does them, I will show you whom he is like. He is like a man building a house who dug deep and laid the foundation on the rock. And when the flood arose, the stream beat vehemently against that house, and could not shake it, for it was founded on the rock. But he who heard and did nothing is like a man who built a house on the earth, without a foundation, against which the stream beat vehemently, and immediately it fell, and the ruin of that house was great. So I'm about to give a sermon on a sermon. You see that Jesus covers a lot of material here in a short amount of time. We may not be used to the rapid movement and sudden shifts in ideas. A commentator, William Barclay, comments Quote, this may be an instance of the Jewish method of preaching. The Jews called preaching karas, which means stringing beads. The rabbis held that the preacher must never linger more than a few moments on any given any topic, but in order to maintain interest, must move quickly from one topic to another. So that could be what Jesus is doing here. Nonetheless, I believe there are some major underlying principles. Jesus was establishing for those who would follow him, or those who are ready following him. And I list three there in the bulletin. 1. Experience true blessings as you suffer. Verses 20 to 26. 2. Love enemies as God loves all sinners. Verses 27 to 38. And three, avoid hypocrisy as you obey Jesus. Verses 39 to 49. First, experience true blessings as you suffer. Verses 20 to 26 The first part of the sermon neatly divides into four blessings in verses 20-23 and four woes in verses 24 to 26. In the Old Testament, authors asserted frequently that true joy, true blessing, belongs to those who fear the Lord, trust in Him, and wait for Him. Jesus continues this line of thought as the greatest prophet. Now consider how paradoxical these verses may sound to a normal, unchurched person. Jesus is saying that following Him does not improve your social and economic status. Discipleship will not get you out of poverty, hunger, sorrow, or rejection. Quite the opposite. Unlike honor societies and degrees from I believe schools, discipleship is a badge of shame in the eyes of the world. Nevertheless, it is worth it. And I emphasize is. Not it will be. Not just because there is a payoff to come. You are in this very moment blessed, even if it doesn't seem like it. As the famous preacher, Charles Spurgeon points out, quote, note with delight that the blessing is in every case in the present tense, a happiness to be now enjoyed and delighted in. It is not blessed shall be, but blessed are. End quote. You do not have to get out of some rut or some painful circumstance before declaring yourself blessed. Jesus has said you are blessed. This might be a total change in perspective for you. Now Jesus could have just said, Blessed are you poor, blessed are you who hunger now, blessed are you who weep now, etc. But thankfully, each beatitude doesn't end at the first comma, but goes on. Those who gave up careers and wealth for Christ to be poor are promised God's kingdom. Those who miss meals for ministry will have their fill at the marriage supper of the Lamb. Those who weep now because of their faith, God will wipe away every tear from their eyes. Those who are hated, excluded, reviled, and cast out for Jesus' sake have their great reward in heaven. So great that right in the middle of a day of persecution, disciples can rejoice and leap for joy. People may think you're crazy, but you are blessed. Their situations parallel what happened to the righteous prophets of old. Now to heighten and emphasize the blessings, Jesus turns our eyes to the other side of the tribunal on the day of judgment. The reverse of the blessings are woes presented in verses 24 to 26. Every soul will stand under God's blessing or curse. There is no middle ground. Woe is a Hebrew interjection, an Anomatopeia. It actually sounds more like oh in the original language. Not the sound we make when we realize something, but more like the sound we make when we face calamity as when we say, Oh no. Many woes or I should say o's will be heard in hell when the rich become poor, the foe become hungry, laughter turn into mourning and weeping. Then it will be eternal regret and suffering for every unsaved soul. Praise God that followers of Christ have brighter days ahead. But for now, suffering is a part of their present reality. Now that doesn't mean that we will be living every waking moment, every second under persecution. Yet at any given moment, any second from now, we could face suffering. Just like many of our brothers and sisters in other parts of the world But those are occasions when we are blessed the most. Much more than when we get a promotion or buy a house So verses 20 to 26 help us endure tough times as a disciple. But that's not all we do. We don't just survive and hold on. Verse 27 begins a series of imperatives that moves us beyond just being blessed as a state of being to being a blessing in an active way of living. And that leads to the second principle. Love enemies as God loves all sinners. Verses twenty-seven to thirty-eight. Now we read up to verse 30 and realize none of these commands align with our natural tendencies. I'm sure the disciples, right off, especially the ones that just became apostles, thought that association with Christ, association with Jesus meant power over foes. But they would be wrong. Verse 31 is often called the Golden Rule, and it is a guide for interpersonal relationships. New Testament scholar D. A. Carson notes its significance. Quote: The golden rule was not invented by Jesus. It is found in many forms in highly diverse settings. About A. D. 20, Rabbi Hillel, challenged by a Gentile to summarize the law, in the short time the Gentile could stand on one leg, reportedly responded, what is hateful to you, do not do to anyone else. What is hateful to you, do not do to anyone else. This is the whole law. All the rest is commentary. Go and learn it. You see how Jesus is different. Apparently only Jesus phrased the rule positively. That means in the face of hostility, Jesus didn't want us to shrink back. Rather, he wanted us to extend love to our enemies. He wants his disciples to be different from the rest of the world. From verses 32 to 34, Jesus asks three questions that all end with What credit is that to you? The word for credit here is the same word for grace, caris, which we have seen four times before in Luke already. We saw the same word in reference to grace which Mary found with God, chapter 1, verse 30. Grace to God which was upon John the Baptist, chapter 2, verse 40. Grace that Jesus had with God and men, chapter 2, verse 52, and words of grace that Jesus spoke, chapter 4, verse 22. You see that up to this point, cares or grace has been with extraordinary circumstances and men. But now we, Jesus' disciples, are invited to experience God's grace. For that to happen, we must go beyond loving those who love us, doing good to those who do good to us, lending to those who pay us back. See how in reply to each rhetorical question, Jesus begins with, for even sinners. Disciples of Jesus are called to a higher standard. We must stop trying to even the score Make an unfair situation equal. Restore the balance. Avenge the fallen, etc. etc. When we stop striving to get even, we situate ourselves for God's grace. We create a deficit that God promises to fill and exceed Your reward will be great. Of course, reward should not be the sole motivation for obeying Jesus. We see in verse 35 that when we love our enemies, we get a chance to show off our Heavenly Father. When we lower ourselves in humility before our adversaries, we will be the sons of the Most High. When we lend without expecting payment and do good to those who do evil to us, we in a miniature way reflect God the Father, who is kind to the unthankful and evil. As we see in verse 36, we must be merciful, just as our Father is merciful. Now to be clear, these commands are not promoting work salvation. You don't become God's children by good works. At the moment of salvation, we are regenerated and born again by the life-giving power of the Holy Spirit, and through his power, we become sons and daughters of God. That is accomplished by God alone without any assist from us. We just trust in his saving work. But those born again are new creation. With new desires, new power from above to obey and follow Jesus. God's children who cry out, Abba Father, will live out their calling They will live as sons of the Most High. Jesus continues this section with more specific applications in verses 37 to 38. If we are to love our enemies, we should not judge or condemn. Now, these commands do not forbid the judicial system or appointment of judges in society. But warn against the human tendency to criticize severely and find fault with our neighbors. Instead, we ought to forgive and give With each of these commands there is a promise of reciprocity from God. A biblical image of giving is provided in verse 38. Again, William Barclay is helpful. Quote: The Jew wore a long robe down to the feet and round the waist a girdle. The robe could be pulled up so that the bosom of the robe above the girdle formed a kind of outsized pocket in which things could be carried. So the modern equivalent of the phrase would be people will fill your pocket. But we gotta be careful not to apply this as just primarily about financial giving, right? Even though that could be a major application. The command to give here is in the context of judgment, condemnation, and forgiveness. So it is more likely that the disciples are asked to give second chances, the benefit of the doubt, an ear to our antagonistic neighbors. All of these acts, and there's plenty, all of these imperatives fit the profile of a Jesus follower who live their uh who love their enemies as God loves sinners. Disciples of Jesus must strive to live lives consistent with their calling. Because we belong to the kingdom of heaven, we are rejected by the kingdom of the world. We should expect that. Because we are God's children, we will live as sons and daughters of the Most High. Now, the direct opposite of Such consistency, sincerity, and integrity is hypocrisy. And that leads to the next point. Avoid hypocrisy as you obey Jesus. Verses 39 to 49. At the root of hypocrisy is losing sight of our perfect example found in Jesus and those who try to imitate him. We may turn inwardly to ourselves as guides or fallible teachers and role models. The inevitable downfall is vividly pictured in verse 39. Two blind men falling to their doom. To avoid such a faith, we must follow Jesus, who is perfect. There is no hint of hypocrisy in him. He leads us in paths of righteousness. We will never be above Jesus, our teacher, but we can be like Him. To avoid the pitfalls of hypocrisy. We must have a clear view of Jesus who goes before us. We must keep our eyes on him. And when we see Jesus clearly, we can see ourselves clearly and then see others clearly. And that's the point of verses forty-one and forty-two. And Jesus, I don't know if you know this, but he has a sense of humor. Have you ever seen a man with a beam of wood stuck in his eye trying to help others? I'm not sure if this was actually an incident because remember Jesus was a carpenter. I wonder if it happened to one of his colleagues or something. What does it mean for us to look at others to help them? Jesus tells us to look for fruit in verses 43 to 45. The quality of fruit reveals the identity of the root. What is true in plant nature is true in human nature. As we reveal with our mouths, our actions, what lurks in our hearts. If our everyday speech does not systemally reflect our confession of Christ, we have some reasons to doubt the so-called faith. Now, just to make the connection here, note how this fruit inspection does not contradict the prohibition against judging others that we saw a few verses ago. Now, even if we don't condemn people, right, we do not do away with discernment. We must always be discerning. Genuine faith in Christ produces fruit. There is a famous saying attributed to the reformer Martin Luther. Quote, we are saved by faith alone. But the faith that saves is never alone. We are saved by faith alone, but the faith that saves is never alone. End quote. So now we based on this principle, which I believe to be biblical, we can comfort those who produce good fruit and warn those who show no fruit, lest they become hypocrites. As verse 46 says, true disciples do not merely call Jesus Lord, they follow Jesus as Lord in their words and actions. Moving from the illustration found in nature, Jesus shifts to an architectural one. Faith that is obedient. True faith is pictured as an unshakable house built on a firm foundation. Faith that is shallow, false faith, is pictured as a house without foundation. The same deluge affects both, but only the house founded on the rock remains. Someday there will be a day of destruction, judgment day, when all will stand before God. Are you ready for that day? All of us will breathe our last breath on earth and stand before our Maker to either enter everlasting life in heaven or everlasting torment in hell. I am telling you this moment that if you have rested the hopes of heaven on your good works, how you compare relatively to fellow humans, you will be swept away by God's wrath. Build your trust upon the firm foundation of Jesus Christ and his work. He is the stone which the builders rejected, but has now become the chief cornerstone. You will not be disappointed that last day if you trust in him and follow him For now, experience true blessings as you suffer if you are a disciple. Love enemies as God loves all sinners. Avoid hypocrisy as you obey Jesus. Jesus made all of these demands of his disciples, and he was fully aware that they would fail him many times over. He knew that when he chose his twelve, they would flee from suffering, despise their enemies, and be disobedient hypocrites. Us too. He knew our sins before we came to him, and he knows our failures even after we became Christians. But our Lord is merciful. Not only did he demand, he met the demands of penalty for our sins. Jesus declared blessings for disciples who would courageously suffer for him, but he himself courageously suffered for us. He became poor, hungry, mournful, hated, excluded, reviled, cast out for our sins. For our blessings, Jesus became a curse for us at the cross, taking God's wrath upon himself. He told us to love our enemies, and he himself did just that. He prayed for those who crucified him. Father forgive them, for they do not know what they do. While we were still enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his son. Jesus suffered for our hypocrisy, bad fruit. evil speech, corrupt hearts, disobedience, though he himself was full of integrity, good fruit, good treasures in his heart And perfectly obedient to God the Father. Risen from the dead and sitting in heaven, Jesus calls each of you to be his disciples Will you respond? He has provided all that you need to follow him as a disciple. He has told you plainly the commands. He has secured the forgiveness for the times you fail. He has granted the power for the time to succeed. Come follow him today. Let's pray.

And by our sinful nature, we are selfish and self-centered people. So rather than being mad at this unnamed man who refused to redeem, we should see ourselves in him. Our first instinct and priority are to preserve ourselves, our possessions With that in mind, let's start with verse 1. While Ruth and Naomi are sitting and waiting, Boaz went to the gate of Bethlehem to sit. Just to be clear, he's not sitting around and doing nothing. According to the commentary of F. B. Huey Jr. , the City Gate was, quote, a kind of outdoor court. The place where judicial matters were resolved by the elders and those who had earned the confidence and respect of the people. A place for business and as a kind of a forum or public meeting place. Here Boaz locates the closer Kinsman Redeemer he spoke of back in chapter three, verse twelve, and pulls him aside. We still don't know the exact nature of this man's relationship with Elimelech, only that he's closer to him than Boaz. The author of Ruth decided to leave it out along with the exact relationship to Elimelech, probably to protect his reputation. The Puritan minister Matthew Poole write, quote, doubtless Boaz both knew his name and called them by it, but it is omitted by the holy writer, partly because it was unnecessary to know it, and principally in way of contempt. As is usual, and a just punishment upon him, that he who would not preserve his brother's name might lose his own, and lie buried in the grave of perpetual oblivion. So harsh words from commentators. Next in verse 2, Boaz gathers ten men to be witnesses of the transaction about to take place. These elders were respected and well-known men of the city. Next in verse five, Boaz reveals that if he really wants to redeem the piece of land, there's more to do. As you know, Naomi was too old and long past the years of childbearing. But Ruth wasn't. The Redeemer refuses in verse 6 and asks Boaz to take his place. So there's a lot going on here, so let's slow down and let's analyze these verses in more depth. David Howard Jr. comments on two interpretive issues. And two questions. First, he asks, quote, why did Naomi appear so destitute early in the book if she in fact had owned property such as this? Now, the author of this book does not answer this question. Perhaps the property was taken over by someone else when the family moved to Moab many years ago, depriving her of any fruits of that land. And here's Howard's answer, quote, assuming that he did not know about Ruth initially, undoubtedly he saw an opportunity for an improvement in his own will. Even if he were obligated to care for Naomi, she was old, and the field would have been his when she died, presumably in the not so distant future. However, Ruth's presence suggested that she or the son born to her by this man would retain or regain rights to the land after Naomi's death. Thus he would have endangered his own wealth by assuming the care and keeping of Ruth and any other children along with Naomi. So his an answer was in essence, I do not have the resources to do this. John Reed essentially agrees with Howard and asks that if Ruth bears a son He would inherit not only the land but a part of the redeemer's inheritance as well. To seal the deal, the anonymous relative had to give his sandal to Bois. The sandal represents the God-given rights to walk on a property as his own. And we see that symbolism in Deuteronomy 1, Deuteronomy 11, Joshua 1, and 14. Deuteronomy 25, verses 5 to 10 gives the most detail concerning this symbolic custom. There you see that if the man refuses to raise up his brother's name as the Redeemer The widowed wife would come up to him in the presence of witnesses to take his sandal, spit on his face, and give him a shameful name. But this man is spared from such shame because Boaz took his place and no one was dishonored. So only the removal of the sandal took place in verse 8. To return to the point I made at the beginning, it's easy for us to vilify this man who refused to redeem brute. But really, we as fallen humans are closer to this man than Boaz. We would rather preserve our own legacies inheritance, plans, then help others, whether neighbors or relatives. Now Paul has to tell saved born-again Christians in Philippians 2 verses 3 to 4. Let nothing be done through selfish ambition or conceit, but in lowliness of mind, let each esteem others better than himself. Let each be looked out not only for his own interests. but also for the interests of others. And you read the rest of that chapter and Christ is the perfect example of that. Now, if saints have to be told to stop being selfish and conceited, how much for the unsaved, right, who don't have the example of Christ or the indwelling spirit? Indeed, the refusal to redeem, to help others, to save others is common. But Boaz through uh Boaz, though he's a sinner like us, was not common in this occasion. He possessed noble faith. And that leads to the second principle. The realization of redemption is noble. Boaz does exactly what the other guy should have done. He addresses the ten-seated witnesses and the others standing and watching. The emphasis in verse 9 is on the material possessions that were at risk. The emphasis in verse 10 is the marriage covenant with root that would be the key to redemption. John Reed again notes how every member of the family is mentioned in these two verses, verses 9 and 10. And the key figure here, the channel of their lasting legacy and blessing, Ruth the Moabites. Truly, God has not forsaken his kindness to the living and the dead, as it was said. back in chapter two verse twenty. Boaz's proposal is formally approved by the witnesses and the people of Bethlehem in verse eleven. The prayer of the people in that verse is amazing because Ruth the Moabites, once an outsider, is compared to the two great matriarchs of Israel Ruth was barren as Rachel once was, but the people intercede for her. The phrase, may you prosper, is literally may you make valor or make qair. You may recall from last time that the word is very context sensitive in chapter 2 verse 1. The word is used to introduce Boaz as a man of great wealth. In chapter 3, verse 11. Boaz himself uses the word to praise Ruth as a virtuous woman. Now, here in chapter 4, verse 11, the townspeople wish that Boaz and Ruth would have Cair together. Prosperity in marriage. Not prosperity primarily in wealth, but prosperity in God's kindness. I say dwell as a family in Ephrata, which is another name for Bethlehem. They pray that when the name of Boaz is mentioned in the town, people would praise the name of Yahweh. In verse twelve, the people invoke another prayer, this time comparing the house of Boaz to the house of Paris, his ancestor. This connection is also appropriate as the story of Paris' mother Tamar and Judah has key affinities with the story of Ruth and Boas. The widow of Rud found a redeemer in Boaz to perpetuate the name of Malon, her late husband. So also the twice widowed Tamar found in Judah a redeemer to perpetuate the name of Er, her late husband. Now there are of course stark contrasts. The entire story of Genesis 38 is a complex one of irresponsibility. Immorality and guile from Judah and Tamar. But Ruth and Boaz have been nothing but noble in pursuing and realizing the redemption. Ruth is a feel-good story because good guys win. Of course not every act of nobility is rewarded like this. But we need reminders, and God knew that we needed reminders through this book, that God makes provisions for redemption and rewards those who are redeemed in this life and next. And that leads to the next point. The reward of redemption is lasting. In verse 13, we fast forward to the next year or two. Boaz and Luth marry and have a son. In verse 14, we hear from the women of Bethlehem again, first time in a while as a separate group. In the first chapter, when Naomi returned to Bethlehem, the women were shocked to see her destitution. Her response to their shock in verse 20 and 21 in chapter 1 was this. Do not call me Naomi. Call me Mara, for the Almighty has dealt very bitterly with me. I went out full, and the Lord has brought me home again empty. Why do you call me Naomi, since the Lord has testified against me? And the Almighty has afflicted me. But see how things have changed under God's providence. Now, the same group, the women of Bethlehem, say, Blessed be the Lord. The Lord who brought her home again empty has not left her to stay without a close relative, without a Goel. Like the elders and the people at the gate who asked for the fame of Boaz's name, the woman asked that this newborn name be famous in Israel. In the first half of verse 15, the woman also prayed that this child would be a source of her restoration in life and security as she faces her latter days on earth. In the second half of verse 15, we get to the blessing that Ruth has been to Naomi. The deep bond that began in the journey from Moab is now celebrated by the women. At the end of chapter one, while I'm sure Naomi was appreciative and grateful for Ruth, she was so engulfed in grief that she didn't even as much introduce her daughter-in-law as she arrived home. The joy of a faithful daughter-in-law evidently did not quench the sorrow of losing her husband and her two sons. But here we are. The woman exclaiming, Your daughter-in-law who loves you is better to you than seven sons. And look at the fullness of Naomi who came to the town empty. Boaz has become like a son to her, and Ruth is worth many sons. Now in verse 16, Naomi practically has a new lease in life. The afflicted one who has who once asked that her name be called Mara, bitter, is now paired with the name of the newborn, Obed, whose name means servant or worshiper. The bitter shock of is this Naomi is replaced by the joyous news in verse 17. There's a son born to Naomi. As she has become a nurse for Obad, the same takes on even more significance. The word for son in Hebrew, then, is the same word used to describe a descendant of multiple generations She's practically the mother and it really a mother as well. Ovet himself will grow up to be the father of Jesse, who is the father of David. The book of Ruth ends with a genealogy from Paras to David in verses eighteen to twenty-two. As I mentioned before, Salman was not the father of Boaz in the way we as modern English speakers understand the word father commonly. Genealogies can skip some generations. So Salman was an ancestor, forefather, probably a great-great-grandfather of Boas. But the point here is that the line is unbroken and Ro Root's role has been instrumental. While all these events were monumental in the lives of these individuals, they were but small pieces of puzzles in the grand picture that God is creating. God has a vision for what he wants to accomplish, and it's a wonderful privilege to be in his hands. Derek Kidner comments, quote, God's hand is all over history. God works out his purpose. Generation after generation. Limited as we are to one lifetime, each of us sees so little of what happens. A genealogy is a striking way of bringing before us the continuity of God's purpose through the ages. The process of history is not haphazard. There's a purpose in it all. And the purpose is the purpose of God. To be used for God's purpose is in itself a great reward. He has designed his redemption to be rewarding and lasting. So all the lessons we learn from this chapter and the entire book, in fact, points us to the beauty of a greater redemption. The redemption from our sins. Now, among us gathered here or listening online, those who don't really think that sin is not a big issue, right? If you don't think sin is a big issue, I want to point you to passages that reveal the seriousness of your predicament. In Romans 6, Paul uses the illustration of employees and wages to describe what kind of life we live apart from Christ. In that chapter, we are told that our occupation is slave of sin. And wages we earn as that slave is death, eternal condemnation in hell. Our master is Satan, the prince of the power of the air, according to Ephesians 2. There's nothing in us to change our position. No one could save us, no priest No prophet, no king from this world. They lack the power to save, and even if they have such power, there will be no willingness. As I said, the refusal to redeem is common. For scarcely for a righteous man will one die. Yet perhaps for a good man someone would even dare to die. We in need of redemption is neither righteous nor good. Because we have sinned in thought, words, and actions, rebelling against God But our God is not common. God demonstrates his own love towards us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us. He is extraordinary in power, grace, love, and kindness. Hear his gentle words spoken to his people. Fear not, for I have redeemed you. I have called you by your name. You are mine. He redeemed us, not from a distance. He sent Jesus, God who became man, who became for us our prophet, priest, and king. When no one would step up to save us, Jesus stepped up as our kinsman redeemer, our very own version of Boaz. But Jesus is more noble than Boaz in realizing our redemption. The price Jesus paid was not cash or property. Our place in heaven has been secured through the ultimate sacrifice of Jesus on the cross. In Jesus, we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins, according to the riches of his grace. After making this payment, he rose from the dead and ascended to heaven, proving to all that he truly is a redeemer. The redemption he has accomplished is not temporary, but eternal. And so is the inheritance that comes through him. See that in Hebrews 9, 12 and 15. The reward of Christ's redemption is everlasting. If you have not been redeemed by Jesus, please know that the payment has already been made. It's finished. All you need to do now is to turn away from your own efforts to redeem yourself. Your own good works. Your own life of sin. Nothing you do will change your occupation as a slave of sin, accruing the wages of eternal death. Repent and put your faith solely in Jesus and no one else. He is the able and willing Redeemer who can transform you into a slave of righteousness. He is noble and kind, realizing the redemption that is eternally rewarding. Not only do we become servants of righteousness, but children and heirs of God and co-heirs with Christ. Not only do we become male and maidservants of God, we become the bridegroom and bride of our groom Jesus As his betrothed wife, know that Jesus Christ will return to be with us forever. Be confident in his works of redemption. I am his and he is mine, bought with the precious blood of Christ. Let's pray. Lord, we pray that as we look at these words that we may have heard all our lives growing up in the church, Redemption, salvation, advent, resurrection. Pray that they will not become hackneyed, that they will not be vain to us, mundane to us, but that every time we hear the word redemption or redeemer, that our hearts Well up in gratefulness with love for you, you who have loved us first, that we will redeem we were redeemed Through the blood of your son Jesus Christ, that we will remember the price that was paid for our salvation. Whether we've been walking with you for months or whether we've been walking with you for many years and decades. Pray that we will remember each and every day the mercies that are new, the price that has been paid, that you are our great redeemer, and your son is coming back. to take us home, to take us as his bride. For that we will live in purity here on earth. Just living in pursuit of sanctification by the power of the Spirit. We thank you, and we pray all these things in Jesus Christ's name. Amen.

sermons.text: If we study the Bible, we have to study people. This book is filled with real stories of real individuals, and that helps us to be real Even when we see names at the bottom of our hymn pages, and I hope then you look into them. For example, consider Connie Deber, my former pastor's wife. who put old words to a new tune and added a new chorus to the song Afflicted Saint to Christ Draw Near Late 2013, Connie was diagnosed with thyroid cancer. Then came multiple operations, radiation. Hormone changes, extreme body temperature and mood swings, back pain, insomnia Now, if I was in her position, I would have shrunk back from the public limelight. She, however, chronicled her journey in a digital diary filled with Thanksgiving, prayer requests, and quotes. And then published her collection in a book, In Brohi Will Hold Me Fast, A Journey with Grace Through Cancer, in 2017. A year later, she worked on this modern rendition of Afflicted Saint. Many of you can testify firsthand and secondhand what pain and suffering can do to an individual's faith. On one hand, the fiery trials reveal authenticity of faith. At the same time, so-called faith, the imitation brand, turns out to be lacking authenticity. Instead of getting stronger, it fades away. Some emerge with the song on their lips and worship in their hearts Others turn away cursing God and bitter in their soul. So I believe in Hannah we have a model of suffering and true faith which we can emulate. So let's turn to 1 Samuel chapter 1. You'll find the passage in the bulletin insert. Otherwise you'll find the book of 1 Samuel, right after the book of Ruth we just finished. 1 Samuel chapter 1. Now there was a certain man of Ramatine, Zophim. Of the mountains of Ephraim, and his name was Elkanah, the son of Jeroham, the son of Elihu, the son of Tohu, the son of Zuf, an Ephramite. And he had two wives. The name of one was Hannah, and the name of the other Tanina. Tanina had children, but Hannah had no children. This man went up from his city yearly to worship and sacrifice to the Lord of hosts in Shiloh. Also the two sons of Eli, Hopni and Phineas, the priests of the Lord, were there. And whenever the time came for Elkanah to make an offering, he would give portions to Panina his wife, and to all her sons and daughters. But to Hannah he would give a double portion, for he loved Hannah. Although the Lord had closed her womb. And her rival also provoked her severely to make her miserable, because the Lord had closed her womb. So it was year by year when she went up to the house of the Lord that she provoked her. Therefore she wept and did not eat. Then Alkana her husband said to her, Hannah, why do you weep? Why do you not eat? And why is your heart grieved? Am I not better to you than ten sons? So Hannah arose after they had finished eating and drinking in Shiloh. Now Eli the priest was sitting on the seat by the doorpost of the tabernacle of the Lord. And she was in bitterness of soul and prayed to the Lord and wept in anguish. Then she made a vow and said, O Lord of hosts, if you will indeed look on the affliction of your maidservant, and remember me, and not forget your maidservant, but will give your maidservant a male child, then I will give him to the Lord all the days of his life, and no razor shall come upon his head. And it happened as she continued praying before the Lord that Eli washed her mouth. Now Hannah spoke in her heart, only her lips moved, but her voice was not heard. Therefore Eli thought she was drunk. So Eli said to her, How long will you be drunk? Put your wine away from you. But Hannah answered and said, No, my lord, I am a woman of sorrowful spirit. I have drunk neither wine nor intoxicating drink, but I poured out my soul before the Lord. Do not consider your maidservant a wicked woman For out of the abundance of my complaint and grief I have spoken until now. Then Eli answered and said, Go in peace, and the God of Israel grant your petition which you have asked of him. And she said, Let your maidservant find favor in your sight. So the woman went her way and ate, and her face was no longer sad Then they rose early in the morning and worshipped before the Lord and returned and came to their house at Rama. And Al Kana knew Hannah his wife, and the Lord remembered her. So it came to pass in the process of time that Hannah conceived and bore a son, and called his name Samuel, saying, Because I have asked for him from the Lord. Now the man Al-Kanah and all his house went up to offer to the Lord the yearly sacrifice and his vow. But Hannah did not go up, for she said to her husband, Not until the child is weaned, then I will take him. That he may appear before the Lord and remain there forever. So Alcana, her husband, said to her, Do what seems best to you. Wait until you have weaned them. Only let the Lord establish his word. Then the woman stayed and nursed her son until she had weaned him. Now when she had weaned him, she took him up with her with three bowls, one epah of flour and a skin of wine, and brought him to the house of the Lord in Shiloh. And the child was young. Then they slaughtered a bull, and brought the child to Eli. And she said, O my lord, as your soul lives, my lord, I am the woman who stood by you here, praying to the Lord For this child I prayed, and the Lord has granted me my petition which I asked of him. Therefore I also have lent him to the Lord. As long as he lives, he shall be lent to the Lord. So they worship the Lord there. The passage naturally breaks in verses 4 and 20, so that we have three subunits as a result. From each section, we can derive three principles. First, God uses individuals for grand purposes. Verses 1 to 3. Second, God permits suffering for intense devotion. Verses 4 to 19. That's the main portion of this chapter. Third, God receives worship for answered prayers, verses 20 to 28. First, God uses individuals for grand purposes. This principle is a good place to start because we can compare and contrast Root, whom we just studied, and Hannah. The commonalities include proximity in location and timeline. Ruth and Boaz were at Bethlehem, about six miles south of Jerusalem, in the territory of Judah. Elkanah and Hannah were from Ramatheim, Zophim, about six miles north of Jerusalem, in the territory of Epra. Both women lived near the close of the Dark Judges period, around 1100 BC, but Hannah undoubtedly came later. They both faced harsh realities of life, especially family difficulties. Recall that Ruth was widowed and childless Instead of returning to her parents, she followed her mother-in-law Naomi to Israel to be a stranger in a foreign land. Boaz, their Redeemer, eventually married Ruth and provided for them both from his wealth. From what we see here, Hannah too married a wealthy man, but Elkanah does not match Boaz's character. Here's what likely happened. At first, El Kana was singly devoted to his wife Hannah. But once he realized that she was barren, he took a second wife to have sons and secure an heir. This arrangement never goes well in the Bible. Polygamy and its modern form, polyamory, violate the one-man, one-woman principle of marriage God designed from the beginning. Instead of persevering in praying for Hannah as his ancestor Isaac did for Rebekah, he followed Sarah and Abraham, resorting to polygamy. This is a surprising and sad compromise considering O'Kana's heritage Eugene Merrill notes that according to 1 Chronicles 6, you can go there and look it up, quote, he was a Levite by lineage, but an Ephraimite by residence, end quote. More specifically, he was a Koetite, responsible for the sacred furniture and vessels of the tabernacle. You see that in numbers 3. So Al Kana should have done better as a family leader. At least in verse 3, we see him taking his family up to Shiloh to perform his annual sacrificial duties, probably at one of the three festivals that Maos had to attend, according to Exodus 23 and Deuteronomy 16. Though Al-Kanah was certainly disappointing, it gets worse at the second half of verse 3. And we're going to talk more about this in the next chapter, but the sons of Eli were terrible priests, unfit to serve as Shiloh. They were sacrilegious and sexually deviant, fighting fun of the tabernacle. So Hannah faced all kinds of unfavorable family, social, and religious circumstances. She lived in a dark time of history, and dark was her soul individually. But still God uses individuals for his grand purposes. Everyone has a part to play in God's overarching plan. I like how commentator David Sumura summarizes the background information for our reflection. Quote Regardless of how desperate the situation looks outwardly, God is certainly preparing his chosen individuals in order to fulfill his plan and purpose according to his sovereign will and gracious concern for his people. If an incident in a woman's ordinary family life could be such a significant step in the eternal plan of a saving God, Each day can be no less significant to a believer for God's plan and purpose. Do you believe that God uses individuals for his grand purposes? If so, let's not be paralyzed by fear. Yes, it's true that we're living in times darker than the era of judges. You may want to retreat from literal and figurative viruses that infect the society. But remember that Jesus called us to be the light of the world, sitting on a hill that cannot be hidden. We may complain and grumble and feel alone. We don't have to let circumstances affect our individual attitudes and choices. Remember what Paul said to Philippians in chapter 2, verses 14 to 15. Hope you reflect on it. Do all things without complaining and disputing. That you may become blameless and harmless, children of God without fault, in the midst of a crooked and perverse generation, among whom you shine as lights in the world. Now on this topic, how can we practically avoid complaining and disputing so we can be used for God's grand purposes? How do we employ our speech in a way that pleases the Lord? From Hannah's example, we learn that prayer is the way to go. And that leads to the second principle. God permits suffering for intense devotion. In verse 4, we get to the main portion of the narrative. In this verse and next, we see Al Kana favoring Hannah over Panina and the children he had through her. But every yearly act of his kindness was an occasion for a provocation, provocation so harsh that Hannah wept bitterly and refused to eat. Her husband tried to console her in verse 8 and gives all us husbands a lesson on what not to say to a grieving wife. I think Elkanah should have expanded on what the narrator says twice in verses 5 and 6. Yes, her God has closed her womb, but he can also open her womb. That back was not lost on Hannah. So in verse 9, after sitting through the meal, she approached the entrance of the tabernacle with Eli the priest nearby. She went with a bitter soul, prayerful lips, and tearful eyes. Though overcome with emotion, she manages to articulate her longings to God in a vow. In verse 11, we see the contents of her vow and we learn about Hannah's view of God, herself, and her son, if the Lord chooses to give her. While the narrator already mentioned the name of Yahweh Seba'ot, or Lord of hosts, in verse 3, Hannah is the first person in the Bible to address God directly with that name. Now, when we talk of hosts, we're not talking about hospitality. We're talking about armies. Armies of supernatural angelic beings who do the Lord's bidding. David invoked that name of the Lord of hosts in his showdown with Goliath in 1 Samuel 17. Prophets saw him as the minister of justice, Isaiah 31, Jeremiah 11. But God not only cares for the great national and political matters, he also cares for individuals, the little people. So then oppressors of widows and orphans, employers who unjustly withhold wages from their employees, racists who persecute immigrants. The Lord of hosts will hear their cries for justice. See that in Malachi 3, verse 5, and James chapter 5, verse 4. Lest your thing is just an Old Testament thing. That's why Hannah called on this name as her rival made her life miserable. While exalting the name of the Lord of hosts, Hannah humbled herself as the maidservant three times in one verse. But she was not so debased to the point that she could not ask, seek, and knock. No, true humility is not self-absorption or self-pity, but looking beyond yourself and asking the Lord to look upon your affliction. It's not self-effacement, but asking Him to remember you and not forget you. The Bible is clear in places like Romans 5 and 2 Corinthians 7. that intense suffering and intense sorrow of various kinds can be good, provided it leads to intense devotion. That's true whether God says yes or no to your specific prayer request Hannah's specific prayer request was a male child. The son would be a Levite and Coedite, just like his father Elkanah, and was already destined to serve in ministry. But Hannah is adding that her son will be given to God all of his days, not just 20 years from age 30 to 50 as prescribed in Numbers 4. You go two more chapters to number six and see that the child would be a Nazarite, just like Samson was in Judges chapter 13. No razor shall come upon his head ever, and though it's not stated here, no alcohol will he drink either When we approach God's throne in prayer, often we ask Him to give and give, but we resolve to give nothing to Him. Not that he needs it, but if I were to transcribe every word of your prayer this past week, what percentage of your prayers would you be would you be giving to God? Ibisamura again is impressed with such willingness in Hannah to give and compares her to A Abraham, who offered Isaac. In Genesis 22. I think he thinks maybe Hannah did even better. He writes, quote, here Hannah promised and gave. There Abraham was promised and was ordered to give. So let's continue with verse twelve. Perhaps Hannah was so tired and weary from grief that though she started audibly soon her voice faded. Her lips were moving, but no words came forth. But she was genuinely praying before the Lord. Now Eli had his doubts about her character, and that shows how bad the times were. Adam Clark writes, quote, The fact that Eli supposed her to be drunken and the other of the conduct of Eli's sons already mentioned proved that religion was at this time at a very low ebb in Shiloh. For it seems drunken women did come to the place and nude women were to be found there. But Hannah distinguishes herself from such deplorable characters and explains in verses 15 and 16. She has not filled her stomach with wine. Rather, she is emptying her heart of grief. So then Eli gives her a proper blessing, which turns out to be a confirmation of God's answer of yes. In response, Hannah, whose name means favor, asks for lasting favor from Eli. The priest's words comforted her, and so she ate. Her countenance was restored, and next day her family returned home, where the Lord remembered Hannah. Hannah's intense suffering has led her to intense devotion. That devotion amiss prayer is in itself a blessing. But our God, our gracious God, gives more. Sometimes the very thing we asked for. In response, it is only right that we return to Him in worship. And that leads to the third principle. God receives worship for answered prayers. In verse 20, we are told Hannah became pregnant and named the boy Samuel. The reason for that name is because she asked for him from the Lord and she was heard by God or Shemal. When time came for El Kana to visit Shiloh again, this time Hannah stayed home to nurse her newborn. His response in verse 23, only let the Lord establish his word means something close to let God's will be done in general. He's not saying some prophetic word was spoken over the child. That word will come later. As Eugene Merrill notes, the customary period of nursing and weaning lasts three years according to Jewish tradition found in works like 2 Maccabees. And when it was time to hand over Samuel to the priests, Al Kana and Hannah brought with him extravagant gifts and sacrifices, like a bushel of flour. The three bowls may appear excessive, but the number probably corresponds. to the boy's age, and also compensation for the priestly staff at Shiloh who will raise the child. After all, he's still young and needs much attention After the sacrifice, Eli is entrusted with Samuel.
