Hebrews 7. 25, he's also able to save to the uttermost those who come to God through him, since he ever lives to make intercession for them. What a delight that we have a Savior who not only provided our salvation by dying on the cross, but who still intercedes for his people. And that includes you and me today. So that concludes our look at the suffering, death, and exaltation of the Messiah seen in these servant passages of Isaiah. These are not just general prophecies of some great leader. They are very specific prophecies concerning the global mission of the servant to bring justice and righteousness to the world. They prophesy of the suffering and death of the servant for our sins, and they prophesy of the servant's rejection by men, but his ultimate exaltation. And as uh we are, um, if you're if you follow a a church calendar, we're in the Lenten season and we as we approach Good Friday and then Easter Sunday in uh about uh three and a half weeks, four weeks from now. I would urge you to look at these passages again. You really have only two options concerning biblical prophecy, but especially concerning the prophecies that we have just looked at And that is, you can try to explain them away, as uh many modern Jewish interpreters do, and sadly uh others as well, by saying the servant is some idealized figure, or the nation of Israel itself. But then how can the mission of the servant be to restore Israel if Israel is the servant? It doesn't make any sense. How can a nation die for the individual sins of its people? Such an interpretation simply doesn't make sense. Or you can recognize, as the Ethiopian eunuch uh did once Philip explained Isaiah 53 to him, that this is an amazing prophecy. of the suffering and death of Jesus Christ, the Son of God, that he died in our place for our sins and rose again. And like that eunuch in Acts 8. 39, you can receive him. as your savior and go away rejoicing, which is what the text says there. It's your choice But the evidence is overwhelming. There is no reason for us to fear anything, for Christ has conquered death, and we can and should rejoice in all that He has done for us. Let us join with the angels in singing with a loud voice, as it says in Revelation 5. 12, Worthy is the Lamb who was slain to receive power and riches and wisdom and strength and honor. and glory and blessing. May God be praised for his amazing grace. Let's pray Heavenly Father, so easy for us sometime

sermons.title: Days of Our Lives (Psalm 90)
sermons.speaker: Sung Cho
sermons.text: The council has decided that I should bring the members of Faith Bible Church. a new expositional material for this week, even though we are not able to gather. But as I was praying and thinking about the appropriate message, I looked back at my older sermons and landed on a file from 2018, December 30th. It was the last Sunday of the year and I delivered a sermon to my former church, preaching from Psalm 90. I began that sermon listing all the significant events of 2018. In Russia, Vladimir Putin was re-elected for a fourth term. The North Korean leader Kim Jong-un crossed over the DMZ to meet with the South Korean president. In Thailand, over 10,000 people were involved in the intense 17-day rescue operation of a boys' soccer team In England, Prince Harry married Meghan Markle in Saint George's Chapel, closer to home. The ongoing wildfires of California had destroyed almost 2 million acres of land as of December 21st. Truly, 2018 was a was an eventful year. But as I think about the first three months of 2020, the first 81 days of this year, perhaps it will not be far-fetched to say that we are having one of the most memorable years of our lives. I think that would be the case even if the rest of the year looks completely normal. I mean, we've already went through bushfires in Australia The assassination of Iranian General Qasam Salomani, and the crash of the global stock market, and of course the COVID-19 pandemic. Who knows what other events lay ahead of us in 2020? A wise man instructs us in Ecclesiastes 7. 14 In the day of prosperity, be joyful, but in the day of adversity, consider. Surely God has appointed the one as well as the other So that man can find out nothing that will come after him. It is true that we can't predict the future unless God reveals it to us. And when we are faced with adversity, we are led to reflect. But now, how exactly should we reflect? Thankfully, we have in the Bible many exemplary men and women who have to evaluate their own lives and the events therein. Today I want to focus on one individual, Moses. In a few places in the Bible, such as Exodus 15, Deuteronomy 32 to 33 and Psalm 90, today's passage, we have Moses' poetic reflections of God. His people and his own experiences as their leader. That means that Psalm 90 is the earliest Psalm we have available. It is more difficult to pinpoint exactly when Moses wrote this. I've heard suggestions as early as we forced Exodus to the final year of the wilderness wandering. But whatever the date, Moses had his share of excitement and disappointments in his life. He had days he felt like a one, as he had to endure over and over again, the complaints of the people. He had days he felt like a ten, like he was on top of Mount Sinai. What do you do with all this? How do you process it all? If you ever feel like Moses, let's read Psalm 90 together. And see what we can learn. Psalm 90, we're going to read the entire chapter Psalm 90. A prayer of Moses, the man of God. Lord, you have been our dwelling place in all generations. Before the mountains were brought forth, wherever you have formed the earth and the world, even from everlasting to everlasting you are God. You turn man to destruction and say, Return, O children of men, for a thousand years in your sight are like yesterday when it is past, and like a watch in the night You carry them away like a flood, they are like a sleep. In the morning, they are like grass which grows off. In the morning it flourishes and grows up. In the evening it is cut down and withers. For we have been consumed by your anger, and by your wrath we are terrified. You have set our iniquities before you, our secret sins, in the light of your countenance, for all our days have passed away in your wrath. We finish our years like a sigh. The days of our lives are seventy years, and if by reason of strength, they are eighty years. Yet their boast is only labor and sorrow, for it is soon cut off, and we fly away. Who knows the power of your anger? For as the fear of you, so is your wrath So teach us to number our days that we may gain a heart of wisdom. Return, O Lord, how long? And have compassion on your servants. O satisfy us early with your mercy, that we may rejoice and be glad all our days. Make us glad according to the days in which you have afflicted us. The years in which we have seen evil, let your work appear to your servants, and your glory to their children. And let the beauty of the Lord our God be upon us and establish the work of our hands for us. Yes, establish the work of our hands. It is my hope that we can learn from Moses how to look to God hopefully as we look at ourselves honestly. I think there are three lessons in this psalm. 1. God provides eternal security. Verses 1 to 6 2. We are sinful mortals, verses 7 to 11. And 3, we must wisely beg God for help. Verses 12 to 17. First, we must learn that God provides eternal security. Moses knew this truth, and that's why he prays, and that's why he is a man of God. He understood that God is not only a dwelling place for his generation alone, but for every generation. When Moses penned verses 2 to 6, I am nearly certain his mind was wandering back to the book of Genesis. In the beginning, God and the rest is history. God is eternal. There is no beginning or end with him. And what are we compared to him? God was there when the first man was formed out of the ground, when we were formed in the womb. He will be there when we return to dust. What are our ephemeral lives in his eyes? What is a millennium in his sight? A day past? A night watch? Grass that sprouts and withers within twenty-four hours. God has creatively designed us to find security and meaning outside of ourselves. In him alone. I feel as if I've been taught this all my life. I remember reading a child as a child the story of the three little pigs. You know how it goes. The first pig builds a house from straws, the second from sticks, the third from bricks. Next the big bad wolf comes to announce, then I'll huff and I'll puff and I'll blow your house in. In the version I read, the first two pigs survive the catastrophe and run into the third pig's house. We repeatedly, earnestly, long after security. Have you recently and prayerfully confessed, Lord, you have been our dwelling place in all generations? Because I come from a broken family, I used to seek shelter in friendships. That's no fault of my friends, it's my fault. Perhaps you guys felt or still feel the same way. But while I still value friends, I've learned to wean myself away from them. Friends of nearly 20 years of my life are now in other parts of the world. My best man and my wedding now live in Texas. Others are leading busy lives everywhere, elsewhere. It's difficult to see them regularly, even though in my college years I would spend nearly every day with them. Imagine if my security was solely based on their proximity and quality time with them, I would be the most miserable. Moses knew how to rest in God. He knew how after the disaster of 1445 He knew how 40 years later, while blessing one of the tribes of Israel, just before they entered Promised Land. These words are from Deuteronomy 33, verse 27, and they are similar to Psalm 90, verse 1. Deuteronomy 33 verse 27. So eternal God is your refuge, and underneath are the everlasting arms. What would it look like for you to find solace in this truth that God is our refuge, dwelling place, and underneath are his everlasting arms? How could you bless others with these words? Here's an example I found. Anthony Showwalter was leading a singing school in an Alabama church in 1887. When he returned to his boarding house room one night, two letters awaited him. Both were from former students, and both men told of their recent loss of their wives. Mr. Show also wrote back seeking to comfort the young men in the midst of their grief. But what to write? When he came to the end of each letter, he wanted to include a Bible verse. He picked Deuteronomy 33. 27, The eternal God is thy refuge, and underneath are the everlasting arms. He pondered the words of that verse as he penned them into the letters, and the lyrics of the chorus of Leaning on the Everlasting Arms came to his mind He wrote to his friend Elisha Holtman, explaining that he had a chorus but no verses. Mr. Holtman wrote back with the rest of the words of this famous hymn. And you know what they are. Leaning on the everlasting arms is the constant thread of the song. The refrain repeats the phrase and adds, safe and secure from all alarms. The verses are filled with the benefits of having God as our refuge. What a fellowship, what a joy divine, what a blessedness, what a peace is mind. Second verse, oh how sweet to walk in this pilgrim way. Oh how bright the path grows from day to day. Finally, what have I to dread? What have I to fear? I have blessed the peace with my Lord so near. Indeed, we need to lean on the everlasting arms because we are mortal creatures. As one preacher said, God is eternal, we are ephemeral. It seems like the most obvious course of action is to turn to this eternal God for refuge. But we have a serious problem. It's called sin. We are not only mortals by design, Genesis 1 and 2, we are mortals by choice. Verse of Genesis 3 That choice is the willful rebellion against God, manifest in our daily thoughts, words, and actions, the refusal to seek Him. Verses seven to eleven emphasize that we are sinful mortals. Far from deserving God's haven, we see in verse seven. that we are consumed by his anger and dismayed by his wrath. Why is God angry? As we see in verse 8, we can't stand before God because iniquities stand between him and us. As another writer laments in Psalm 130, verse 3: If you, Lord, should mark iniquities, O Lord, who could stand? We can't enjoy God's presence because our secret sins are brought into light. Because of our sins, we read in verses 9 and 10 that both the quality and quantity of our lives are diminished. Under God's fury, our days have declined, our years are but of breath, lasting seventy to eighty years, filled with labor and sorrow and fleeting. That is just a hint, only a taste of God's fearful wrath. Moses can only wonder what the full measure of it might be in verse 11. Moses had abundant reminders of God's anger during his lifetime. He was front and center when God judged Egypt and Pharaoh through a tenth place. He heard the screams of firstborns and groans of their parents fill the streets. He saw an entire army drown in the depths of the Red Sea. He entered the clouds that covered Mount Sinai where God's glory rested. Exodus 24, 17 records The sight of the glory of the Lord was like a consuming fire on the top of the mountain in the eyes of the children of Israel. He saw the ashes of Nadab and Abihu, sons of Aaron, devoured by that very fire. He witnessed the defeat in the hill country under the sword of Amalekites and the Canaanites. As his fellow countrymen were routed, Moses knew that they were done for. He knew that sin was people's greatest problem in every generation. Therefore, we do not deserve to have God as dwelling place in any generation. If we are truly honest with ourselves, and if we would confront the total depravity of our human condition, we would arrive at the same conclusion as Moses. We would see God and his wrath as necessary, imperative to make sense of this universe. The English-American poet W. W. H. Alden adopted many ideologies over the first few decades of his life. They ranged from post-Froudian psychology to Marxism, but the common denominator underlying them all was his basic belief of man's goodness. That belief would be seriously challenged one faithful night when he went to watch a movie in Yorkville, a neighborhood in the Upper East Side of Manhattan, New York City. Biographer Humphrey Carpenter recounts the experience. It was largely a German-speaking area. and the film he saw was Sig in Poland, an account by the Nazis of their conquest of Poland. When Poles appeared on the screen, he was startled to hear a number of people in the audience scream, Kill them He later said of this, I wondered then why I reacted as I did against this denial of every humanistic value. The answer brought me back to the church. Soon after the Yorkville incident, Alden wrote these words in a poem. Either we serve the unconditional, or some Hitlerian monster will supply, An iron convention to do evil by. Alden came face to face with sin in all its ugliness, and he could no longer hold on to the naive conviction that humans are basically good. Not only that, he saw the need for an absolute morality for man, even if it means their damnation. While Alden's poetry does not matter inspired Psalm 90, he was on the right track in his discovery of depravity and search for the unconditional. And what Alden had as a troublesome urge, Moses had as firm revelation, firm conviction. The wickedness of man, which the poet saw at the cinema, God sees constantly with his holy gaze. And we are not just speaking of sins that grab the headlines. God sees all. Read again in verse 8: You have set our iniquities before you, our secret sins in the light of your countenance. Like a surgeon with a sharp scalpel, God penetrates our sins to reveal the filth of our sins. He penetrates our hearts. We read in Hebrews 4, 12 to 13. For the word of God is living and powerful, and sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing even to the division of soul and spirit, and of joints and marrow. and is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart. And there is no creature hidden from his sight, but all things are naked and open to the eyes of him to whom we must give account. Please know that there is no hiding our evil from God. So it seems then God cannot be our hiding place. He is justly angry with us because we are sinners. We deserve his wrath in hell. Theologian John Murray wrote a helpful definition of God's wrath. The holy revulsion of God's being against that which is the contradiction of His holiness, that manifests in a positive outgoing of the divine displeasure. The holy revulsion of God's being against that which is the contradiction of his holiness that manifests in a positive outgoing of the divine displeasure There is no holding back God's righteous anger. How can we ever hope to calm a vengeful, immortal God? We can't. But Moses knew dimly, but Christians today know clearly in full detail. About a millennium and a half after Moses, God sent his son, born of a virgin, Jesus Christ, to live a perfect life and die on the cross. What happened at the cross is what we call propitiation, the pacification or appeasement of God's just anger. Jesus took the full brunt of God's fury on behalf of sinners. The wrath of God was satisfied. Jesus rose from the dead as proof of this truth and ascended to heaven. Now he offers salvation to you. If we would humbly repent and trust in Jesus Christ, we can become objects of his mercy. We don't have to remain as objects of his wrath. Please turn to Christ before it's too late. Our time on earth will pass by like the blink of an eye. We are not guaranteed a single moment beyond the present. Every breath we breathe could be our last. Please email or call me if you want to have God as your dwelling place, not consuming fire. I beg of you that you would beg of God for salvation. That leads to the third point of Psalm 90. Whether we need to initiate our relationship with Christ for the first time or we have been walking with the Lord for years. We must wisely beg God for help. From verses 1 to 11, Moses has been a narrator. Recounting God's greatness and human frailty. Finally, we have Moses entreating and asking. There are many requests, at least one request per verse. Verse 12, teach us. Verse 13, return, O Lord, and have compassion on your servants. Verse 14, O satisfy us. Verse 15, make us glad. Verse 16, let your work appear to your servants. and your glory to their children. Verse 17, let the beauty of the Lord our God be upon us and establish the work of our hands for us. Do these entreaties and requests echo the desires of your heart? Moses' appeals are firmly grounded in sober self-awareness and God awareness. We need both. Self-awareness and God awareness in these dark times. For example, look again in verse 12. Because we are mortals, we should learn to budget our days like the way we budget our money. We have limited time on earth. This is wisdom. This is wisdom we can offer to God, God who is everlasting. We ought to offer Him such a wise heart. Paul most likely had this verse in mind when he wrote Ephesians 5, 15-17. See then that you walk circumspectly, not as fools, but as wise, redeeming the time because the days are evil Therefore do not be unwise, but understand what the will of the Lord is. I'm willing to bet that you already value your time and even quantify it to small increments. I bet if I looked at your calendars, they are filled with events, deadlines, and flights I probably don't need to ask you to keep yourself busy. We've been wired since childhood to go from one event to the next, commute from one location to another. Well this pandemic has forced us to come to a screeching halt and reassess. So now What would the rest of 2020 look like if we were to consciously devote blocks of time to understanding the Lord's will and live wisely? To help us answer this question, let's continue to verse 13 and again observe God's eternality and our mortality in Tam. We need God to return to us because we are servants who return to dust, as we saw in verse 3. There's much wisdom here. The question, how long, is a perfect demonstration of actively waiting for God in prayer. Would you learn to pray more starting today, eagerly anticipating the presence of God? And ask the Spirit to help us start tomorrow morning with prayer. Verse 14 provides the template. We can ask at breakfast. Oh, satisfy us early with your mercy, that we may rejoice and be glad all our days. Yes, satisfy us even if each day starts to look the same. Speaking of joy and gladness, if life has been rough lately, we can look forward in hope and pray, as in verse 15. Make us glad according to the days in which you have afflicted us, the years in which we have seen evil. We can open up the Bible in individual or family worship time and lift up these words to God in verse 16. Let your work appear to your servants, and your glory to their children. Or what if you were to recite verse 17 as you return to work, whatever that may be, or work from home? And let the beauty of the Lord our God be upon us and establish the work of our hands for us. Yes, establish the work of our hands. How would your attitude and your calendar be different with all these applications of Psalm 90? How will you live the days God has appointed for you? Someone once observed that a wasted life is really nothing more than a collection of wasted days. The first step to avoiding a wasted life is to know the Lord. Know that God is our dwelling place through Jesus. Though we are sinful mortals, Jesus died on the cross in our place. In contrite, humble confession, we ask for God's salvation and growth in wisdom, joy, and holiness. With these truths in mind and heart, life is no longer drudgery or meaningless. Life is filled with good and bad things, seasons of joy and seasons of sorrow, and for all of them we ought to be thankful. And all of these give way to the best days to come in heaven. Perhaps you will say amen to the words of Samuel Rutherford, the great Scottish pastor. The sands of time are sinking, the dawn of heaven breaks, the summer morn I've sighed for, the fair sweet morn awakes. Dark, dark hath been the midnight, but day spring is at hand, and glory, glory dwelleth in Emmanuel's land.

sermons.title: Friends in Low Places
sermons.speaker: Sung Cho
sermons.text: Though my years in the States are more than double my years in Korea, my time in my home country is precious. I was there in the formative stages of my life. It was there that I first went to school, first went to church, first prayed, first read the Bible, first learned about Jesus. I saw snow snow for the first time. It was there that I first explored a world that seemed full of Avengers. So when it was time to become naturalized in US, I held on to my Korean name as a link to my past. I relinquished the chance to adopt some westerning I considered Sean. By the way, do I look like a Sean to you? My wife says no In those first years at US, there was a mixture of old and new. I arrived at an airport that looked similar to the one I left. It was snowy in Maryland, late December of nineteen eighty-nine, which was nothing new. Except there was that one time I found myself locked out in front of my elementary school building as snow piled on. In the Korean town I grew up in, you didn't close for snow until unless it was like two feet I had a lot of classmates with yellow hair, which was new. Math was really easy. I remember being pulled out of the normal English classes to be with other immigrant children. To learn basic grammar and vocabulary. Though they were from different parts of the world, we felt a sense of connection as we learned a new language and culture together. That's similar to the scenario that Daniel found himself in. You may know him best as that elderly man who was thrown into the lion's den This might be the most familiar story of Daniel, but it took place later in his life. I w I want to focus on an episode in his life when he was younger and with friends who shared the immigrant experience with him. But before we turn there, let's get to know his background a little bit. In Cartermish, 605 BC, Nebuchadnezzar II. The king of Babylon fought against the Allied forces of Assyria and Egypt. The Babylonians won and sought to establish control over the region. Daniel's homeland, Judah, mistakenly allied with Egypt, and the Babylonians punished them for it. Judah lost their independence, temple treasures, and some of their royal and noble men. These men had to be young, likely from thirteen to seventeen years old, without physical defects, handsome, smart, and promising students. They were taught and trained in the Babylonian language and literature for three years in preparation for service at the royal courts. Among those chosen were Daniel, Hananiah, Mishhael, and Azariah. The Babylonian chief official gave each new names. Beltashazzar, Shadrach, Mishak, and Abednego respectively There was one major problematic requirement with their Babylonian enculturation. All the trainees ate from the king's table While Daniel had no issues with the name change and foreign education, the royal cuisine included dishes not allowed in Jewish diet, including sacrificial meals dedicated to idols. Eating such food is tantamount to fellowship and agreement with false beliefs and deities. Abstaining from the table would allow the Jewish men to maintain their integrity and obedience to God. But it would also mean rejecting and insulting the most powerful man in the nation. We see, however, in chapter 1 verse 8 that Daniel was determined to follow the scriptures His boss is worried that he would get into trouble if Daniel and his friends look unhealthy without food from the king's table. The chief had every right to be scared. King Nebuchadnezzar was known for his cruelty, gouging out of King's eyes just after killing his sons in front of him Or burning other rulers in fire. We see this in Jeremiah 39, verses 6 to 7, 29, verse 22. But he convinces him to allow a diet of vegetables and water for ten days. At the end of the trial period, their appearance looked healthier than those who ate meat. Within three years, the four men surpass all others in wisdom and knowledge as well. Here's the good beginnings. We are only in chapter 1 of this book, and already we see teenage followers of God making tough choices. Such choices will determine their future. These four young men, well educated, successful, and working for the most dominant power in the Middle East, started out as wide-eyed strangers there. We may not be taken captive like them, but we do live between two cultures. I mean that the choices Daniel and his friends made have some applications for us today Our core identity is not American, Asian, or African. We do not even belong to this world. Here's what Jesus said in John 15 verses 18 to 19. If the world hates you, you know that it hated ye before it hated you. If you were of the world, the world would love its own. Yet because you are not of the world, but I chose you out of the world, therefore the world hates you. Paul tells us in verse twenty of Philippians chapter three, Our citizenship is in heaven, from which we also eagerly wait for the Saviour. The Lord Jesus Christ. Hebrews 11, verses 13 to 16 tells us concerning some believers of the Old Testament. These all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off, were assured of them, embraced them, and confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth. For those who say such things declare plainly that they seek a homeland. And truly, if they had called to mind the country from which they had come out, they would have had opportunity to return But now they desire a better, that is a heavenly country. Therefore God is not ashamed to be called their God, for he has prepared a city for them. Finally, Peter wrote in his first letter, chapter 2, verse 11, to the New Testament saints like thus. Beloved, I beg you as sojourners and pilgrims, abstain from fleshly lusts which war against the soul. So if we identify ourselves as foreigners and exiles in this world, if we are determined to abstain from simple desires and wage war against them, Perhaps we can continue to learn from the example of Daniel and his friends in the next crisis they faced. Let's turn to chapter 2 together and look at the first 23 verses. Now in the second year of Nebuchadnezzar's reign, Nebuchadnezzar had dreams, and his spirit was so troubled that his sleep left him. Then the king gave the command to call the magicians, the astrologers, the sorcerers, and the Chaldeans to tell the king his dreams. So they came and stood before the king. And the king said to them, I have had a dream, and my spirit is anxious to know the dream. Then the Chaldeans spoke to the king in Aramaic, O king, live forever! Tell your servants the dream, and we will give the interpretation. The king answered and said to the Chaldeans, My decision is firm. If you do not make known the dream to me and its interpretation, you shall be cut in pieces, and your houses shall be made an ash heap. However, if you tell the dream and its interpretation, you shall receive from me gifts, rewards, and great honor. Therefore, tell me the dream and its interpretation. They answered again and said, Let the king tell his servants the dream and we will give his interpretation. The king answered and said, I know for certain that you would gain time, because you see that my decision is firm. If you do not make known the dream to me, there is only one decree for you. For you have agreed to speak lying and corrupt words before me till the time has changed. Therefore, tell me the dream, and I shall know that you can give me its interpretation. The Chaldeans answered the king and said, There is not a man on earth who can tell the king's matter. Therefore no king, lord, or ruler has ever asked such things of any magician, astrologer, or Chaldean. It is a difficult thing that the king requests, and there is no other who can tell it to the king except the gods, whose dwelling is not with flesh. For this reason the king was angry and very furious, and gave the command to destroy all the wise men of Babylon. So the decree went out, and they began killing the wise men, and they sought Daniel and his companions to kill them. Then, with counsel and wisdom, Daniel answered Arioch, the captain of the king's guard, who had gone out to kill the wise men of Babylon. He answered and said to the said to Eriok, the king's captain. Why is the decree from the king so urgent? Then Ariath made the decision known to Daniel. So Daniel went in and asked the king to give him time that he might tell the king the interpretation. Then Daniel went to his house and made the decision known to Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah, his companions, that they might seek mercies from the God of heaven concerning the secret. So that Daniel and his companions might not perish with the rest of the wise men of Babylon. Then the secret was revealed to Daniel in a night vision. So Daniel blessed the God of heaven Daniel answered and said, Blessed be the name of God forever and ever, for wisdom and might are his. And he changes the times and the seasons. He removes kings and raises up kings. He gives wisdom to the wise and knowledge to those who have understanding. He reveals deep and secret things. He knows what is in the darkness, and life dwells with him. I thank you and praise you, O God of my fathers. You have given me wisdom and might, and have now made known to me what we asked of you, for you have made known to us the king's demand I'm stopping the reading here because I'm not going to focus on the prophetic content of the stream. I do hope that if the Lord tarries, we will study the apocalyptic visions together. But today, I just want to focus on the man Daniel, his friends, and his example. As we look at Daniel, we can observe three qualities to imitate. Daniel 1 seeks wise understanding of the crisis. one to sixteen, two, finds prayerful support of friends, verses seventeen and eighteen, and three, praises the great name and acts of God verses nineteen to twenty three First Daniel seeks wise understanding of the crisis. Verse 1 tells us that Nebuchadnezzar had a disturbing dream during the second year of his reign. But how do we reconcile that timestamp of second year with the three years of training Daniel and his friends just completed, as we see in chapter 1, verse 5? Chapter 2 verse 1 is most likely speaking of the second full year of his reign. If a Babylonian king's reign began in the middle of the year, that year would not count as his first year. since it won't amount to twelve months. When the year cycle begins again, that would be reckoned as the king's first year of reign. Now on to the dream. It's possible that Nebuchadnezzar could not recall the details of the dream. Not that he kept the information from his subjects It's also possible that he had some recollections, some vague memory of it, in bits and pieces. We're not entirely sure. Instead of admitting that he forgot, he designs to test their loyalty and or skill. When they couldn't give what he wanted and thought he was unreasonable, they faced his wrath. Daniel learned of this incident from Ariok, the king's executioner. Note how in verse 14 that he conversed with counsel and wisdom Not panic, not anger. Those are natural first instincts of natural men. Counsel and wisdom befit the godly saint. After gathering sufficient information, he goes to meet Nebuchadnezzar himself and successfully secures more time. Perhaps Daniel spoke with gentleness that assuaged the king. A soft answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger. Proverbs 15:1. The king's wrath is like the roaring of a lion. But his favor is like dew on the grass. Proverbs nineteen twelve We are living in a time of crisis that reveals what's inside our hearts. Panic, fear, anger, racism, idolatry. A good diagnostic question to ask is this, where do we turn for wisdom? I'm not saying you shouldn't read the news or keep up with the latest information on the pandemic. But true wisdom is not found in the world. It is found in God, who reveals himself to us and hears our script, hears our prayers. That leads to the second point. Daniel finds prayerful support of friends. In verses 17 and 18 we get a glimpse into Daniel's personal spiritual life. He has an emergency prayer meeting with Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, his roommates at home. All they had was each other in this strange land, no temple for congregation, no elders and priests to consult. They had no parents or siblings to turn to. Since they were all made eunuchs, they would never have families of their own either. Together they faced an unprecedented obstacle In Genesis, we know that Joseph rose to power in Egypt by interpreting dreams. That would have encouraged these men. But then again, Joseph at least knew what the dreams were before he interpreted them. Daniel and his friends were desperate, and their prayers were earnest. We can imitate their passion as well as the prayer life of other biblical heroes like Elijah. James chapter 5, verses 16 to 18 reminds us of the power of corporate prayer. Confess your trespasses to one another, and pray for one another, that you may be healed. The effective, fervent prayer of a righteous man avails much Elijah was a man with a nature like ours, and he prayed earnestly that it would not rain, and it did not rain on the land for three years and six months. And he prayed again, and the heaven gave rain, and the earth produced its fruit. Of course, the greatest prayers were offered up by Jesus, the God of man. He prayed, Father, glorify your name. John 12, 28. Jesus, like Daniel, asked three of his closest friends to pray with him at the Garden of Gethsemane. Unlike Daniel, Jesus didn't get much support because Peter, James, and John fell asleep. Alone, Jesus prayed three times for God's will to be done, not his. God the Father answered these prayers He was glorified. Jesus drank the cup of God's wrath at the cross and arose from the dead. The Father's will was done. And it is because Jesus prayed and went to the cross, the grave and heaven, that we can pray to our Father in heaven It's all accomplished by the work of his son Jesus. There's nothing you or I can do to act to it. Salvation is A gift from God. And it is ours with repentance, turning from ourselves and our way of living, and faith, turning to the living Christ. And because of Jesus, we have access to heaven. Hear these words of assurance. Romans 5, verses 1 and 2 says, Therefore, having been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ. through whom also we have access by faith into this grace in which we stand, and rejoice in the hope of the glory of God. Ephesians chapter 2, verses 17 and 18 tells us. And he came and preached peace to you who are afar off and to those who are near. For through him we both have access by one spirit to the Father So as the writer of Hebrews says in chapter 4, verse 16, let us therefore come boldly to the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy and find grace to help in time of need. Now that we know how we can speak with the Father through Jesus, let's go back to the example of Daniel and his friends. When is the last time you really prayed? Prayed like your life depended on it? When is the last time my prayer meetings looked like the one at Daniel's home? Maybe the current health and economic crises will lead us to be so fervent and so desperate So that we are their big prayers bigger than ever before in accordance with God's great power. Instead of worrying about temporal matters such as food, drink, or clothing, Jesus told us to seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness. And all these things shall be added to you. What if we were to ask for bigger, greater things from God, rather than things with expiration dates? That God would save that stubborn atheist. That a city would re would turn to God. That rulers would repent. Perhaps we don't ask big things because we have a small view of God. Let us ask now for great things in accordance with God's greatness. And that leads to our third point. Daniel praises the great name and acts of God. During the night, God reveals the mystery of Nebuchadnezzar's dream. For the contents of the dream and its interpretation, you can read on with the rest of the chapter later. But first, upon this revelation, Daniel immediately praises God. He doesn't run to the king right away, though maybe a part of him wanted to. He prioritizes worship. He prayed to receive revelation, so now he prays to give glory. First, note the names of God. Verse 19 has God of Heaven. Back in verse 10, the astrologers complained to the king, there is not a man on earth who can tell the king's matter. They are hundred percent accurate. No amount of human intelligence and inspiration can achieve this feat. Only the God of heaven can do it. Because as you read in verse 20, wisdom and might are his In verse 23, there is God of my fathers. Not only is God spatially above us, dwelling in heaven, he is chronologically prior to us. He has chosen the Israelites to be his people. He's been in the divine promise business way before Daniel and his friends. And there's something personal about verse 23. From verses 20 to 22, God is referred to in the third person, he, his, and him. But here, Daniel switches to the more direct second person, you. God is willing to relate with us closely and not from a distance. He exists not only in heaven, but on earth with us. He is not only high above us, but he is down here near us. Not only does Daniel praise God's name, he highlights his acts. In other words, God backs up his great reputation with firm action. In verses 21 and 22, his power and wisdom are proven by the way he changes the times and the seasons. He removes kings and raises up kings. He gives wisdom to the wise and knowledge to those who have understanding. God reveals deep and secret things. He knows what is in the darkness, and light dwells with him. In these verses, we learn these general truths about God's wisdom and power. Now in verse 23, Daniel recounts how he specifically and graciously shares them. Praise God that we are not talking to an empty room on the other side of the phone. That we don't leave a message to God in prayer and he never calls back. He reveals his ways and deep things in his word and providence. We can trust that God's answers to us, his children, are for our good and his glory. Daniel is thankful and confident that God's answer is the correct answer. Keep in mind, Daniel hasn't gone to the king yet to confirm the dream to be true. He hasn't checked the answer sheet. But he's already certain that the answers are correct and he will pass with the hundred because God gave him the answer. He says in the second half of verse 23, You have given me wisdom and might, and have now made known to me what we asked of you. For you have made known to us the king's demand. One last thing about verse 23. Note how Daniel uses the first person plural. God, you have made known to me what we asked of you, for you have made known to us the king's demand Daniel knows that he could not have survived this ordeal without the prayer of his friends. So Daniel was the only one to see the divine vision. He immediately shares the contents with his friends. Because they prayed as one, they celebrate God's answer as one. Because Daniel, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego sowed in unison. They reap in unison. If the four wept together, they would rejoice together. Pray that we as Faith Bible Church can have a similar testimony at the other side of this trial. As we seek wise understanding of the crisis at hand, I hope that the world will see in us peace and joy and security in the gospel. As we seek and find prayerful support from each other, may the world know the love that we have for the Lord and one another. Let's not have circumstances hinder us from praising the great name and acts of God. Yes, we need friends to share these ups and downs of life. But no one in this world can be your strength and portion forever. Whom am I in heaven but you? And there is none upon earth that I desire besides you. My flesh and my heart fail. God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever. Psalm 73, 25 to 26. Jesus is God who can fulfill that desire. But at the same time, he is man and our close friend. Let's sing about this truth in our final hymn. What a friend we have in Jesus.

sermons.title: Wisdom in Psalms
sermons.speaker: Sung Cho
sermons.text: This week, I'm sharing with you a special topical sermon on wisdom in Psalms. We usually turn to books like Proverbs and Ecclesiastes for Wisdom, but I was provided an opportunity to look into this recently, and I thought I would share with you my findings. There are several ways to approach wisdom and psalms. One way is to look up keywords like wise or wisdom in a concordance or Biblegateway. com and concentrate on the multiple occurrences in the book of Psalms. Or one could compare what this book says about wisdom in the context of other poetic books in the Bible, such as Job, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, and Song of Solomon. Yet another way is to classify certain chapters of Psalms into a genre called wisdom psalms. But this is not an easy task, as scholars have debated for decades as to what exactly makes a psalm a wisdom type. Commentator Craig Broils considers three characteristics. One, emphasis on teaching skillful living, not on addressing God directly in worship. 2. Usage of formulate expressions of wisdom literature like blessed is, numerical sayings, and acrostics. And three, inclusion of wisdom themes like instruction for daily living, and the problem of the prosperity of the wicked. So I'll be mainly using this approach of looking at wisdom psalms One more thought from Craig Broils, a practical note of warning, which I'll paraphrase. Even if we were to identify certain verses dealing with wisdom or certain portions of the book as wisdom psalms, We must be wary of the modern thinking that worship and wisdom, church and school, corporate singing and daily living are incompatible, separate, distinct, and should stay that way. But let no foolish or irreverent man separate what God has joined together. Wisdom and worship. There is wisdom in the context of worship, and there's worship in the context of wisdom Psalm one eleven is a good example of this mixture. Praise the Lord. I will praise the Lord with my whole heart, in the assembly of the upright and in the congregation. The works of the Lord are great, studied by all who have pleasure in them. His work is honorable and glorious, and his righteousness endures forever. He has made his wonderful works to be remembered. The Lord is gracious and full of compassion. He has given food to those who fear him. He will ever be mindful of his covenant. He has declared to his people the power of his works in giving them the heritage of the nations The works of his hands are verity and justice. All his precepts are sure. They stand fast forever and ever, and are done in truth and uprightness. He has sent redemption to his people. He has commanded his covenant forever. Holy and awesome is his name. The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom. A good understanding have all those who do his commandments, his praise endures forever. You see how study, mind, truth, precepts, wisdom, understanding are comparably mixed. With thanksgiving from the heart, praise of God's mighty works and his attributes. And what's true in the Old Testament is true in the New. Again, there's worship in the context of wisdom. And there's wisdom in the context of worship. In his letter to the Romans, Paul worships God as he concludes chapter 11. Oh, the depth of the riches, both of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and his ways past finding out! For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has become his counselor, or who has first given to him, and it shall be repaid to him? For of him and through him and to him are all things, to whom be glory forever. Amen. Worship and wisdom. Elsewhere he tells the Colossian church in chapter 3, verse 16. Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom, teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord. Psalms have lasting relevance both in Israel's original context and the church in its worship setting. And so, in such corporate worship settings, the manifold wisdom of God is revealed to the church through the word, and further through the church for his glory. Ephesians 3:10. Worship and wisdom. There's something sublime, wonderful, supernatural, and I can say confidently. Wise every time a local church gathers for worship. Now I miss my brothers and sisters in Christ and gathering together on Sunday mornings And I hope that we can join together very soon. Now I've jumped too far into the application in the New Testament. Let's go back to the topic of Psalms and wisdom. Stringing together various passages, I want to explain to you Three major concepts or principles that summarize biblical wisdom from the Psalms. 1. Reading and meditating on the Word Two, the righteous and the wicked in contrast. And three, fear and trust in the Lord From the onset of the collection of Psalms, we see a major emphasis on reading and meditating on the word. Right away in Psalm 12, we hear this about the blessed man. His delight is in the law of the Lord, and in his law he meditates day and night. The Bame of Psalm 19 is neatly divided into two parts. First, six verses dealing with what theologians call general revelation of God from his creation. natural order of the universe and providence. Paul summarizes the function of general revelation in Romans 1. 20 His invisible attributes are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made, even his eternal power and Godhead So that they, all humans, are without excuse. And then the second part of Psalm 19, which is what I want to focus on, is about special revelation. God supernaturally speaking to us through his word. I'll read for you verses 7 to 11. The law of the Lord is perfect, converting the soul. The testimony of the Lord is sure, making wise the simple. The statutes of the Lord are right, rejoicing the heart. The commandment of the Lord is pure, enlightening the eyes. The fear of the Lord is clean, enduring forever. The judgments of the Lord are true and righteous altogether. More to be desired are they than gold, ye, yea, than much fine gold Sweeter also than honey and the honeycomb. Moreover, by them your servant is warned, and in keeping them there is great reward. Before the days of Amazon book rental, I remember feeling the dread at the beginning of each semester as I walked to the university bookstore. I would fork out hundreds of dollars to buy textbooks. Since I majored in business, I knew that fairly soon later editions, better authors, and the rapidly changing world would make my recently purchased copies. obsolete. But as we just read, the Bible contains God's perfect laws, pure testimonies, right precepts, pure commandments, fearful contents, true and righteous judgments. The Bible is the greatest textbook ever because its author is God, and it will never be obsolete. So then it is more precious than finest gold or the fanciest meal. As David puts it, the benefits of the scriptures are many. It restores the soul, makes the simple wise, rejoices the heart, enlightens the eyes, warns us, and rewards us. As Paul would tell Timothy, all scripture is given by inspiration of God and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction and righteousness. that the man of God may be complete, thoroughly equipped for every good work. In the longest chapter in the Bible, Psalm 119, we find more benefits of reading and meditating on the Word. In verses 97 to 100, in particular. Oh, how I love your law. It is my meditation all the day. You, through your commandments, make me wiser than my enemies, for they are ever with me. I have more understanding than all my teachers, for your testimonies are my meditation. I understand more than the ancients, because I keep your precepts. As you know, a third of our church is composed of men and women in their 70s, 80s, and 90s. Some who were born before World War II, I will not be matching you in life experience anytime soon. So then what can I offer you, wise and experienced saints? What weight or authority do I have if I'm younger than some of your sons and grandsons? The only way I can adequately lead you is to read and meditate on his word and speak from it and live by it. This is wisdom. And as we read the Bible, what we find in it, even at a cursory glance, is that there are two ways to live. That leads to the next point, the righteous and the wicked in contrast. We live in a pluralistic culture in which drives the idea that there are many paths to God. And as long as you're sincere and earnest, it doesn't matter which religion you follow. But it is clear from the word that there are moral absolutes. There's only one way to heaven. Jesus said, I am the way, the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me. It is also clear that there are only two ends to human destiny, two paths, right and wrong, two ways to live. The entire collection of Psalms begins with this assumption that there is way number one, the way of the wicked, where sinners and scoffers traverse. And way number two, the way of the righteous. The wicked path leads to destruction. Even if, for the time being, they prosper and seem to be on the winning side at the expense of the righteous. The day of judgment will reveal the consequences of their choices. Then as David says in Psalm 37, they shall soon be cut down like the grass and wither as the green earth. Like the splendor of the wet metals shall vanish. Into smoke they shall vanish away. The sons of Korah echoed David. The one who prospers apart from faith in God, a man who is in honor yet does not understand, is like the beasts that perish. The wicked is far from the law, and thus far from salvation. But then there is the way of the righteous. The righteous one who delights in God's law is like a tree planted by the rivers of water that brings forth its fruit in its season. Whose leap also shall not wither, and whatever he does shall prosper. Such is the way we mark the blameless man and observe the upright Such is the man of peace. However, such ones are marked by their enemies as targets for persecution. They surround and trap the righteous, but when their perseverance is awarded in the end, the wicked will see it and be grieved. He will gnash his teeth and melt away. At this point you might say to me, I want to follow the path of righteousness, or I am already following the path of righteousness. Now please don't be offended as I'm about to challenge your confidence in this matter. I don't know who's listening, so I have to say this. Please consider my next words to be an act of love because I will be most unloving if I don't tell you about heaven and hell, and that many won't be in heaven. Jesus, the most loving person ever, said the following in Matthew seven, thirteen-fourteen: Enter by the narrow gate. For wide is the gate, and broad is the way that leads to destruction, and there are many go in by it. Because narrow is the gate, and difficult is the way which leads to life, and there are few who find it. Not everyone is clamoring to go through this small gate and narrow way, like those fighting their way to Costco for toilet paper and disinfecting wipes. The statistics are not in our favor. Well, you might still believe I'm one of the few, the proud. I'll get to heaven on my own merit and in my own effort Just in case you think that the Bible reinforces such notions, let's turn to Romans 3, 10 to 18. Romans 3, 10 to 18. There is none righteous. No, not one. There is none who understands. There is none who seeks after God. They have all turned aside. They have together become unprofitable. There is none who does good. No, not one. Their throat is an open tomb. With their tongues they have practiced deceit. The poison of asps is under their lips. Whose mouth is full of cursing and bitterness. Their feet are swift to shed blood. Destruction and misery are in their ways. And the way of peace they have not known. There is no fear of God before their eyes. So the same Bible that says follow the path of righteousness also says there is none righteous, not even one, none who understands, none who seeks for God. Zero, zil, chip, nada. Allah turned aside from God to become useless. We are comprehensibly sinful to the core in our throats, tongues, lips, and teeth which go down to the paths of destruction and misery, away from the path of peace. We have no fear of God. Recognizing this perilous spiritual condition of ours is foundational. This is wisdom. That leads to the third principle. Fear and trust in the Lord. The first principle led us to God's revealed word in the Bible Secondly, opening up that book, we learn quickly that there are two paths open to us, the path of the righteous and the path of the wicked. We will not be going down the path that leads to everlasting life because we do not have the will to do so. So is there no hope Jesus did say there will be few who will live. They are those who fear the Lord True wisdom is not found in complete isolation in some ivory tower experience. True wisdom is relational, that is, in a relationship Not with the greatest authors on of earth, but the greatest author in heaven. It's not found in pride, pomp, and circumstance. but humility, brokenness, and in reverence towards God. One scholar writes, quote, Wisdom is to be found with God and nowhere else, and unless the quest for wisdom brings a man to his knees in awe and reverence, knowing his own helplessness to make himself wise Wisdom remains for him a closed book. End quote If I got your attention, if you feel your need to look beyond yourself for salvation, let's go on to the next steps David knew the relief one experiences from the gospel. God looks at him as if he has no sins on his record. He says at the beginning of Psalm 32, Blessed is he whose transgression is forgiven, whose sin is covered, blessed is the man to whom the Lord does not impute iniquity. And in whose spirit there is no deceit. David understood that he is counter-righteous apart from doing good works by God's grace alone. He knew no amount of good deed will make up for the wicked sins on his record. He knew this gift could be received by faith in God and repentance from unbelief. To receive God's gracious gift of righteousness credited to his spiritual account, David confessed his need of it. In the same Psalm he confesses in verses three to five, When I kept silent, my bones grew old, through my groaning all the day long. For day and night your hand was heavy upon me, my vitality was turned into the draught of summer Saylah, I acknowledge my sin to you, and my iniquity I have not hidden. I said, I will confess my transgressions to the Lord, and you forgave the iniquity of my sin. Wait, is it that simple? Yes, on your end. But know that forgiveness has a price. There was a great cost of lifting the weight of God's hand from you. Somebody else's body has to be wasted away. Somebody else groaned. Somebody else was smitten, stricken, and afflicted by God's hand. Somebody else's vitality had to be drained away. That somebody else is the substitute Jesus, who died on the cross in David's place and in the place of all those who trust in him. The reason that saints can walk in the path of righteous is that Jesus died as if he walked in the path of the wicked. He faced hell on the cross so that we can reach heaven. God the Father made him Jesus who knew no sin to be sin for us That we might become the righteousness of God in Him. On the third day, Jesus rose again from the dead and told his disciples, who were still confused about the cross, These are the words which I spoke to you while I was still with you, that all things must be fulfilled, which were written in the law of Moses and the prophets and the Psalms concerning me. And he opened their understanding that they might comprehend the scriptures. Then he said to them, Thus it is written, and thus it was necessary for the Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead the third day. And that repentance and remission of sins should be preached in his name to all nations, beginning at Jerusalem. He then ascended to heaven and awaits his glorious return. Until then, we must continue to spread the good news of Jesus Christ. Who is the power of God and the wisdom of God? So I'm here to beg of you to repent and trust in Him for righteousness. And eternal life. This is wisdom For those who those of you who already trust in Jesus, revere and worship him here on earth, walking in the path of righteousness by Spirit's power until you reach heaven. Fear and trust are not just one-time acts, but a way of life. Wisely worship him. Be worshipful in your wisdom You have cried out to him for salvation and he has heard you. Now it remains for you a life of holy obedience by the power of the Holy Spirit Savor his goodness, trust in him, fear him. Do not be dismayed when the godless grow rich. Be grateful and satisfied for the safety of your home. Prospect of a stable career, the warmth of your family, the unity you enjoy with your brothers and sisters in Christ. The one who lives by faith will not be afraid of evil tidings, his heart is steadfast, trusting in the Lord. Fear and trusting God above all else. The solution to our fears in life isn't overcoming them with our courage. The solution really is fearing someone who is greater than our fears. Jesus said, do not fear those who kill the body, but cannot kill the soul. but rather fear him who is able to destroy both soul and body in hell. Our natural instinct is to distrust, distrust those we fear. But the biblical command is to trust the one we fear, not only to get out of hell and to get into heaven, but in living for him on earth What does a life dedicated to wisdom and worship of God? His scriptures, his son Jesus, who makes us righteous, and continual fear and trust in him look like It may look a bit like the life of Aiden. Aiden was born in a tiny farming community in West Pennsylvania right near the end of the 19th century. When he was a teenager growing up in Akron, Ohio, he heard the gospel and he was saved. The 17-year-old overheard a street lay preacher proclaim Quote, if you don't know how to be saved, just call on God, saying, Lord, be merciful to me, a sinner. End quote. He arrived home that day, climbed into his attic, and did just that. Aiden came from a poor family background, and the home situation was so bad that he could not even complete high school, let alone college or seminary. But his passionate prayer life, forged in the dingy corner of his basement, and his desire to preach the gospel would not be denied God opened up ministry opportunities, eventually leading to pastorate positions in West Virginia, Ohio, Illinois, and Ontario, Canada. His gift of preaching was broadcast on radio, recognized by his denomination, the Christian and Missionary Alliance, and eventually by the larger evangelical community. He even became the editor of his Denominations magazine. How does such a man, poor, without formal training, become such a great instrument of God? How did such a man become the author of more than forty books, including classics, The Pursuit of God, and the Knowledge of the Holy, and be hailed by some as a twentieth-century prophet? Here's how one biographer describes the process. Quote: Aidan W. Tozer educated himself by years of diligent study and a constant prayerful seeking of the mind of God. With Tozer, seeking truth and seeking God were one and the same thing. For example, when he felt he needed an understanding of the great English works of Shakespeare He read them through on his knees, asking God to help him understand their meaning. This procedure was typical of his method of self-education With no teacher but the Holy Spirit and good books, A. W. Tozer became a theologian, a scholar, and a master craftsman in the use of the English language. Here is a man who was wise because he worshiped. Here is a man who worshipped because he was wise. Here is a man who revered the word, understood the gospel of righteousness, justification by grace alone, through faith alone, and feared the Lord all the days of his life. And with that fear, he embarked on a life of wisdom. I pray that every one of us would live such a life from this moment onward.

sermons.text: What is it about forensic drama that fascinates us? Silent Witness. CSI Crime Scene Investigation. Bones. All follow the careers of those who attempt to master the art of forensic pathology in attempts to explain sudden and unexplained deaths. By studying the deceased body, the main characters and the audience along with them gain insight into the underlying narrative. Who attacked the victims? How did they meet their fates? These questions lead to more inquiries. Why did the criminal carry out the nefarious act? We marvel at the modern technology and the science of deduction. Though it's fiction, I remember watching and wondering whether there really are people like Sherlock Holmes out there. In one modern interpretation of the character, Sherlock studies a lady dead on the floor. Within a few minutes, he deduces the following. Victim is in her late 40s. Professional person going by her clothes. I guess something in the media going by the frankly alarming shade of pink. She's traveled from Cardip today, intending to stay for one night. That's obvious from the size of her suitcase. She's been married for at least ten years, but not happily. She had a string of lovers, but none of them have known she was married. The wedding ring, ten years old at least. The rest of her jewelry has been regularly cleansed. But not her wedding rings. State of her marriage right there. The inside of the rings are shinier shinier than the outside. That means they're regularly removed. The only polishing they get is when she works them off her finger. It's not for work. Look at her nails. She doesn't work with her hands. So what? Or rather who does she remove her rings for? Clearly, not one lover. She never sustained the fiction of being single over time. So more likely, a string of them. Simple. To that, Watson exclaims, Brilliant When Lestrade wonders about Cardiff, Charlotte Sherlock continues. Her coat is slightly damp. She's been in heavy rain within the last few hours. No rain anywhere in London in that time. Under her coat collar is damp too. She turned it up against the wind. She's got an umbrella in her left pocket, but it's unused and dry. Not just wind. Strong wind. Too strong to use an umbrella. We know from her suitcase that she's staying overnight, so she must have come at this decent distance. But she can't have traveled more than two or three hours because her coat hasn't dried. So where has there been heavy rain and strong wind within the radius of that travel time? Cardiff To that, Watson shouts, Fantastic Now as interesting as it may be to shadow a genius like Sherlock, I find it cold and robotic to study a dead body like that. The only time I've seen corpses are at funerals. The atmosphere there is one of respect, reverence, and affection. The body has been prepared for the service and building. The terrible narratives behind the death may be put aside for the time being and left to the professionals. Of course, such professionals do what they do because they have a dispassionate objectivity in the task ahead of them. As he stood watching Jesus die on the cross, John the Apostle would not qualify as one of those objective scientific professionals. Nor was there a need for them. There was no mystery surrounding that death. Judas, one of the twelve, betrayed Jesus, who was innocent. The religious leaders were jealous and framed the popular teacher. John just saw his master and close friend die an excruciating death reserved for the worst criminals of the empire. No forensic pathology is needed to confirm the cause of death from such a public execution. Jesus died on the cross from exhaustion, dehydration, and heart failure But to the keen eye of John, who wrote what he saw, so we may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that believing we may have life in his name There was something about those wounds and the way he died that led him to investigate the scriptures What this beloved disciple found at the cross was that there was a new beginning and a new ending that came from Jesus' death. Let's read his account in John 19, 31-37. John nineteen, thirty-one to thirty-seven Therefore, because it was the preparation day, that the bodies should not remain on the cross on the Sabbath, for that Sabbath was a high day, the Jews asked Pilate that their legs might be broken. and that they might be taken away. Then the soldiers came and broke the legs of the first and of the other who was crucified with him. But when they came to Jesus and saw that he was already dead, they did not break his legs. But one of the soldiers pierced his side with the spear, and immediately blood and water came out. And he who has seen has testified, and his testimony is true. And he knows that he is telling the truth, so that you may believe. For these things were done that the scripture should be fulfilled. Not one of his bones shall be broken. And again, another scripture says, they shall look on him whom they pierced. We know the straightforward facts. Jesus died on the cross with two others before Sabbath on a Friday. That much is clear from every gospel writer But to understand how Jesus gave us a new beginning at the cross, we have to move here from the early part of the New Testament to the early part of the Old Testament. Here's a quick recap. The descendants of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, later named Israel, known as children of Israel. were chosen by God and found haven in the powerful nation of Egypt during a famine. They stayed there for a total of 430 years and became a numerous people. With such dramatic increase in numbers, a certain Pharaoh began to worry that a revolt might take place. So he enslaved and oppressed them. But all these circumstances led up to God's great deliverance of his people through his servant Moses. God displayed his sovereignty and power through ten plagues that finally broke the yoke of slavery. That tenth plague was the most severe of them all. The tenth plague took place literally hours before Israelites' departure from Egypt, starting at midnight. God worked in the darkest hours of the night to give them a bright new dawn. The tenth and final plague is called the plague of the firstborn Because the Lord went through the land and targeted all the firstborns among the Egyptians and animals. The only way to be spared from such sudden death and bereavement was to formally join the congregation of Israel and then participate in the Passover meal. The details of the Passover meal are described in Exodus twelve. I'll read there from verse five to thirteen. Your lamb shall be without blemish, a male of the first year. You may take it from the sheep or from the goats. Now you shall keep it until the fourteenth day of the same month. Then the whole assembly of the congregation of Israel shall kill it at twilight. And they shall take some of the blood and put it on the two doorposts and on the lintel of the houses where they eat it. Then they shall eat the flesh on that night, roasted in fire, with unleavened bread and with bitter herbs they shall eat it. Do not eat it raw, nor boiled at all with water, but roasted in fire, its head with its legs and its entrails. You shall let none of it remain until morning, and what remains of it until morning you shall burn with fire, and thus you shall eat it. with the belt on your waist, your sandals on your feet, and your staff in your hand. So you shall eat it in haste. It is the Lord's Passover. For I will pass through the land of Egypt on that night, and will strike all the firstborn in the land of Egypt, both man and beast, and against all the gods of Egypt I will execute judgment. I am the Lord Now the blood shall be assigned for you on the houses where you are, and when I see the blood I will pass over you, and the plague shall not be on you to destroy you when I strike the land of Egypt. Hence the name Passover. But beyond the name, we see the manner in which this meal is prepared and eaten. There is haste and urgency. Where's the attire? I admit to you that usually after church morning service, I come home and the very first thing I do is to get out of my suit and change into something more comfortable before lunch. The Israelites did the reverse for this meal. They have to put on their belt, get their shoes on, and grab their walking stick, and then eat the meal. No loosening the belt as they ate. Since the lamp is killed at twilight just before dark, they will have to quickly apply the blood on the doors. They will not expand time and energy to sever the limbs or guff the animal for easier consumption. The entire thing is roasted. The unleavened bread is also important. The feast of unleavened bread is so closely related to Passover, chronologically and conceptually, that they are considered synonymous. You see that in Luke 22 verse 1, Acts 12, 3 to 4. Just before and during the seven-day feast, yeast is removed from home, and bread without yeast baked and eaten. Again, this practice communicates urgency. The unleavened crisp mazzo only requires four ingredients, flour, salt, water, and olive oil. Compare that to a typical collar bread, which also requires sugar, egg, and of course yeast. Certain varieties of colorbread add honey, raisins and rceprin. After the first rising the dough is rolled into robe-shaped pieces which are braided. Seeds may be added to the dough or sprinkled on top. Both egg and water kala are usually brushed with an egg wash before baking to add a golden sheen. One online recipe for Kala bread has 12 steps compared to six steps for baking unleavened bread. Again, urgency and haste. We will return to the connection between Passover lamb and unleavened bread, so keep that in mind There's a few more details about the meat we haven't discussed yet. We read in Exodus 12, verse 46, In one house it shall be eaten, ye shall not carry any of the flesh outside the house, nor shall you break one of its bones. That instruction at the end about not breaking the bones is crucial. It is not a detail missed by John the Apostle at the cross. As I said at the beginning, John may not be a forensic pathologist or a medical doctor, but he had special insight at the cross. It was no happenchance that Jesus was crucified in Jerusalem just at the time of the Passover feast. It was no coincidence that the bones of Jesus were preserved like the bones of lambs slaughtered that day. It was no accident that John the Apostle was there to witness these things. God intended to show John, Israel, the church, and the rest of the world The crucifixion shows how his just retribution passed over sinners and fell on the Savior. Praise God for both demonstrating his righteousness while also demonstrating his love for us who were his enemies. From the beginning of the gospel, John has been foreshadowing and anticipating this climax of the cross. John the Baptist, the forerunner, proclaimed in chapter 1, verse 29. Behold the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world. Also, just before his death, as Jesus was parched with thirst, we read in chapter 19, verse 29, that a jar full of sour wine was standing there. So they put a spongeful of the sour wine upon a branch of hyssop and brought it up to his mouth. Again, this is no minor irrelevant detail. It's another clue to this equation of Jesus as the Passover lamb. Back in Exodus 12, verse 22, Moses instructed, You shall take a bunch of hyssop and dip it in the blood which is in the basin and apply some of the blood that is in the basin to the lintel and the two door posts The proclamation of Jesus as the Lamb of God, the hyssop branch raised to his lips And the preservation of the bones all add up to John's conclusion that Jesus is our Passover land. Just in case that you think that this is just a far-fetched, later developed idea of John. Let's go to Paul in his letter, 1 Corinthians 5, chapter 5. Here's the context. Paul is upbraiding the Corinthian saints for tolerating someone who is unrepentantly and publicly living in gross sexual sin. Paul condemns this unnamed man using his apostolic authority, and then he gives this church specific instructions to gather together and practice church discipline. In verses 6 to 8, he explains why they must do this using the two holidays of Passover and the beast of unleavened bread. Let's read the verses. Your glorying is not good. Do you not know that a little leaven leavens the whole lump? Therefore purge out the old leaven, that you may be a new lump, since you are you truly are unleavened. For indeed Christ, our Passover, was sacrificed for us. Therefore, let us keep the feast, not with old leaven, nor with the leaven of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth. Paul is speaking to a church that is made up of Jews and Gentiles, yet Christ has become the Passover lamb for all of them. I can tell you that I have never properly celebrated the Jewish Passover with all its formalities But by repenting of my sin and trusting in Jesus Christ, he has become my Passover lamb in my stead. The parallels are plenty. I deserve death and condemnation to hell forever because of my sins of thought, word, and actions. Like the firstborns that evening, I should face God's wrath. But because the blood of the Lamb was applied to me, I am forgiven of all my sins. So the punishment that was due to me passed over me and landed squarely on Christ crucified, the Lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world. And now I am set free from the bondage of sin. My process of leaving behind the world and its influence of malice and wickedness has begun. It is similar to the way the Israelites left behind Egypt and its influence. Because of Jesus and what he did at the cross, I have a new beginning. And not only that, I have a new ending. This journey as strangers on earth, this sojourning and pilgrimage, is guaranteed to end in success because of Jesus. While I can say I'm going to him, he is really coming to me. Here's what I mean When Jesus was pierced with the spear, it wasn't just because the soldiers had to verify whether he was dead. Yes, the flow of water and blood confirmed a ruptured heart, and John may have known that, but our witness is John the fisherman, not Dr. John Watson. The apostle was more interested in fulfillment of Scripture from Zechariah 12. 10 So to understand the new beginning at the cross, we have to go back to the beginning of the Old Testament to Exodus 12. To understand the new ending at the cross, we have to go back to the end of the Old Testament to Zechariah 12. A little background about Zechariah. He was one of the three post-exilic prophets, along with Haggai and Malachi, who spoke on behalf of God to the descendants of Judah. By post-exilic, I mean that they minister in the period after the Babylonian captivity, after the Persian authorities took over and allowed their subjects to return to their land. This was about a thousand years after the Exodus. We gather from other books like Nehemiah and Ezra. Now Zechariah belongs to a priestly family and his father's name is Barekiah, but he is more often connected with Ido, his grandfather. It's likely his father died early in his life so that his grandfather raised him. He is described as a young man in Zechariah 2. 4, though specific age cannot be determined. Zechariah began his ministry two months after Haggai and their ministry overlapped. We see that in Ezra 5. 1 and 6. 14. Together, they encouraged the returned remnants to rebuild the temple and hope in the coming vindication of the Lord. Though Cyrus the Great allowed them to build the edifice almost two decades prior, they faced opposition and discouragement when local enemies petitioned to Xerxes against them. Finally, they received the support of King Darius, who ruled from the year 521 onwards, and discovered Cyrus' original memorandum in the archives. With God's providence and message, the community worked hard to finish the temple in about four years. Zechariah was likely active at least two of those four years, though we don't really know when he stopped. Zechariah 1-1 and 7 and 7-1. Though their overall purposes were the same, Zechariah differed from Haggai in his approach. Hag Eye's work is a short, simple prose delivered in the course of four months Zechariah's scope far exceeds that of Haggai, and in fact is broader than all other minor prophets, prophets not named Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and Daniel.
