While he too was often simple and direct, his prophecies contain visions and oracles that deal with distant future. Also exceptional are the numerous predictions of the coming Messiah. His book can be divided into two major sections, chapters 1-8 and 9-14. In the first section, we have a series of eight visions. The second part deals with the end of the age and the messianic kingdom that follows. So not only is the Prophet concerned with the more immediate completion of the temple building, he goes far beyond that to the future in the last few chapters Future shapes the present. Our passage for today is nestled in that second section that runs from chapters 9 to 14. We can break down this section further into two more parts, chapters 9 to 11 and 12 to 14. There's a key word in chapter 9 verse 1 and repeated in chapter 12 verse 1. Chapter 12 verse 1. Burden. The word is found in the headings of various prophetic passages in Isaiah, Ezekiel, Nahum, Habakkuk, and Malachi. Most often the word burden signals a weighty and menacing judgment against an enemy of Israel. We witness such power in Zechariah 9. 1, as God's word is spoken against the land of Hadrach, a city in the vicinity of Damascus. Nations around Judah are judged and their bad fortunes are good news for God's own. The second burden begins in chapter 12. This is again a vision of the future. At the end of the seven-year tribulation, just around the time of Jesus' return, his second coming, here's the scene. Like the previous message, surrounding peoples are condemned because they oppose Judah, the capital city Jerusalem, and the royal house of David. In that day, God will empower the beleaguered city to be a weapon, so that it becomes a cup of drunkenness and a very heavy stone. with his leaders inflamed like a firepan and a torch. In that day God will defend and save the outskirts of Judah as well as the inhabitants of Jerusalem. With all the impressive displays of power here, you might think that God's work among men will only be external. But as God of Israel works against his people's outer turmoil, he also works in his people's inner turmoil. Let's read verses 10 to 11. And I will pour on the house of David and on the inhabitants of Jerusalem the spirit of grace and supplication. Then they will look on me, whom they pierced. Yes, they will mourn for him as one mourns for his only son, and grieve for him as one grieves for a firstborn. In that day there shall be a great mourning in Jerusalem, like the mourning at Hadad Riman in the plain of Megido. This is nothing short of a miraculous national revival. Israel outside of the church in the present age will return to the Lord, pray and ask for forgiveness. As a nation, they have rejected God's Son, Jesus the one they have pierced. The Spirit works in them to create genuine repentance and grief for their sin. Their weeping is so bitter that it will resemble that of parents bereaved of their only child or firstborn, like those who suffered in the tenth plague in Egypt. Another comparison is made to the weeping of Hadad Rimmon in the plain of Megidd. There the last good king of Judah named Josiah died during a battle The loss of such a beloved ruler struck everyone hard. So in a similar way, these people will mourn for another good king, better yet, the perfect and holy king. The Messiah whom they have previously rejected. In this decisive moment, the resurrected Messiah stands before them for salvation. At the last possible moment for repentance, just before judgment, God works in the hearts of his remnant to save them as they look upon their Savior, whom they have pierced. John probably didn't understand all these prophecies at first. But as he filled his mind with contemplations and reflections on that strange late afternoon, as Jesus' body was laid to rest He would not be stuck at the cross. He had to move to the empty tomb and even beyond that, to the vision of his second coming. It turns out John's reflections on Zechariah were correct. He saw at Pathmas a preview of his return in Revelation 1. 7. Behold, he is coming with clouds, and every eye will see him, even they who pierced him, and all the tribes of the earth will mourn because of him. Even so Amen. Now let's connect the dots of the cross, Jesus' resurrection and his second coming. Jesus had to die to be our Passover, to save us from sin. But if Jesus did not rise from the dead, he could not be the one to deliver his people in the future. Not only did Christ die for our sins according to the scriptures, he was also buried and rose again the third day according to the scriptures. Scriptures like this one. Zechariah 12, 10-11. Not only seeing him pierced for our transgression and humiliation But pierce for our final redemption in glory. Now we as a church won't be on earth seeing this final deliverance, but following Christ out of heaven as it returns. But at any rate, for all the saints, this is the common glorious ending, a new ending that has been made possible, because Jesus died on the cross and rose from the dead. So ask so I ask all of you as you meditate on the cross and celebrate the resurrection. That your thoughts would be led to worship Jesus our Passover. Hallelujah! The Lamb of God for sinners slain. The new beginning. But also look forward to the new ending with the resurrection and ascension. God making all things new. A prayer for that end. Lifted up to the Father through faith in his son, the pierced Messiah is as follows. Grant us grace to sing your praise, round your throne through endless days. Ever with the sons of light. Blessing, honor, glory, might

sermons.title: Peter's Good News
sermons.speaker: Sung Cho
sermons.text: If you're like me, you might say that one benefit of these strange circumstances Is the chance to introspectively consider important basic definitions. I think of words like faith, hope. Love, joy, mercy, grace, born-again, and gospel. Words that we may take for granted and seem like Christian jargon to the unchurched. Words that overlap in mean and need specific clarifications, even in the best minds. For example, let's talk about hope. I'll present to you John Piper's findings from Romans and Hebrews in a string of quotes Ordinarily, when we express hope, we are expressing uncertainty. But this is not the distinctive biblical meaning of hope Biblical hope is not just a desire for something good in the future, but rather biblical hope is a competent expectation and desire for something good in the future. There is a moral certainty that the good we expect and desire will be done. It is different from, say, mathematical or merely logical certainty. I would suggest that faith is the larger idea, and hope is a necessary part of biblical faith. Hope is that part of faith that focuses on the future. Faith can look back to creation as well as forward. So faith is the larger idea, it includes hope, but is more than hope. You might put it this way. Faith is our confidence in the Word of God, and whenever that word has reference to the future, you can call our confidence in it hope. Hope is faith in the future tense. With all that in mind, the message of future we uh future hope we offer to you is the gospel. And you can have faith in that message today. I want to introduce you to a man who believed in the gospel named Peter. He used to be a fisherman in Galilee until he met Jesus of Nazareth. After spending a few years following him, he came to the full conviction that he is a sinner and needs to repent. And Jesus is the Son of God. Who died for him and rose from the dead. After Jesus ascended to heaven, Peter spent the rest of his life sharing the gospel of hope to others. Here we see him in a letter to fellow Christians spread throughout the Roman Empire in the first century, reminding them of the good news of Jesus Let's read first Peter one, one to nine Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ, to the pilgrims of the dispersion in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bidnia. Elect according to the foreknowledge of God the Father, in sanctification of the Spirit, for obedience and sprinkling of the blood of Jesus Christ. Grace to you and peace be multiplied Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, for according to his abundant mercy has begotten us again to a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead. to an inheritance incorruptible and undefiled, and that does not fade away, reserved in heaven for you were kept by the power of God through faith for salvation ready to be revealed in the last time. In this you greatly rejoice, though now for a little while, if need be, you have been grieved by various trials. That the genuineness of your faith, being much more precious than gold that perishes, though it is tested by fire, may be found to praise, honor, and glory at the revelation of Jesus Christ. whom having not seen you love. Though now you do not see him, yet believing, you rejoice with joy inexpressible and full of glory. Receiving the end of your faith, the salvation of your souls. From our passage today, I believe we have three assumptions of the gospel and four assertions of the gospel. The three assumptions are one. God gets all the glory. Verses 1 to 3. 2. We need God's mercy. Verse 3. And three, we need rebirth. Verse three. The four assertions are one, our hope is alive. Verse three. 2. Our security is eternal, verses 4 to 5. 3. Our joy is enduring. Verse 6 and 4. Our faith is rewarding. Verses 7 to 9. We start with the three assumptions of the gospel. First, we assume that God gets all the glory. If we turn back to verse 1, we see Peter addressing believers from various parts of Asia Minor, modern-day Turkey. What binds all these people together? How are they united? The answer is in verse 2. The God of the Bible, one God in three persons, is the Father, the sovereign election, and eternal foreknowledge. It's the Holy Spirit, his initial and continual positional and progressive work in setting Christians apart for salvation and obedience, respectively. It's Jesus, his blood, with this cleansing power to forgive our sins. That's the abundant Trinitarian source of grace and peace that flows to all the saints. No wonder in verse 3, Peter begins the body of his letter with the blessing, a good word that properly belongs to God, not to us. That's why we sing praises to Him even when we can't gather as a congregation. That's why we lift up prayers of adoration. That's why we offer ourselves money, time and energy to the Lord The gospel is the good news because God ultimately gets all the glory Second, we assume that we are a people who need God's mercy. A simple definition of mercy is this: mercy is God not giving us what we deserve. So what is it that we do deserve? Well, not heaven. Certainly not intimacy with the holy God. Because all of us have sinned in thought, word, and action. We all deserve rightfully and fully God's wrath. Striving in our own strength to observe God's commandments and get to heaven is pointless. All that the law does for you is give proof that you deserve a guilty verdict. Because we deserve punishment, we need to beg God for mercy. And we don't need a little bit of mercy. We have sinned abundantly. Therefore, we need mercy abundantly. At every Holy Communion, which is one of the two ordinances that define a local church, I try to make this assumption of our need for mercy abundantly clear. Here's what I say. The Lord's suffer is for sinners. If you consider yourself a person who sins, you are welcome to join us. At the same time, the sufferer is for a specific kind of sinner, the one that confesses Christ as Savior and repents from sin. I say to you, if if you have never confessed Christ as Savior, if you don't understand what repentance means, please email our church Our leaders will explain how we're all people in need of a savior, what it means to receive God's mercy, and turn away from your old life. Speaking of old life, thirdly, verse 3 assumes that we need a new birth, new creation, rebirth, or what we commonly call regeneration. Our lives are so messed up by our poor choices, our self-destructive habits, our demented thought patterns, and our rebellion against God that a mere remodeling will not do. If I may use a home and garden television illustration, we can't ask Chip and Joanna Gaines to come and fix our spiritual problems. We can't paint over our iniquities or renovate our dilapidated hearts. Stains of our sins will never be wiped away. In our own strength, we can't even repent properly. No fixer upper here. The only solution is to burn it, all of it. Sin and sinners alike. We need a miracle, not renovation, not renaissance, not reform Rebirth, regeneration, renewal. Jesus spoke on this topic of being born again with a teacher of Jerusalem named Nicodemus, who was confused and wondered if he had to go back into his mother's womb. Jesus patiently explained to him that rebirth is based on God's work through his son and his Holy Spirit. One God and three persons is at work, and he deserves all the glory. Look at what Paul says about regeneration in Titus 3, 4-7. When the kindness and the love of God, our Savior toward man, appeared, not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to his mercy he saved us. through the washing of regeneration and renewing of the Holy Spirit, who he poured out on us abundantly through Jesus Christ our Savior. That having been justified by his grace, we shall become heirs according to the hope of eternal life. Here's an axiom about your need for rebirth. Born once, die twice. Born twice, die once. Here's what I mean. All of you have a physical birthday. If you don't have a second spiritual birthday, you will die twice. Once when you breathe your last breath on earth, and second when you enter the eternal lake of fire. That's where we're headed, unless we have a second spiritual birthday. If you are born physically and reborn spiritually, that is born twice, you will only face physical death, die once in a momentary struggle into eternal bliss. Of course, if Jesus returns right now, a Christian won't die at all. But you see the general rule here for most of redemption history So these are Peter's three assumptions of the gospel: God's glory, our desperate need for mercy, and our need for God's regenerating work. And then there are four assertions of the gospel. First, our hope is alive. Peter asserts that Jesus' resurrection is the hope for our own resurrection. Every time we meet on Sunday, the first day of the week, we gather to celebrate again and again the day Jesus rose from the dead. We don't meet on Fridays as a church as if to commemorate a life well lived, past tense. As if the death of Jesus was the end of the story. We gather on Sunday, on the Lord's Day, to celebrate the life living, present, Jesus who will live forever, future He lives again to die no more. Our hope is alive because Jesus is alive. Saying, have you considered what exactly occurred at the time of your salvation? What happens after your second birthday? You don't gain muscles or lose wrinkles from a fountain of youth. No. But Jesus is the source of living water a gracious gift which becomes in us a fountain of water springing up into everlasting life. John 4. 14 Even though our outward man is perishing, yet the inward man is being renewed day by day. 2 Corinthians 4, 16. Because of Jesus, your life now has life. You are no longer wayward, but heavenward. We can go on and be more specific about this hope. Christians not only have hope for their spirits, but for their bodies as well. Humans possessing a physical form is God's idea. He called it good. God always intended for us to have a material body. The spirit of a Christian goes directly to God after death, but we await our new bodies to be given later. Since the effects of sin have tarnished our fallen physical form, we need a new tent or dwelling place for our immaterial being. That's what we hope for. And Christ has given us a visible and tangible preview of this new body when he rose from the dead as the first fruits of resurrection. We find details of this hope in 1 Thessalonians 4 and 1 Corinthians 15. In an appointed time, Christ will descend with a loud command, accompanied by the voice of the archangel and God's trumpet to escort believers to heaven in resurrected bodies. Our brothers and sisters in Christ, who died before us, will be at the head of the line to meet him in the air. If God wills that we are alive on earth at this blessed event, Our perishable flesh will turn imperishable in a blink of an eye. We don't know when it will happen, but we are certain it will happen. And could you imagine this happening right now? All of a sudden, the persecuted churches are friends in Christ battling cancer. A Christian war veteran, disabled and crippled, battling post-traumatic stress disorder. A sister in Christ who was sexually abused. They will be transferred to eternal life with no trace of sense effects in their bodies. Let's take comfort in this future hope right now in the present. Peter's friend John speaks about this same hope in his first letter, chapter 3, verses 1 to 3. Behold, what manner of love the Father has bestowed on us that we should be called children of God Therefore, the world does not know us, because it did not know him. Beloved, now we are children of God, and it has not yet been revealed what we shall be. But we know that when he is revealed, we shall be like him, for we shall see him as he is. And everyone who has this hope in him purifies himself, just as he is purified. All our worldly hopes of success, money, romance, education All lose their luster and wither over time. Everything is subject to entropy. Not so with our hope in the gospel. Jesus rose from the dead, never to die again. Our hope corresponds to that historical reality, and we won't be disappointed. And so our hope is secure in heaven. Peter's second gospel assertion is that our security is eternal. When you think of birth, you think of children. When you think of children, you think of inheritance. That is also true in the gospel, but um tenth times better. When you experience rebirth, you become God's child. When you become God's child, you are his heir and co-heirs with Christ. See what's yours in Jesus, what treasures are laid in store for you? An inheritance incorruptible and undefiled, and that does not fade away, reserved in heaven for you. Consider what kind of inheritance this is. Just as our hope is eternally assured, our inheritance is eternally secure. It is safe and locked away for you, not in any place on earth where moth and rust destroy, where thieves break in and steal. Our birthright is in heaven. Note also in verse 5 how not only our inheritance, but we ourselves, the inheritors, are secure. Not by our power, but by God's power. Not through works, but through faith. We possess not only salvation from penalty and power of sin in the past and present. But guaranteed guaranteed to be ours is salvation ready to be revealed in the last time. Salvation from presence of sin in the future. Adoption into God's family is open to you all through repentance and faith in Jesus Christ. Now, faith is not just a prayer you recited when you were in Sunday school. It's a lasting affection for Jesus in a genuine relationship with him. Peter will talk more about faith later in this passage, but for now, here's a story I heard from Rabbi Zacharias that illustrates the reward of inheritance that comes to us through faith. A man owned a lot of paintings, a very wealthy man who had a son. The son used to go into the city streets and would often talk to a beggar. The beggar took a liking to this young man and one day gave this young man a portrait he'd painted of him So the young man took it to his father, who was an art connoisseur, and the father thought to himself, well, it's not a very good painting, but we'll hang it up in the gallery because it's supposed to be of my son Many, many years went by, and the young lad stopped coming to visit the beggar. And the beggar finally went to the gates of the palace and said, I don't see that young man anymore. The palace guards said, Well, he died very suddenly. The beggar was very unhappy to hear the news, and he said, Can I see his father? And they said, Yes. The beggar said to the father, I have done another picture of your son, just like the other one. I want you to have it. He gave it to the father, and the father hung up the painting beside the other one. Not long afterwards, the father suddenly passed away too, and the beggar heard about it. He also heard that all the art in the palace was going to be auctioned. So he asked if he could go in. An auctioneer came and saw all the point paintings on the walls. The connoisseurs were there, and they were all going to bid on them. There in the middle of the this collection were hanging the two paintings of his son done by this beggar. That were not very good at all. The auctioneer said, we're going to have an auction. But the first paintings to go are the ones of the young lad here. And then we'll proceed with the rest. They said, we're not interested in them. Just get on with the he said, no, no. We must begin with these. But nobody bid. So the beggar put his hand in his pocket and took out a handful of pennies and said, I want to bid on the young man's paintings. Nobody else competed for the few pennies. The gabble was sounded and he got the son's portraits. As the beggar took them and was about to leave, the gabble sounded again, and the auctioneer said, I have some news for you. Behind the paintings of this young man are the words, Whoever bids on these gets the whole gallery. See how we are like the beggar with affections and faith, like the paintings, crude and as crude as they may be. But he who acknowledges the Son has the Father also. 1 John 2, 23 He who did not spare his own son, but delivered him up for us all. How shall he not with him also freely give us all things? Romans 8. 32 I has not seen, nor ear heard, nor have entered into the heart of man the things which God has prepared for those who love him. 1 Corinthians 2. 9. No wonder Peter talks about joy in verse 6. That leads to Peter's third gospel assertion, our joy is enduring. We Christians ought to be the most hopeful, the most secure, and hearing this verse, the most joyful. If you have been a believer for a long time, consider how your life has changed with regard to joy and how stable that joy has been during these unstable times. I'm glad you're a regular attendee of a gospel present a preaching church. It's good that you know your Bible, but are you joyful? I must admit, even with all the years of studying and learning, my struggle for joy is ever present. The world pulls us toward cynicism and pessimism. But we must find our happiness and contentment in what we already know. If we have joys of heaven for the long term, we can endure trials of earth for the short term. That's reason enough to rejoice. Now, the way we maintain our joy is through faith. In fact, joy is very closely wrapped up with faith, as evidenced by verse 8. So let's move on to that fourth assertion of the gospel. Our fate is rewarding. To be clear, eternal and spiritual rewards of genuine faith in Jesus Christ are without a hint of doubt ours in the present. But there are those who preach a false gospel promising that if you have enough faith, you will have health, wealth, and prosperity on earth You know who had the greatest faith in God and still suffered? Jesus. That's the perfect, obedient Son of God, and he trusted the Father until the end. But where did that land him? At the cross. Trusting in God does not always land you at a happy place, not in this fallen world. One local pastor wrote about Jesus on the night he was arrested, quote, Christ's convulsive struggles in the Garden of Gethsemane It's the clearest proof that personal peace is an unreliable indicator that you're in God's will. Sometimes faith sweats blood. The same truth applies to us. We are disciples who are not above our teacher, servants not above our master. Matthew 10, 24. But as we follow in Christ's footsteps, we learn that the trials we face do have a purpose. That purpose is explained in verses 7 to 9. Our faith is tempered, heated, and cooled over and over again to ultimately reflect the brilliance of God's glory. Only the crucible of the cross-centered life will produce a precious, steely, persevering faith that brings praise, glory, and honor at Jesus' second coming. Our sole salvation is the promise and the outcome. Because we have faith in this outcome and in Jesus Christ, our present circumstances in dark and confusing times Do not spoil our inexpressible and glorious joy in Christ. Now you might ask, if God knows everything, what need is there for him to find our faith to be genuine? One commentator says Quote, our faith isn't tested because God doesn't know how much or what kind of faith we have. It is tested because we often are ignorant of how much faith or what kind of faith we have. Do you and those around you know how much or what kind of faith you have? Life throws unexpected curveballs like this pandemic and other tests of faith. How do you react? What is your mood and speech like when freedom is limited, when our finances are in peril? How are your spiritual disciplines without the normal structures and patterns for support? Can the proof of your faith be found in this season? In addition to your further study and application of this passage, sing and meditate on a verse of that hymn. How firm a foundation it goes. When through fiery trials thy pathway shall lie, my grace all-sufficient shall be thy supply. The flame shall not hurt thee. I only design Thy draws to consume and thy gold to refine. Our fiery trials are many. Our faith is that precious gold to be refined. Our draws to be consumed by God's design are every weight and the sin which so easily ensnares us, which we resist by the Spirit's power. Cast out while running in this race of faith. Hebrews 12. 1. Finally, to prayer I pray that your faith, your joy, your security, your hope in the good news of Jesus Christ can be on full display this week. May your hope pulsate with life. May your security be unshakably firm. May your joy leave you speechless. May your faith be unbreakable.

sermons.title: Psalm 40: Saints Who Go Down Must Come Up
sermons.speaker: Sung Cho
sermons.source_file: Psalm 40 - Saints Who Go Down Must Come Up.txt
sermons.text: As a teenager growing up in a church youth group, I would attend at least two retreats a year. There was one time when I returned from a winter retreat that I experienced an inner turmoil. It was literally another mountaintop experience, late December. Lots of singing, lots of praying, lots of sermons. Lots of discussions in small groups, lots of basketball, etc. All the typical things youth group retreats consist of. But just as the retreat concluded, I felt somewhat depressed. The feeling lingered all the way down the mountain and back home. I remember speaking with my youth pastor's wife who noticed and pulled me aside and asked me what's wrong. I told her, I don't see the point of going to these grand winter retreats every late December. Making promises to God only to fail just a few weeks, if not days, into the new year. Promises like, I'll do my quiet times every day. Three chapters a day means I'll finish the Bible in a year. I'll pray for all my friends and church members regularly. After numerous cycles of promises made and promises broken, I was fed up with my own faithlessness. The pastor's wife's response was gracious and wise. She drew a picture in my head. Imagine a line running horizontally from left to right, but zigzagging up and down. The upward summits are good times in your spiritual life, and the pits are the low points. All that you may feel and experience is this nauseating sensation and discouragement as if you are not getting anywhere. But beauty as a whole, a life devoted to God, and a soul captured by God, surely makes an upward ascent in the grand scheme of things. Even if it's ever so slight in a single season, even if a free fall catastrophe into the valley immediately follows a mountaintop experience, The next peak just might be higher than ever before. Generally speaking, a true believer's maturity and depth of relationship with God will be on the gradual rise. The picture stayed with me even to this day. I know the illustration is overly simplistic and could use more nuance, but I appreciate how it visualized my inner struggles at that time and comforted me. I suppose we would all appreciate it if our spouses, friends, or family can accurately peer into our souls. Just like the way ultrasound reveals the inner structures of the body, wise counsel can reveal the inner structures of the spirit. What's going on inside of me, you might ask, and your trusted soul physicians would tell you what's wrong. And the spiritual tools for these soul physicians would be God's word More specifically, I would point to the 150 chapters that make up the Psalms. John Calvin called the book of Psalms Quote, an anatomy of all the parts of the soul. He explains, quote, for there is not an emotion of which anyone can be conscious. That is not here represented as in a mirror. Or rather, the Holy Spirit has here drawn to the light all the griefs, sorrows, fears, doubts, hopes, cares, perplexities In short, all the distracting emotions with which the minds of men are wont to be agitated. The other parts of Scripture contain the commandments which God enjoined his servants to announce to us. But here, The prophets themselves, see they are exhibited to us as speaking to God. Draw each of us to the examination of himself in particular. in order that none of the many infirmities to which we subject, and of the many vices with which we abound, may remain concealed. Anatomy of all the parts of the soul is an apt description of Psalms. Let's take a look at one of them, Psalm 40, to find vocabulary and expression for our struggles, whether we are on a mountaintop or valley. Let's read it together. To the chief musician, Assam of David I waited patiently for the Lord, and he inclined to me and heard my cry. He also brought me up out of a horrible pit, out of the miry clay, and set my feet upon a rock. and established my steps. He has put a new song in my mouth. Praise to our God. Many will see it and fear, and will trust in the Lord. Blessed is that man who makes the Lord his trust, and does not respect the proud, nor such as turn aside to lies. Many, O Lord my God, are your wonderful works which you have done, and your thoughts toward us cannot be recounted to you in order. If I would declare and speak of them, they are more than can be numbered. Sacrifice and offering you did not desire. My ears you have opened Burnt offering and sin offering you did not require. Then I said, Behold, I come. In the scroll of the book it is written of me. I delight to do your will, O my God. and your law is writ within my heart. I have proclaimed the good news of righteousness in the great assembly. Indeed, I do not restrain my lips, O Lord, you yourself know. I have not hidden your righteousness within my heart. I have declared your faithfulness and your salvation. I have not concealed your loving kindness and your truth from the great assembly. Do not withhold your tender mercies from me, O Lord. Let your loving kindness and your truth continually preserve me. For innumerable evils have surrounded me, my iniquities have overtaken me, so that I am not able to look up. They are more than the hairs of my head, therefore my heart fails me. Be pleased, O Lord, to deliver me. O Lord, make haste to help me. Let them be ashamed and brought to mutual confusion who seek to destroy my life. Let them be driven backward and brought to dishonor who wish me evil. Let them be confounded because of their shame, who say to me, Aha! Aha! Let all those who seek you rejoice and be glad in you. Let such as love your salvation say continually, The Lord be magnified. But I am poor and needy. Yet the Lord thinks upon me. You are my help and my deliverer. Do not delay, O my God Please note that the words before verse one are part of God's inspired scriptures. To give a brief background, David was the second king of the United Kingdom of Israel around 1000 BC, about a thousand years before Christ. He rose to fame as a court musician and a warrior in King Saul's army. Though he was destined to be king himself later, his ascension to the throne was quite difficult. Saul grew jealous of him and his military success and tried to hunt him down. As a fugitive, David refused to take the opportunities to kill the king and take the throne. Instead, he waited until it was his time. He is considered an ideal king. A man after God's own heart, though his moral and family failings are well documented. He wrote many psalms throughout his life, and at times they provide deeper insight into his soul. But we do not know what specific life circumstances led to the drafting of Psalm 40. G. Morgan Campbell, a British preacher, thinks it may have been around David's coronation as he reflected upon all the troubles he endured. But was it when he was anointed as ruler over Judah in 2 Samuel 2, or when he was anointed king over all the tribes of Israel in 2 Samuel 5? Whatever the occasion, we know that his life was filled with troubles before he became king and afterwards too. He shed much blood and made great wars according to 1 Chronicles 22 verse 8. As for the structure, one commentator divides up this chapter into two parts. One, Praise for Past Troubles, verses one to ten. And two, prayers for present troubles, verses 11 to 17. The basic flow of David's thought goes like this. Because God helped me in the past, I can pray to him in the present. First, let's look at the praise for past troubles in the first ten verses. In the first three verses, we hear David's testimony filled with vivid images, slimy pits, mud, and mire, all fittingly describing David's former distress. He went from instability to stability, from a hole to a rock, from sinking sand to a firm place to stand. What results from such experience are a new song and a hymn of praise to cause others to see, fear, and trust the Lord. This desire to see others trust in the Lord leads to the Beatitude in verse 4. True happiness is found in trusting in God alone. Not in boasting in self-worth or empty promises. According to verse 5, there are multiple reasons for such focused and singular devotion. God's many wonders, providence, and benevolent thoughts for us. I like Derek Kippner's commentary on this verse. Quote, The past is full of his miracles. The future follow his plans. The focus of the first five verses was God and what he has done and those who share David's faith. The emphasis of the next five verses is on David's personal devotion, though as you can see at the end of verse 10, though the congregation is always in David's sight. Note how many times we see the pronoun I from verses 7 to 10. I said, I come, I delight, I have proclaimed, I do not restrain, I have not hidden, I have declared, I have not concealed. We observe how David expresses his individual dedication using liturgical vocabulary. Though he wasn't a priest, he was pious and familiar with the requirements of Moses and Levitical rituals. So it's not surprising that in verse 6 he knows all the different sacrifices, offerings, burnt offerings, and sin offerings. But David knew what God desired most: obedience. That obedience is expressed with the image of opening his ears This might sound a bit strange to us. We turn to commentators who offer different explanations. One explanation is that David is referring to the law for Hebrew servants in Exodus 21, verses 1 to 6, and Deuteronomy 15, 12 to 18. After six years of service to a master, a servant becomes a free agent and could leave if he or she chooses. But if the servant desires to stay, he or she is taken before the judges, then to the door or doorpost, to have his or her ear pierced to it as a mark of lifelong service. Other commentators take the expression as a general description of David's readiness to listen and obey with ears open. Regardless, the main idea is captured in the way the Greek version of the Old Testament, used by the writer of Hebrews, renders the phrase Instead of my ears you have opened, we find a body you have prepared for me. We can envision a person's whole self upon the altar before the Lord. What does this mean? God is more interested in living sacrifices of his saints themselves than in dead sacrifices of animals. He is concerned with offering of ourselves more than our resources, giving 100% of ourselves more than the 10% of our money and time. A heart passionately burning for him more than burnt offerings. Remorse and repentance from sin more than offerings for sin. This is what Saul failed to realize when he disobediently spared the Amalekite king and kept the spoils of sheep and cattle. Samuel confronted him about it, and the insecure king confessed that he feared men more than God and thus disobeyed him. In words very similar to these verses, Samuel rebukes Saul in 1 Samuel 15, 22 to 23. Does the Lord delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices as much as in obeying the Lord? To obey is better than sacrifice, and to heed is better than the fat of rams. For rebellion is like the sin of divination. And arrogance like the evil of idolatry. Because you have rejected the word of the Lord, He has rejected you as king. In verse 7, David comes forward as the better king and says that he is ready to obey God's will, as recorded in the law of Moses. Which includes the requirements for the king. But God's desires are not merely externally written in the scriptures. In verse 8. David says he internalizes them in his heart through memorization and meditation. Now you might be impressed with David's passion. He's giving his testimony, motivating others to trust God, and offering himself to his service. He certainly looks better than many other kings that came after him, but if this song only leads you to revere David, you would be on the wrong track. It should lead you to ultimately honor the son of David, Jesus Christ, who is David's Lord. Here's how we honor Jesus. Turn with me to the aforementioned letter to the Hebrews, chapter 10, where the writer cites Psalm 40. The writer presents Jesus' superior sacrifice over all the animal sacrifices under the Levitical system. Let's read the first 14 verses there. For the law, having a shadow of the good things to come and not the very image of the things, can never with these same sacrifices, which they offer continually, year by year, make those who approach perfect. For then would they not have ceased to be offered For the worshippers once purified would have had no more consciousness of sins. But in those sacrifices, there is a reminder of sins every year, for it is not possible that the blood of bulls and goats could take away sins. Therefore, when he came into the world, he said, Sacrifice and offering you did not desire, but a body you have prepared for me. In burnt offerings and sacrifices for sin you have no pleasure. Then I said, Behold, I have come. In the volume of the book it is written of me, to do your will, O God. Previously saying, Sacrifice and offering burnt offerings and offerings for sin you did not desire, and nor had pleasure in them, which are offered according to the law, then he said, Behold, I have come to do your will, O God. He takes away the first that he may establish the second. By that will we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all. And every priest stands ministering daily and offering repeatedly the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins. But this man, after he had offered one sacrifice for sins forever, sat down at the right hand of God, from that time waiting till his enemies are made his footstool. For by one offering, he has perfected forever those who are being sanctified. Back to David for a second. As impressive and inspiring as David's devotion may be, the man after God's own heart has faltered often. He was an adulterer, a murderer, and a bad father. Even if the son of Jesse lived hundreds of years and dedicated every minute of his life to God, it would not amount. to a fraction of Jesus' word. Even if David brought every priest in the land together, every animal for slaughter. drained every drop of blood from their bodies, and even laid himself down on the altar. He could not blot out a single sin from his record, let alone someone else's Neither could any Levitical priest, as the writer of Hebrews, makes clear. But Christ's sacrifice is so much better. He lived a perfect life. Not merely a man after God's own heart, but both God and man at the same time with the pure heart. He lived a blameless life, fulfilling the law in all his demands. He took that unblemished offering of his body to the cross as the great high priest. He perfects all of us who are blemished and imperfect when we come to him repenting and believing in his death, resurrection, and ascension. Once we grasp the Father's plan to send His Son to die for us, When we fully appreciate this gospel of grace and mercy which redeems Jews and Gentiles, we are led to the same conclusion as Paul in Romans 12. 1. I beseech you, therefore, brethren, by the mercies of God, that you present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable to God, which is your reasonable service. with Jesus' sacrifice of sin already accepted by the Father and provided for us in the gospel We only have to offer in response sacrifices of praise, thanksgiving, and charity to others, as Hebrews 13, 15 to 16. And such sacrifices are meant to be public, as we see in verses 9 and 10. What binds these two verses together is the phrase, the Great Assembly. David's open ears lead to open lips. Though God's righteous ways are in his heart, it does not stay there. He does not just delight within, but he also declares without. This song demonstrates that to be devoted individuals, we must be in a devoted community. Our faith is not simply an individual matter, but a corporate one So I suppose you can say that one major lesson in our soul's anatomy is that we are not just individual cells or parts, but we form organs and systems together. Paul makes it abundantly clear in the New Testament that we are many parts of one body in Christ manifest locally. With a community of worshippers who carry out God's will according to Christ's example We can face the struggles in the present and ahead of us. That's the focus of verses 11 to 17. As I said at the beginning, the first ten verses were about past troubles. The remaining verses make up a prayer for the present troubles, which consists of two kinds of pains. In verses 11 to 13, the suffering is more inward, with blinding sin being the principal cause. In verses 14 to 16, troubles come outwardly from persecutors and mockers. The rescue from both is explicitly mentioned in verse 17 in God who is David's help and deliverer. In verse 11, David wishes for divine mercies for his human faults. He asks that the same loving kindness and truth of God declared in the past, verse 10, would preserve him in the present. Verse 12 reveals some sin that has caught up with the man. There are innumerable consequences of iniquities, like a pack of wild beasts chasing him. We're thankful that we don't have to pay the eternal consequences of sin in hell, but we must face temporal consequences of sin on earth for our own discipline and character growth. Like David in verse 13, we learn to cry out to our Lord in bad times, just as we praise him in good times. We shift our focus in verses 14 and 15. This time the source of David's troubles come from those who seek his life, those who wish him evil. Those who are ready to pounce on his mistakes, pointing and exclaiming, aha! But our psalmist asks the Lord to avenge him. To put them to shame, to confuse them, to drive them back, to dishonor them, and to confound them. Such maledictions belong to those who seek his life Benedictions belong to those who seek the God of Israel, those who rejoice and are glad in Him, as we see in verse 16. Without minimizing the troubles of life, David can say with those who love God's salvation: The Lord be magnified. Finally, in verse 17, we have David's omission of his spiritual poverty and neediness. Instead of yet the Lord thinks upon me, I believe the New American Standard Bible is more accurate in translating the phrase as a request, let the Lord be mindful of me. His request is based on his understanding of God, his help and deliverer. He asks for speedy rescue from his present troubles. A short illustration to end. There's a story about a man who fell into a pit and couldn't get himself out. A subjective person came along and said, I feel for you down there. An objective person came along and said, it's logical that someone would fall down there. Buddha said, your pit is only a state of mind. A realist said, that's a pit. A self-pitying person said, you haven't seen anything until you've seen my pit An optimist said, things could be worse. A pessimist said, things will get worse. The story ends with Christ coming to save the man from the pit. Perhaps this psalm can be an epilogue to this story. Perhaps the rescued man will go and join a local church to speak of all that God has done for him. And hopefully he will testify of how Christ has descended from the heavens to take our place in the pit of God's judgment. Christ devoted his body as a substitute in our place, paying the price for our sins. And if the man falls again during his pilgrimage on earth, he will know to pray for deliverance because of what God has already done. He knows that since his soul is secure from the deepest and darkest pit of hell, the lesser pits of earth are only meant for his discipline and growth. His struggles with personal sins within and persecutions without will continue in the present, but he can cry out to the same Savior who rescued him in the past. O Lord, make haste to help me. Do not delay, O my God. Maranathdah, O Lord, come.

sermons.title: Naboth's Vineyard
sermons.speaker: Sung Cho
sermons.text: Late November of twenty eighteen, a licensed psychologist contributed an article to a Florida newspaper entitled The irony of Black Friday following Thanksgiving. You can guess by that heading what the piece is about The long lines, people camping out in the dark, customers trampling each other, old ladies fighting over the last George Foreman grill. All happening within 24 hours of Thanksgiving dinners, where families gathered together to say grace, count their blessings, and ask, what are you most thankful for this year? The psychologist condemns the, quote, ultra-materialistic aspects of our culture. But at the same time observes this, quote, We feel most grateful for things that transcend the trappings of our world, like family, good friends, the awe of nature, or our spirituality. As far as I know, this author is no theologian or preacher. He runs a psychological service agency, not a Christian counseling organization. This wasn't in the pages of Christianity today, but it was in Florida today. But all his talk of materialism, gratefulness, and transcendence is rather convicting. Are we seeking first the kingdom of God and its righteousness? Well, there are many reasons for our ungrateful attitudes and many passages we can study. I want to focus on one particular passage in the Old Testament and one sin, the sin of coveting. First, a definition. What is covenant? We talked a bit about this topic during our series on the Ten Commandments. While God gave us desires and means to fulfill those desires legitimately, coveting is a specific kind of desire that has grown out of control. Most of us are familiar with the Tenth Commandment in Exodus 20, verse 17. You shall not covet your neighbor's house, you shall not covet your neighbor's wife nor his male servant, nor his female servant, nor his ox, nor his donkey, nor anything that is your neighbor's You find the word covered in your English translation twice in that one verse Interestingly, that word in the original language is the same word found in Song of Solomon, chapter 2, verse 3. In that verse, the bride desires to be in the presence of her lover. The verb for desire is the same as the verb for coveting elsewhere Similarly, in chapter 2 of Genesis verse 9, before Adam and Eve ate the forbidden fruit, God gave them abundance of desirable trees. They just decided to go for that one tree God did not allow Since the beginning of time, we have foolishly followed our desires at the cost of sinning and transgressing God's laws and neighbors' boundaries. With that in mind, let's turn towards the passage for today, 1 Kings 21. As you go there, I'll provide brief background information on King Ahab. During his time, Israel was divided into two nations, one in the north with the same name, Israel, and the one in the south named Judah. Ahab's father Omri founded a major dynasty in the north and established Samaria as the capital. Ahab surpassed his father in wickedness and married Jezebel, the princess of Sidonians. Together they opposed the true prophets of God like Elijah. and established worship of foreign idols. But even though Ahab was wicked, God gave him victory over the enemies. The Aramenians and their leader Ben-Hadad. Ahab was foolish to spare Ben-Hadad, however, and God sent the prophet to condemn him for that poor decision. You can read verses 42 and 43 in chapter 20 to see what happened just prior to the vineyard incident. Then he said to him, Thus says the Lord, because you have let slip out of your hand a man whom I appointed to utter destruction. Therefore, your life shall go for his life, and your people for his people. So the king of Israel went to his house, solemn and displeased, and came to Samaria. Let's continue right into chapter twenty-one. And it came to pass after these things that Naboth the Jezreelite had a vineyard which was in Jezreel, next to the palace of Ahab, king of Samaria. So Ahab spoke to Naboth, saying, Give me your vineyard, that I may have it for a vegetable garden, because it is near, next to my house, and for it I will give you a vineyard better than it. Or if it seems good to you, I will give you its worth in money. But Naboth said to Ahab, The Lord forbid that I should give the inheritance of my fathers to you. So Ahab went into his house, sullen and displeased, because of the words which Naboth the Jezreelite had spoken to him, for he had said, I will not give you the inheritance of my fathers. And he lay down on his bed, turned away his face, and would eat no food. But Jezebel his wife came to him and said to him, Why is your spirit so sullen that you eat no food? He said to her, Because I spoke to Nabet the Jezreelite, and said to him, Give me your vineyard for money, or else if it pleases you, I will give you another vineyard for it. And he answered, I will not give you my vineyard Then Jezebel, his wife, said to him, You now exercise authority over Israel. Arise, eat food, and let your heart be cheerful. I will give you the vineyard of Navith the Jezreelite. And she wrote letters in Ahab's name, sealed them with his seal. and sent the letters to the elders and the nobles who were dwelling in the city with Nabat. She wrote in the letter saying, Proclaim a fast, and seek Naboth with high honor among the people and see two men, scoundrels, before him to bear witness against him, saying, You have blasphemed God and the king, then take him out and stone him, that he may die. So the men of his city, the elder and nobles who were inhabitants of his city, did as Jezebel had sent to him, sent to them. as it was written in the letters which she had sent to them. They proclaimed the fast and seated Navat with high honor among the people And two men, scoundrels, came in and sat before him, and the scoundrels witnessed against him, against Nabat in the presence of the people, saying, Naboth has blasphemed God and the king. Then they took him outside the city and stoned him with stones so that he died. Then they sent to Jezebel, saying, Nabat has been stoned and is dead. And it came to pass, when Jezebel heard that Nabat had been stoned and was dead, that Jezebel said to Ahab, Arise, take possession of the vineyard of Nabat the Jezreelite, which he refused to give you for money. For Nabat is not alive, but dead. So it was when Ahab heard that Nabeth was dead, that Ahab got up and went down to take possession of the vineyard of Naboth, the Jezreelite. Then the word of the Lord came to Elijah the Tishvite, saying, Arise, go down to meet Ahab, king of Israel, who lives in Samaria. There he is in the vineyard of Nabat, where he had gone down to take possession of it. You shall speak to him, saying, Thus says the Lord, have you murdered and also taken possession? And you shall speak to him, saying, Thus says the Lord, in the place where dog licked the blood of Nabut, dog shall lick your blood, even yours. So Ahab said to Elijah, Have you found me, O my enemy? And he answered, I have found you because you have sold yourself to do evil in the sight of the Lord. Behold, I will bring calamity on you, I will take away your posterity, and will cut off from Ahab every male in Israel, both bond and free. I will make your house like the house of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, and like the house of Baashah, the son of Ahijah. Because of the provocation with which you have provoked me to anger and made Israel sin And concerning Jezebel, the Lord also spoke, saying, The dogs shall eat Jezebel by the law of Jezreel. The dog shall eat whoever belongs to Ahab and dies in the city, and the birds of the air shall eat whoever dies in the field. But there was no one like Ahab who sold himself to do wickedness in the sight of the Lord, because Jezebel, his wife, stirred him up. And he behaved very abominably in following idols, according to all that the Amorites had done, whom the Lord had cast out before the children of Israel. So it was when Ahab heard those words that he tore his clothes and put sackcloth on his body, and fasted and lay in sackcloth, and went above mourning. And the word of the Lord came to Elijah the Tishvite, saying, See how Ahab has humbled himself before me. Because he has humbled himself before me, I will not bring the calamity in his days. In the days of his son, I will bring the calamity on his house. I want to state four big ideas from the author. 1. Covering destroys us verses 1 to 4. 2. Coveting leads to more sins. Verses 5 to 10. 3. Covenant corrupts a society. Verses 11 to 16. And 4. Coveting will be judged. Verses seventeen to twenty-nine. First coveting destroys us Not just psychologically or emotionally, though that certainly happens. Ahab was already in a terrible spiritual state, and coveting exacerbated it. As we saw in the last verse of chapter 20, Ahab went to his home sullen and displeased by the prophetic words sent to him. And now, again in chapter 21. Verse 4, we have the same phrase, his house, swollen and displeased. He thought he could cheer himself up by acquiring more things. But he learned money cannot buy happiness. You can picture Ahab sobbing and muttering to himself in a dark room. Ahab did not handle criticisms well, and he did not easily take no for an answer, though he lived in the physical comforts of a palace He was in a bad place, spiritually speaking. He thought that by purchasing valuable physical estate, he could forget about his vulnerable spiritual state. In contrast, Navith was content and loyal to God and his family. Even before Israelites possessed the promised land, God has parceled out the land to individual tribes and families in accordance with His will. Nabit's portion was in Jezreel, a city strategically located near major roads. It was a city of great military and commercial relevance. It was in the valley with the same name, Fertil, with a nearby strand grapes and olives. Nabat was blessed, and he was a good steward, knowing that the vineyard was not his to give Ahab only has to realize that the vineyard was not his to take. Have you ever felt vexed and displeased about what you can't have? Could it be that you have unresolved issues with God, a problem with disobedience and idolatry? Jesus told us to not worry about food, drink, clothes or tomorrow. If Jesus told us to not fret about our basic needs, how much more shall we be free from coveting extraneous wants? The rest of scriptures is clear about how riches are ungratifying and the desire for riches is even dangerous. See for example Ecclesiastes 5. 10, Matthew 13, 22, and 1 Timothy 6, verses 6-19. What happens when coveting gets its way in our hearts? That leads to the second point. Coveting leads to more sins. In verse 5, we see Jezebel is concerned about her husband refusing to eat. I'm sure any woman would be concerned about her man having a bad day at work. So she asks, What's going on? Note Ahab's recollection of Nabod's refusal at the end of verse 6. I will not give you my billion. But that's not all that Nabod said. The way Ahab was presenting Nabot's words, it makes it seem like he was unreasonable, petty, and harsh. Ahab was so far from God at this point that all he could focus on is what he can't have, not why he can't have it. From verses 7 to 10, we gather that Jezebel formed a plan to get the vineyard, maybe without Ahab's foreknowledge initially. writing, sealing, and sending the letters. But he must have eventually learned about the plan because Elijah condemns him directly later The fasting would set the stage, as such days are usually proclaimed, to seek God's mercy for some evil or calamity that has befallen his people. Like what happened after Joshua's defeat at I, the scapegoats had to be identified. Except Nabat didn't covet like Achan, Ahab did. Nabit would be framed as the scapegoat. The two false witnesses were needed, and they were present to assure the crowds that he has violated Exodus chapter 22, verse 28. So Nabat would face the same fate as Shalomid's son in Leviticus 24. Ahab's vexation and sullenness were met with Jezebel's alacrity and callousness. They have the chemistry of the worst kind. They were a match made in hell. If only Ahab knew what Proverbs chapter 26, verse 7 says. Ahab had many things, but it doesn't seem like he really had a true friend who would dare wound his pride. If you think about it actually, David and Elijah were the closest things he had to friends. Because they told him the truth. So if you're struggling with coveting, go seek out a true friend who's not afraid to tell you the truth. And point you to Christ as the greatest treasure. Otherwise, desires unrestrained gain momentum and progressively gets worse James writes in chapter 1, verses 14 to 15. Each one is tempted when he is drawn away by his own desires and enticed. Then when desire has conceived, it gives birth to sin, and sin when it is full-grown, brings forth death. How true is that in this story? Now you might say, yes, Ahab's desire led to Nabat's death, but there's a far worse type of death here. And that's the spiritual depth for people like Ahab. Those out of fellowship with God. So in this chapter, sin goes unchecked, coveting goes unchecked, and then spreads to society and corrupts it. That's the third point. The letters arrive at their destinations. The elders and the nobles of Jezreel do not veto or revoke the executive order, so now covenant corrupts the city. Verse 11 shows the agreement. And then verses 12 to 13 show the near verbatim agreement between Jezebel's wishes and the compliance of Jezreelite rulers. From 2 Kings 9, verse 26, we learn that the leaders went above and beyond their duties and killed Nagar's sons as well. To clear the path completely for Ahav. They report their dirty deed to the queen The queen tells her king, and the king all he cares about is that Mabot is dead, and he can get what he wants. See this three-part progression from Ahab's internal coveting to Jezebel's external actions to the compliance of so-called leaders. A preacher and an expositor, Alexander McLaren, notes how all three were equally wicked. But they represent three different types of wickedness. Ahab was wicked and weak. Jezebel was wicked and strong. Her co-conspirators, the elders and nobles of Jezreel, were wicked and subservient. Just because you don't have a certain kind of personality, you're not a go-getter, you're not a type A, doesn't mean that you're not wicked. You could be a more go-with-the-flow kind of person. Or you allow others to manipulate you, though you occupy a place of responsibility. Wickedness doesn't just look like Jezebel. It could look like Ahab or the rulers of the city. No leader courageously protested against this plot. No elder protected his young. The nobles were ignoble. But let's be honest, if we were in the place of those leaders, would we have done much better? Will our voices be heard calling out against injustice? There are plenty of corrupt power-mongers like Ahab and Jezebel, and there are plenty of victims like Nabat and his sons today. What will we do as saints? Now just to be clear, we can't redeem the culture, but we can show them the redeemer. We can't save the world, but we can point to them, point them to the savior of the world We shine our light with our good testimony and good fruits in prayer and in hopes of their conversion. We also need to warn them of the judgment to come. That leads to the fourth point, coveting will be judged. In verses 17 to 19, God sends his prophet Elijah to confront Ahab, just as he was rapaciously claiming the vineyard like a vulture. Verses 20 to 24 record the prophet's scolding remarks. Ahab thought that he was getting an amazing bargain, but it came at the cost of his soul. He sold himself to do evil, so the Lord will repay evil to him. He was about to add to his house, but God is going to destroy his house. Ahab and his family would suffer, just as he caused suffering for Naboth and his family. His father Omri's dynasty will fall just as the two previous dynasties fell before him. The houses of Jeroboam, Ba'asha, and Omri were all wicked and caused the people to sin. So they all fall, according to the words of prophets, through mutinous conspiracies. The house of Ahab will not even get a proper burial as dogs and birds will eat their corpses. The narrator, probably Jeremiah, joins Elijah in condemning his wickedness and idolatry in verses 25 and 26. Now I want the chapter to end at verse 26. I wish it did. But we must go on to verse 27 to 29. We must realize that God extends his mercy to the worst of sinners We learn in the next chapter that Ahab's repentance seems short-lived and shallow, but the emphasis here is that God is gracious, bountiful, and rich in mercy. We could spend time speculating whether Ahab was truly saved, whether he ended up in heaven, but a better exercise would be this. Consider whether you understand fully how your coveting will be judged. Consider how you need to ask or seek God's forgiveness. You may find it preposterous that I am asking you to repent of coveting. You might say, I'm not like Ahab. I didn't let my desires get out of control. What's the big deal? What harm has my covering done? But remember that what Ahab did was wicked in the sight of the Lord. Verses 20 and 25. Even if the world doesn't see it, God does. By breaking the tenth commandment, you shall not covet, you are actually breaking the first commandment. You shall not have any other gods before me. It is clear that coveting is idolatry, according to Colossians chapter 3, verse 5. You are putting a person, a status, or an object in place of God. We have coveted and practiced idolatry, so we deserve his wrath forever. But like I said, those last few verses of this chapter are there to signal to us that God's grace is available. God is holy, yes, but he is also merciful. That mercy can be better understood if we can perceive not only the injustice that Nabat suffered But the greater injustice that Jesus suffered. So we turn from 1 Kings 21 to Matthew 21. In a parable, Jesus explains that like Naboth, he was the rightful heir of the vineyard of God's kingdom. The father sent him to collect the fruits of that vineyard, but the tenants, the religious leaders of the day, upon identifying him as the owner's son, out of jealousy threw him out and killed him. That parable predicted Jesus' suffering. Jesus, though innocent, was wrongfully accused by false witnesses. and he was sentenced to die as a criminal outside the city of Jerusalem. Like the Old Testament counterpart A plot was hatched by the leaders of the city in conjunction with other rulers. But that's not the end of the story. Jesus is not merely a victim. He is the victor. If you continue to read Matthew 21, Jesus says that the stone which the builders rejected has become the cheap cornerstone. If you continue to read to the end of the Gospels, the resurrection proves Jesus' story doesn't end as a tragedy. He died for our sins and he rose again from the dead. They said Nabbat is not alive but dead. But I tell you, Jesus is not dead, but alive. He died specifically to pay the penalty of every covetousness, every injustice, every bloodshed, every wickedness. If we repent and turn from our sins and trust in Jesus Christ, who died for our covetousness, we will be forgiven Jesus, unlike Ahab, is the good and benevolent King who doesn't take life, but lays down his life so that we may enjoy him forever. What need do we have to covet? We are complete in Christ. Would you make this confession to the Lord as a prayer? Yea, justified, O blessed thought, and sanctified, salvation wrought. Thy blood had pardoned bought for me, and glorified I too shall be. Complete in thee, each one supplied. And no good thing to me denied, since thou my portion, Lord will be, I ask no more, complete in thee.

sermons.title: Church Family (2 Tim 1:1-5)
sermons.speaker: Sung Cho
sermons.text: As this pandemic continues, we have a chance to reflect upon the most important and essential matters of life. like family and religion. Not surprisingly, the message of our culture conflicts with biblical definitions of both. Take as an example the story of a girl named Tess that is very typical. Quote, change was the accepted norm for tests at home. For one thing, she had no idea who would be there when she walked in the door. Her full brother, one of her step- or half-siblings, her old mom, her new old mom. For the guy her dad was in a relationship with now, one constant was grandpa. Tess loved to listen to the old stories he told about how families used to be one mom, one dad, two kids, and a dog. Those stories seemed quaint now compared to the reality of her diverse and rapidly changing family. Yoga was a good way to center herself in light of constant shifts, but sometimes even that wasn't enough to quell the sometimes chaotic nature of her post-modern home. Do we as Christians have any say in the definition of family? We should honor marriages and protect it. Marriage is honorable among all, and the bed undefiled. We know family is God's idea. And even before the fall, he wanted male and female to marry and be fruitful and multiply. God chose Israel to carefully teach his revelation from generation to generation. In the New Testament church age, the stress on the importance of family continues. Paul wrote about love, submission, obedience, and patience required in the Christian household. But Paul was aware that in this fallen world, not everyone in the family would follow God. He knew that one spouse can come to Christ. while the other can become hostile to Christ and even desert the Christian. Our Lord Jesus Himself felt such tensions during his ministry, marrying his mother and his brothers Thought he lost his mind and wanted to come restrain him. But Jesus wasn't discouraged. He asked, who is my mother or my brothers? He turned toward his disciples and said, Here are my mother and my brothers. For whoever does the will of God is my brother and my sister and mother. Jesus' family consists of those who hear God's word and do it. Later, when his disciples began to cost the following him, Jesus encouraged them with these words. Everyone who has left houses, or brothers, or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or aunts. For my name's sake shall receive a hundredfold and inherit eternal life Now this verse in Matthew 19, 29 is not some claim to prosperity, but I truly believe that Jesus envisioned the church family. to be a partial fulfillment of this promise of a hundredfold. Even if we lose our earthly family members, we gain Christ most importantly And secondly, we become part of God's family. Dr. Paul, who also talked about how the church is a wonderful, extended family. It's even greater than the family of Israel in the Old Testament. Consider how ethnically diverse the church is, made up of both Jews and Gentiles. Paul did not believe in two churches, but one in which brothers and sisters from completely different backgrounds can share table fellowship. He believes in one household of faith where we sow and reap in the Spirit and do good to each other. In that sense, Paul truly was a family man. He loved, led, and served the church family like a protected father. laboring mother, and responsible brother. The burden he had for the churches he founded are evident all throughout the book of Acts and his letters. He would even write epistles from prison to encourage them. He did precisely that in 2 Timothy. 2 Timothy is one of three letters written near the end of his life called pastoral letters. They are named that way because Paul wrote three letters to two pastors named Timothy and Titus, who served at Ephesus and Crete, respectively. But they are more than just his assistants or disciples. They are his true children. And as their responsible spiritual father, he prepares them for ministry ahead of them. as his own ministry is about to come to a close. But you might wonder why did Paul write Timothy twice? There are indications in this second letter that this young pastor was discouraged, weakening spiritually and in need of exhortation. By one count, there is a total of 33 imperatives from Paul throughout the letter, reminding and urging Timothy to be strong and preach, among other things. The fact that Paul writes this letter is quite amazing, because he writes it from his second and final imprisonment in Rome, knowing that he is about to face martyrdom. Like any good parent, he knew he had to be strong for his spiritual son. In this manner, God intended the church to be a family where we bond and strengthen one another. As we think about these matters, let's look at 2 Timothy 1, verses 1 to 5, to see how the church family is formed. Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ, by the will of God, according to the promise of life which is in Christ Jesus, to Timothy, a beloved son. Grace, mercy, and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord. I thank God whom I serve with a pure conscience, as my forefathers did. As without ceasing I remember you in my prayers night and day, greatly desiring to see you, being mindful of your tears, that I may be filled with joy. When I call to remembrance the genuine faith that is in you, which dwelt first in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice, and I am persuaded is in you also. I believe the church family is created through one, lives changed by the gospel, verses one to two. 2. Devotion shared with past saints, verse 3, the first part of verse 3, 3a. And three, joy experienced with present believers. The second part of verse 3, 3b, to verse 5. First, lives changed by the gospel, verses one to two The entire reason why we can even talk about a spiritual family is the gospel. Without the death and resurrection of Christ, there is no promise of life. Without repentance from sin and genuine faith in Jesus, there is no conversion. Unless it was in God's will for the resurrected Jesus to confront the Christian persecuting Saul directly on the road to Damascus, there is no Paul, the apostle to the Gentiles. Without the radical transformations of both Paul and Timothy, there is no radical bond between the two. There is no grace, mercy, and peace that unite the two as family apart from God the Father and God the Son, Lord Jesus Christ. This is why I love listening to testimonies. Though we may live completely different lives, our lives converge at the cross. You may not have the immigrant experience I had in the late 80s. You may not understand what it means to be an Asian minority in the states. But like you, I am created in God's image. I am a sinner who has rebelled against God in thought, word, and actions. You and I deserve God's wrath. But Jesus died on the cross in my place, paying the penalty I deserve. Having completed his work, he rose from the dead and ascended to heaven Awaiting the day of his return to judge the world. I place my faith in Jesus as a teenager, knowing that no amount of good works or good intentions can save me from hell. My only hope of heaven is Jesus and his finished work on the cross. I pray your hope of heaven is the same. If so, we are a family who share lives changed by the gospel. There are even more blessings that come from the gospel. Secondly, God's family is formed by devotion shared with past saints. Look again at the first part of verse 3. I thank God whom I serve with the pure conscience as my forefathers did. To be clear, Paul's main point is that he is grateful for Timothy as he prays for him. But as he begins this letter, note how Paul avows his devotion to God. He can confidently affirm that one, he is internally consistent with his own conscience, and two, externally consistent with the ways of his forefathers. Now Paul is not boasting that he is perfect, but he is saying that he serves God to the best of his ability, according to the measure of his knowledge. He does not violate his internal moral radar, that is, his conscience, as it has been shaped and transformed by God's revelation in Christ and the Word. Paul's devotion is also in line with the legacy of his forefathers. Now Paul's past relationship with his ancestors is complicated. Back in his pre-Damascus days, Paul was advancing in Judaism, rapidly surpassing his peers. He was more zealous for his ancestral traditions than any of them. But being zealous did not mean that he was in the right. Like I said already, he persecuted the church, and by extension, he persecuted the head of the church, God's anointed Jesus. Paul is actually living contrary to his ancestors because they worship Jesus the Messiah, albeit in their limited scope of knowledge. So we must understand that by becoming a Christian, Paul wasn't faltering as a Jew. In fact, he's a better Israelite for it. He wasn't betraying his roots as a Benjaminite. He wasn't forsaking Moses as his enemies accused him of doing Paul stands in a long line of saints, justified and saved by grace through faith alone. He's affirming the promises made to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. He's proclaiming that the covenant made to David is fulfilled in his descendant Jesus. What's amazing is that we also stand in this line of faithful saints. The writer of Hebrews lists many heroes of faith from the Old Testament until he reaches the New Testament times. The saints of old have arrived ahead of us to the finish line. now dressed in white, watching us as we run our race of perseverance. We may not be connected to them ethnically, but we are related through the common faith in the same Christ and God. Why is this so important? Well, I think we have instinct and longing to belong not only to a family in the present. We also want to be proud of our heritage. One summer around the 4th of July, I saw this cool commercial for ancestry. com. A company that helps you trace back to your family roots. A crowd of people assemble at the Pennsylvania State House, Independence Hall, in Philadelphia. They take turns reading some lines of the Declaration of Independence signed in the year 1776. Racially diverse individuals sit, stand, and pose in imitation of the famous oil on canvas painting by John Trumbull. As they finish reading the concluding lines, the camera zooms out and a caption appears. Quote, everyone we've assembled here is descended from a signer of the Declaration of Independence. Unlock your past. Inspire your future. What would it feel like to get your Ancestry. com test results back and you realize you're a descendant of Thomas Jefferson Or somewhere in your genealogy, there is Benjamin Franklin. Who knows if we do a genetic test, what we'll discover? Perhaps we're from a royal line. Maybe we can boast of national heroes in our family history. But whether you go and sign up for ancestry. com or not, I'm going to hijack their model for illustration purposes. Unlock your past, inspire your future. The writer of Hebrews tells us that by faith we are connected to saints like Abel, Enoch, Noah, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Joseph, and Moses. By faith, we look back to Christ who already came, while they looked forward by faith to the same coming Christ. Paul unlocks the blessed truth that we are justified by faith alone, just as Abraham and David were. Abraham became the father of all who believe in Jesus, even Gentiles. Does that inspire your future? How's that for ancestry? So up to this point we see that through the good news of Jesus, Paul is not truly alone in prison. He has a band. Paul stands in connection with the future. He anticipates his home in heaven as his time draws near to the end. Paul also stands in connection with the past, believers of lore in the ancient scriptures. Finally, he stands in connection to the present with his fellow saints on earth as he reflects joyfully on the common fate shared with Timothy, Timothy's mother, and his grandmother. The third essence of God's family is the joy experienced with present believers. As that said, the main point of these verses is that Paul is thankful for Timothy. Paul prays for Timothy, remembers him, and longs to see him. The feelings are mutual as Timothy has shed tears for Paul. But such intentional prayer and memory do not leave Paul wistful and forlorn. A real fruit of his prayer for Timothy is overflowing joy. I present a challenge for all of us. Is it possible that we are not complete with joy because we don't remember our church family and pray for them? Maybe because all we pray for are our advancements, our successes, our relationships, and our future, that we only experience a tiny drop of joy. What if we long for others and remember their tears? What if we looked beyond ourselves to others' needs? What if we celebrated what God is doing in others? Paul informs us that joy is the purpose of his intercessory prayer. What Paul remembers most about Timothy is his sincere faith. Paul has seen his share of insincere faiths during decades of ministry. In the same chapter he mentions Phagellus and Hermogenes who abandoned Paul, verse 15 Later he mentions that Himeneas and Belatus are men who stray from the truth, chapter two, verses seventeen to eighteen.
