And Damas loved the world and left him as well. Chapter four verse ten. But Timothy isn't like them. His faith is steady, like the faith of his grandmother and his mother. We haven't seen the names of Lois and Eunice before, but we can gather from here and axe the following information. During Paul's first mission trip, he and Barnabas visited a city in modern-day Turkey named Lystra. There, Paul shared the gospel and healed a man lame from birth. This miracle created a stir in the city. And much to the dismay of these missionaries, the crowds tried to worship Paul and Barnabas as Hermes and Zeus, respectively. They wouldn't be so popular for long though. Soon, Jews from nearby cities came and turned the people against Paul. They stoned them and left them for dead. The Paul just got back up and returned into the city. He left next day for Derby and had fruitful ministry there, but Paul came back once more to Lystra on his return route. There were evidently enough genuine believers in the city since Paul and Barnabas appointed elders for the congregation there. During Paul's second mission trip, we first hear about Timothy and his mother. Who likely became followers of Christ during Paul's evangelistic work and Lystra It is safe to assume that Timothy's grandmother, Lois, was also converted at the same time. We also learned that Timothy was a half-Jew because Eunice is a Jew and his father was a Greek. We don't hear anything else about Timothy's unnamed father, perhaps because he died prior to these events. Lois and Eunice must have taught Timothy much about the Old Testament scriptures. That's why after conversion, the young man became quickly competent. in church life. As believers in his town Lystra, a neighboring town of Iconium, spoke well of him. So Paul recruited Timothy to help him in his mission trips. The young man was circumcised to have access to synagogues. Over the years, Timothy became Paul's valuable co-worker, faithful representative messenger, and irreplaceable son in faith. Timothy was endowed with spiritual gifts in accordance with prophecy. For all these reasons, Paul is joyful. Let's talk for two applications here. First, I want to stress again the adjective that is attached to Timothy's faith. Sincere In some versions we have genuine or unfeigned. Let's consider for a second its opposite meaning. Fake, hypocritical, skin deep. You see, shallow, nominal Christianity is not new, is not a new problem. It existed even in Paul's time. Many so-called believers only wanted to look holy or be praised. At the first sign of trouble, they are out the door. That means sadly we can't have genuine family relationships with everyone that comes to our churches. We must warn those who may have deceived themselves into thinking they are saved, when in fact they are headed for eternity without Christ. The second application has to do with the four people here: Paul, Timothy, Lois, and Eunice. What these verses demonstrate is the full realization of what an intergenerational church could look like. Look how different they are in life stages. Timothy was probably in his teenage years at conversion and at the time of this letter in his 30s. He's still considered relatively young as a church leader Paul was probably in his 60s, old enough to be Timothy's father. Perhaps Eunice is a bit younger than Paul in her 50s, and maybe Lois the grandmother was in her 70s. Yet these men and women were united and struggling in the same faith That's what a church is supposed to look like. Believers from different generations laying aside differences to serve God together. Now, I'm not saying it's easy. Timothy probably felt insecure as a leader of those older than him. But Paul told him to be an example to them. He wouldn't have told him that if it wasn't possible. Let me speak to those who are younger. After years of college where I spent so much time with friends my age at a Christian fellowship group I have difficulty relating to the older members of my home church. But having faithful Christians from different generations is a good thing. We have so much to gain from our older brothers and sisters. I also want to speak to the older generation here. You have the potential to positively impact younger believers at this church. And it's not only by having official positions at Sunday school teachers, elders, or deacons. You can invite younger couples and singles informally for dinner fellowship and show them hospitality. You can send a thoughtful email asking for their prayer requests Do you want this church to have a future? If so, the older men and women must make disciples. It's not too late. A pastor named Dave Harvey told the story of a woman named Jerry. She was married to her husband, Albert, for 42 years. In the last eleven of those years, she stood by him as he battled cancer. Thankfully, God used these trials to draw Albert and Jerry to God and to each other through the gospel. But Albert's time had come. Jerry was strong in her faith, but she went through the normal process of deep grief She lost sleep, she had apathy, mental listlessness, and sometimes even forgot what Albert looked like. But her faith began to come alive again First, she found the will to get up in the morning, leave the house. She remembered that others were suffering, and she made herself available She met with her pastor to ask how she could serve the church. She got a flexible job so that she can build her schedule around her ministry. She didn't wallow in pity, but found direction through her faith. Jerry eventually sold her house and moved into a smaller place. But her enthusiasm never shrank. She regular regularly studied God's Word and read good books. She embodied Titus 2, 3 to 5, and became a wonderful disciple maker. One younger woman, a mother, testified, quote, Through Jerry's example and honesty, she has encouraged me and exhorted me to greater love for my Savior. and greater diligence with my family. Not only that, but I now have a vision for how God will meet me when I am older. End quote Dave Harvey ends the story with the words of Jerry herself, quote, A wise person is always preparing for the next stage. Well, I'm in the deep winter of my life. I want to live preparing for what's after that. I want to spend my time and money in a way that recognizes eternity. After citing this quote, Harvey revealed that Jerry is his mom. There are still untold stories like Jerry's where an older believer inspires a younger one. It's like the way Eunice, Lewis, and Paul impacted Timothy. I hope that the spiritual family here can have similar testimonies. We are saved by the same gospel. We stand in a long, unending line of those who are justified by grace alone, through faith alone, in Christ alone. We share joy with all the saints on earth, the church family which provides encouragement in this journey. Let's remember these truths as we look forward to reuniting again as church family.

sermons.title: Word-Saturated Worship
sermons.speaker: Sung Cho
sermons.text: Imagine that you've just moved to Northern California You end up in a beautiful city of about 90,000 called Redding. As a mature Christian, you made it a priority to find a church to join. Impossible to ignore is a non-denominational megachurch in town called Bethel Church with approximately 11,000 members. So you decide to visit the College View campus. You step out of the car, stand in awe of the modern facility. And you are welcomed warmly into the 10:30 a. m. worship service. They are ministries of all life stages, from nursery to youth group to young adult to men's ministry to senior ministry. They have an amazing and talented worship band. The sermon was different than what you're used to, with tons of emphasis on miracles. There was some reference to angel feathers and gold dust. That sounded strange, but you try to be open-minded You come home impressed by the grandeur of the experience. You tell your friends back in Maryland about it. They aren't as excited as you and they begin sending you warnings and articles like, quote, nine things you should worry about, the Bethel Church movement. I'm sorry, nine things you should know about the Bible Church movement, and quote, from the Gospel Coalition website, and quote, what are the greater works for believers? John 14, 12, and quote from The Grace to You website. What will you do? Beto people seem to be genuine and caring. They've invited you over for lunch and they want to keep a help you get acclimated to the city. Also, you've been to small churches all your life. This would be a step in a new direction. Perhaps you'll be in a similar situation in the future. Perhaps you're not sure how to guide your children and grandchildren in finding a good, solid church where they live. This hypothetical situation is meant to introduce us into today's topical sermon. I don't typically prepare topical sermons, but these are not normal days. As we're forced to stay home on Sundays, as we observe how other churches operate. We might ask the following questions. Why are some worship services and churches, quote, better than others? By what standard is one Sunday experience superior or inferior to another? If you said conformity to biblical standards, you're correct. And so I want to point you to this biblical idea. The Bible not only dictates what we should worship that we should worship God, but it also dictates how we should worship God. The Bible not only dictates that we should worship God, but it also dictates how we should worship God. Not just who, when, where and why, but how. A key passage is John 4, 21 to 24. While Jesus was talking to the Samaritan woman, he said Woman, believe me, the hour is coming when you will neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem worship the Father You worship what you do not know. We worship what we We know what we worship for salvation is of the Jews. But the hour is coming, and now is when the true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth. For the Father is seeking such to worship him. God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth. We know from this passage, the Who, God who is revealed throughout the Old Testament, not just the first five books, he must be worshipped. From creation to new creation, the constant why of worship is God's glory. We learn about the relevant when, a time inaugurated by Jesus, God's Son in the present church age. We learn about where? It's not the physical locations of Mount Gerizim or even Jerusalem upon Mount Zion, but from saints all over the world. But the focus of our discussion is how we ought to worship God. He is no longer concerned with the physical shadows of Levitical worship and its sacrificial system. These anticipated heavenly things and good things to come. Hebrews 8 and 10. Now we worship in spirit as God is spirit, and we worship him according to the truth of Scripture. As Don Whitney writes, quote, the boundaries of evangelical spirituality are the written self-revelation of God. Yet there are still divisions on how of worship The main debate is between two principles. One, the regulative principle of worship and two, the normative principle of worship. First, the regulative principle of worship, henceforth RPW. It is described well in the two 17th century Reform documents, the Westminster Confession, Chapter 21, of Presbyterian Puritans And the second London Baptist Confession, chapter 22, adopted by particular Baptists. The former describes it like this, quote, The acceptable way of worshipping the true God is instituted by Himself, and so limited by His own revealed will. that he may not be worshipped according to the imaginations and devices of men, or the suggestions of Satan, under any visible representation, or any other way not prescribed in the Holy Scripture. RPW adherents err on the sign of caution to say whatever is not commanded in the Bible should be forbidden. The adherents of the normative principle of worship, NPW, agree that our worship must conform to explicit teachings of the scriptures. But with regard to whatever not commanded in the Bible, they are more liberal. Whatever is not forbidden should not be condemned necessarily. There have been extremes on both sides. On the excessive side of RPW are some churches with roots in the Restoration Movement. They hold that only a cappella singing is allowed as instruments are not prescribed in the New Testament. On the excessive side of NPW are seeker-sensitive churches with all kinds of creative yet superfluous elements. Such elements can distract us from the word. Though I lean towards RPW, I'm not here to settle the debate. I simply want to promote what I believe the Bible says we should do during worship. I found Livin Duncan helpful in identifying five elements of biblical corporate worship. Read the Bible Preach the Bible, pray the Bible, sing the Bible, and see the Bible. First, we read the Bible. Public Bible reading is a consistent practice throughout redemption history. Exodus, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Second Kings, Nehemiah. If synagogue worship influenced early church worship, scripture reading could be one tradition that was passed along. Before Jesus sat down to teach at the Nazareth synagogue, he stood up to read Isaiah. Luke 4. During his missionary trips, Paul strategically targeted synagogues in cities. There the law and the prophets were read weekly. Acts 15, 2 Corinthians 3. At Phisione and Antioch, the synagogue ruler invited Paul to give an exhortation after the reading. Acts 13. As a number of Gentile converts grew, the Jewish Christians couldn't just take them to the synagogues as God didn't want Gentile saints to become Jewish proselytes and live under the law. So just as the Jews did on the Sabbath, Christians gathered on Sundays to read the scriptures. They not only procured the Old Testament, but also the letters, the Gospels, and the prophecies from apostles and eyewitnesses of Jesus and his ministry. But they did more than just read the Bible. Instruction begins, not ends, with scripture reading Take for example 1 Timothy 4. 13. After the reading, there are exhortation and doctrine. What's the difference between the two? According to commentator Dwayne Lipbin, quote, the distinction between this and the former term is by no means clear-cut. The two merge into each other, yet teaching, doctrine in NKJV, Didaskalia may refer primarily to a more catechical treatment of the truths of the Christian faith. The two terms occur in Romans 12, 7-8 And are there related to spiritual gifts? End quote I tend to think that good exhortation emphasizes wise insight into people, while good doctrine emphasizes wise insight into the word. But you need both. Both exhortation and doctrine must occur in corporate worship. We need both pastors and teachers for exhortation and doctrine, for the equipping of the saints. Ephesians 4, 11 to 16. The way to have both in one activity is to preach the Bible. Consider what churches are asking you to do every week. We are asking you to give up time and energy in your precious weekend, the golf course, extra sleep, a chance to get away, etc. What do we have to offer as a church that's worth such sacrifice? God's word. Look no further than the Bible to learn the value of the Bible. Psalm 19, 7-11 says, The law of the Lord is perfect. Converting the soul. The testimony of the Lord is sure, making wise the simple. The statutes of the Lord are right, rejoicing the heart. The commandment of the Lord is pure, enlightening the eyes. The fear of the Lord is clean, enduring forever. The judgments of the Lord are true and righteous altogether. More to be desired are they than gold, yea, than much fine gold, sweeter also than honey and the honeycomb Moreover, by them your servant is warned, and in keeping them there is great reward. Psalm 119, 105 says, Your word is a lamb to my feet. and a light to my path. 2 Timothy 3, 16-17 says, All scripture is given by inspiration of God. and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness, that the man of God may be complete, thoroughly equipped for every good work. There's nothing else worth preaching. No wonder Paul tells Timothy in chapter 4, verse 1 to 2. Our charge you therefore before God and the Lord Jesus Christ, who will judge the living and the dead at his appearing and his kingdom. Preach the word. Be ready in season and out of season. Convince, rebuke, exhort with all long-suffering and teaching. The word exhort and teaching here is similar to exhortation and instruction in 1 Timothy 4. 13. But you see how preaching encompasses both. You can't preach without absorting But preaching is more than exording. You can't preach without teaching, but preaching is more than teaching Joseph Bayer defines preaching as follows in his lexicon. Quote: One, to be a herald, to officiate as a herald. 1a to proclaim after the manner of a herald, 1b, always with the suggestion of formality, gravity, and an authority which must be listened to and obeyed 2. To publish, proclaim openly, something which has been done. 3. Use of the public proclamation of the gospel and matters pertaining to it. made by John the Baptist, by Jesus, by the apostles, and other Christian teachers. End quote. As a herald, I have to preach with dying people in front of me and the reality of God's kingdom behind me. On the pulpit I speak on behalf of the kingdom of heaven advancing. There's an immediate urgency and desperation to see people saved and transformed for his glory. I'm not here for an academic lecture. I'm not here for an enlightening TED Talk. As an emissary of the kingdom, I joined other faithful preachers in imitating Paul in 2 Corinthians 5. 20. We are ambassadors for Christ, as though God were pleading through us. We implore you, on Christ's behalf, be reconciled to God. For this end, I shall preach what the Bible says. I ought to be an expository preacher who explains the scriptures. I follow the lead of Charles Simeon, who said, quote, My endeavor is to bring out of Scripture what is there, and not to thrust in what I think might be there. I have a great jealousy on this head, never to speak more or less than I believe to be the mind of the Spirit in the passage I am expounding. That should be the goal of every individual instance of preaching, to plumb the depths of scriptures. But over time, we should also endeavor to preach the entire breadth of the Bible through surveys and broad strokes. After all, Paul said to the Ephesian elders in Acts 20, verse 27, that he has not shunned to declare to them the whole counsel of God. I doubt Paul preached every single verse of the Old Testament. It's more likely that he provided the big picture along with key details. So the pastor and guest speakers have an awesome responsibility at the pulpit. But the sermon is not the only time there's exhortation and instruction. We must also pray the Bible. Paul prescribes prayer in church life and men are to lead representative prayers. 1 Timothy 2. 8. The translation of 1 Timothy 2. 8 is more accurate in the New American Standard Bible than the New King James Version It's not that Paul wants men to pray everywhere like the public park or the city hall. Rather, Paul wants men everywhere, that is, all throughout the world, to pray specifically in public assemblies. See chapter 3 verse 14 to 15. When I say pray the Bible, I mean that we should be biblical in our prayer content We may close our physical eyes in prayer, but our spiritual eyes must always be open to the word. One way to do this is literally praying a prayer in the Bible, like the Lord's Prayer, But a far more practical application is found in Acts 4. It's not only an example of praying scriptures, but also scriptural praying. Here is the Jerusalem Church's corporate prayer in response to persecution, starting from verse 24. Lord, you are God who made heaven and earth and the sea and all that is in them. who by the mouth of your servant David have said, Why did the nations rage and the people plot vain things? The kings of the earth took their stand, and the rulers were gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ. For truly against your holy servant Jesus whom you anointed, both Herod and Pontius Pilate With the Gentiles and the people of Israel were gathered together to do whatever your hand and your purpose determined before to be done. Now, Lord, look on their threats and grant to your servants that with all boldness they may speak your word. by stretching out your hand to heal, and that signs and wonders may be done through the name of your holy servant Jesus. This prayer is both empowered by the scriptures and laced with scriptures. See how the beleaguered Jerusalem saints first address God with reverence. They acknowledge his absolute sovereignty as the creator of the universe. drawing from passages like Exodus 20. 11 and 2 Kings 19. 15. But the main scripture at the forefront of their minds is Psalm 2, 1 to 2. In that passage, they not only see the future struggle of Gentile nations against the Messiah and his kingdom. They also see in it the past futile attempts to stop God's rule through Christ. The kings of earth and rulers correspond to Herod, Pontius Pilate, Jewish and Gentile authorities who can do nothing to thwart the plan of redemption. The early church, endowed with all their apostolic gifts of signs and wonders, asked for courage in their witness. We benefit from their example of prayer. As they meditated on the Bible and reflected on their predicament, they could not help but praise God and petition Him. But to adoration and supplication, we can add confession and thanksgiving. When we consider all the demands of Scripture, how can we not acknowledge our shortcomings? How can we say we have not transgressed in thought, word, and deed, sinned in omission and commission? 1 John 1, 9-10 says, if we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness. If we say that we have not sinned, we make him a liar, and his word is not in us. And of course, we cannot help but thank God as we meditate on his promises and blessings. We see thanksgiving time to prayer in Philippians 4. 6 and Colossians 4. 2. Just as preaching the Bible requires preparation, so do corporate prayers. First, we can start individually with a specific verse or passage. Evan Howard in his book, Praying the Scriptures, writes Quote, to pray the scriptures is to order one's time of prayers around the particular text in the Bible. Then we apply ACTS, adoration, confession, thanksgiving, and supplication. Finally, if we are praying before others, we remember the general biblical principle for our local church gatherings in 1 Corinthians 14, 26. Let all things be done for edification. The way to guarantee edification in prayers is this. Prepare prayers that are informed by scriptures and inform others of scriptures. Our prayers must be in line with Bible, and often that means our prayer lines contain the Bible. This means that you should listen carefully to representative prayers. Don't put your brain and heart on cruise control during the first half of the worship service. Pray along and also sing along. That leads to the third point. Sing the Bible. Actually, that should be the fourth point. With all the debate out there about the acceptable music styles, We can at least agree on what's said in Colossians 3:16. Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom, Teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord. The parallel passage in Ephesians 5, 18-21 teaches us that, among other things, spirit-filled church members speak to each other by singing scriptural content. It's true that there's no mention of instruments in New Testament passages that relate to church life. But if instruments can be used to aid congregational singing, I think they can be justified. If a piano, guitar, or percussion can help us sing in temple and in tune, I think we should have instruments. But when we can't hear our voices or each other because of a worship band or an orchestra, when accompaniment do much more than accompany the vocals, We need to deem them as hindrances to singing the Bible. Whatever choices our church makes instrumentally, we can resolve to sing the Bible by literally singing the Bible, as some do with Psalters, and or by singing scripturally rich songs. Take for example the hymn Rock of Ages and his first few words. Rock of Ages cleft for me, let me hide myself in thee. There are so many scriptural allusions in just 12 words. First, the address rock of ages. In Isaiah 26, verse 4, we are told Yahweh is worthy of trust. as the everlasting rock. In KJV and NKJV we have everlasting strength, but the original word there can mean both rock and strength Next we learn that this everlasting rock or the rock of ages was clept. What did the lyricist mean to do here? You may recall from Exodus 33 that Moses wanted to see God's glory, but if he were to gaze upon God's face, he would die. So the Lord gave this instruction in verses 21 to 23. Here is a place by me, and you shall stand on the rock. So it shall be while my glory passes by, that I will put you in the cleft of the rock, and will cover you with my hand while I pass by. Then I will take away my hand and you shall see my back, but my face you shall not be seen. Keep this incident in mind as we continue to First Corinthians ten and Colossians three. The second person in the Trinity, God the Son, was the pre-incarnate Christ and the spiritual rock. that followed the Israelites, providing for them. 1 Corinthians 10, 1 to 5. Christ is the everlasting rock, the rock of ages, worthy of trust, then and now. So the author of this hymn, Augusta's top lady, confesses, let me hide myself in thee, just as Moses hid in that cleft rock in the wilderness. So we can say with Paul that our lives are hidden with Christ in God. When Christ, who is our life, appears, then you also will appear with him in glory. Colossians 3, 3 to 4. The reason that we are able to live forever in glory is that we die to sin through Jesus. When we sing that Jesus a rock was clept, Top Lady was referring to the crucifixion as the next lines clearly indicate. At the cross, the rock was clept for me. Jesus died on the cross for our sins, accepting God's wrath and punishment of hell in our place. While we were still sinners, Christ died for us. Romans 5. 8. On the third day after his death, Jesus rose from the dead and ascended to heaven. And he will return here in the future day of judgment. Meanwhile, we have a chance to repent and believe in Him for salvation. There's no place to hide from God's righteous anger. But amazingly, God the Father has provided a hiding place in God the Son, the rock of ages, cleft for me. We hide from God, in God. We hide in Christ by repenting from self-reliance and trusting in Jesus alone for eternal life. I hope these hymn lyrics whet your appetite for God's Word. But there's one more activity for worse saturated worship. We see the Bible through the ordinances. I first spoke about the two Protestant ordinances early in 2019, Baptism and Lord's Supper. You can listen again to these sermons online, the Holy Communion of the Church, February 17th, and the Mission of the Church, February 24th. These two ordinances are commanded by Lord Jesus at the Great Commission and the Last Supper, respectively. They visualize biblical truths of salvation in Christ, and they are given to the church. While the marriage covenant functions similarly, it was given to all humanity. But of course, we are enlightened to appreciate clearly and fully what it signifies. Baptism and Lord's Supper are given to the church specifically. And we know from Romans 6, 1-11, and 1 Corinthians 11, 17-34, what each ordinance signifies respectively. They are visible words, as the reformers call them. They're God-ordained object lessons. Also, these are by nature communal practices. You can read the Bible alone, you can pray alone, you can sing alone. But you cannot have baptism and Lord's Supper without your local church. By the public act of baptism You are professing your faith in Jesus and formally entering visible church membership. Acts 241. To be baptized, at minimum, you need a representative baptizer, as the Ethiopian eunuch had with Philip. Chapter 8, 26-40. Also, Paul reminds the Corinthians to discern the Lord's body, that is the local church, during the supper and wait for one another. Taken together, if baptism is the rite of initiation, the Lord's Supper is the recurring family meal of the local church. We look forward to resuming these communal activities in the near future. I hope that as we prepare to regather as church, you will appreciate all that takes place during the worship service. Reading, preaching, praying, singing, and seeing the Bible. Until then, please take up the practice of reading, praying, and singing at home. As Matthew Henry has said, they who pray in the family do well. They who read and pray do better. But they who sing and read and pray do best of all. But playing your worship times with the Lord are saturated by the word.

sermons.title: Revelation 1:1-3
sermons.speaker: Sung Cho
sermons.text: A pastor tells a story of two men in a museum who see a painting of a chess game. One character in the painting looked like a man, the other looked very much like the devil. The man was down to his last piece. The title of the painting was Checkmate. One of the two men looking at the painting was an international chess champion. Something about the painting intrigued him. He began to study it. He grew so engrossed that the man with him got a little impatient and asked what he was doing. The chess champion said, Something about this painting bothers me. I want to study it a while. You go ahead and wander around. When the friend came back after a while, the chess master said, We must locate the man who painted this piece. We must tell him he must either change the picture or change the title. I have determined there is something wrong with this painting and I am an international chess champion. His friend asked, What's wrong with the painting? The man replied, It's called Checkmate, but the title is wrong. The king still has one more move. To the untrained eye, to the uninitiated, your view on life could be aptly described as checkmate. You feel like it's over. You have this sinking feeling that with this pandemic, our economy, personal health problems, relationship issues, there's no way to win You believe the scripture, the truth of scripture, that Jesus sits upon the heavenly throne and all authority has been given to him in heaven and on earth. But instead of that glorious vision, you can only see Jesus as that lone piece on the chessboard. Your despair has led you to forget the truth that God is in control. All you can see is the devil smirking at you across the table, and all you hear are mockers. Where is the promise of his coming? For since the fathers fell asleep, all things continue as they were from the beginning of creation If you are discouraged in this manner, I'd like to change your misnomer. The title of your worldview you have adopted. But it won't be because I am Pollyanna-ish or because I believe in the progress of humanity Far from it, I point you to scriptures and think that you may have underestimated the King of Kings. We may underestimate the power of that one move, his glorious return from heaven. Others may say he is only one man, but you should know he is the one and only God man. Our king still has one more move, and we will win. If we are to understand this truth better, we must know the whole counsel of God. That means we must be familiar with the contents from Genesis all the way to Revelation. But perhaps you feel like studying that last book is daunting. Thankfully, the first few words of the book are quite inviting and welcoming. Let's turn to the first three verses. The revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave him to show his servants, things which must shortly take place And he sent and signified it by his angel to his servant John, who bore witness to the word of God and to the testimony of Jesus Christ, to all things that he saw. Blessed is he who reads and those who hear the words of this prophecy, and keep those things which are written in it, for the time is near. As we wait for Jesus' second coming, let's resolve to take three actions corresponding to the three verses. One Be servants of Christ who revealed in the past. 2. Be witnesses of Christ who saves in the present. 3. Be obedient to Christ who returns in the future. First, be servants of Christ who revealed in the past. In verse 1, we have a rare instance of a book titled actually embedded in the book itself. Sure, there are salutations, introductions, and prefaces in the New Testament narratives and epistles, but titles like the letter to the Galatians or the Acts of the Apostles. were not added until later, after the completion of the inspired contents. John the Apostle, on the other hand, begins with the title that encapsulates what follows. Revelation comes from apocalypse, which means uncovering to show what's hidden. Seems straightforward enough, but there are disagreements concerning what follows, the phrase of Jesus Christ. Is this phrase the object or the subject of revelation? In other words, is Jesus the one revealed object or the one revealing subject? You can see by the sermon point I've shared that I lean towards the latter. I believe John is emphasizing that Jesus is the revealer. Of course, a case can be made that Jesus is the one revealed. After all, Jesus' revelation from heaven is where this book is headed. Also, commentators note that in the New Testament, most instances of the same grammatical construction, that is, revelation of this or that, convey something to be revealed. But I agree with Robert Thomas who favors Jesus as the revealer and points to the abundance of passages in the book of Revelation itself. Jesus as the revealer addresses the seven churches in chapters 2 to 3, exposing their corporate sins and recognizing their good works. John learns later that Jesus as the Lamb, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the root of David, has prevailed to open the scroll and to lose its seven seals. And verse 1 itself makes clear that Jesus transmits divine revelation from God the Father to his mediating angel, who then signified it to John. Signifying need not be taken to mean that this prophecy is opaque or impossible to interpret. We find the same word used to accurately predict three concrete historical events. Jesus' crucifixion. Peter's martyrdom, and the widespread famine during Emperor Claudius' reign. John then writes down for the rest of the servants, us Christians in general. Next, we should not miss the significance of the phrase, things which must take place. We find the same exact phrase in the Greek version of Daniel 2, 28-29. In that chapter, Daniel teaches King Nebuchadnezzar the prophetic content of his dream Which outlines history from his kingdom of Babylon to the kingdom of heaven, Jesus will establish. Here is the final scene of that vision in verses 44 to 45. The God of heaven will set up a kingdom which shall never be destroyed, and the kingdom shall not be left to other people. It shall break in pieces and consume all these kingdoms, and it shall stand forever. Inasmuch as you saw that the stone was cut out of the mountain without hands, and that it broke in pieces the iron the bronze, the clay, the silver, and the gold. The great God has made known to the king what will come to pass after this. The dream is certain, and its interpretation is sure. So Daniel knew that history would culminate with the advent of the Messianic kingdom But he spoke from a distant past before the rise and fall of the intervening kingdoms like Persia and Greece. Similarly, Jesus spoke of what must happen in the future before his return. Our Lord warned us that first there will be the beginning of sorrows. Nation will rise against nation and kingdoms against kingdom, and there will be famines, pestilences, and earthquakes in various places. Matthew 24, 7 to 8. So we know that the phrase things which must take place refer to end-time events. But in what sense is it going to take place shortly? I mean, it's been about 2,000 years and counting. Commentator Alan Johnson helps by explaining that the adverb shortly primarily communicates iminency. Quote, the church in every age has always lived with the expectancy of the consummation of all things in its day. Immincy describes an event possible any day, impossible no day. Here's an illustration. Among the less enviable and more forgettable memories we have in our adult experience is Waiting at the Maryland Motor Vehicle Administration. You receive a piece of paper with a letter and a number from a worker. Let's say you got E97. You spend your time waiting. You see E94, E95, and E96 flash on the displays, and you see someone go to take care of her business with the representative. Now you know that your time will come shortly But what was promised to you at the beginning of the MVA process was not quantifiable time like forty minutes or an hour. You, E97, were only promised that you would go after E96. Consider the three customers ahead of you as events rather than people. E94 is the first advent of Jesus. E-95 is the death, resurrection, and ascension of Jesus. E96 is the church age, the present epoch, when the fullness of Gentiles comes into the kingdom. while Israel is blinded as Romans 11. 25 tells us. Now you know Jesus' second coming is next, but it turns out E96 is taking longer than expected. But you know it's okay. It's more than okay. Because between Jesus' ascension and his return, not only are you saved, but there's a possibility that Your family, friends, neighbors, people all over the world will hear the gospel and be saved. So you hold on to that sheet of paper knowing that your time of deliverance is coming shortly. In the same way, we hold on to the revelation of Jesus Christ firmly and eagerly. We live as servants. We tell others about our Savior and Lord with one eye in the heavens, waiting for our time of deliverance. and the other eye on the lost, those destined for eternal destruction. And so we feel the urge to preach the gospel to them. That leads to the second action. Be witnesses of Christ who saves in the present. There's a special emphasis on testimony in verse 2. In this one verse there are Two words, a verb, bore witness, and a noun, testimony. They have a common etymological root, and so we see that John testifies what Jesus has testified. As Adam Clark notes, quote, John had visions from heaven, but he described them in his own language and manner. He used simple common Greek language in his style to write down the contents. Yet the apostle understands that that content consisting of all things that he saw. Is authoritative. God's very own word. So the line of communication goes like this God the Father speaks the word. God the Son testifies to that word. A mediating angel transmits Jesus' testimony. John the servant bears witness to Jesus' testimony. Other servants receive John's testimony. But what are we to learn from this process? I just want to point out two applications First, let's reinforce our primary designation as servants. For that end We should note our location in this line of communication. We are not at the beginning of the line for sure. Not even near the beginning or the middle. To use military terms, we are not a general, colonel, major, captain, sergeant, but more like a private. We are at the bottom of the hierarchy as normal Christian servants who receive God's word. That should humble us. The best of us, the most insightful and knowledgeable among us, cannot escape our lowly position. Those right above us, the foundational apostles of the early church, set an example for us. If such men were humble servants, how can we not humble ourselves? 2 Corinthians 12, 1-6 indicates that John is not the first to see visions of heaven in the apostolic age. And those privileged to see them were not to boast in such revelations. Paul teaches us that if we do boast, it should be in our weaknesses, infirmities, and humble circumstances. 2 Corinthians 11, 22 to 33. It should not be because we have great Bible knowledge and know how to interpret all the signs of this book. We must remember that we are mere recipients and witnesses, not innovators or visionaries. Speaking of which, the application, the other application, is that we are to be faithful witnesses. The test of Christlikeness is our persevering testimony. In verse 5, we see that Jesus Himself is the faithful witness. He is introduced to the Laodiceans as the Amen, the faithful and true witness. Chapter 3 verse 14 Verity and fidelity are qualities found in witnesses like John himself, exiled to Patmos for his ministry. 1-9. Or consider Antipas at Pergamos. Who gave his life to martyrdom? Not coincidentally, the word martyr comes from witness, chapter 2, verse 13. Many others in the future will face the same fate, whether martyred for their witness, chapter 6, verse 9, attacked and killed by the Antichrist. And beheaded for not taking his mark. If all that sounds intimidating, please know that similar trials are already taking place in the world as we speak. They occur in smaller localized settings as prelude to the universal tribulation to come. And let's say God by His good Providence permits us to face such troubles here and now. Will you be a faithful witness? The answer is the same as before. Revelation 12, 11 tells us the key to victory over the evil one. They overcame him by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony, and they did not love their lives to the death. We can be bold in our witness to the point of martyrdom, because we are covered by the Lamb's blood. We can share the good news of Jesus Christ, even if that means bad news for our comfort here. And to be Christ's good servant and his faithful witness, we must stay in his word. That leads to the third point. Be obedient to Christ who returns in the future Verse 3 is the first of seven Beatitudes or Blessings in the Book of Revelation. Others are found in chapter 14, 16, 19, 20, and 2 are found in chapter 22. Blessings number 2 to 5 relate to the martyrdom of tribulation saints, moral purity during intense trials, marriage suffer of the Lamb, and the first resurrection unto glory. Blessings 6 and 7, both in the final chapter 22, serve as symmetrical bookends to the first one here in chapter 1. Far from being esoteric, impractical, or elusive, this book begins and ends with promises of blessing for those who put these words to action. So it behooves us to read, understand, and keep this book of prophecy, that is, interpret and apply it. Interestingly, there is a switch from the singular to the plural in verse 3 that gives some insight into the practices of the early church. One person stood to read while everyone else sat and listened. Since paper and ink were precious commodities back then, and the printing press was still about 1300 years away, the most efficient way to transmit scriptures was to have someone read it aloud during a congregational meeting. But it was not enough to listen and understand. Individuals and churches must keep those things which are written in it, for the time is near. Like I said earlier, Jesus' second coming is imminent or could happen any moment. So as James said, we ought to be doers of the word and not hearers only, deceiving ourselves. Blessings await those who read, understand, and keep this prophecy. We miss the time of reading and preaching scriptures in corporate church worship, but we don't have to miss out on reading in our individual home worship. Praise God that we have access to the Word via print or online. As for understanding the prophecies, we are thankful that we have the entire Bible. All the books that came before Revelation are essential in understanding this last book. You have to speak and be fluent in the language of the Bible, as it were, to understand Revelation. Commentator David Guzig writes, Though it is filled with signs, the Book of Revelation is accessible. To those who have an understanding of the first 65 books of the Bible, and especially an understanding of the first 39 books of the Bible, the Old Testament. The book of Revelation is rooted in the Old Testament. It contains more than 500 allusions to the Old Testament and 278 of the 404 verses in Revelation. That is almost 70%. Make some reference to the Old Testament. We are also thankful to have some 2,000 years of history of interpretation, a lengthy bibliographical list of commentators, pastors, teachers, and scholars. I'm thankful for their insights, not only their honest and humble attempts at interpreting the text, but their lessons of applying the text. Currently, the council is reading some sermons from John Charles Rile, J. C. Ryle, an English evangelical Anglican bishop from the 19th century. He wrote and delivered a sermon on these three first three verses of Revelation entitled The Reading Which Is Blessed. He says much to encourage us to read this book. He finds in it a number of useful lessons, many blessed and comfortable truths scattered up and down, all over. intelligible to the simplest comprehension, and yet full of food for the most spiritual mind There is hardly a chapter from which a man may not draw some striking and edifying thought if he perseveres in humble prayerful study of the whole book. He shall find in almost every page verses which shall richly repay his pains They shall shine out on him like stars in the dark bolt of heaven in a moonless night They shall refresh him like an oasis in the wilderness and make it impossible for him to say, all is barren. They shall sparkle like precious stones on the shore as he walks by the deep waters of the mysterious book, and make him feel that his journey in search of treasure is not in vain. Ryle goes on and provides specific examples of such stars, oases, and precious stones. He tells us that there is much about the Lord Jesus Christ in the book. There's much about the desperate corruption of human nature. There is much about hell. There is much about heaven. There is much about the prospects of the saints. There's much to show the folly of depending entirely on the powers of this world for the advancement of Christianity. There's much in the book of Revelation to show the painful childishness of the vast majority of Christians, true Christians all over the world. Finally, there is much to show the safety of all true believers in Christ, whatever may come upon the world. Indeed, there is enough in this book to occupy those who have studied scriptures all their lives, and those who have just begun their heavenly journey. There's everything from elementary gospel basics to advanced eschatology, from rudiments of salvation to tough lessons of sanctification. And while you may get excited about the complex details, God has designed us to be blessed from reminders of simple truths as well. So it seems appropriate that before you read the revelation of Jesus Christ, you should review the gospel of Jesus Christ. It goes like this and it never gets old. God created us in his image to live with him and live for him But we, like the first man Adam, rebelled against our Creator. We have done wrong, sinned, and broke God's law in our thoughts, words, and actions. We have fallen short of his glory by doing what we should not do, and not doing what we should do. So like our first parents, we deserve to be cast out of God's blissful paradise. But our loving God never left us without hope and promise of redemption. That promise of returning to paradise, to the ultimate, to the intimate presence of the Lord. is guaranteed through the seed of the woman, the seed of Abraham, the Lion of Judah, the son of David, all fulfilled in one person. All throughout the Old Testament, saints were anticipating the Messiah, that is Christ, who would save sinners. Jesus came with the perfect light, and he saved us by dying on the cross in our place, paying the penalty for our sins. On the cross, Jesus took the consequences of our sins, the full wrath of God, hell reserved for sinners, so that we may enter into heaven. He took upon himself the curse of the book of the law, so that we would receive the blessings of this book of prophecy. Our Lord finished the work of salvation, died, was buried, and rose from the dead on the third day. He showed many proofs that he was alive and ascended to heaven. Now he extends his mercy to you. Because there is no other way for us to be saved except by grace as a gift. Heaven cannot be earned by your good works. Jesus already did all the work required. All you need to do is turn away from yourself, from self-confidence and self-loathing. And trust in him alone for salvation. Now we live on earth as Jesus' grateful servants who have received his revelation. We live for him as unashamed witnesses for Christ who saves the lost. We live to testify to the gospel the power of God to salvation for everyone who believes. We are to read this book of Revelation, understand it. And keep it as we await Jesus' return. Our King still has one more move, and we will win.

sermons.title: Revelation 1:4-8
sermons.speaker: Sung Cho
sermons.text: Earlier this week, I took a virtual trip back about a century I read some letters from the First World War kept by the Imperial War Museums. According to their website, quote, during the First World War, letter writing was the main form of communication between soldiers and their loved ones. Helping to ease the pain of separation. The British Army Postal Service delivered around two billion letters during the war. In nineteen seventeen alone, over nineteen thousand mailbags crossed the English Channel each day. Transporting letters and parcels to British troops on the Western Front. Here are snippets of various letters. Patrick, a schoolboy, to his father, quote, Dear Daddy, I hope you are not alarmed. You should not be, unless you know where one of the Zeppes, Zeppelin airships, went. I have heard that it raided London up the strand and caused heavy casualties. But this I know because I saw and so did everyone else in the house. Sailor Teddy to his sister Gertie, quote, Give my best love to everyone at home. I often think about you all, I am yours ever. Emily to her fiance Private William, quote, Don't think, dear, I am worrying unnecessarily about you, because I know God can take care of you wherever you are. Just from these short quotes, we not only get a taste of early 20th century But we also understand better the longing hearts of those who loved each other and look forward to the end of war. As we continue into the introductory chapter of Revelation, the final book of the Bible We understand better the longing hearts of first century saints who love each other and look forward to the end of the age. And while we are presently wait still waiting, we can learn from their example. Let's see what occupied their minds and hearts. From chapter one, verses four to eight John to the seven churches which are in Asia. Grace to you and peace from him who is and who was. and who is to come, and from the seven spirits who are before his throne, and from Jesus Christ, the faithful witness The firstborn from the dead, and the ruler over the kings of the earth, to him who loved us and washed us from our sins in his own blood, And has made us kings and priests to his God and Father. To him be glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen. Behold, he is coming with clouds, and every eye will see him, even they who pierced him. And all the tribes of the earth will mourn because of him. Even so are men. I am the Alpha and the Omega, the beginning and the end. says the Lord, who is, and who was, and who is to come, the Almighty I believe there are three principles from these verses. One, know God as your source of grace and peace. Verse 4 to the first part of verse 5. 2. Praise God for saving us through Jesus. The second part of verse 5 to verse 6. 3. Wait for God who will send Jesus. Verses 7 and 8. I will spend most time on the foundational first point. In fact, more than half of the sermon will be on it. So we begin with this principle: know God as your source of grace and peace. In the first three verses we had a book title, a look into the channel of divine communication, and an invitation to receive blessings from reading, understanding, and keeping the prophetic contents of the book. As we go on with verses 4 and 5, note that this book has features similar to New Testament letters. That is. There's a standard introduction with the writer, the address C, and the greeting The writer is John, the son of Zebedee, the brother of James. John lived a long time, and at this point he was the last living member of the Twelve Apostles. He needs no elaborate introduction here, as most knew and recognized him as an apostle. He had widespread influence and authority among the churches, as we can see it in his Gospel and Letters. We'll discuss how he ended up at Patmos later, but before Patmos, we know from tradition that John settled at Ephesus. A port city located conveniently near the Aegean Sea. We know from Acts 17 to 19 that the church there started decades ago with strong initial missionary presence. Apostolic ministry, numerical and spiritual growth, and plurality of elders. It was a leading church in the Roman province of Asia. Other churches in the area include congregations at Troas, Colosse, and Heropolis. And we will learn about the six other churches near Ephesus in our future studies of Revelation 2-3, Lord willing. Now that we know a little bit about the writer and the addressees, let's talk about John's greeting. It starts out like the greetings of Paul's letters. During our study of the Thessalonian epistles, we discussed why Paul may have put grace and peace together in the opening words. According to Ben Wutherington, quote, Paul customizes the greeting. The standard Greek greeting was chirane, which just happens to be from the same root as the word caris, which we translate as grace. The standard Jewish greeting was, of course, shalom or peace. Paul combines the two standard greetings in order to properly greet both the Gentiles and the Jews in his audience. Witherington also suggests the possibility that Paul's audience was mostly Gentile, since he always puts grace before peace. Perhaps that's the case with John and his audience too. But whatever the demographics of the recipients, the source of grace and peace is clear. The triune God. After the phrase grace for you and peace, there are three instances of the same Greek preposition, a pol, accurately translated as from. Two in verse four and one at the beginning of verse five. These three instances of from introduce us to God the Father, God the Holy Spirit, and God the Son. Three distinct persons in one and the same divine essence, who dispenses grace and peace The Father is described as the one who is, and who was and who is to come. This title emphasizes his sovereignty, self-existence, and self-determination. It also brings to mind God's name of Yahweh in Exodus 6. Yahweh means He is thou He is. And when he says in the first person that I am that I am, he's saying he's not at the mercy of circumstances or environment like us. He is in absolute control of himself. That is, not only is he self-existent, but he is self-determinate. He will be what he will be, just as he was who he was, and he is who he is. So in Exodus, the Pharaoh and his forces could not overcome his people because of what Yahweh has determined for them. The same in Revelation, in a grander scale, Satan and his forces will not overcome his people because of what Yahweh has determined for them. Grace and peace from our Father in heaven. Next, the Holy Spirit is described as the source of grace and peace. But his title is somewhat strange. The seven spirits who are before his throne. How is one person of the Spirit described as seven? We need all the help we can get, so let's look at all the relevant passages in Revelation. There are three. Chapter 3, verse 1, chapter 4, verse 5, and chapter 5, verse 6. And all three instances add the description of God. In chapter 3, verse 1, the church at Sardis is introduced to Christ who has the seven spirits of God. In chapter 4, verse 5, just as we see here, the seven spirits are around the throne. but visualized as seven lambs. In chapter 5, verse 6, we are told that the Lamb of God who has been slain has seven eyes, which are the seven spirits of God sent out into all the earth. As you can see by the capitalization of spirits, the translators of New King James Version hold to the view that the seven spirits are collectively the Holy Spirit. The other view is that these seven spirits are celestial beings, powerful yet not divine. I think the first view is the better one. Here are some reasons. With the exception of two passages, chapter 11, verse 11, chapter 13, verse 5. All instances of the word spirit or pneuma in Revelation, that's 23 total, refer either to the divine spirit of God or demonic spirits. Angelic beings are distinctively described as angels. Angulas. Most importantly, there is a very very serious contextual problem with the angel view. In the immediate context, The notion that grace and peace could come from supernatural yet less than God beings, equal and at the same level as God the Father and God the Son, is heretical Such an idea contradicts the message of Revelation itself in chapter 19, verse 10 and chapter 22, verse 9. But we should still try to explain further how the Holy Spirit can be called seven spirits. Some, like John Wolford, turn to Isaiah 11. 2 to look for seven designations of the Spirit. But Robert Thomas suggests a better passage for consideration. Zechariah chapter 4 verse 1 to 10. There we have that famous word, not by might nor by power, but by my spirit in verse 6. And we are told that the seven lambs are the eyes of the Lord which scan to and fro throughout the whole earth. Verse 10 We compare these details with Revelation chapter 4 verse 5 and chapter 5 verse 6 and we have the following links. Seven spirits are seven lamps. Revelation 4. 5. Seven lambs are the seven eyes. Zechariah 4. 10. Seven eyes are the seven spirits of God. Revelation 5, 6 So with all these cross-references between Revelation and Zechariah, we are warrant to understand seven spirits of God as the singular Holy Spirit. Since God is everywhere, Psalm 139, we have reasons to understand seven symbolically. Seven is appropriate to describe God's perfect omniscience and omnipresence. Grace and peace from the Holy Spirit of God. Last but not least, we have God the Son as the source of grace and peace. It may feel out of place to have the second person of the Trinity come third, but perhaps John wrote in this manner to prepare for his elaboration in the second half of verse 5. The Divine Son has a human name, Jesus, whose very name signifies that he will save us from sins. He holds the title of Christ, which is the Greek translation of Messiah. The word means anointed one. In Jesus Christ, we have all three offices of prophet, priest, and king. These offices began with an inauguration ceremony where precious oil is poured over the head of the individual. Most often we think of the Messiah as king from the line of David, and we are encouraged to do the same here. Faithful Witness, Firstborn, and ruler over the kings of the earth, bring to mind Psalm 89, a psalm inspired by God's covenant with David in 2 Samuel 7. Listen to verses 35 to 37 and see how they help us understand Jesus' title of faithful witness. Once I have sworn by my holiness, I will not lie to David. His seed shall endure forever, and his throne as the sun before me. It shall be established forever like the moon, even like the faithful witness in the sky, Selah. Interestingly, Jesus is compared to the sun and the moon, signs of heaven that also serve as signs of God's fidelity to his promises. But while old covenant saints looked up to the moon in dark times for visible assurances of their salvation, we have something much better. We, as new covenant saints, can look to Jesus in dark times for assurance. He is a faithful witness. A living testimony of our living hope As for the titles of firstborn and ruler over the kings of the earth, they help explain each other. Firstborn is a special title for the heir who has the right to family inheritance. But depending on the context, it's not only or even necessarily about being chronologically prior. as in first in time or oldest in the family. It could be more about being first in place or exalted in the family. Many nations existed before Israel. Yet the Lord caused Israel firstborn. Exodus 4. 22 The same emphasis on the highest position is found in Psalm 89, verse 27. I will make him, my firstborn, the highest of the kings of the earth. So then the title of firstborn has to do with Jesus' destiny, to be the favored king above all other kings, like David, his forefather. But just as Jesus is a witness more faithful than the sun and the moon, he is king better than David. That's because Jesus is not just the firstborn, but he is the firstborn from the dead. Peter preached this truth in Acts 2, because David's tomb was occupied. While Jesus' tomb was empty. Paul makes the same argument. Jesus is the firstborn from the dead because he was the first to have a resurrected body. Believers are destined to inherit same bodies and become like Christ. So, he is the firstborn among many brethren. Grace and peace from Jesus, the Son of God For those who are considering their eternal destiny, let me tell you, grace and peace that comes from God the Father, God the Spirit, And God the Son can be yours through the gospel. The gospel is the good news. But first, the bad news. We have all sinned in thought, word, and actions against the Holy God. Heaven belongs to him, and he permits entrance according to his perfect standards. So who could enter then? No one. Apart from Jesus, our destiny is hell, the place of God's wrath. But here these words from Romans five one to two Therefore, having been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom also we have access by faith into this grace in which we stand. And rejoice in hope of the glory of God. Though we are guilty of sin, we can be declared just, justified by faith, apart from works. We can have peace with God through Jesus. We can have access into grace by faith We can stand in the day of judgment. We can rejoice in hope of the glory of God. There's nothing you can do to earn grace and peace. Jesus has done all the work, dying on the cross, taking on the entire wrath of God in our place. He rose from the dead and ascended to heaven, waiting for the day of his return. Until then, we are to live for the Lord Recognizing our triune God as the source of all grace and peace. That leads to the second point. Praise God for saving us through Jesus. If the first half of verse 5 emphasizes who Jesus is, the second half emphasizes what Jesus has done. And it starts with love. Recall the words of 1 John 4:10. In this is love, not that we loved God, but that he loved us and sent his son to be the propitiation for our sins. The cross was the ultimate public display of God's affections. Yet God's justice and God's love are not mutually exclusive. But they meet at the cross. I like the way David Platt puts it. Does God hate sinners? Absolutely. Look at the cross Jesus is enduring what we are due. Does God love sinners? Absolutely. Look at the cross. Jesus is saving us from all we are due. And because Jesus loves us, he cleansed us. Some Bible translations have released us, freed us, or set us free instead of washed us. In the original Greek, the difference between loose and wash is the difference of one letter, and they are homonyms. Even though both ideas are biblical, sin as enslaving and sin as contaminating, the majority of Greek texts have it correctly here as wash. The soiling power of sin is well documented. It has power to defile nations. Because of sin, we have ample evidence of the corruption of our flesh, manifest both in deeds and words. Sin provides proof of our inner evil, even while outwardly we may look polished and clean. There's nothing of our own that will cleanse us from our sin. But as we sang earlier, What can wash away my sin? Nothing but the blood of Jesus. What can make me whole again? Nothing but the blood of Jesus And now thanks to Jesus, we have experienced forgiveness and cleansing from all sins. Verse John 1. 9 says, if we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins. And to cleanse us from all unrighteousness We go on to Revelation 1. 6 and see that not only did Jesus love us and cleanse us, he clothed us in dignity. We read there that He has made us kings and priests to His God and Father. We get this double vestiture, royal and priestly. Because Jesus our Lord holds both offices forever. We can be kings because He is the King of Kings, King of Israel, and the ruler of all nations We can be priests because he is the great high priest. What great names are bestowed upon us? As kings and priests, we have authority and access to God, and we invite others to receive the same privilege. But glory and honor never rest with us as if we have done something special As his royal priesthood, we are to proclaim his praises and give thanks to him. So we can say with John the Apostle, to Him be glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen. All that we know about God thus far, and all that God has done for us up to this point are enough to occupy us for eternity of worship. But Paul reminds us as it is written, Eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor have entered into the heart of man the things which God has prepared for those who love him. John here anticipates the things which God has prepared for those who love him. He does this by reflecting on scriptures as he waits for Jesus' second coming. That leads to the third point. Wait for God who will send Jesus. Before John writes down what he saw regarding Jesus, he sees Jesus through what's already written down. Before John was in the Spirit, heard the word, and turned to see the Lord in Revelation 1. 12, he was inspired by the Spirit. Went to the Word and turned his pages to see the Lord. The first passage that came to his mind in Revelation 1. 7 is Daniel 7, 13 to 14. There we read this about the Messiah: Behold, one like the Son of Man coming with the clouds of heaven. He came to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him. Then to him was given dominion and glory and a kingdom, that all peoples, nations, and languages should serve him. His dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom the one which shall not be destroyed. This appearance of Jesus, the one like the Son of Man, will be good news for us who eagerly await his coming, but bad news to those who oppose him. As for the rest of verse 7, you may recall that John was at the crucifixion to witness Jesus being pierced with the spear. The soldiers did this to confirm his death. That wound, though, became an invitation for further study. A study of Zechariah 12, 10-12. That chapter describes the plight of Jerusalem in the end times and its dramatic and miraculous rescue. Just before the kingdom of Sharizen, there will be a national repentance and revival, as every eye will see him, even they who pierced him. But whereas Zechariah was focused on Israel, John here and Jesus in Matthew 24, 30, had a broader international perspective And all the tribes of the earth will mourn because of him. Even so, Amen. Even to the last possible minute, as Jesus descends from heaven, the Lord will grant one final chance for the entire world population to repent. What a merciful God! All these promises are guaranteed by the Alpha and the Omega. The Beginning and the End. These titles are based on the divine name of the first and the last from Isaiah 41, 44, and 48 The point is the same. God is the first to exist. So he is the first, like the first letter of the Greek alphabet, alpha. He is the beginning because he has no beginning. Even if all fails, God will outlast all others. So he is the last, like the last letter of the Greek alphabet, Omega. He is the end because he has no end. And using merism, we know that he is not only at the points of the beginning and the end, he is in everything between. Thus, you have no reason to doubt God's promises. Verse 8 is a quote from God, but is it the voice of the Father or the Son? The titles of Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end. and who was, who is, and who is to come, or a slight variety of it, can refer to both persons of the Trinity. What tips the scale to the option of God the Father is the title of Almighty. The one who sits on the throne, distinct from the Lamb, It's the Father who holds that title of Almighty throughout Revelation. But the main point is that we don't have to doubt the promises of Jesus' return because we know the divine character of the one speaking. Rather than doubt, why not enjoy his blessings in the present? We can patiently and faithfully wait for God who will send Jesus. We can experience grace and peace from our triune God. We can praise Jesus for his saving work. Let's pray. Lord, we know that in this broken world Grace, peace are in short supply. There's racism, there's rioting, there's unrest, there's injustice. But we thank you that true grace and peace comes from you, your son, and the Spirit. May we trust in you. May we look to you. May we praise you at this time. And we praise your son for saving us. And we eagerly await his coming. When the kingdom will be established. We pray all these things in Jesus Christ's name. Amen.

sermons.title: Revelation 1:9-11
sermons.speaker: Sung Cho
sermons.text: I once heard a definition by the preacher, Adrian Rogers, that stuck with me. He was talking about a fanatic. He said, quote, a fanatic is someone who loses direction and doubles his speed. Just to get the picture in your head, I'll repeat, quote, a fanatic is someone who loses direction and doubles his speed. When I'm driving and I get lost because my GPS acts up, I should slow down to get my bearings A fanatic, however, would say, nope, I'm going to go hundred miles per hour now. It's insanity. Now it's important to be passionate. Paul says that Christians, as God's own special people, must be zealous for good works. Titus 2. 14. We are to be fervent in our love for one another. 1 Peter 1. 22. But we are not fanatics rushing to nowhere. We have we must have a purpose. We work for something and someone We are dependent on him and his directions in his instruction manual, the Bible. As we consider all the strife and angst around us and maybe even in us, we don't want to be fanatics. We should seek a clear biblical direction and steadfastness in pursuing that path For help in that endeavor, we turn to the example of the apostles, the earliest followers of Jesus. Specifically, as we continue in the first chapter of Revelation. We turn to the example of John, the son of Zebedee. So let's go to Revelation 1, verses 9 to 11. I, John, both your brother and companion in the tribulation and kingdom and patience of Jesus Christ. was on the island that is called Patmos for the Word of God and for the testimony of Jesus Christ. I was in the Spirit on the Lord's day. And I heard behind me a loud voice, as of a trumpet, saying, I am the Alpha and the Omega. The first and the last end. What you see, right, in a book, and send it to the seven churches which are in Asia To Episus, to Smyrna, to Pergamos, to Diatera, to Sardis, to Philadelphia, and to Laodicea I believe from these three verses we have three principles to live by. One, know the purpose for which you suffer. 2. Hear the Lord who is sovereign. 3. Share the word which the saints need. You'll find those points at the back of your bulletin. Like last week, I'll spend most time on the first point. First, know the purpose for which you suffer As you read again verse 9, if you're like me, you might be fixated on the word tribulation. Poor John, you might say. He's old. He's the last remaining remaining member of the Twelve. He appears alone on an island Here's how Pat Moss is described in various sources. According to Robert Thomas, it is an island in the Icarian Sea, 40 miles west of Miletus, among a group of islands called the Dodacanis. It is shaped like a crescent with its horns facing eastward. It's a key stopping place for those sailing between Ephesus and Rome. According to BiblePlaces. com, it is about 7. 5 miles long from north to south and about 6 miles east to west. Joseph Siss describes a firsthand experience in nineteenth century, quote, Less than a year ago I passed that island. It is a mere mass of barren rocks, dark in color, and cheerless in form. It lies out in the open sea near the coast of Western Asia Minor It has neither trees, nor rivers, nor any land for cultivation, except some little nukes between the ledges of rocks There's still a dingy grotto remaining in which the eight apostle is said to have lived, and in which he is said to have had this vision. A chapel covers it, hung with lamps kept burning by the monks. Just from the looks of it, even to this day, Patmos was a fitting place for banishment. According to historians Pliny and Tacitus, the Romans often sent their prisoners to these kinds of islands. That background fits in the verse 9. John was most likely exiled to Patmos for the word of God and for the testimony of Jesus Christ. This phrase and the earlier mention of tribulation lead me to believe that the apostle wasn't on the island voluntarily as if on a mission trip. Though he was forcibly banished there during the reign of Emperor Domitian. Second century tradition says that after the ruler died, John was allowed to return to Ephesus. It would be easy for anyone in John's situation to despair. But if we look at verse 9 again, we would probably agree with Joseph Sice. Quote: John was at the time in exile upon a lonely and desolate island, but neither seas, nor alps, nor ages, can sever the bonds by which Christians are united to each other or to Christ their Lord. The inseparable bonds by which Christians are united to each other are indicated by the two titles John uses to introduce himself: your brother and companion. Though John's natural parents and adopted mother undoubtedly passed away by now, though his blood brother faced martyrdom many decades prior He had a family. He was connected not only to the congregation at Ephesus, but all those who profess Christ as Lord. He's a member of the household of God. He has siblings in God's family who do the will of the Father. There's a family bond with fellow believers. If brother brings to mind a warm, intimate home, the other title, companion, brings to mind hard work as a team. The word companion comes from fellowship, which is one of those church jargons that could use some explanation. The essence of fellowship isn't having a potluff meal while bantering about local sports or politics. It's a lot more serious. At a minimum, it's a word used in contractual partnerships, such as the fishing business that John and his brother James shared with Peter. But fellowship can go way beyond business Fellowship can be about common religious commitment, such as the one shared between pagan worshippers and demons at sacrificial altars. Fellowship is the deep covenantal bond between those who share the bread and cup of the Lord, those who are together forgiven and saved by Jesus. Fellowship is an unbreakable love triangle, established as Christ loved us first, and in response we love Him and we love one another. In Christian fellowship, we share our lives with Christ and share our lives with each other. Fellowship means sharing work, sharing resources. But even as all Christians share this deep bond, they're unable to have fellowship with false teachers and unbelievers. John goes on to name three specific commonalities shared in his fellowship with the churches: tribulation, kingdom, and patience of Jesus Christ. Taken individually, they're not difficult to understand. Tribulation here is more specific than human suffering, but more general than the great end-time tribulation just prior to Jesus' return. When he returns, we can say the kingdoms of this world have become the kingdoms of our Lord and of his Christ, and he shall reign forever and ever. Revelation 11:15 That's the kingdom. And until that day, we must exhibit patience in our present troubles. Seems simple enough But it is the connection between the three that's interesting. Tribulation, kingdom, and patience are tied together grammatically with a single article in what is called a hendiadist. Typically in a hendiadist, two words are combined with a conjunction and This is preferred over an adjective noun construction. So back at grammar school. An example would be Shakespeare's use of sound and fury Which has a different rhetorical effect than furious sound. Now John here takes three, not two words, and binds them together He and his brothers and sisters have a tribulation-resistant, kingdom-focused, Jesus Christ-motivated patience. It's like he's trying to say, Together we have a type of patience for the sake of Jesus' name that can endure tribulation as we wait for the kingdom. See how Hendiadus can be more efficient. Tribulation, kingdom, and patience come in a package when we trust in Jesus Such perseverance until the end is required by all the saints and only possible as God empowers us. This truth is confirmed elsewhere. Paul and Barnabas told young churches, as they were strengthening the souls of the disciples, exhorting them to continue in the faith. We must through many tribulations enter the kingdom of God. Acts 14, 22 Paul told the Philippians, to you it has been granted on behalf of Christ, not only to believe in him, but also to suffer for his sake. Philippians 129. Paul told Timothy, if we endure, we shall also reign with him. Second Timothy two twelve. Peter encouraged patience in view of Christ's coming glory. 1 Peter 4. 13 and 5. 1. And that future glory is absolutely worth the press suffering. If we minimize or ignore the suffering that comes to Jesus' disciples, we're not doing anyone favors. Not Christ, not the church, not the prospective Christian. We should let them know what they're signing up for, just as Jesus and his followers, like John did. Now I gave this illustration from Ray Comfort before, but I think it's worth repeating. Two men are seated in a plane. A stewardess gives the first man a parachute and instructs him to put it on as it will, quote, improve his flight. Not understanding how a parachute could possibly improve his flight, the first passenger is a little skeptical Finally, he decides to see if the claim is true. After strapping on the parachute, he notices its burdensome weight and he has difficulty sitting upright Consoling himself with the promise of a better flight, our first passenger decides to give it a little more time.
