Because he's the only one wearing a parachute, some of the other passengers begin smirking at him, which only adds to his humiliation. Unable to stand it any longer, our friend slumps in the seats, unstraps the parachute, and throws it to the floor. Disillusionment and bitterness fill his heart because, as far as he is concerned, he was told a lie. Another stewardess gives the second man a parachute, but listen to her instructions. She tells him to put it on because at any moment he will be making an emergency exit out of the plane at 25,000 feet. Our second passenger gratefully straps the parachute on. He doesn't notice its weight upon his shoulders or that he can't sit upright. His mind is consumed with the thought of what would happen to him if he jumped without it. When other passengers laugh at him, he thinks, you won't be laughing when you're falling to the ground. Let's now analyze the motive and the result of each passenger's experience. The first man's motive for putting on the parachute was solely to improve his flight. As a result, he was humiliated by the passengers, disillusioned by the unkept promise, and embittered against the stewardess who gave it to him. As far as he is concerned, he will never put on one of those things on his back again. The second man put on the parachute to escape the danger of the upcoming jump. Because he knew what would happen to him without it, he had deep-rooted joy and peace in his heart. Knowing he was saved from certain death gave him the ability to withstand the mockery of the other passengers. His attitude toward the stewardess who gave him the parachute was one of heartfelt gratitude. Now listen to what the contemporary gospel message, the false gospel. Put on the Lord Jesus Christ. He will only give you love, joy, peace, fulfillment right now, on demand. In other words, he will improve your flight. In an experimental fashion, the sinner puts on the savior to see if the claims are so. What does he get? Temptation, tribulation, and persecution. The other passengers mock his decision So what does he do? He takes off the Lord Jesus Christ. He is offended for the word's sake. He's disillusioned and embittered, and quite rightly so. He was only promised peace, joy, and fulfillment, and he got trials and humiliation. His bitterness is directed at those who gave him the quote good news. His latter end is worse than the first. Another inoculated, bitter backslider But if we let them know that being a Christian means enduring tribulation, as we patiently wait for the kingdom, we are giving the true biblical gospel. We can suffer together and encourage one another. But even as we comfort each other, we must have our ears open to the word. And that leads to the second point. Hear the Lord who is sovereign. We see in verse 10 that while John was on the island of Patmos, he was in the spirit. John Wolver defines the phrase in the spirit as follows: carried beyond normal sense into a state where God could reveal supernaturally the contents of this book. Benten Hort thinks it is a quote state in which the ordinary faculties of the flesh are suspended and the inward senses opened, end quote. We can't be sure exactly how it happened, but we can be sure the Holy Spirit empowered John's spirit to have this ecstatic visionary experience while still in Pat Moss. As for the timing of the experience, we are told it happened on the Lord's Day. Some commentators, like Ethelbert Bollinger, take this to mean the day of the Lord predicted by the Old Testament prophets. Another view is that it refers to the first day of the week, that is Sunday. In support of the view that John meant the prophesied end-time day of the Lord, The day of Christian worship is elsewhere called something else, first day of the week, in the Gospels, in Acts, and First Corinthians. But against this view, one, the day of the Lord is grammatically distinct from Lord's day. And two, at this point in the book, John has not, quote, entered into the virtual future. So the view that the Lord's Day refers to Sunday has slight edge over others. Possibly this was the first time Sunday was referred to as the Lord's Day, a practice followed by second century Christians nearby in Asia Minor. So exiled in Patmos in spirit-induced trance on a Sunday, John hears the voice of Jesus. He heard a great voice behind them like the way Ezekiel heard the voice of the Lord behind them in Ezekiel 3. 12 But while Ezekiel heard a sound like a great thunder or earthquake, John heard a sound resembling a trumpet. David Owen notes that throughout this book, loud sound or voice communicates importance or solemnity of the upcoming utterances. The resemblance to the trumpet also adds a note of authority. And what is spoken is this? I am the Alpha and the Omega, the first and the last. We've seen the title of the Alpha and the Omega before in verse 8, and I came to the conclusion that there it refers to the Almighty God the Father. But here it's definitely Jesus, the Son of Man, who takes the same title for himself. We can see that it's from verse 13 that this is Jesus. So while the title of the first and the last is reserved for Jesus in this book, chapter 1, 2, and 22, the title of the Alpha and the Omega is shared with the Father. As I said last week, alpha is the first letter of the Greek alphabet and omega the last letter These titles together communicate that Jesus is sovereign and in control. Jesus shares the divine essence of the Father, but is distinct in personality. He, the uncreated one, exists first, and he will outlast all. And he is on the side of John and his beleaguered companions. We may feel like an insignificant title or an iota in the annals of history. We may feel like no one cares about our church or our journey of faith. Well know that you are in the hands of Jesus, the Alpha and the Omega, the first and the last. He gives you eternal life. You shall never perish. Neither shall anyone snatch you out of his hand. All authority has been given to him in heaven and on earth. He is the originator and the completer of your faith What a privilege we have through our sovereign Lord. We need these reminders constantly. And that leads to the third principle: share the word. Which the saints need. John, though he was the disciple whom Jesus loved, did not only think of himself and his relationship with Jesus. His purpose as an apostle like Paul was to build up others. So here, his calling is to write down what he sees and hears, the first of twelve similar commands throughout the book. We get the impression that if he wasn't given such a command, he would have kept the contents of his vision to himself, as Paul did decades prior. In 2 Corinthians 12. The contents are written on a papyrus scroll, not in books like the ones we see or we think of today. Commentators note how the seven churches listed are located near the roughly circular route that clockwise begins at Ephesus and ends at Laodicea. But not all were equally populous or influential. And some well-known cities in the region, like Colossae or Herapolis, Troas, and Tralis, were left out. The distances between the cities range from thirty to forty miles. The messengers may have read the contents of Revelation at each stop produced a copy of the entire book, and then moved on to the next congregation. The practice of reading letters addressed to other churches was already established by Paul earlier in the century, Colossians 4. Now there is a lingering question of Y seven or Y D seven. I believe the seven churches are real historical churches in late first century. But respected names like Dwight Pentecost go beyond that And to see them also prophetically representing seven periods of church history. I find this approach to be overly subjective But I do think it is important for every church in every age to study what Jesus says to these congregations. As we already saw in Revelation 1. 3, there are blessings for all that read, understand, and keep these words. Lord willing, we'll get to chapters 2 and 3 and get to know each church better. For now, we can focus on these simple rudimentary truths. Our suffering has purpose. Our Lord is sovereign. We need his word These are truths for our well-being. But we can also share these truths to a hurting world. You don't have to look far these days to find hurting people. Just turn on the news. Open up a newspaper. Scroll through Twitter. I think about the anger felt by those discriminated, hurt, and even killed because of skin color. I think about the fear and disrespect experienced by dedicated policemen who have sworn to serve and protect. I think about the sorrow of those who lost loved ones on both sides of the struggle. As we reopen our church doors, we should invite such hurting ones to meet Jesus. For those who don't know, hear this good news. God created all of us in his image, and that's all of us, no matter what skin color we have. But we are all sinners too. Sinners in thought, word, and actions, whether it's hate, envy, greed, racism. We're all guilty of breaking God's laws, one way or another. We deserve God's wrath in hell But Jesus, the Son of God, became man like us. But he never sinned. He voluntarily laid down his life in our place. He gave his perfect life on the cross to pay the penalty for our sins as our substitute. He rose again from the dead on the third day and ascended to heaven. Before he returns, he offers you the gift of eternal life. It cannot be earned or deserved. Can only be received as a gift by grace alone, through faith alone, in Jesus Christ alone. Turn away from yourselves and turn to Him. We as Faith Bible Church are recipients of this grace. So now we tell those left unsatisfied by the empty promises of the world: join us. They will never find true, lasting justice out there. Movements may fail and activists might be forgotten, but the Church of Jesus will not succumb, not even to the gates of Hades. Though we love USA, we don't pretend that it's a perfect nation. But we can show those hurting a perfect kingdom. The kingdom of heaven, where citizens are redeemed by the blood of the Lamb, out of every tribe and tongue and people and nation. Even now we are elect from every nation, yet one over the earth, her charter of salvation, one Lord, one faith, one birth. Earthly rulers and authorities will disappoint and fail us, but we have a sovereign Lord in heaven, the Alpha and the Omega. The first and the last. We have visions of its glory to comfort us, even as visions of violence and routing distress us. Let's look to his word. Let's look to the Lord. Let's pray. Mid toil and tribulation and tumult of her war, she waste the consummation of peace forevermore. To with the visions of visions glorious, her longing eyes are blessed, and to the great church victorious shall be the church at rest. Lord, we come before you devoted, focused, knowing ourselves. In this grand vision, in this grand plan of your redemption history. Lord, we are your people. And we look to each other as brothers and companions in tribulation, kingdom, and patience of Jesus Christ. Lord, may our eyes be focused. May our eyes be turned to our Lord Jesus in heaven, who is in combo Lord, may we look to your word, the visions of your of the future kingdom. May those words comfort us. May we not lose direction May we not be fanatics in the wrong way. Will we seek to seek to uh honor you in our lives? Pray all these things in Jesus Christ's name. Amen.

sermons.text: Ed Stetzer, a popular Christian author once wrote, People have a remarkable ability to make Jesus in their own image. Arguably, the most well-known and the most beloved painting of Jesus, Head of Christ, by Werner Salman Depicts Jesus with blue eyes and long hair, a white man, even though the Bible is clearly against such depiction. I mean the very first chapter of the New Testament is there to debunk such myths. For some, the doctrine of incarnation and messianic prophecies are not enough. Some want the Son of God to be near us in more ways than that. That's their belief. Many want him to be an American, a Republican, maybe even a Tim Teble fan. He warns, quote, this is unhealthy. We are to be conformed to his image, not conforming him to ours. We are to be conformed to his image, not conforming him to ours. How true that is. It's a lesson for us if we are to grow individually and corporately as Faith Bible Church It's a lesson we gain from our study of Revelation chapter 1. Commentator Robert Thomas notes, quote, The titles of Jesus Christ found in the introductions to six of the seven messages in chapters two and three are drawn largely from this vision of chapter 1, 12 to 20. And its descriptive phrases. Only the message to Laodicea, chapter 3, 14 to 22, is devoid of one of these. It is apparent that the appearance of Christ in this vision is designed to emphasize the aspects of his nature. That are most relevant to the needs and circumstances of the seven churches who are the primary recipients of this book. End quote. Going further, we look to Christ and we search for relevance to the needs and circumstances of our church as the secondary recipients of this book. If we are to conform to Christ, we must see Him as He presents Himself in the Word. So what does this vision of Christ teach us about himself so that we may worship him and be like him? How can we see Jesus as the Holy Spirit guides us, not according to the flesh For that endeavor, let's turn to chapter one, verse twelve to sixteen of Revelation. Revelation one, verse twelve to sixteen Then I turned to see the voice that spoke with me, and having turned, I saw seven golden lampstands. And in the midst of the seven lamb stands, one like the Son of Man, clothed with a garment down to the feet, and girded about the chest with the golden band. His head and hair were like were white like wool, as white as snow, and his eyes like a flame of fire. His feet were like fine brass, as if refined in a furnace, and his voice as the sound of many waters. He had in his right hand seven stars. Out of his mouth went a sharp two-edged sword, and his countenance was like the sun shining in its strength This first century vision teaches us four lessons directly relevant to twenty-first century churches like ours. 1. Jesus cares for churches with authority. 2. Jesus has sagely wisdom and sees all. Three, Jesus exemplifies purity and speaks with power. And four, Jesus controls and judges in heavenly glory First, Jesus cares for churches with authority. John turned around to locate the source of the voice that spoke the words of verse eleven. But first, he sees the seven golden lamp stamps. Now we don't have to look far to figure out what these represent. We learn in the last verse of chapter 1, verse 20. The seven lampstands which you saw are the seven churches. Now, this imagery has its roots back in the Old Testament. Moses relayed the instructions to build a lamb stand with seven lambs, which is known as the menorah. Zachariah saw something similar in his fifth night vision But this is a single lampstand, whereas John saw seven separate lampstands. What is the significance of these lamps? In every dispensation, God's people are to shine their lights in the world. For example, the Israelites were told in Isaiah 58, verses 1-12, that their practice of praying and fasting must be accompanied by good works that promote justice and mercy. That way their light shall break forth like the morning and dawn in the darkness. Now to the New Testament. Jesus told his followers, You are the light of the world. A city that is set on a hill cannot be hidden. Nor do they light a lamp and put it under a basket, but on a lampstand, and it gives light to all who are in the house. Let your light so shine before men that they may see your good works and glorify your Father in heaven. And we must always remember the true source of our light. Adam Clark writes, quote, A lamp is not light in itself, it is only the instrument of dispensing light. And it must receive both oil and fire before it can dispense any. So no church has in itself either grace or glory. It must receive all from Christ its head, else it can dispense neither light nor life. So that's why we see in verse thirteen, in the midst of the seven lamb stands, one like the Son of Man. The one like the Son of Man recalls the vision of Daniel. This being is none other than the Messiah. The one who, in the vision, was given dominion and glory and kingdom. That all peoples, nations, and languages shall serve him. His dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away And his kingdom, the one which shall not be destroyed. That's in Daniel seven, thirteen to fourteen. Jesus, because he is the Son of God from the beginning, he is the Son of Man who will judge in the end. The second half of verse 13 describes the attire of Jesus, his robe and his girdle. His garment went down to the feet, which could refer to the garb of the high priest. The band around his waist, just below the armpits, also matches the priestly description. But such articles of clothing were also worn by dignitaries, royalty, and princes. Now, as splendid and dazzling as the high priest or an Oriental king may be, we must remind ourselves that we are dealing with authority and majesty. That surpasses even theirs. We go beyond the realms of earth to take a look at celestial beings. We find that Jesus resembles angels and even surpasses them. The connection to Daniel 10, 5 is striking. There the prophet encounters an angelic being clothed in linen whose waist was girded with the gold of Upas. We find similar clothes on Angels of Judgment in Revelation 15, 6. But even more striking and interesting is Ezekiel's vision in chapter 9. This figure in Ezekiel has an ink horn, and he is tasked to put a mark on the foreheads of the men who sigh and cry over all the abominations in Jerusalem. Interestingly, later in the book of Revelation, God's servants will also receive a mark on their foreheads to be spared from judgment. So all these connections and cross-references point to this basic truth. Jesus has heavenly authority. So, putting together his position among the lampstands and his attire, we can say Jesus cares about us, and he does so with authority. He is like us, yet so different from us. That's what makes him perfect in caring for us. He is the head far above and above and over the universal church. Yet the Son of Man moves close to us in the midst of local churches. This Son of Man, born on earth, is rolled and girded in the dignity of heaven But it's not just about where Christ is from, it's also about how long he's been around. And that leads to the next point: Jesus has says leave wisdom and sees all. Moving up from the rope to the sash to Jesus' head, John describes the following: His head and hair were white like wool, as white as snow. This description is very similar to the one in Daniel 7. 9, where God the Father is described. But as Henry Sweet observes, it is not unusual for the names of God the Father and the praises due to him to be shared with God the Son. Thus here we are reminded that Jesus, the Son of Man, always existed as the Son of God. The Nicene Creed, formulated in 325 A. D. , captures this truth that our Lord Jesus Christ is, quote, begotten from the Father before all ages. God from God, light from light, true God from true God, begotten, not made, of the same essence as the Father. Through him all things were made. Jesus, though he has a birthday and we can count his definite days on earth, he is the ancient of days. Next, John meets the penetrating gaze of Jesus with eyes like a flame of fire. Now, if angelic beings have fiery eyes, how much more Jesus? In the Gospels, Jesus' eyes were keen to detect callous hearts, true belief. Insincere faith, corruption of the temple ministry, and denials of Peter. That same gaze will be upon all mankind in the end. As the Father has committed all judgment to the Son. The fire in his eyes corresponds to the fire reserved for the day of the Lord. Jesus searches the hearts of the saved and the unsaved, those in the past, present, and future. No one can escape his notice. Are you ready to look upon those eyes? If not, we are here. To give you a message. Before you meet Jesus as your judge after death or at his return, please meet him as your savior now. It is appointed for men to die once, but after this, the judgment. There is no second chance in purgatory or reincarnation. That's why the life you live now is so precious and the choices you make so consequential You must not wait a moment longer to hear the good news and respond in repentance and faith. Here's the good news. The same Jesus, with eyes like a flame of fire, looked at the lost multitude and felt compassion for them. He looked with the same compassion at hurting individuals, those whose lives have been ravaged by death. Those eyes have shed tears for sinners in the course of his mission to rescue them from hell. To complete that mission, Jesus went to the cross. Though he has never committed a sin in thought, word, or act, he died for us who have broken his commands. He took our place on the cross to pay the penalty for our sins as substitute. On the third day he rose again from the dead, defeating death by death, and ascended to heaven. Jesus washed us from our sins in his own blood, became the firstborn from the dead, and someday as he returns to earth, every eye will see him, even they who pierced him. Now the question remains for you. Will you look at the eyes of compassion now, or look at his eyes of fiery judgment when it's too late? The time to repent and believe is now. Turn away from yourself as the source of joy and righteousness. Confess that you do not and you cannot live up to the demands of God's word in your own strength. Trust in Jesus Christ alone for eternal life and receive it as a gift. Once we make this individual decision, we join God's family corporately, but we're not teleported to heaven upon conversion We have work to do here on earth. Facing the uncertain world with certainty of salvation We will need to take off our cross and follow Christ in his teaching and example. That leads to the third lesson. Jesus exemplifies purity and speaks with power. Back in verse thirteen, we saw that Jesus was in the midst of the lampstands. Here in verse 15, we focus on his feet, which by themselves suggest movement. In this context, we are speaking of his movement among the lampstands, the seven churches of Asia. Jesus is not just standing there watching while local churches wane and their wicks fade away. He moves towards them and gives them a vision of himself. As for the feast's appearance like fine grass, as if refined in furnace, there is this idea of purity It is a type of purity unknown in this world, purity of heavenly origins. Through the process of refiners, fire, drosts, and impurities are removed, and a glowing metal results But this kind of purity is about moral character. It is the pure character of Jesus which we strive to follow. In the second half of verse 15, we return to the quality of Jesus' voice. Back in verse 10, we heard John heard what sounded like a trumpet. That same voice now resembles the sound of many waters. If the trumpet suggests authority, the sound of waves suggests immense power. The voice of Jesus by himself surpasses the force of multitudes, singing in unison. It is the same voice prophesied by Ezekiel as he saw God's glory returning to the Jerusalem temple in the end times. Taken together, the sight of Jesus' feet and the sound of his voice reinforce the idea that Jesus is teaching us by example and words what sort of church we should be. Consider the message Jesus has for the church at Diatera in chapter 2, verses 18 to 29. He is introduced again as one with fine with feet like fine brass. Jesus begins by recognizing their works, love, service, faith, and patience, but they have compromised their purity. They have tolerated sexual immorality and idolatry to the point they have spread into the congregation. Now there were those who were caught in the depths of Satan. Not only did they need to hear Jesus' voice, they needed a vision of his purity. By the way, Kerry will lead us in an in-depth study of this church and other churches later on Wednesday night. For now, let's return to chapter 1, verse 16 for our final lesson. Jesus controls and judges in heavenly glory. John sees in the right hand of Jesus seven stars. We will see this again as Jesus addresses believers in Ephesus and Sardis. His hand may communicate protection, like the good shepherd carrying his sheep, or control as the king over his regent or messengers. I think control is the better interpretive option as sovereignty and authority of Jesus are stressed throughout this book. The seven stars require more interpretive work. We begin by looking down to verse 20, and we see that the seven stars are the seven messengers. Or in NKJV, it should say seven angels. But the Greek word angelos could refer to angelic or human messengers. So we'll have to do a further study of verse 20 to better understand verse 16. And there are four interpretive options for the stars. They're one, guardian angels over the churches. 2. Personified spirits of the churches. 3. Chief Overseers of the Churches. Four representatives but not unique sole leaders of the churches. So I'll try to repeat those as I go again Henry Alford is a key proponent of the guardian angel view. His assertion is this, if people groups or neophytes can have guardian angels, why not churches? And angels are represented as stars elsewhere in the Bible. There are some problems with this view, though. If we take the channel and sequence of divine communication back in chapter 1, verse 1 to 3 seriously, here's what we would have with this view of verse 20. God the Father sent his revelation to Jesus. Jesus commissioned this heavenly angel. The angel sent the message down to John on Patmos John sent it back up to guardian angels. The guardian angels then sent it back down to Jesus' servants in the seven churches. What a circuitous route of revelation. Angel, John, Guardian Angels, Churches. Seems a bit strange. Another problem is that these messengers appear to be part of the congregation. So they too are part of the second person plural of commands to turn away from sins Now how could such rebukes apply to holy angels? The second view adhered by Isman Beckwit is that the stars are personified spirits of churches. It's a little abstract. Personified spirits of the churches. This interpretation does better to connect the representative messengers to the respective congregations. But the required abstract double symbolism here complicates matters. We should expect Jesus' explanations of symbols To lead to literal meaning, not yet another symbol. But in this case, stars represent messengers that again mean something else A star is a symbol for an angel who is a symbol for the church. As William Lee points out, then the stars are essentially identical to the lampstands. In the third view, we have messengers in flesh and blood, stars that occupy heavens, symbolize highest positions in hierarchy These starry leaders could be wise and turn many to righteousness, or corrupt and lead many astray. But this idea of a singular supreme ruler over a church or local church contradicts the biblical concept of plurality of elders. The fourth view is that the messengers serve as church representatives or delegates among multiple leaders, but they are not the only leaders in their congregations. Epaphroditus and Epaphras, leaders sent to represent the churches of Philippi and Colossae, respectively, are prime examples of such delegates. In Paul's times, there was a policy of churches selecting and sending representatives to help the apostles. We see that in 2 Corinthians 8. It appears John also benefited from such messengers. I think this view is the best, as it is the least problematic. Ultimately, these messengers would serve the Lord as his mouthpieces. The message itself would come from the Lord When Jesus opens his mouth to speak, there is certainly life and salvation. But there is also death and destruction. We see in the middle clause of verse 16, out of his mouth went a sharp two-edged sword. This visualization of Messiah's judgment has been predicted in Isaiah, previewed here by John, and ultimately fulfilled in Jesus' return. Just as Jesus' fiery eyes penetrate through our facade, his mouth speaks the word of God, which is living and powerful, and sharper than any two-edged sword. Piercing even to the division of soul and spirit, and of joints and marrow, and is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart None will escape his judgment in the end. But there's also a present application for us. Of course, we are to be like Jesus in that, as Paul tells us, we are to yield the sword of the Spirit, which is the Word of God, in our external spiritual warfare. But we must also look inwardly to ourselves. We must surrender ourselves to the introspective power of the word. Just as Mary suffered as the mother of Christ, we should expect God's word to cut us inwardly as followers of Christ. Here's an example for us as a local congregation. At the church in Pergamos for those who hold to false doctrines. Those who were faithful to Jesus had to practice church discipline and urge the disobedient to repent. If they don't, Jesus would come to fight against them with the sword of his mouth. Jesus has the right to judge sinners and judge churches in this manner because he is the Son of God. The third and final clause of verse 16 says, and his countenance was like the sun shining in his strength. If the righteous who love the Lord shine like the sun, and if a mighty angel, if mighty angel's face clothes like the sun, how much brighter is Jesus God's beloved Son, in whom he is well pleased. We ought to hear him, as the Father commanded. Jesus controls and judges in heavenly glory. I believe we will hear Jesus better if we can see him better. And both seeing and listening are experienced through our study and meditation of the Bible. How will seeing Jesus as he is transform you? Please listen to these words of this 19th-century hymn by Anna Bartlett Warner. We would see Jesus where the shadows lengthen across this little landscape of our life We will see Jesus, our weak faith to strengthen for the last weariness, the final strife We will see Jesus, the great rock foundation, whereon our feet were set by sovereign grace. Nor life nor death, with all their agitation, can thence remove us if we see his lace. We would see Jesus. Senses all too blinding, and heaven appears too dim, too far away. We would see thee to gain a sweet reminding that thou hast promised our great debt to pay. We would see Jesus. This is all we're needing. Strength, joy, and willingness come with the sight. We would see Jesus dying, risen, pleading, then welcome day and farewell, mortal night. Let's pray. Lord, we pray that every time we open up your word. In our personal devotions, as we listen to a sermon or a 10-day Bible study, where we come with an expectation May we come with a heart of hope that you have something for us that will transform us. That if we get a glimpse of who you are, That our lives will be changed. We can become we can grow cynical, we can feel like we will never change. Or we may even feel like there's nothing to change in us. We repent of such an attitude. Lord, may we be transformed and amazed as we stand in the presence of your Son. Though we will do this We cannot do this truly at this point until your son returns. But we pray that we would look to your word And we'll look with hope of our future glorification as we see the glorified Jesus Christ risen and ascended to heaven. And it is in his name we pray. Amen.

sermons.text: Martin Luther King, Junior, Marco Polo, Nelson Mandela, John Bunyan, Miguel de Cervantes Boethius, Dante Alighieri, Paul of Tarsus, John the Apostle All of these produced memorable works of literature while imprisoned, held in bondage against their will. Is it their willpower, courage, or strength of character that led to their indelible marks in history? Is it their innate genius, rich well of experience, or some eureka moment? Paul and John would no doubt tell you that their position is one of privilege and grace. They weren't apostles because of birthright or inheritance. They were chosen by Jesus, the Messiah. And much of their writings were composed in confinement or forced isolation. But God would not be limited by their limitations. He would work in spite of them. When conditions looked bleak, while all things looked dead and barren around them, Jesus gave them something worth writing about. Let's learn how John got such an opportunity. Let's turn to Revelation one, seventeen to twenty And when I saw him, I fell at his feet as dead. But he laid his right hand on me, saying to me, Do not be afraid. I am the first and the last. Verse 19 is the Lord's confirmation of Samuel as his prophet. Not only was the Lord with him, he made sure that his words never fall to the ground. That means the predictions he made always came to pass. That was a sure sign of the true prophet who speaks in the name of the Lord in Deuteronomy eighteen and first Samuel nine. Like other prophets, Samuel could not help but speak God's truth to the people. As a result, the Israelites all throughout the land knew that Samuel was really God's spokesperson, a prophet of the Lord. People everywhere in Israel recognized Samuel The chapter ends with another appearance of God in Shiloh, but see how again the point of emphasis is on the word of the Lord, which is heard, more than the visionary experience, which is seen. The word is what's lasting and most relevant for the saints of Samuel's day and saints of today. And through God's selection and calling of Samuel, Shiloh and Israel as a whole transform. No longer can it be said that the word of the Lord was rare in those days. There was no widespread revelation. Now the word became abundant, and widespread was the news that Samuel was God's choice prophet. For the Lord revealed himself to Samuel in Shiloh by the word of the Lord. Such encounters through the Word will be the means of Samuel's growth. And so the prophet learned to speak for God without fear. Over 3,000 years later, the basic principle remains the same. If we are to speak for God, we must learn what God has spoken. To speak God's word, we must listen to God's word. To overcome fear of men, we must fear God above men. Learn to listen to Him. Listen to learn about Him. Learn to speak for Him. Throughout the church history, simple truths like these have advanced the gospel. Of course, God can directly speak for himself or send one of his angels. But we like Samuel are called by God so that through us he might call many to salvation. Not just me, all of us. Her the Great Commission. The principle of Romans 10, 14-15 continues today. How then shall they call on him? In whom they have not believed? And how shall they believe in him of whom they have not heard? And how shall they hear without a preacher? And how shall they preach unless they are sent? As it is written, how beautiful are the feet of those who preach the gospel of peace, who bring glad tidings of good things. These verses are not just for missionaries and pastors. It's for all of us. Whether you are old like John in Revelation or young like Samuel in this chapter. God wants to speak to you so that you may speak to others about God. As we sing our last song, let's remember why you have that Bible. That the light of Christ might be seen today in our acts of love and our deeds of faith. Speak, O Lord, and fulfill in us all your purposes for your glory. Let's pray. Lord, we come just as we are Lord, in need. Lord, we want to simplify our faith in some ways. Yes, we want to grow in our knowledge of your word and to know it from cover to cover. But Lord, we want to hear you. We come like a child. We come like Mary. No, we want to imitate your son, who took time, to really pray and get away from the crowds, get away from the busyness of life. Lord, even as a pastor, Lord, I find it a struggle to get away from everything, to just hear your voice. I'm sure that all of us struggle in some ways, even in our retirement, or even when we're have low in our schedules We pray that you would help us to listen, to learn, to speak for you And even our devotions, we pray that it will not be just about us. It's what we can get out of your word and what we can learn. But Lord, we want to benefit others. Lord, send us Eliz in our path. Send us people in our path who need to hear your word. Christians, non-Christians. Ailing Christians, Christians who are doing well. May you send Samuels into our lives that may speak to us your word. We pray that you were you would be glorified and your word would spread. Pray all these things in Jesus Christ's name. Amen.

sermons.text: Well it seems much of our spiritual warfare consists of resisting the allures of the world. One temptation among many poor pastors is what's called the church growth movement. It started with good intentions to instill a missionary mindset in local churches to better reach the lost. But the respected author Ed Stetzer outlines major problems with the movement as it stands now. I just want to focus on one today. There is what Stetzer calls the Americanization of the movement. In short, their leaders turned into corporate sales consultants. and their message became a sales pitch. They envisioned churches as American businesses, and their principles were reduced to one, two, three steps. Easy one, two, three. Richard Helverson, in his book, The Church Between Gospel and Culture, wrote, quote, When the Greeks got the gospel, they turned it into a philosophy. When the Romans got it, they turned it into a government. When the Europeans got it, they turned it into a culture. When the Americans got it, they turned it into an enterprise. End quote. And how tragic is that? Sometimes pastors leading the way. Turning a holy ministry into a corporate business. I hope many American pastors can speak in good conscience with Paul in 2 Corinthians 2. 17. We are not as so many peddling the Word of God, but as of sincerity, but as from God. We speak in the sight of God in Christ. But it's a temptation. Getting results. Filling the seats. Keeping up with the Joneses, that is, other chap other churches rapidly growing. Pray that we as a church resist worldly principles and stay in his word. I believe today's passage in 1 Samuel 4 will empower us for that endeavor. Let's turn there now. First Samuel four And the word of Samuel came to all Israel. Now Israel went out to battle against the Philistines and encamped beside Ebenezer, and the Philistines encamped in Abek. Then the Philistines put themselves in battle array against Israel, and when they joined battle, Israel was defeated by the Philistines, who killed about 4,000 men of the army in the field. And when the people had come into the camp, the elders of Israel said, Why has the Lord defeated us today before the Philistines? Let us bring the Ark of the Covenant of the Lord from Shiloh to us, that when it comes among us, it may save us from the hand of our enemies. So the people sent to Shiloh that they might bring from there the ark of the covenant of the Lord of hosts, who dwells between the cherubim. And the two sons of Eli, Hophni and Phineas, were there with the Ark of the Covenant of God. And when the Ark of the Covenant of the Lord came into the camp, all Israel shouted so loudly that the earth shook. Now, when the Philistines heard the noise of the shout, they said, What does the sound of this great shout in the camp of the Hebrews mean? Then they understood that the Ark of the Lord had come into the camp. So the Philistines were afraid, for they said, God has come into the camp, and they said, Woe to us, for such a thing has never happened before. Woe to us, who will deliver us from the hand of these mighty gods? These are the gods who struck the Egyptians with all the plagues in the wilderness. Be strong and conduct yourselves like men, you Philistines, that you do not become servants of the Hebrews as they have been to you. Conduct yourselves like men and fight. So the Philistines fought, and Israel was defeated, and every man fled to his tent. There was a very great slaughter, and there fell of Israel thirty thousand foot soldiers. Also the Ark of God was captured, and the two sons of Eli, Hopti and Phonaias, died. Then a man of Benjamin ran from the battle line the same day and came to Shiloh with his clothes torn and dirt on his head. Now when he came, there was Eli sitting on a seat by the wayside watching, for his heart trembled for the ark of God. And when the man came into the city and told it, all the city cried out. When Eli heard the noise of the outcry, he said, What does the sound of this tumult mean? And the man came quickly and told Eli. Eli was 98 years old, and his eyes were so dim that he could not see. Then the man said to Eli, I am he who came from the battle, and I fled today from the battle line. And he said, What happened, my son? So the messengers the messenger answered and said, Israel has fled before the Philistines, and there has been a great slaughter among the people. Also your two sons, Hophni and Phineas, are dead, and the Ark of God has been captured Then it happened when he made mention of the ark of God that Eli fell off the seat backward by the side of the gate, and his neck was broken, and he died, for the man was old and heavy. And he had judged Israel forty years. Now his daughter-in-law, Phineas' wife, was with child due to be delivered. And when she heard the news that the ark of God was captured, and that her father-in-law and her husband were dead, she bowed herself and gave birth, for her labor pains came upon her. And about the time of her death, the woman who stood by her said to her, Do not fear, for you have borne a son. But she did not answer, nor did she regard it. Then she named the child Ichabod, saying, The glory has departed from Israel Because the Ark of God has been captured, and because of her father-in-law and her husband. And she said, The glory has departed from Israel, for the Ark of God has been captured. I believe there are three lessons for us individually and corporately One spiritual defeat occurs without faith in God. Verses one to eleven 2. Spiritual demotion happens without godly leadership, verses 12 to 18. And three, spiritual despair results without proper perspective on God, verses 19 to 22. First, spiritual defeat occurs without faith in God. The first sentence in verse 1 is a transitional hinge statement that connects chapters 3 and 4. We are reminded of how Samuel grew and heard God's call to be a prophet. Through the young man, God's word was widely known. The word of Samuel in his capacity as prophet is essentially the word of God. That was obvious and plain to everyone That's why what happens next is perplexing. Why didn't the leaders consult with the young prophet? Isn't it a good idea to seek the Lord before a major battle? It could be that the elders of Israel relied on their experience instead of God. Perhaps they were too prideful to take advice from Samuel. But the mouthpiece of God was right there in Shiloh. They really could have used some health. Understandably, without eyes of faith, Philistines would look undefeatable. Here's a little background on them from commentator Eugene Merrill, quote: The Philistines, Israel's principal enemy during the period of the Last of the Judges, were a non-Semitic people. whose origins were most likely in Crete or in some other part of the Aegean Sea area. They came to Canaan in two different migrations, one as early as Abraham's time, and the other about 1200 BC. They lived in five main towns on the southern Canaan coast: Gaza, Ashkelon, Ekron, Gath, and Ashtod. They were technologically advanced, pioneering in the use of iron and in other skills. With such power and knowledge, the Philistines were a force to be reckoned with, formidable clothes, superior to the Israelites in the worldly sense. Philistines camped in Afek, a site about 25 miles west of Shiloh, and Israelites two miles west of Afek in Ebenezer. As they clashed, verse 2 records Israel's humiliating defeat. In verse 3, we read that the elders are shocked by the results. They blame God instead of taking responsibility. Instead of humbly seeking His will, they come up with a solution that is wrong on so many levels They say, let us bring the Ark of the Covenant of the Lord from Shiloh to us, that when it comes among us it may save us from the hand of our enemies. What motivated this idea? Perhaps multiple strands of ill-conceived thoughts weave together here. There's a bit of pragmatism, reliance on what worked on the past, more than reliance on God Himself When Joshua and the Israelites fought against Jericho, they took the ark and marched around the city for a week, and on the final day its walls fell down with much fanfare and shouting. But it wasn't the ark, the priests, the trumpets, the method. The writer of Hebrews reminds us: by faith, the walls of Jericho fell down after they were encircled for seven days. Instead of trusting in what worked before, they should have trusted God Himself. There's also superstition. Instead of faith in the holy God, the people had faith in holy things. They thought it, the ark, would save them from their enemies. They should have recognized God as Savior. Charles Spurgeon suggests, quote, instead of attempting to get right with God, these Israelites set about devising superstitious means of securing the victory over their foes. In this respect, most of us have imitated them. We think of a thousand inventions, but we neglect the one thing needful. They forget the main matter, which is to enthrone God into life. to seek to do his will by faith in Christ Jesus. End quote It is truly sad that they forgot the main matter, to enthrone God in life, especially since the ark was a visible reminder of divine majesty. David Samura points us to various passages that describes it as God's footstool, 1 Chronicles 28, Psalm 99, 132, Lamentation 2. The full picture is that of God sitting above the highest heavens with angels at his feet. The angels at his feet include cherubim. Their worship of God is visualized on the golden slab or the lid of the ark, what is called the mercy seat We can take in that scene with the help of that hymn we just sang at the beginning of the service, Let all mortal flesh keep silence. At his feet the six-winged seraph, cherubim with sleepless eye, veil their faces to their to the presence. As with ceaseless voice they cry, Alleluia, Alleluia, Alleluia, Lord Most High. These were wonderful truths taught through the Ark and the Holy Articles. God designated them to lead us to awe and reverence. But instead of reflecting on such matters, we see in verses 4 and 5 that they quickly turned to a plan to bring the ark to their camp. The fact that Eli's sons were there suggests that Eli agreed to do. This foolishness. On top of pragmatism and superstitions, they seem to be attempting manipulation Trying to get God to come out of the tent like a genie out of a bottle. Commentator Henry Ellison thinks, quote, their idea was that God should be forced to fight for them. If he was not willing to do it for their sake, he would have to do it for his honor's sake. End quote We turn aside to the enemy camp in verses 6 to 9. Initially, the Philistines were surprised and scared by this new tactic of Israel. They, like many nations at that time, believed deities could directly fight wars. They knew about the Egyptians who enslaved Israel, how God struck them with plagues, but they seemed imprecise with their facts. Israelites were not polytheists. The plagues against the Egyptians didn't happen in the wilderness, but in their homeland. At any rate, the Philistines rally and muster up the courage to fight, afraid of becoming slaves to Israel, as they have been to them. They win again and we see the disastrous results of verse in verses 10 and 11. Before they brought the ark to the camp, they lost about 4,000 men. After they tried their godless strategy, 30,000 foot soldiers fallen, the Ark of God captured, and the two sons of Eli slain. We'll take in all of this in a moment, but let's stop to reflect here. Pastor Kenneth Chatfin offers a good insight. Quote, We eventually all learn what Israel discovered in battle against the Philistines. Having the paraphernalia of God and having God are not the same. Thomas Constable goes further, quote, The paraphernalia that modern believers sometimes rely on in place of God include a crucifix, a picture of Jesus, or a family Bible positioned conspicuously in the home, but seldom read. These things, as good as they may be, are no substitute for a vital personal relationship with God. It's sobering to realize that one can adorn walls with posters and plaques of Bible verses and be completely devoid of godliness It's scary to think that one can be superstitiously arrayed in religious clothing. Retreat t-shirts, Christian school uniforms, purity rings, what would Jesus do bracelets? Yet not clothed in Christ. We may not be so different from Pharisees of Jesus' day. Who ostentatiously made their blackteries fraud and enlarged the borders of their garments God will not be charmed or summoned at your bidding. Eli, Hophni, Phineas, and the elders of the people should have known better. Their failure teaches us the second lesson. Spiritual demotion happens without godly leadership. From verses twelve to eighteen, we see the news of the defeat reaching Shiloh. An unnamed messenger from the tribe of Benjamin runs there, literally disarrayed dirt on his head, a look a proposed to the horrific tragedy on the battlefield. Eli was worried most for the ark and on the lookout at a gate for any update. But because he was old and blind, he did not first notice the messenger entering the city. Once the citizens' outcry reached his ears, he learned what happened. The flight, the slaughter, the death of his sons. What pushed them over the edge, literally, was the capture of the ark. It was more than the old man could take. His weight and brittle bones caused his death as his neck broke. That's the ignoble end to Eli's 40-year rule as judge. Eli's influence had to end because his leadership was ungodly. All that the man of God said to him in chapter 2 confirmed through Samuel in chapter 3 came true. I'll reread chapter 2, verses 27 to 34, if you want to flip back. This is what the man of God said to Um Eli. Thus says the Lord, did I not clearly reveal myself to the house of your father when they were in Egypt in Pharaoh's house? Did I not choose him out of all the tribes of Israel to be my priest, to offer upon my altar, to burn incense, and to wear an ephod before me? And did I not give to the house of your father all the offerings of the children of Israel made by fire? Why do you kick at my sacrifice and my offering which I have commanded in my dwelling place? And honor your sons more than me to make yourselves fat with the best of all the offerings of Israel, my people. Therefore the Lord God of Israel says, I said indeed that your house and the house of your father would walk before me forever. But now the Lord says, Far be it from me, for those who honor me I will honor, and those who despise me shall be lightly esteemed. Behold, the days are coming that I will cut off your arm and the arm of your father's house, so that there will not be an old man in your house. And you will see an enemy in my dwelling place, despite all the good which God does for Israel. And there shall not be an old man in your house forever. But any of your men whom I do not cut off from your my altar shall consume your eyes and grieve your heart. And all the descendants of your house shall die in the flower of their age. Now this shall be a sign to you that will come upon your two sons, on Hopni and Phineas. In one day they shall die, both of them. There's no prediction of Eli's death, but at this point he has lost all will to live before his body hit the ground. It's a tragic end. Pray for your spiritual leaders. Carrie and I are supposed to be the spiritual leaders of the church, but let's not stop there. Husbands and fathers are supposed to be spiritual leaders at home. Like Eli, the urgency of the moment and the pressure of the crowds can sway us easily. We might become complacent and tolerant about sin over time. We may treat lightly the holy ministries we're entrusted with. Sadly, everyone suffers when leadership fails. We see that in the rest of the chapter. That leads to the third lesson. Spiritual despair results without proper perspective on God. In verses nineteen to twenty-two, what was supposed to be a joyful event in life becomes a time of despair. When the news of the defeat and the taking of the ark reached Eli's daughter-in-law, the wife of Phineas, she was already close to giving birth to her son. Ordinarily, this would have been a glorious day. But it was a sad day for herself and her people She lost her father-in-law and the father of her child. She becomes a mother just as she becomes a widow. And that not even that long. P. Kyle McArthur writes, quote, The death of the grandfather is balanced by the birth of a grandson, but the cheerless event brings no hope to the cursed family. End quote. Her despondency and dejection are evident in her initial silent reaction to the woman around her. And when she does speak, she names the son Ichabod, which means, where is glory? In her mind, the glory of Israel has departed with the capture of the ark. But in reality, God's glory and presence are not circumscribed or limited to any physical space or object. Eugene Merrill notes, quote, to the pagans it was conceivable that God could be taken into exile, Isaiah 46, 1 to 2. But the Israelites should have known that their omnipresent God could not be taken away from them. How hedden Israel's perception of God had become. Indeed, heaven and the heavens of heavens cannot contain him The Most High does not dwell in temples made with hands, let alone a small ark Yahweh, the creator of heaven and earth, will display his glory everywhere, even in enemy territory. If I may use a sports analogy, God of Israel is not disadvantaged in playing away from his home field. We will see this clearly in the next few chapters. But for now, this chapter holds up a mirror to our own sinful souls Perhaps you have done well this week, but I'm willing to bet you weren't sinless, though not as dramatic as the loss to Philistines. I'm sure you faced spiritual defeat. Or you may have failed as a leader as Eli did, and you rightly deserved emotion. Or you've been so negatively affected by sin, so deep in despair. They lost proper perspective on God and who He is Now for some this kind of talk may be confusing, especially if you think Christians are supposed to be perfect. Well, I speak for all the saints here that we we are not perfect We have our shares of defeats, demotions, and despairs. But then what makes us different from non-Christians? It's this we've been shown mercy and forgiveness of sin, the root of our struggles Such grace is found in the good news of Jesus, the gospel. We remind ourselves of the gospel regularly and repeatedly through the word and one of the two ordinances, the Lord's Supper And here's the gospel, the good news. God has formed all of us in his image to represent him in the created order and glorify him. But we have sided with the enemy, the devil, in rebellion against our maker in mad mutiny. We have sinned against him in thought, word, and deed, and now live in bondage to Satan. Unless we return to God, we face punishment in hell. But we cannot and would not return to God in our own initiative. Not with our wicked hearts. He had to initiate. While we were far from being righteous or good, while we were still sinners and enemies. God demonstrated his love as he sent Christ to die for us. Jesus, as God's Son and the righteous and good man, took our place on the cross. Taking upon himself the wrath we deserve. We know this payment was accepted because he rose from the dead and ascended to heaven. Now he offers all. Righteousness by his blood. Salvation from wrath. Reconciliation with God. Joy for eternity. We can be victorious over sin and hell by surrendering to Christ, repenting and trusting in Him alone for the gracious gift of salvation. Again, being a Christian does not mean you don't face setbacks. But even though sin is an ongoing reality, we can get back up. But make no mistake, I'm not saying get back up in the power of the indomitable human spirit. Get back up in the power of the Holy Spirit. As your loving Father reminds you of the gospel, the good news of his Son Jesus Christ. Let's turn to the words of His promise. Gather at the assembly of His saints. Come humbly to the Lord's table. Let's pray. Lord, we look back at the failures of Israel and Lord We see how we have failed. We may rely on things that have worked before. We may rely on things and patterns and cultures and Traditions. Help us to let go of those things, to trust in you, that we may have victory in our spiritual lives. Lord, we pray for leaders. paper leaders in our homes, in our churches, that we would make the tough choice to follow you and lead others to do the same. Pray that even as we see things fall apart around us, that we will not be in despair. But see that no matter what's going on going on around us, We know that the one who is seated in heavens, that you are in control. Lord, may we not forget these truths. Pray all these things in Jesus Christ's name. Amen. Let us arise and sing
