We lived uh we had moved to Rehoba Beach, Delaware for ministry and we were living near the boardwalk, and so I had a habit of getting him up in the mornings uh or getting him a dress when he woke up early and taking him for a wagon ride w so my wife could sleep in and uh our other son could sleep sleep. So I would I would do that. And so we were out for a walk uh on a morning. It was in January. I had him all bundled up in his coat and his parka and he was about a year and a half old perhaps. And I walked for about an hour, bought a cup of coffee, ate a donut, read the paper while I was pulling the wagon behind me. He's back there And I just know he's as contented as he can be. And I got about, well, I got within the block of our house and I turned around and the wagon was empty. Alright, so that was jolt. That's a something you never forget, right, parents? You just never forget those kinds of things. And so it's as vivid today as it was then. And So I had an empty wagon and no sun and didn't know where he could possibly be. I've been walking for an hour And the wagon was noisy because it had loose nothing bolts. So if he had cried out or whatever, I may not have heard him when he fell out. So I immediately said, I'm in big trouble with my wife. I better go find him. And uh so I headed out. Now he was found. I'm not gonna tell you that whole story because I don't have time, but I'll tell you he was found. And I understand a little bit of this idea of losing something precious and finding it. I found him quickly. And there was great rejoicing, I assure you, as I took him in my arms and held him. And so for Jesus to tell this kind of story, to focus our attention on lost and found, everybody's thinking about that. You may not have lost a sheep. You may not have lost a coin. You lost something. Everybody has lost something. I lost my wallet in a gas station a couple years ago, and it was returned to me intact. You know, so it's it doesn't have to be a sheep or a coin, it can be all kinds of things. And that's to help us understand the mentality of God. And his son in his quest for those who are considered on the margins of society, the tax collectors and the sinners, those that religious people would consider unclean. Jesus uses this term sinner to accommodate the Pharisees. Interestingly enough, it doesn't show up in the third parable. The prodigal son, just the first two. But he uses this terminology to help bring home his point that a sinner has been found Picture angels in heaven. You ever just sit around and just take three minutes and think about angels rejoicing in heaven? What does that look like? How do angels rejoice? Do angels dance? Do they sing? Do they jump for joy? Do they do high fives? Do they bump elbows? I don't know what angels do when they rejoice, but I'd love to see it And Jesus thinks that's important enough to bring out at this point joy in heaven over sinners repenting. I don't know if that fits your model of heaven or not. C. S. Lewis once said, joy is the serious business of heaven. And I think his point was that we need to rethink our view of heaven because here we find out that the angels are rejoicing. Over one who repents. And angels don't even understand salvation like we do. And yet they know something has happened, and it's a big deal. So let me just conclude with an encouragement to us today Think about the tax collectors and sinners in your life, and think about the Pharisees and the Sadducees. And I know that when I think about the Pharisees and the Sadducees, I never want to put myself in that category. I always want to think, yeah, I would be like these other guys who want to hang out with Jesus, but sometimes we need to d take a ruthless look at ourselves and ask, what are the qualities of Pharisees and s and scribes, and would I be one of them? Do I have pharisaical tendencies? And perhaps I might isolate myself from the very people that God has targeted. For repentance, because I have a pharisaical attitude towards them. I love what I see of Jesus in this chapter And in the book of Luke, his comfort in being in the company of those despised by the religious leaders of his day. And it makes me want to be in that crowd that says, I'm listening. I'm coming to be in his presence. to sit at the table with him. I want to hear every single word he says. I want to see every facial expression, every body uh gesture that he makes. I want all of that because he has the answers and he's the one who cares for those who are marginalized We thank you, Lord Jesus, for the portrait that we see of you in your word in this passage. How wonderful it is to realize that the poor and the needy can come, That the tax collectors and sinners can be comfortable in the company of one like you. Oh, I want to be like that. I want tax collectors and sinners to want to hang out with me. And I want to to hang out with them like you would. Give us that kind of heart. Thank you for who you are. In Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.title: Israel Demands a King
sermons.speaker: Sung Cho
sermons.text: When one speaks of religion, politics is just around the corner Let's say I give you a list of contemporary moral issues and ask you to categorize them as either religious or political. Here they are. Abortion. Racism. Kingdom of God. In my opinion, none of these topics are exclusively religious or exclusively political. With abortion and racism, we must be thoroughly equipped in biblical anthropology. We must understand the doctrine of God's image in humanity to counter our society's false views. As for the kingdom of God, we do not think of it in the abstract or deem it distant and far away. When Jesus returns, an angel will announce, the kingdoms of this world have become the kingdoms of our Lord and of his Christ. And he shall reign forever and ever. That's in Revelation eleven, fifteen Sometimes the religious and the political are so closely aligned that we can't see one without the other. Sometimes we get a peek into someone's religion through her politics. Vice versa, we see someone's politics through his religion. How about ourselves? Is the hope of our hearts in a political party or a candidate? Is our souls security In a certain form of human-ruled government, we reveal our cherished values in our politics and religion. So you can understand why G. K. Chesterton once quipped, quote, I never discuss anything except politics and religion. There's nothing else to discuss. End quote. In today's passage, I hope you will observe with me an important intersection between politics and religion. In brief, we are challenged to recognize our God as king. That's the simple lesson. I don't have any genius ideas about politics. Just recognize God as king. That's the basic point. But I think there's other things we can learn. So let's read 1 Samuel 8 together and see what truths we can learn. First Samuel eight Now it came to pass when Samuel was old that he made his sons judges over Israel. The name of his first son was Joel, and the name of his second, Abijah. They were judges in Beersheba, but his sons did not walk in his ways. They turned aside after dishonest game, took bribes, and perverted justice. Then all the elders of Israel gathered together and came to Samuel at Ramah and said to him, Look, you are old, and your sons do not walk in your ways. Now make us a king to judge us like all the nations. But the thing displeased Samuel when they said, Give us a king to judge us. So Samuel prayed to the Lord. And the Lord said to Samuel, Heed the voice of the people in all that they say to you. For they have not rejected you, but they have rejected me, that I shall not reign over them. According to all the works which they have done since the day that I brought them out of Egypt, even to this day. with which they have forsaken me and served other gods, so they are doing to you also. Now therefore, heed their voice However, you shall solemnly forewarn them and show them the behavior of the king who will reign over them. So Samuel told all the words of the Lord to the people who asked him for a king. And he said, This will be the behavior of the king who will reign over you. He will take their sons and appoint them for his own chariots and to be his horsemen, and some will run before his chariots. He will appoint captains over his thousands and captains over his fifties. will set some to plough his ground and reap his harvest, and some to make his weapons of war and equipment for his chariots. He will take your daughters to be perfumers, cooks, and bakers And he will take the best of your fields, your vineyards, and your olive groves and give them to his servants. He will take a tenth of your grain and your vintage and give it to his officers and servants. And he will take your male servants, your female servants, your finest young men, and your donkeys and put them to his work. He will take a tenth of your sheep, and you will be his servants. And you will cry out in that day, because of your king whom you have chosen for yourselves, and the Lord will not hear you in that day. Nevertheless, the people refused to obey the voice of Samuel, and they said, No, but we will have a king over us, that we also may be like all the nations, and that our king may judge us and go out before us and fight our battles. And Samuel heard all the words of the people and repeated them in the hearing of the Lord. So the Lord said to Samuel, Heed their voice and give them and make them a king. And Samuel said to the men of Israel, every man go to his city. I think there are three lessons for us from this passage. One, weakness of human leaders should lead us to God. That's verses one to six. 2. Rejection of God as king results in disaster. Verses 7 to 18. 3. Stubbornness of sinful people is permitted as judgment. That's verses 19 to 22. First, weakness of human leaders shall lead us to God. There are two weaknesses, moral and physical The first corresponding to Samuel's sons, and the second corresponding to Samuel. Joel and Abijah had the vigor, youth, and energy on their side. But they lacked the faith and the integrity of their father. Samuel had the faith and the integrity, but his vigor, youth, and energy were fast waning The younger judges exhibited moral weakness. The older judge showed signs of physical weakness. Specifically, we read in verse 3 that Samuel's sons did not walk in his ways. They turned aside after dishonest gain, took bribes, and perverted justice. Tragic consequences of such corruption, especially corruption among leaders, are recorded throughout the Old Testament. Moses warned Israel that a bride blinds the eyes of the wise and twists the words of the righteous. That's in Deuteronomy 16, 19. Proverbs warned, a wicked man accepts a bribe behind the back to pervert the ways of justice. That's in 1723. Later, prophets also warn Israel against corruption and its consequences. There's a violent bloodshed of innocence in society. Isaiah 33, 14-15. Ezekiel 22, 12 to 13. Habakkuk 1, 2 to 4. The righteous and the poor are marginalized. See that throughout Amos 5. And not much has changed since the days of ancient Israel. Here and now, in the present age. Assault against human dignity continues through dishonesty and injustice. More victims are added daily. The unborn in the womb, the elderly in isolation, the minority in discrimination, the lowly in the margins God have mercy on us and our leaders Only if there were younger versions of Samuel. Now it is true that Samuel was getting up there in age, as seen in verses 1 and 5. The man does not deny it. He's probably around 50 years old, and he's definitely slowing down. He could continue as a spiritual leader, but he's no Gideon or Samson. He's no longer fit for battle against enemies like the Ammonites, new threats from the east side of Jordan. The people were also probably concerned about the Philistines that they would rise up again as Samuel grows greater. But it's not as if Samuel's youth gave them victory in the first place. I don't know how these elders forgot the lessons from the battles with the Philistines. They forgot the tumors, the thunder, mizfah, ebenezer. Does our God the King need men with vigor, youth, and energy? Does our eternal God grow uneasy as Samuel grows old? Have we not known? Have we not heard? The everlasting God, the Lord, the creator of the ends of the earth, neither faints. Nor is weary. No one is holy like the Lord, for there is none besides him, nor is there any rock like our God. That's what Hannah said back in chapter 2, verse 2. I'm sure Samuel reminded them to trust God above all during his time as a prophet and judge. As he grew older, I bet he reiterated the words of Gideon before him. That's in Judges 8:23. I will not rule over you, nor shall my son rule over you. The Lord shall rule over you. In response, the Israelites should have done what they did in the previous chapter. Repentance. Worship, prayers, fasting, confession, sacrifice. Samuel pointed them back to God many years ago at that battle of Mitzvah. It wasn't Samuel that saved them in the first place. It was the Lord. So it's fine that the Israelites said, look, you are old and your sons do not walk in your ways. But what if they said right after that Instead of now make us a king to judge us like all the nations, they said, now pray for us to God our King to judge us directly, unlike all the nations. What if they said, We know you're growing old and your sons are corrupt, but we trust God will lead us with or without strong human leadership? What if they said, our special significance is not in having a king like all the other nations, but we shall be to God a kingdom of priests and a holy nation. Alas, that's not what they say. But what the Israelites refuse to do, namely praying to the Lord, Samuel does in verse 6. So let's stop here for some applications to the moral and physical weaknesses You see in human authorities drive you to trust God more and more? It's a good question to ask anytime, but especially poignant in election year. Do the moral and physical weaknesses you see in our candidates lead you to deeper trust in God? Good leaders, sadly, do not live forever. Bad leaders, mercifully, do not live forever. We should not be looking for an earthly king to solve our problems. Sadly, the Israelites did look for an earthly king to solve their problems because they have rejected the divine king. And that leads to the second point. Rejection of God as king results in disaster Feeling underappreciated and unwanted, Samuel went to the Lord who assured his prophet that it was not him they were rejecting. In reality, they were rejecting God Himself. We see in verse 8 that idolatry was the problem. Idolatry can be an image of a false God, or it can be an image of an ideal human king. They broke the first commandment because they did not put God first. This present sin was completely aligned with the past sin of Israel from the days of Exodus, the journeys in the wilderness, and even their more recent struggles in the Promised Land. They got out of Egypt long ago, but they still needed to get Egypt out of them. They as a people have forgotten how bad it was under the harsh rule of the Pharaoh, the king of Egypt. What is sad about this chapter is that God would have eventually given them a king. God is not anti-king per se. He promised Abraham and Sarah and their grandson Jacob that kings would come from them and their seed. Jacob predicted that the scepter of rule would remain in the tribe of Judah, his son. Moses anticipated that people would want a king and gave strict guidelines in Deuteronomy 17. And in due time, God would have raised up a royal root of Jesse and the seed of David. Ultimately, God had plans to give the world the greatest king. His own son, Jesus. He is perfectly qualified to rule as both Son of God and Son of Man, divine and human, perfect in every way. Why would anyone settle for anything less? Why be like other nations when they are God's special possession? Well, the Israelites decided to settle for less. Now they have to put up with the behavior of their king. The original word for behavior in verses 9 and 11 is mishpat, and it's often translated as judgment elsewhere. But it has a wide range of definitions. And depending on the context, it could also mean custom, such as that of priests in chapter 2 verse 13. team or behavior as such as that of rulers as seen here. Some commentators note how this rhetoric could be a word play, satire, or sarcasm. It's as if God is saying, Oh, you want the judgment of the king? All right, I'll give you the judgment of the king And we don't have to go through all the details of his behavior to figure out that it's going to be bad. David Guzick observes from verses 11 onward, quote, The Lord gives fair warning. Most kings are takers, not givers, and they come to be served, not to serve. If Israel wants a king, they must realize he will be a taker, not a giver, and they will be his servants. Verse 11, he will take your sons. Verse 13, he will take your daughters. Verse 14, he will take the best of your fields, your vineyards, and your olive growth. Verse 15 He will take a tenth of your grain and your vintage. Verse 16, he will take your male servants, your female servants, your finest young men, and your donkeys. Verse 17, he will take a tenth of your sheep. Take, take, take, take, take, take. No wonder we read in verse 18, and you will cry out in that day because of your king whom you have chosen for yourselves. And the Lord will not hear you in that day. Going back to Deuteronomy 17, we see the contrast between the king the people choose versus the king the Lord God chooses. The ideal king does not add, accumulate, or multiply horses, wives, silver, and gold. The typical king does add, accumulate, and multiply for himself. He builds a hedge of protection and privilege for himself at the expense of his subjects. This is what a normal monarchy looked like in a fallen world. They chose this over theocracy, God's benevolent direct rule. Rejection of God as king results in disaster. Like I said above, the king the Lord God chooses is none other than Jesus from the line of David The people should have been satisfied with the promises and prophecies of his coming to sustain them in faith. So their faith would ultimately be in God, not in man. Their faith will be rewarded because the Messiah is not like the kings of other nations The New Testament reinforces how Jesus our King is different than other kings. The Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve and to give his life a ransom for many. He was among his followers as the one who serves. The teacher and the Lord washed their feet. Though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, that you through his poverty might become rich. Jesus, being in the form of God, did not consider robbery to be equal with God, but made himself of no reputation, taking the form of a bondservant. Coming in the likeness of men and being found in the appearance as a man, he humbled himself and became obedient to the point of death, even the death of the cross. The king of human choosing takes and takes for himself to be exalted over all. The king of God's choosing gave himself a ransom for all, gave himself for us. The king of human choosing enslaves us to be his people, just as kings of other nations do, zealous to work for him. The King of God's choosing redeems us and purifies for himself his own people, his own special people, zealous for good works. 1 Timothy 2 and Titus 2. Will never truly be satisfied with the fellow sinner ruling over us. Why not serve the sinless Jesus? Why not get to know him? The one who gives, gives, gives and gives. Now, if you want to know him as Savior, you must know him as King. Please make no mistake. There's no such thing as accepting Jesus as Savior without accepting Jesus as Lord. That's like saying I accept Jesus as a Jew and a Nazarene, but not as Christ. The very identity of Jesus and his title of Christ, the anointed one. Points to the kingship of Jesus. Give yourself to Jesus Christ the King. Because Jesus Christ the King gave himself to you. He will accept you, though you have nothing to give him. Though you may be poor, weak, sinful in thought, word, and deed, repent and trust in him alone, not in your works. He offers you eternal life, the life he purchased with his own life, die on the cross in your place, rose again from the dead, and awaits the day of his return. To earth, to judge as the wrathful king. Make the choice now to meet Jesus as the merciful King. Those who persistently reject God as king are in grave spiritual danger, a precarious position, a step away from eternal punishment. In fact, because of their unbelief, they stand condemned already. John 3:18 says, He who does not believe is condemned already, because he has not believed in the name of the only begotten Son of God. That leads to the third point. Stubbornness of sinful people is permitted as judgment So we wrap up this chapter with Samuel as the goal between the people and God. Samuel is faithful to transmit to the people all that the Lord has told him, and vice versa. Sadly, the people refuse to listen. They maintain their position and dig in their heels. In their minds, the era of judges is over. Let the monarchy begin. The final verse records how God let them lets them have their way. This is a tragic moment. Stubbornness of simple people is permitted as judgments. judgment. Let's apply this individually. We've talked about stubbornness and how it's related to being stiff-necked. I shudder to think what would happen if God unleashed me and let me go my own way. I'm so thankful that he has mercifully brought me back to myself back to himself time and time again. I hope that none of us, for no one we love, gets all that we want for ourselves. That's not a good thing. That itself is a judgment. Stubbornness of simple people is permitted as judgment. Let's apply this corporately in our culture. As we watch in horror the downward spiral and decadence of our society, know that we are not merely headed towards judgment or condemnation. We are already under judgment. As Paul said in Romans, the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men who suppress the truth and unrighteousness. He already gave the idolatrous humanity over to uncleanness, vile passions, and debased mind. Okay, so depressed yet. Um, here's some good news. We who submit to Christ can rest assured that God is in control. A king will not rise from Israel, and even evil governments that appear to run amok are not outside of God's sovereignty. Samuel will transition from judge to kingmaker, but that's not without the Lord's permission. God is in control, even in dark times of human stubbornness. The Israelites have made their choice. But what about us? What about you? I'll mention some uh closing applications for the unbeliever, the believer, the church, the political-minded person, and the religious-minded person. First, I address the unbeliever once more. You think you are your own boss and ruler, but your kingdom will not last, and you will not survive the day of judgment. Make that life-altering choice to enthrone him as king. Submit to the righteousness of God instead of establishing your own righteousness. To the believer, we must grow in our submission to Jesus, our King. Continually submit to God and resist the devil, as James tells us Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, as our Lord Jesus told us. To the church, let's continue to pray and stay in his word. As your pastor, I often hear prayer requests and concerns about the state of our nation. Really, the best we can do for each other is to pray and remind ourselves of biblical truths. God is King. He's in control. Jesus, the head of the church, is also the King of kings and the Lord of Lords. To the political-minded person who consumes a lot of news and is very concerned about the politics of today, seek God's grace. Yes, our nation may shake and someday crumble to pieces. Our leaders are weak morally and physically. But the writer of Hebrews, I think, gives us two grace verses. That are, I guess you can say political, but it's also spiritual at the same time. Since we are receiving a kingdom which cannot be shaken. Let us have grace by which we may serve God acceptably with reverence and godly fear. That's Hebrews 12, 28. Let us come boldly to the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy and find grace to help in time of need. Chapter 4, verse 16. We find and claim grace at that throne room. Visit there often. Find Jesus, the King of glory and of grace. Our sympathetic high priest sitting at the right hand of the Father. He's in control. Finally, to the religious mind that individual Christian who don't really care about politics, my political statement is that you would ask God would reign in you, reign in us through his spirit. That he would be king. If you don't know how to ask for this, perhaps this Puritan prayer from Valley of Vision can be an inspiration. O God of the highest heaven, occupy the throne of my heart. Take full possession and reign supreme. Lay low every rebel lust. Let no vile passion resist thy holy war. Manifest thy mighty power and make me thine forever. Thou art worthy to be praised with my every breath, loved with my every faculty of soul, served with my every act of life. As we close, we will sing a song based on this very prayer. Let's make our religious and political statement. The Lord is the great God and the great King above all gods. Let's pray. Lord, we come before you confessing. Our rebellion, that we come before you confessing our weakness, moral weakness, physical weakness. That we don't deserve to sit on the throne where you rightfully sit. We confess that we have rejected you And at times, even in our walk, even in our sanctification, or that tendency, that inclination to reject you and make ourselves the king. Lord, it creeps back. Pray that you'll give us the power through your Holy Spirit. Lord, we confess that we are stubborn. We want it our way. Lord, when you challenge us and when you show us gently and lovingly and kindly through your word and persuasively, we still say no. And Lord, we confess that when we say you are king, and when we sing these songs and hymns, and when we read these passages, Lord, we have not been good servants. But we're thankful that we find forgiveness in your Son Jesus Christ. Who is the humble king who showed us, not only forgiving us of our sins, but showing us how to live a life that is pleasing to you. So we pray that as we sing this last song and as we meditate on your passage, on your word, may we be able to say more than ever before, in a new way, each and every day, that you are King over our lives. Pray all these things in Jesus Christ's name.

sermons.title: Saul Chosen to be King
sermons.speaker: Sung Cho
sermons.text: Adventure. When is the last time you went on an adventure I remember the adventure of going to and from church through the shortcuts and main roads of Degu, hymns and Bible lessons ringing in my head. I remember as a walker, the neighborhoods and apartment complexes of Laurel in my commutes to and from school. More recently, I remember during our summer honeymoon exploring Florence, a beautiful Italian city that appeared calm and serene, yet alive and busy at the same time. You might notice that I'm feeling stuck at home recently. Maybe you do too. So I wanted to recall the thrill of adventure I looked up some famous quotes on the topic. See if you can relate to these quote. Every man's life ends the same way. It is only the details of how he lived and how he died that distinguish one man from another. That's Ernest Hemingway. Quote, an adventure is only an inconvenience, rightly considered. An inconvenience is only an adventure, wrongly considered That's G. K. Chesterton. And then quote, not all who wander are lost. That's J. R. Tolkien. The Bible is filled with adventures too. Many of its protagonists have followed God's call to unknown and strange places, learning valuable lessons. Living and dying in unique ways. Now we may not think immediately of Saul in this today's passage as a protagonist That's probably because we primarily view him as a tragic figure and the enemy of David. But try to read today's passage without thinking too much about that ending. See where his life is headed chronologically, step by step, turn by turn, chapter by chapter, instead of as a panoramic whole. By doing so, I believe we can learn valuable lessons for our own adventures. So let's read the chapter together. It's 1 Samuel chapter 9. There was a man of Benjamin, whose name was Kish, the son of Abiel, the son of Zeror, the son of Bakorath, the son of Abiah, a Benjamite, a mighty man of power And he had a choice and handsome son, whose name was Saul. There was not a more handsome person than he among the children of Israel. From his shoulders upward he was taller than any of the people. Now the donkeys of Kish, Saul's father, were lost. And Kish said to his son Saul, Please take one of the servants with you, and arise, go and look for the donkeys So he passed through the mountains of Ephraim and through the land of Shalisha, but they did not find him. Then they passed through the land of Sha'alim, and they were not there Then he passed through the land of the Benjamites, but they did not find them. When they had come to the land of Zup Saul said to his servant who was with him, Come, let us return, lest my father cease caring about the donkeys and become worried about us. And he said to him, Look now, there is in this city a man of God, and he is an honorable man. All that he says surely comes to pass. So let us go there. Perhaps he can show us the way that we should go. Then Saul said to his servant, But look, if we go, what shall we bring the man? For the bread in our vessels is all gone, and there is no present to bring to the man of God. What do we have? And the servant answered Saul again and said, Look, I have here at hand one fourth of a shekel of silver. I will give that to the man of God to tell us our way. Formerly in Israel, when a man went to inquire of God, he spoke thus, Come, let us go to the seer. For he who is now called a prophet was formerly called a seer. Then Saul says to his servant, Wilset, come, let us go. So they went to the city where the man of God was As they went up the hill to the city, they met some young women going out to draw water and said to them, Is the fear here? And they answered them and said, Yes, there he is, just ahead of you. Hurry now, for today he came to the city, to the city, because there is a sacrifice of the people today on the high place As soon as you come into the city, you will surely find them before he goes up to the high place to eat. For the people will not eat until he comes, because he must bless the sacrifice Afterward, those who are invited will eat. Now therefore, go up, for about this time you will find them. So they went up to the city. As they were coming into the city, there was Samuel coming out toward them on his way up to the high place. Now the Lord had told Samuel in his ear the day before Saul came, saying, Tomorrow about this time I will send you a man from the land of Benjamin And you shall anoint him commander over my people, Israel, that he may save my people from the hand of the Philistines. For I have looked upon my people because their cry has come to me. So when Samuel saw, the Lord said to him, There he is, the man of whom I spoke to you. This one shall reign over my people. Then Saul drew near to Samuel in the gate and said, Please tell me, where is the seer's house? Samuel answered Saul and said, I am the seer. Go before me to the high place, for you shall eat with me today, and tomorrow I will let you go and will tell you all that is in your heart. But as for your donkeys that were lost three days ago, do not be anxious about them, for they have been found. And on whom is all the desire of Israel? Is it not on you and on all your father's house? And Saul answered and said, Am I not a Benjamite of the smallest of the tribes of Israel, and my family the least of all the families of the tribe of Benjamin? Why then do you speak like this to me? Now Samuel took Saul and his servant and brought them into the hall and had them sit in the place of honor among those who were invited. There were about thirty persons. And Samuel said to the coat, Bring the portion which I gave you, of which I set to you, set it apart. So the cook took up the thigh with its upper part and set it before Saul. And Samuel said, Here it is. What was kept back? It was set apart for you. Eat, for until this time it has been kept for you since I said I invited the people. So Saul ate with Samuel that day. When they had come down from the high place into the city, Samuel spoke with Saul on the top of the house. They arose early, and it was about the dawning of the day. The Samuel called to Saul on the top of the house, saying, Get up, that I may send you on your way. And Saul arose, and both of them went outside, he and Samuel As they were going down to the outskirts of the city, Samuel said to Saul, Tell the servant to go on ahead of us. And he went on, but you stand here awhile that I may announce to you the word of God If we are to embark on an adventure of our own Please keep three principles close to your heart. One, God's providence despite ignorance. 2. God's design over human plan. Verses 15 and 17. 217. 3. God's grace for the humble. Verses 18 to 27. First, God's providence despite ignorance. Let's look at the first fourteen verses of this chapter, which may seem quite mundane at first. Pastor Ray Bowler, however, sees here God's guiding, almighty hand in Saul's life and by extension and application in our lives as well. I find Fowler's outline of this chapter and his four subdivisions of verses 1 to 14 very helpful. Fowler teaches from verses 1 and 2 that God is at work in your family background. From verses 3 to 4, God is at work in interruptions and setbacks. Next in verses 5 to 10, we learn that God is at work in the people he has placed around you Finally, from verses 11 to 14, we learn that God is at work in the timing of events. And I'll repeat those for you. Are you aware that God is at work in your family background? We may find it trivial, but we know from verse 1 the names of Saul's grandfather, great-grandfather, great-great-grandfather, and great-great-great-grandfather. Aren't the name of the father and the name of the Benjamin tribe enough? You may think so. I may think so, but sorry, the Holy Spirit inspired these words as much as he inspired John 3. 16. If indeed all scripture is given by inspiration of God, then there are lessons here too Saul was privileged to come from a wealthy and prominent family in Gibeah. Kish was a mighty man like Boaz or some of the other warriors in the Bible. And he was blessed with good genes. As R. P. Gordon wrote, quote, if a king is to be distinguished by his physical appearance, then Saul is every inch a king. We'll see how he handles such privileges, but regardless for the role of king, he definitely looks the part. As for us, we may not fully understand why we have our last names, why we were born to this family or that, why we look like this or that. But we must not be ignorant of God's providence in our own family background. God's hand is not only evident in the many generations of Saul's family, are you aware that God is at work in interruptions and setbacks? Kish loses his donkeys and commissions his son to go search for them with one of his house servants. The place names in verse 4 are hard to pin down, but one scholar surmises an itinerary. The search party may have proceeded northward from Gibeah to the uplands of Ephraim, turning then westward, then southward, and finally eastward. In other words, they wandered in every direction. The interruption and setback got Saul out of his home and closer to Samuel. We must not be ignorant of God's providence in interruptions and setbacks Not only in family and unplanned events, are you aware that God is at work in the people He has placed around you? Just when Saul was about to give up, his servant makes a key suggestion to visit a man of God nearby. When Saul was afraid of breaching decorum by going to the seer empty-handed, This servant found money for the honor area. David Samura believes this servant is none other than Ziba, a high-ranking servant and steward of this household. We'll learn more about him later. For now, can you think of people like Ziba in your life? Consider all the turning points of your life. And individuals who pointed you to the Lord in the right direction. We must not be ignorant of God's providence and the people He has placed around us. Not only in family, life events, and people, are you aware that God is at work in the timing of events? Saul and the servant arrived right when the young women came to draw water. That day Samuel was at the city, and that day a sacrifice was scheduled. The ladies say they will surely find them before he goes up to the high place to eat. That's exactly what happened next You see how everything came together at the right moment. We must not be ignorant of God's providence in the timing of events. What are the benefits of such awareness as opposed to ignorance of God's providence? I encourage you to look this up. The Heidelberg Catechism is helpful in supplying an answer along with proof passages. And this is question number 28. And the question is, what does it benefit us to know that God has created all things and still upholds them by his providence? Answer. We can be patient in adversity, thankful in prosperity. And with a view to the future, we can have a firm confidence. In our faithful God and Father, that no creatures shall separate us from his love. For all creatures are so clean completely in his hand that without his will they cannot so much as move. Patience, gratitude, confidence, mark the one who is constantly aware of God's mighty hand of providence. Seek to understand providence by faith. Another mystery that we seek to understand by faith is God's grand plan. That leads to the second lesson. In verses 1 to 14, the narrator told the story from Saul's point of view. In verses 15 to 17, we switched perspectives and learned that Samuel was expecting Saul. He received revelation a day prior and confirmation at the encounter, this is the king that Israel was waiting for. He will be anointed as the commander and rule over them. By the way, the predictions of Saul's success here do not contradict all the warnings of the previous chapter. Saul may be the answer to the people's cries now, but later people will cry out because of him, and God will not answer then. For the moment, let's observe God's design over human plan. Prior to this Saul was just another guy. Yes, he was good looking, but he didn't have any position per se. I'm sure he wasn't the first person to go search for his father's donkeys But this encounter with Samuel is the moment his life diverges from the typical Israelite. He is destined for leadership, combat, greatness. His homesickness and anxiety are frustrations of mere human plans. God had greater designs for Saul, who had no idea three days ago when he left home The very straightforward application of this principle is that we should not boast in our plans. Our plans are always subject to divine veto. You know, 2020 with a rude interruption of all that we scheme for ourselves. Our careers, our finances, our goals, our relationships, everything has been affected Now we are reminded of James 4, 13 to 16. Come now, you who say, Today or tomorrow, we will go to such and such a city, spend a year there, buy and sell, and make a profit. Whereas you do not know what will happen tomorrow. For what is your life? It is even a vapor that appears for a little time and then vanishes away. Instead, you ought to say, if the Lord wills, we shall live and do this or that. But now you boast in your arrogance. All such boasting is evil. So don't boast in your arrogance. Qualify your big plans with the important phrase, if the Lord wills. Remember, Proverbs 16, 9. A man's heart plans his way, but the Lord directs his steps. If we discuss our grand future plans with our spouses, our parents, our bosses, how much more shall we discuss them in prayer with our God the King? Though we feel weak and insignificant in this confusing and harsh world, you will find that He cares for you. You will know by experience that all things work together for good to those who love God, to those who are called according to his purpose. And that leads to the third point, God's grace to the humble, or for the humble Saul's life is changed forever as he meets Samuel. The future king is overwhelmed with the prophet's kindness in verses 19 to 20. Invitation to the sacrificial feast the same day, the next day, discussion of all that is in his heart. That's probably his long-laid aspirations for politics. Assurance that the donkeys have been found, and the conferring of the kingship on him, on whom is all the desire of Israel. I believe Saul's response to grace in verse 21 is one of genuine humility and meekness. There's no need to think he was being two-faced or read his tragic end into his hopeful beginning here. Again, let the story unfold, shot by shot, scene by scene. On a side note, I find that interesting that the story of Saul of the New Testament had a bad start, but a good ending. The story of Saul of the Old Testament had a good start, but a bad ending. Saul, the son of Kish, had a good start due to his realistic assessment of his tribe and family. Being from town of Gibeah and the tribe of Benjamin was not something to be proud of at this point in Israelite history. You may recall from the final few chapters of Judges why. The tribe of Benjamin was wicked and stubborn in tolerating and defending the evil of Gibeah. The other tribes defeated the Benjamites in the ensuing civil war. Saul's tribe was severely decimated, so much that the fellow Israelites feared its extinction. And that's not good, not a good at all. But remember God's grace to the humble Samuel takes this man who questions his word and seats them in the place of honor at the table Recall Jesus' parable we read earlier. Thanks to Samuel, Saul has to glory in the presence of those who sit at the table with him. He learned by firsthand experience the lesson of that parable. He who humbles himself will be exalted. Because Saul humbled himself privately to Samuel, he was exalted publicly at the hall before the guests. But that's not all. As a distinguished guest, Saul was served a distinguished meal David Samurai notes how the cook brought before him the meat portion normally set aside for the priest as prescribed in Exodus 29-27. It's as if the priest is saying, I'm usually the one to eat this choice and sacred portion, but I want you to have it, Saul. This is a visible demonstration of God's grace for the humble. After their meal, they returned from the high place to the city. Samuel spoke to him privately, presumably reinforcing these lessons of grace. Early next day, Samuel calls Saul to the same spot and tells him to get ready to depart. Near the outskirts of the city, Saul is instructed to send his servant ahead of him. That way Samuel can announce God's word and anoint him as ruler God's grace in Saul's life magnifies moment by moment, day by day, place by place. What about God's grace in your life? Let the favor shown to Saul be a lesson for the New Testament saints. There's a common principle of grace between the meal which Saul attended and the Lord's Supper we attend monthly. Both are beautiful pictures of divine grace shown to the humble, undeserving, the lowly. But we are so much more privileged than Saul. We are invited to enjoy the presence of our God, the King of the universe, who takes his time to meet us in fellowship. But please know and remember that this intimacy came at a great cost. We don't deserve to be near God. He is holy, morally perfect. We are sinners to the core in our thoughts, actions, and deeds. We offend them actively and passively. We must pay for breaking God's laws. So how do we get to be with them? Jesus paid the price of entrance and the seat at the table. The cost was this, he died on the cross in the place of sinners like you and me, taking upon himself the torment of hell. As proof that he has paid it up in full, he rose from the dead and ascended to heaven. He now offers eternal life as a free gift, not as a reward for works. This grace is for all who humble themselves in repentance and faith. With this gift of grace, we can thrive in our adventure, our pilgrimage on earth, joyfully, thankfully, courageously We experience his grace through faith in Christ, even as we face dangers and uncertainties It's good to remind ourselves that God's almighty hand and ever-present power governs the affairs of the universe. He has a grand plan of redemption and glory for his king and his people. He bestows grace to the humble. What about those who don't have faith in Christ? What does their story consist of? Rival worldviews offer such disappointing alternatives. Some say nothing governs history and stories of our lives, just chance Others have said fate determines all things. It's interesting to look at how Greek storytellers like Homer and Hesiod personified fate. The fates were the three daughters of Nyx, the goddess of the night. Not a good start here. One daughter would simply spin thread from a spindle The second would measure out a given piece of thread, which signify the length of life. And the third would cut the thread and thus signify death. In Greek, her name literally means the inevitable. Even the mighty Zeus had to bow to the fates. They were independent, arbitrary, capricious. They govern all events of human history and all events of a single life. How bleak and depressing is that? Here's the truth. Instead of being at the mercy of three faith sisters, we are the three persons of the Trinity. The Bible teaches that our Father is the grand weaver. Neither death nor life can separate me from the love of Christ God's Son. The Holy Spirit abides with me forever. With God's providence, plan, and grace in our favor, life is not an accident, inconvenience, a wandering. Life is a grand adventure in which we are assured a happy ending. Let's pray. Lord, we're thankful that you are sovereign and Lord, we believe in providence And Lord, we go through each day and we don't even understand the full significance Of the events that occur in our lives. Lord, but we know that you have a plan, and we are part of that plan. And Lord, you have called us to salvation to be part of this grand kingdom plan that you have. And Lord, we can only come and participate in this grand scheme of things. Not because we have done something great. But all we can say is we're sinners. We're undeserving. Am I not a sinner? Who bring nothing before this holy God of the universe. But we're thankful for the grace shown to us. Lord, grace shown to the humble that you exalt us. May we never take that for granted May we live each day, trusting in you, living confidently, joyfully Knowing that you are writing the story of our lives, you are weaving us into your grand plan. We're thankful and we pray all these things in Jesus Christ's name.

sermons.title: Saul Anointed as King
sermons.speaker: Sung Cho
sermons.text: In his book The Call, author Oz Guinness recounts a story of a prominent businessman who spoke at a conference near Oxford University. The speaker said, quote, as you know, I have been very fortunate in my career and I've made a lot of money. Far more than I ever dreamed of, far more than I could ever spend Far more than my family needs. His face revealed determination. and character. But suddenly his outward intensity faded and sorrow emerged. He continued with a single tear rolling down his cheek. Quote To be honest, one of my motives for making so much money was simple. To have the money to hire people to do what I don't like doing. But there's one thing I've never been able to hire anyone to do for me. Find my own sense of purpose and fulfillment. I'd give anything to discover that. Last time I checked, purpose and fulfillment are not for sale on Amazon or available for pickup at a local store. They cannot be found near or far in this world. It's sobering to see that even those who find their earthly calling, their so-called dream jobs Fail to discover what's essential in life. I'm here to tell you that you will not be satisfied until you are satisfied in the Lord As we continue in the story of Saul, we see a man who had no trouble finding his earthly calling. God and his prophet practically handed it to him on a silver platter. What a privilege to be the first king of Israel. He, like the prominent businessman, would eventually accumulate wealth and power over others But without a vital relationship with God and his grace, he would never find his own sense of purpose and fulfillment. In a word, to be a good king, Saul needs God as king. Let's read today's passage, 1 Samuel chapter 10. Then Samuel took a flask of oil. and poured it on his head, and kissed him, and said, Is it not because the Lord has anointed you commander over his inheritance? When you have departed from me to day, you will find two men by Rachel's tomb in the territory of Benjamin at Zelza. And they will say to you, The donkeys which you went to look for have been found. And now your father has ceased caring about the donkeys and is worried worried about you, saying, What shall I do about my son? Then you shall go on forward from there and come to the Terebin tree of Tabor. There are three men coming going up to God At Bethel will meet you, one carrying three young goats, another carrying three loaves of bread, and another carrying a skin of wine. And they will greet you and give you two loaves of bread, which you shall receive from their hands. After that you shall come to the hill of God, where the Philistine garrison is, and it will happen when you have come there to the city. That you will meet a group of prophets coming down from the high place with a stringed instrument, a tambourine, a flute, and a harp before them, and they will be prophesying. Then the Spirit of the Lord will come upon you, and you will prophesy with them and be turned into another man. And let it be when these signs come to you, that you do as the occasion demands, for God is with you You shall go down before me to Gilgal, and surely I will come down to you to offer burnt offerings and make sacrifices of peace offerings. Seven days you shall wait till I come to you and show you what you should do. So it was when he had turned his back to go from Samuel that God gave him another heart. And all those signs came to pass that day. When they came there to the hill, there was a group of prophets to meet him. Then the Spirit of God came upon him, and he prophesied among them. And it happened when all who knew him formerly saw that he indeed prophesied among the prophets, that the people said to one another, What is this that has come upon the son of Kish? It saw also among the prophets. Then a man from there answered and said, But who is their father? Therefore it became a proverb. It saw also among the prophets. And when he had finished prophesying, he went to the high place. Now Saul's uncle said to him and his servant, Where did you go? So he said, To look for the donkeys. When he saw that they were nowhere to be found, we went to Samuel. And Saul's uncle said, tell me please, what Samuel said to you. So Saul said to his uncle, He told us plainly that the donkeys have been found. But about the matter of the kingdom, he did not tell him what Samuel had said. Then Samuel called the people together to the Lord at Mitzvah and sets the children of Israel, Thus says the Lord God of Israel: I brought up Israel out of Egypt. And delivered you from the hand of the Egyptians and from the hand of all kingdoms and from those who oppressed you. But you have today rejected your God. who himself saved you from all your adversities and your tribulations and you have said to him, no, set a king over us Now therefore, present yourselves before the Lord by your tribes and by your clans. And when Samuel had caused all the tribes of Israel to come near, the tribe of Benjamin was chosen. When he had caused the tribe of Benjamin to come near by their families, the family of Maitri was chosen, and Saul, the son of Kish, was chosen, but when they sought him, he could not be found. Therefore, they inquired of the Lord further, has the man come here yet? And the Lord answered, There he is, hidden among the equipment. So they ran and brought him from there. And when he stood among the people, he was taller than any of the people from his shoulders upward. And Samuel said to all the people, Do you see him whom the Lord has chosen? That there is no one like him among all the people. So all the people shouted and said, Long live the king. Then Samuel explained to the people behavior of royalty and wrote it in a book and laid it up before the Lord. And Samuel sent all the people away, every man to his house And Saul also went home to Gibeah, and valiant men went with him, whose hearts God had touched But some rebels said, How can this man save us? So they despised him and brought him no presents, but he held his peace. To find lasting and true purpose and fulfillment in life We need the Lord and his gifts of grace. And I think of five in particular from this chapter. One, God's confirmation, verses one to eight. 2. God's Spirit verses 9 to 13. 3. God's timing verses 14 to 16. 4. God's promotion verses 17 to 24. And five, God's approval, verses twenty-five to twenty-seven. First, we need God's confirmation. Consider what Saul is going through. I mean, in a matter of few days, he's been wandering through the land. He met a prophet who made him a VIP at a feast. He's been privileged to come be a commander over the nation of Israel, God's own inheritance. He's got precious oil running down his head. He's been told that he's God's anointed He might pinch himself to see if this is all real. God provides something better than a pinch. Samuel tells Saul to look for three confirmation signs on his way to the city of Gilgal. Sign number one: two men will inform him that the lost donkeys are found. Sign number two. Three men on their journey on their way to worship will share some bread with him. Sign number three Saul will be transformed by the Holy Spirit and join a group of prophets in prophesying. Note how Samuel's predictions of each encounter are precise in location and detail. Hills. Ray Fowler notes also how each sign increases in intensity. Saul goes from one man Samuel to two men at Zelza to three man at Zelda. Ta table to group of men, at least four I think, based on the number of music instruments. Fowler also notes that each sign corresponds to what Samuel just did for Saul. The two men confirm Samuel's words in chapter 9, verse 20. Which said, as for the donkeys you lost three days ago, do not worry about them. They have been found. The three worshippers sharing bread is parallel to Samuel sharing his special meat portion. Reserved for priests. Finally, the encounter with the prophets and the Holy Spirit corresponds to Samuel and his symbolic anointing of oil. And more on this third sign a little bit later. For now, observe in verse 7 the outcome of God's confirmation. And let it be when these signs come on come to you that you do as the occasion demands, for God is with you. As God confirms Saul's calling, he can act confidently. He can be assured that God is with him. But this kind of confirmation is not mere intellectual assent to God's word. It's living and experiencing God's Word. Saul went on his way and experienced God's gracious confirmation. And as he continues his journey, there will be more opportunities to confirm his calling. Now we may not receive out of ordinary confirmations like Saul here, but we can in his word Find confirmation in God's promises. They are true, and we can live confidently, knowing God is with us. How can Christians who experience promises of hope, peace, joy be so gloomy and pessimistic? Why so sour? The longer we walk with the Lord, the more confirmation we receive that God is good. We grow better, not bitter. As we find purpose and fulfillment in him. And what does that look like? You know, we sang about it as our first song. Tis so sweet to trust in Jesus, just to take him at his word, just to rest upon his promise, just to know, thus saith the Lord. Jesus, Jesus, how I trust him, how I approved him, o'er and o'er. Jesus, Jesus, precious Jesus, all for grace to trust him more. That's living in God's promises, living in the blessings of faith. And that kind of faith can only be developed in the power of the Spirit. And that leads to our second need, God's Spirit. I find that interesting that in verses 9 to 13 that only the confirmation of the third sign is narrated explicitly. We trust that the first and second signs came to pass that day. I believe the narrator wanted to emphasize here Saul's transformation. And what the scripture emphasizes, we too should highlight. Every leader, king, ruler, take note Not by might, nor by power, but by his spirit This third sign was also distinct from others in that observers recognized the Spirit's influence over Saul. This came as a surprise to friends and acquaintances. They knew Saul as the son of Kish. They knew about the group of prophets, but they found it strange to see the two come together. So mockley was this crew that someone asks, who is their father? Father here is the title of mentor or teacher. Just as Elijah was for Elisha, or there was a leader among the musicians, you can read about that in 1 Chronicles 25 and 2 Kings 2. In other words, what sort of leader of prophets would admit an ordinary man like Saul? Well, only God, gracious to give us purpose and fulfillment through his spirit Now we should stop and ask what exactly happened to Saul in this passage. I guess the big question is, was he saved? We know that Saul turned into another man and God gave him another heart. He was even granted the power to prophesy But the rest of the narrative does not give us much confidence that he was justified by faith. He's not cited as a model of faith anywhere. I tend to believe he was not saved, but I'm not hundred percent sure. And so the question is: if Saul was unsaved, how did he have the Holy Spirit? Now we must understand that certain ministries of the Spirit extend to both the saved and the lost. An individual may be empowered simply for an office or a function in corporate Israel. In Numbers 11, God's spirit that rested on Moses was distributed to the 70 elders. I think the 70 elders were saved. But later in the same book, the spirit came upon Balaam of all people to empower him. To speak for God. I don't think Balaam was saved. The Spirit enabled the judges later for service. And then now here the Spirit equipped Saul for kingship. Later in 1 Samuel 16, the Spirit of the Lord would depart from Saul and come upon David, who was already saved, I believe. But anyway, I think dwelling on the topic of individual salvation is missing the point of the narrative. What is certain is that Saul eventually lost his power to be a good king. Somewhere along the way, he's going to forget his need for God. Not by might, nor by power, but by his spirit J. Oswald Sanders says in his classic book, Spiritual Leadership, quote, There is no such thing as a self-made spiritual leader. A true leader influences others spiritually only because the Spirit works in and through him to a greater degree than in those he leads. That's why we pray for leaders, not only for their sake, but for our sake as well. Now back to Saul, who, through the power of the Spirit, spoke words of prophecy. Through the same spirit, he kept his mouth shut about his kingship until the right time, I believe. That is God's timing. Compared to all that took place from the beginning of this chapter, verses 14 to 16 appear relatively insignificant. It's a rather ordinary conversation between Saul and his uncle, whom David Sumura guesses is Abner, the future commander of Israel's army. Abner seems to perk up hearing Samuel's name. Perhaps he at this point was eager for glory to raise the prominence of his family to national fame. Whether Saul was nervous or wise, we're not certain. Either way, he hides the matter of the kingdom until Samuel breaks the news publicly. Just a quick application here. Waiting in the wings for God's timing is crucial for lasting and true purpose and fulfillment. Abraham waited twenty-five years for the promised son. Joseph spent his youth, late teens and his twenties, as a slave, as a prisoner. Moses was 40 when he left Egypt and he spent another 40 years in the wilderness before fulfilling his purpose. Joshua and Caleb waited 40 years to enter the promised land. David had a target on his back for a long time before he became king. Most importantly, our Lord Jesus waited until he was about 30 years old, getting baptized and beginning his ministry, spending many obscure years. In an obscure city, in an obscure region. Can we wait for God's timing Now, Saul didn't have to wait very long, and that leads to his fourth need, God's promotion. Now God's promotion of Saul as king comes with a bit asterisk or caveat. Even though Saul is destined to rule over Israel, God is most qualified to rule. And just look for just look what he did for them from the time of Exodus until now. He brought up Israel out of Egypt and delivered them from their oppressors. Yet, they have rejected God, their Savior. And they have chosen a lesser Savior. Israel got their final warning. Now, from the second half of verse 19 to the end of verse 21, there is a selection of the king by lot. Two quick observations about this. First, this casting of Lod was a necessary formality to publicly identify the one God has chosen. Samuel knew, Saul knew, and we the readers knew or know the outcome because God has previously revealed it. Now the people will be assured that the selection is according to God's will. And whether God reveals in advance or not, we lean on the truth of Proverbs 16:33. The lot is cast into the lap, but it's every decision is from the Lord. The other observation Fowler makes the keen observation that this process of elimination, tribe by tribe, family by family, all the way to the individual, looks a lot like what happened in Joshua chapter 7. You may recall from there that the Israelites suffered a humiliating defeat against the city of Ai. That's because just prior to this, a man named Achan surreptitiously took the accursed things of Jericho. God was angry with Israel for the foolish choice of one man. And he was brought forward. Now God is again angry with Israel for their foolish choice of one man as king. And he is brought forward. The people made their choice, and Saul must now fulfill his purpose in history. But he doesn't step into his role with fanfare. He's found hidden among the equipment. We're not sure exactly why he shied away from the spotlight, whether it was humility or fear. We don't really know. Perhaps he wasn't excited to take on a role that's doomed to fail from the beginning. Regardless, he displayed a healthy amount of reluctance and distance from power. At this point, at least, Saul focused more on God's promotion than human promotion Of course the people just wanted him on stage and focused on his tangibles, his height, appearance. Do we patiently seek God's promotion for purpose and fulfillment in life? Personality-wise, Saul wasn't what you call a goal-getter. We may have a hard time relating to him because he because in the so-called real world We don't climb to the top without a certain mindset or attitude. But at this specific time, for this specific role of king, everyone wants in place of God. I think it was wise for Saul to tread carefully. We too would be wise by not seizing every opportunity and running through every open door. Starting up every conversation. You know, these days, Saul's reluctance and hesitation would do us good, especially in the realm of politics. I won't go there. Such wisdom and patience will serve Saul in the long run. And that leads to our fifth need: God's approval. God's approval is so vital for meaning, for purpose, fulfillment That's because the approval of men is not reliable. Sure, Saul must have felt an adrenaline rush as he heard the people shouting, Long live the king! He even had godly and valiant men pledging their loyalty to him. But tough times and tensions will come Already there were those who questioned this leadership. It's hard being a leader. Saul would need to seek stability in God's approval, not the shifting opinions of men. To help, Samuel explained the behavior of royalty This is likely a written agreement outlining the expectations of each party, clarifying the relationship between the king and his subject. The document probably included references to passages like Deuteronomy 17, 14 to 20, and even the recent behavior of the king from chapter 8. Will all the lessons Saul learned thus far, and this written reminder of his duty be enough? Will Saul focus on God's approval to find purpose and fulfillment. For now, yes, we see him resisting the urge to avenge himself against his naysayers. As application, we too can resist the urge to live for the approval of men by living for the approval of God. Meditate on Galatians 1:10. For do I now persuade men or God? Or do I seek to please men? For if I still please men, I would not be a bondservant of Christ. True lasting purpose and fulfillment are found in being a bondservant of Christ, living for his approval for the audience of one. As his servants, we find purpose and fulfillment in the Lord. In his confirmation, in his spirit, timing, promotion, approval Purpose and fulfillment are not found in education or career. Paul was taught by the best in Jerusalem. At the feet of Gamaleel. He advanced in Jerusalem, I mean I'm sorry, Judaism, beyond many of his contemporaries, more exceedingly zealous for the traditions of his fathers. But where did that lead him? Enmity against God Himself, Jesus Christ. Without the gracious calling and the revelation of Jesus Christ, He would have been lost. After being saved, he counted all things lost, his education and career included. For the excellence of the knowledge of Christ Jesus the Lord, he counted all things as rubbish, that he may gain Christ. Purpose and fulfillment are not found in wealth or status. Moses, when he became of age, refused to be called a son of Pharaoh's daughter. Unsatisfied, he chose rather to suffer affliction with his people, the people of God, than to enjoy the passing pleasures of sin.
