So Samuel's gentle approach is not working. Time for a more direct approach. He cuts Saul off in verse 16 and cuts to the chase. To get the prideful king to end the eagle trip, the prophet takes him back to his humble beginnings Saul needed a reminder that it was the Lord who anointed him, king over Israel, to be head over the tribes. It was the Lord who sent him on a mission and gave clear instructions. It was the voice of the Lord that Saul rejected. It was the sight of the Lord he should care for most. Another chance to repent, a chance to accept responsibility, another squandered opportunity. Saul's response is a mishmash of distorted half-truths. When it comes to the voice of the Lord, he has selective hearing. Yeah, he went on the mission, but it was not complete. He contradicts himself as he admits he spared the Amalekite king and then says in the same breath, I have utterly destroyed the Amalekites. Perhaps he started fumbling his words as he caught the hard and stern gaze of Samuel. He resorts to blame shifting in verse 21. Basically saying, Samuel, I did my part. It's the people. They spared the spoils, but at least they had good intentions. Saul's conscience has been so seared with poor choices, and his spirit so callous with arrogance. That God's voice no longer got his attention. He needed to understand the gravity of his sin. And that leads to the third principle. Disobedience is underrated as sin. Here's what I mean. Saul didn't take his sin seriously enough. I'll return to verse 22 later, but let's look at verse 23 for now. It's supposed to give a give him a shock. The king has to be taught that his rebellion is just as bad as witchcraft, and his stubbornness is just as bad as idolatry. Does that shock you? The Bible is filled with passages that tell us that all disobedience is disobedience. Whether it's sin of the heart or deed, sin of omission or commission, sin of thought or talk Complete or partial. Jesus warned that a lustful look is tantamount to adultery in the heart. Unjust explosive anger is deserving of hellfire. We may minimize or justify our pet sins while maximizing and condemning the sins of others. We may ignore the plank over our eyes while reaching for the speck in someone else's. Matt Smethurst, a Christian writer, wrote this the other day, quote. An immature person pursues a PhD in other sins while settling for a GED grasp of their own. That's what Saul is, an immature person. He did a good job of expelling mediums and spiritists out of the land. But he did not expel rebellion and stubbornness out of his life. He has rejected God's word, so he is rejected as Israel's king. Another humiliating moment for Saul. Back in chapter 13, verses 13 to 14, Samuel told Saul that he has lost his dynasty. Here, Samuel tells Saul that he has lost his kingship. He's no longer useful as a ruler. Commentator R. P. Gordon diagnoses the fallen king's spiritual condition. Quote: Saul is dead while he still lives. So then Saul's confession in verse twenty four rings hollow He was not truly repentant of his transgression, his fear of man, his sin. He was more interested in saving faith before the people than saving fate before the Lord. Samuel sees to the Pasad and initially refuses to accompany him back to worship. Compromise, pride, disobedience. Saul got into this mess because he refused to listen to God's voice. What is the Lord speaking to you today? David Samura observes, quote, Ironically, Saul became king because of the voice of the people asking for a king. Now he is rejected because he listened to the voice of the people. This irony, this tragedy here. Do you listen to God's voice? Or do you listen to the voice of the people? Saul's tragic end is determined because we know from the Bible the fourth and final principle. Judgment always follows sin. Every choice has a consequence, and that's what Samuel teaches as a rebuking prophet. Saul tried desperately to hold on to his power, but he was left clutching a torn piece of robe. With a prophetic wit, Samuel says, The Lord has torn the kingdom of Israel from you today. And has given it to a neighbor of yours who is better than you. God's judgment here is certain. There's no changing his mind because God is not like Saul, weak in leadership. He is the strength of Israel. Men fail in truth. God does not lie. Even the best rulers second guess themselves. The Lord is relentless. But even if God is unmoving, Samuel isn't. Samuel gives into Saul's pleas in verses 30 and 31 Now the seer is in no mood to worship and celebrate with Saul, but perhaps he did not want to cause widespread panic or rumors by his conspicuous absence. Also, Samuel could follow the trail of the king of Israel, or the rejected king of Israel, to find the king of Amalek. The rebuking prophet is forced to take up the sword to play the part of the executing king. He finishes the job that Saul didn't finish. Judgment always follows sin. Agac could not avoid the bitterness of death. Agag is properly executed, but the judgment of Saul lingers. Samuel as the kingmaker cannot be friendly with Saul anymore. Because he's fired basically and his replacement is on the way. Just a technical note. The first sentence in verse thirty-five and And Samuel went no more to see Saul until the day of his death shall be understood as this. Samuel never again formally met with Saul in a cooperative relationship. That has to be the case because they act they do actually see each other later in chapter nineteen, verse twenty-four, but it's that's not a formal cooperative meeting. For now Samuel returns home to Rama and he plays the part of a burdened pastor. From our vantage point, we may say good riddance to Saul. Samuel, however, grieves for the rejected king and Saul's rejection of God. We all need to learn from this example. How much do we mourn over those in our lives who walk away from the Lord? This should be the emotional burden of every pastor, every Christian parent, every Christian sibling, every Christian friend, and every neighbor with unsaved persons in his or her life. Let's take the names of the lost to the Lord in prayer, both in private and corporately at our prayer meetings. And we pray to God because He is the one who saves We have confidence that the gospel of Jesus Christ is what saves us from compromise, pride, disobedience, and judgment, which is taught in this chapter. This chapter isn't just about Saul's failure. It's about our failures. We're thankful that Jesus saves us. But how did Jesus exactly save us? Now let's go back to verse 22 for a moment and reread it Has the Lord as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices as in obeying the voice of the Lord? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice and to heed. Than the fat of rams. Hope you commit that to memory. It's a timeless lesson. And this is a lesson that David, the next king of Israel, knew. And we can see that this is something that he truly believed in based on Psalm 40, verse 6 to 8. These are David's words. Sacrifice and offering you did not desire. My ears you have opened. Burnt offering and sin offering you did not require. Then I said, Behold, I come. In the scroll of the book it is written of me. I delight to do your will, O my God, and your law is within my heart. Pretty impressed, right? Like David knows much better than Saul. But even David could not obey God and his will perfectly. In fact, no human in history could until a descendant of David, Jesus came. Jesus valued obedience even before he came to earth because he is the eternal Son of God Jesus valued obedience above animal sacrifices, just as David did in Psalm 40. Jesus valued obedience so much that he obediently gave what was most valuable. His own life. Jesus offered his own body on the cross to take away sins, one offering once for all. What priest after priest could not accomplish, sacrificing countless sheep and oxen. Jesus did by himself with his obedient self-sacrifice, making provision for forgiveness of sin and cleansing. We can read all about this in the book of Hebrews, especially chapter 10. When Jesus rose from the dead, he proved his obedient offering was accepted by God the Father. He ascended to heaven and he will return one day to judge all. Now is the time to respond in repentance and faith. Admit that like Saul you have compromised. You have been proud. You have disobeyed God's voice and listened to the voice of the world, the people. You realize now that judgment follows sin. Turn away from your sins and repentance and turn to Christ by faith. Trust in him and his and his perfect obedience We've all messed up and there's nothing we can do to reverse our past to cleanse away our sins. But Jesus never messed up and he offers salvation for all time. For those who are already saved, may the obedience and sacrifice of our Lord Jesus motivate you. Having understood the good news, I exhort you as Paul did in Romans 12:1. I beseech you, therefore, brethren, by the mercies of God, that you present your bodies a living sacrifice. holy, acceptable to God, which is your reasonable service. As we observe the Lord's Suffer, I invite you to revisit the cross where Jesus suffered. Be amazed at his obedience. Be grateful for his sacrifice Made a profound gratitude. Need you to live for him. Let's pray. Lord, we read your word And your spirit convicts us in these fallen kings and fallen rulers, and even saints who stumble, But we see our own sinfulness on display. Lord, there may be a tendency in us to underestimate. Or to think less of our sin, of our compromise, of our pride, of our disobedience, of the judgment that follows sin. But Lord, may we take the words, the prophetic words, seriously. That it was because of our disobedience Because of our ignorance and stubbornness and rebellion, that your son had to come and die for us. Lord, as we spend time reflecting on these things, where we meditate May we be grateful. May we be motivated to live more for you from that great gratitude. Pray all these things in Jesus Christ's name.

sermons.title: Path of Discipleship
sermons.speaker: Sung Cho
sermons.text: In 1904 and 1905, a rich recent high school grad named William Borden was treated to a trip around the world. He saw Asia, the Middle East, and Europe. But during the trip, he felt the burden for the lost and the hurting and expressed the desire to be a missionary. A friend responded in disbelief, lamenting that Bill would throw away his future. It's reported that the young William wrote on the back of his Bible two words. No reserves. As a recent graduate of Yale University, William had before him some high-paying job offers. But though he came from a rich family, he had no greed for money. It's reported that he wrote on the back of his Bible two more words. No retreats. Bill finished his graduate studies at Princeton, where he committed his life to evangelize the Muslims in China. Next, he gave away half a million dollars and left for Egypt in his 26th year to learn Arabic. Within a few months, he contracted cerebral meningitis in Cairo. As the story has it, prior to his passing, the young man wrote two more words on the back of his Bible. Underneath, no reserves, no retreats, no regrets. Can we say the same when it comes to our devotion to Jesus Many are concerned about the political decision 2020, but I may ask whether you made any significant spiritual decisions this year, this year for the Lord. Today we take a break from 1 Samuel and shift back to the New Testament to resume our studies in the Gospel of Luke. Before we read today's passage, which is chapter 9, 51 to 62, let's review what happened earlier in this chapter. Jesus has been in public ministry for some time now. He has the end in sight, and he's been giving a lot of attention to his twelve apostles. He sends them out in a sort of a on-the-job training, granting them power and authority over all demons and to cure diseases. But having apostolic authority wasn't as important as having faith Can they trust the Lord when they're without provisions, whether it's out on the road or out in the deserted place? Their faith needed a lot of work. To grow their faith, they needed to truly understand who Jesus is and what it means to follow him. Peter, as their spokesperson, correctly identified Jesus as the Christ of God, so they had the right profession of faith. But do they have the right progression of faith? After all, Jesus said: if anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow me. The disciples needed the strength of faith to endure suffering from Jesus. They needed eyes of faith to behold the glory of Christ. They needed a humble faith to be childlike and lowly as their master. Indeed, Jesus gave them a perfect example to follow. He didn't just prepare classroom lectures, he showed them real-life demonstrations. He talked the talk and then walked the walk. Jesus didn't just talk about going to the cross, he went to the cross. So, Luke combined both the talk and the walk. He records Jesus' journey from Galilee to Jerusalem and many of his teachings, lessons, and parables on the way. In a large central section, portion of the book, from chapter 9, verse 51 to chapter 19, verse 27. This section is often called the travel narrative, and it's one of the salient features of Luke. Much of the material in this section will show what it means to follow Jesus as Jesus follows the Father's will. So let's begin with the first few verses of this central section, chapter nine, verse fifty-one to sixty-two. Now it came to pass when the time had come for him to be received up that he steadfastly set his face to go to Jerusalem. and sent messengers before his face. And as they went, they entered a village of the Samaritans to prepare for him. But they did not receive him because his face was set for the journey to Jerusalem And when his disciples, James and John, saw this, they said, Lord, do you want us to command fire to come down from heaven and consume them, just as Elijah did? But he turned and rebuked them and said, You do not know what manner of spirit you are of. For the Son of Man did not come to destroy men's lives, but to save them. And they went to another village. Now it happened as they journeyed on the road that someone said to him, Lord, I will follow you wherever you go. And Jesus said to him, Foxes have holes and birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head. Then he said to another, Follow me. But he said, Lord, let me first go and bury my father. Jesus said to him, Let the dead bury their own dead, but you go and preach the kingdom of God. And another also said, Lord, I will follow you, but let me first go and bid them farewell, who are at my house. But Jesus said to him, No one, having put his hand to the plow and looking back, is fit for the kingdom of God. A good way to divvy up this passage is to look at the four conversations Disciples James and John, that's one in verses 51 to 56, and three more corresponding to three would-be disciples in verses 57 to 62. Notice how at each conversation Jesus is addressed as Lord, but do they really understand what it means to relate to Jesus as Lord? And how about us? Since we don't commonly use this word in our society, we need Jesus to teach us what it really means to say Jesus is Lord. So let's listen to him from this passage. As Lord Jesus teaches us four discipleship principles. One Respond to rejection with mercy. Two, expect hardships, three, follow urgently, and four, maintain focus First, respond to rejection with mercy. We begin the travel narrative of Luke with Jesus' keen sense of timing, his Acknowledgement of his destiny. The words time for him to be received up are referring to Jesus' eventual ascension to heaven. To be received of is a noun here in verse 51. And not surprisingly, its verb counterpart is found three times in Acts chapter 1, verse 2, 11, and 22. But reception into heaven meant rejection on earth. The glory road goes to Gogoth. To cross over to the other side, he must face the cross. He did not settle for the path of least resistance. He went through the path of most resistance. Our Lord did not cower from this road. He charged with a confident stride and head forward. He steadfastly set his face to go to Jerusalem. And this reminds us of Ezekiel and his difficult ministry with the people. God had to strengthen him for that. We read in Ezekiel 3, verses 8 to 9. Behold, I have made your face strong against their faces, and your forehead strong against their foreheads. Like Adam and stone, harder than flint. I am made your forehead. Do not be afraid of them, nor be dismayed at their looks, though they are a rebellious house. Prophetic stubbornness matches and surpasses people's stubbornness This determination is what Jesus as the servant of the Lord needed. If you have your Bibles, turn with me andor look later at Isaiah 50. Verses four to nine. So God grants his son there not only the tongue of the learned to speak a word in season to him who is weary. Not only an awakened and open ear, but he grants his son a face like Flint to face the suffering ahead. Verses 6 to 7 show us vividly what's to come in Jerusalem. I gave my back to those who struck me, and my cheeks to those who plucked out the beard. I did not hide my face from shame and spitting. For the Lord God will help me. Therefore, I will not be disgraced. Therefore, I have set my face like a flint, and I know that I will not be ashamed. See now I need to park here to proclaim this gospel truth. The reason that our Lord gave his back, his cheek, and his face to such mistreatment. is to save us. He, the Son of God, came from heaven to earth. As the Son of Man, he went from Galilee to Jerusalem. He was resolute about the solution to sin. And though we, as simple humans, caused the problem, ruined ourselves. And we should be the one to suffer. Jesus lovingly suffered in our place at the cross, rose from the dead, and he was received up into heaven. Now he waits the day of his return to judge all mankind. And he's also waiting for you to turn away from your sins and turn to him for salvation. He offers you eternal life as a gift, not by works. Come to Jesus by faith. And follow him so that like him you too may be received up into heaven. Okay, now back to Luke 9 Jesus sends messengers ahead of him to announce his arrival. Now this wasn't the first time our Lord encountered Samaritans. In fact, he had a divine appointment with them in Sakar, according to John chapter 4. It went from a conversation with the woman at the well to many believing Jesus and even him staying with them for a few days. The village the messengers entered here is probably not the same city, but there's no reason they shouldn't welcome Jesus, except they wouldn't welcome Jesus. What gives? Knowing some background on the Samaritans can help us. See Marvin Pate comments, quote The origin of the Samaritan people seemed to have been intermarrying of Jews from the Northern Kingdom with imported non-Jewish colonists from after the conquest of 722 BC. That's in 2 Kings 17. These mixed Jews Gentiles developed their own translation of the Pentateuch. That's the first five books of the Bible, called the Samaritan Pentateuch, built their own temple of worship on Mount Gerizim. is talked about in John 420, which was later destroyed by John Hyrcanus in 128 BC. And they celebrated their own Passover. End quote. So maybe the Samaritans initially thought that Jesus was here to legitimize their separate existence, religion, and lifestyle. Our Lord had no such intentions. In fact, later in the book of Acts, he would make sure Samaritan Christians submit to Jerusalem church. Here, as unconverted people, they were not ready for that. The Samaritans could not stand the fact that Jesus was just Passing through, not stopping to settle with them. His real mission is in Jerusalem. Not getting the hospitality and the warm welcome Jesus deserved. James and John wanted to command fire to come down from heaven and consume them, just as Elijah did. And perhaps you read these words and appreciate their passion. Who doesn't like passion? They were living up to the name Jesus gave them, sons of thunder. But James and John got carried away with their emotions. They wanted to imitate Elijah in 2 Kings 1, that time when fire from heaven twice consumed the wicked king's men. They wanted to make Sodom and Gomorrah out of the Samaritans. They wanted instant and immediate justice. Sadly, the power and authority James and John received at the beginning of this chapter, the power to heal the suffering, they would rather employ to cause suffering. You know, except for one time with the fig tree, Jesus never performed a destructive miracle. And he was not about to let some hot-headed brothers in his group perform one. James and John have to learn that mercy, not vengeance, is the way of the master. The spirit of revenge they harbored was not from the spirit of Jesus. The spirit came upon Jesus to preach the gospel to the poor. To heal the brokenhearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives and recovery of sight to the blind, to set at liberty those who are oppressed, to proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord. The spirit that came upon the Zebedee was nothing like that. It was bad news. It broke, it not healed. It enslaves, not liberates. It blinds, not illuminates. As James warns us, the wrath of man does not produce the righteousness of God. The sons of thunder came to destroy men's lives, not save them. The Son of Man did not come to destroy men's lives, but to save them. Can we follow Jesus' example? Can we respond to rejection with mercy? There will be ample opportunities for the world to provoke us. Our views on family and marriage will be under attack eventually. Don't expect hospitality and warm welcome from those who consider our values bigoted. What will our response be? Of course, we need to prepare for the worst actions against us, but we also need to prepare for the worst reactions from us. That simple reaction is a quick reflex of wrath, vengeance, and unrighteous anger. Respond to rejection with mercy. As Jesus commanded back in chapter 6, love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, bless those who curse you, and pray for those who spitefully use you. As Jesus preached on the mount, blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy. As we move on from the Samaritan, there's another type of quick reflex that we should be concerned about Pastor Ray Fowler calls the next encounter in verses 57 and 58, the roadblock of hasty commitment. And that leads to the second point: expect hardships. Jesus and his followers leave the Samaritans and go another route. Along the way, Jesus encounters three unnamed men in quick succession. The first one comes up to Jesus and declares, Lord, I will follow you wherever you go. And Jesus said to him, Boxes have holes and birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head D. A. Carson explains this poetic reply: In the immediate context of Jesus' ministry, the saying does not mean that Jesus was penniless, but homeless. The nature of his mission kept them on the move and would keep his followers on the move. Such physical instability is just one of many hardships that await the faithful disciple. But be assured a hardship for Jesus' sake is a privilege. Meditate on Paul's words in Philippians 1:29-30. For to you it has been granted on behalf of Christ not only to believe in him, but also to suffer for his sake. Having the same conflict which you saw in me and now here is in me. So you have two divine gifts: the gift of believing in Christ. And the gift of suffering for Christ, expect hardships And don't let prosperity theology preachers tell you otherwise. They will tell you that if your faith is strong, you will not have pain in this life. I wouldn't touch that with a 10-foot pole. As application, if you happen to turn to a cable channel called Trinity Broadcast Network, you shouldn't assume every program there is safe. I mean some are fine. I saw names like Bill and Gloria Gaither, Greg Lori, David Jeremiah, Veggie Tales. That's a weird list. But I also saw names like Creplow Dollar, Joe Austin, T. D. Jakes, and Bethelmusic. Unless some dramatic repentance took place recently, and I didn't hear about it, I would probably avoid these ministries. They seem generally to overlook or misunderstand passages of hardship like this one. After the first unnamed man goes away, Jesus recruits another. The second man's response and Jesus' reply demonstrates the third principle. Follow urgently. There are some different interpretations of the man's response: Lord, let me first go bury my father. One option is that the father just died, so the man needs some time to grieve. This seems unlikely. If his father just died, why is he out here talking with Jesus right now? Shouldn't he be with others grieving and arranging the funeral? Another option is that the father was sick and on the verge of death. Commentator John Martin wonders whether this man wanted to secure his inheritance before following Jesus This is an intriguing option, but here's the same criticism. If the father was about to die, why is he here? A third option, and I think it's the best one, is that the father was simply elderly and not necessarily about to die right away. The son felt that his filial duty was to stay with him until his passing, whenever that may be. His words may sound pious, but it disguises either fear or double-mindedness. Whatever the underlying reason may be, it's clear he lacked the urgency to follow Jesus. He did not prioritize the kingdom of God enough to go and preach it. Being a follower of Jesus means shifting priorities. No, I mean, in a few months, my wife and I will have to shift priorities for our son. How much more for the Son of God? Your secular work and boss demand you adjust your schedule. How much more your kingdom work and Lord? Accordingly, Jesus' reply, let the dead bury their own dead, shall be understood in the following way: Let the spiritually dead bury their physically dead. Let the spiritually dead bury their physically dead. The kingdom of earth groups humanity between the physically alive and the physically dead. The kingdom of heaven groups humanity as either spiritually alive in Christ or spiritually dead in trespasses and sins. If you're spiritually alive, the world has been crucified to you and you to the world. If you're spiritually alive, you belong to God's kingdom. If you're spiritually alive, you have a spiritual family. And Jesus, he's the ultimate patriarch in the household of God. More important than the patriarch in the household of man Jesus' name supersedes surnames. You belong to Jesus Christ. And he can make radical demands because he is Lord. Because he is King. Because he is God. So are we following urgently? To those with living parents, please know that following Christ urgently is the best way to honor them. Jesus himself honored parents best. He was obedient to his own, Joseph and Mary. He condemned the hypocritical use of tradition to bypass the sixth commandment, as in Matthew 15. He made sure his mother had a caretaker as she grew older and he departed. And while doing all that, he accomplished the will of his heavenly father. I've learned from Christ that the best way to honor my living mother and my late father's name is to honor his name. Of course, urgently reconfiguring priorities requires wisdom, prayer, and counsel. As we consider specific application, let us maintain focus, which is the fourth principle. Joseph Fitzmeier observes this about the final unnamed man in this chapter, quote: The third follower resembles the first in that he spontaneously offers to be a disciple. But also the second one in that he adds a condition. Later he says, plowing for the kingdom means sacrifice. It can tolerate no distractions. Following Jesus means devotion to kingdom work and transcends even ordinary family affection. Sacrifice, no distractions. We must maintain our focus on Jesus. And if we pay close attention to Jesus, we may notice how his mention of the plough harkens back to another incident in Elijah's life. In 1 Kings 19, God commanded Elijah to look for his successor and anoint him. Turned out to be a man named Elisha, the son of Shapat. Elijah found Elisha while ploughing with 24 oxen, which indicates his rich family background. But Elisha left all that behind to pursue his prophetic calling. Yet as he left his home, he made a request to Elijah. Please let me kiss my father and my mother, and then I will follow you. Elijah not only grants this proper farewell, he allows a parting feast. Like Elisha and unlike the previous guy, this third man was willing to follow Jesus almost immediately, but even almost immediately is not good enough. Not when it is following Jesus. Focusing on Jesus meant letting going, letting go of the peripheral. To keep the straightway, one must not be sidetracked by the wayside. R. Ken Hughes provides a helpful summary or commentary. Quote: It was proverbial in ancient culture. Now one could not look back while ploughing and drive a straight furrow. Those who pine after what they left behind, who are always remembering the comforts of home and hurt. Who dream about how life might have been if they had not stepped onto the road with Jesus, who keep looking in the rare view mirror, will not do well on Jesus' road. If we're honest with ourselves, we fail to run the race while looking on to Jesus. We're like Lot's wife. Like Peter who began to sink. We remember, not forget those things which are behind. We reach backwards instead of reaching forward to those things which are ahead. We often fail to maintain our focus on Jesus. And we can review the other principles in this passage, the three principles. Are we following Christ urgently? We may announce, Lord, I will follow you wherever you go, but then we never go anywhere because of hardships. When we face rejection from the world, we lose patience and retaliate with anger. We may call Jesus Lord, but often do not understand fully what it means to follow Him as Lord. Thankfully, our Lord Jesus is merciful. For those here who think that you have to be perfect to follow Jesus, be assured that none of us follow Jesus perfectly. But as Paul testified, the grace of our Lord is exceedingly abundant. We fall and he picks us up again. We stray and he leads us in the path of righteousness for his name's sake. We're prone to wander, yet he never forsakes us, never deceives us. Whatever my God ordains is right. He never will deceive me. He leads me by the proper path. I know he will not lead me. Let's follow this path in faith this week and the rest of our lives. No reserves, no retreats, no regrets. Let's pray. Lord, we see these demands that your son makes of us. And made thousands of years ago, we traversed the old paths of your word And we hear your son beckoning us to follow him. Lord, we confess that we fail. Like John and James, where we don't understand what it means to follow the way of your son. We rather blow up in anger. But we don't know what we're getting ourselves into with the hardships that follow. No, we often put our spiritual lives on the back burner and not follow urgently. No, we're so distracted By what's on the media? We're so distracted by lesser things, shadows, things that are not as important Lord, you speak to us through your word. May you challenge us. May you convict us. May you transform us so that we would follow you. That your spirit would empower us to fulfill the Great Commission, to go to places Where we would ordinarily in our own human strength would be fearful to go to. And we're thankful that your son is with us Your spirit is with us, and we are not abandoned. Pray all these things in Christ's name. Amen.

sermons.title: The Seventy Sent Out
sermons.speaker: Sung Cho
sermons.text: The evangelization of the world in this generation That is the call of the late 19th-century student volunteer movement. Robert Wilder and his sister Grace saw firsthand the dire spiritual needs of India. And they dare to pray for a thousand missionaries to emerge from American colleges and universities. It started with Sunday afternoon studies of foreign missions with five fellow students at their home. With the help of D. L. Moody, the movement grew to hundreds. It soon grew to thousands, with names like John Mott, Samuel Dwimmer, and Robert Speer added to the list. By the 20th century, there were tens of thousands. In the twenty-first century, can we take up the rallying call again? The evangelization of the world in this generation. You might be skeptical Even if we replicate the student volunteer movement, you've got to be thinking, really? The evangelization of the entire world in one generation. One stat I found read that the world population was 1. 6 billion in 1900, 6 billion in 2000, and close to 7. 8 billion now. We may see these numbers and lukewarm churches all around us and be tempted to despair. We might scoff at the need for thousands of laborers when only few show up to church, let alone go to third world countries for Christ. But our Lord did not change the mission or our objectives Just as we read earlier, we the church have Jesus leading us, the Spirit empowering us, and the Great Commission in front of us. And we turn to passages like today's, Luke chapter 10, verses 1 to 12. So that like Robert and Grace Wilder, We too can dream of worldwide evangelization in this generation. Let's go there now. After these things the Lord appointed seventy others also, and sent them two by two before his face, into every city and place where he himself was about to go. Then he said to them, The harvest truly is great, but the laborers are few. Therefore pray the Lord of harvest to send out laborers into his harvest. Go your way. Behold, I send you out as lambs among wolves. Carry neither money bag, knapsack, nor sandals, and greet no one along the road. But whatever house you enter, first say, peace to this house. And if a son of peace is there, your peace will rest on it. If not, it will return to you. And remain in the same house, eating and drinking such things as they give, for the laborer is worthy of his wages. Do not go from house to house. Whatever city you enter and they receive you, eat such things as are set before you. And he will just sit there and say to them, The kingdom of God has come near to you. But whatever city you enter, and they do not receive you, go out into its streets and say, The very dust of your city which clings to us, we wipe off against you. Nevertheless, know this that the kingdom of God has come near you. But I say to you that it will be more tolerable in the day for Sodom than for that city. Uh before my exposition I have to ask you, have you ever had those deja vu spiritual moments where you keep seeing the same verses, hear the same preaching? And feel the same prompting of the Holy Spirit over and over again. I mean, you might even have two Asian American brothers preaching two sermons on the same passage of Luke in the span of about two months right here from this pulpit on two Sunday mornings. Wait, it's happening right now. You you may recall that on September twenty-seventh, I invited Alex Chen from Campus Outreach. As guest speaker, and he delivered a sermon from Luke chapter 10. I didn't assign him this chapter. I told him about our church's need to grow. And he felt led to share from Luke 10. The sermon was entitled The One and Only Method And his main idea was the redeemed man is God's method for his majesty. I encourage you to go take a listen if you haven't already Because maybe God really, really wants us to meditate on this passage. My main sermon idea is that we must not only follow as Jesus commands us And we talked about that last time. But also go as Jesus sends us. Not only follow as Jesus commands us But also go as Jesus sends us. Principles for The sent disciples are as follows. Go with faith and urgency, verses 1 to 4, 2. Rest with peaceful company, verses 5 to 7. And 3. Proclaim with kingdom authority, verses 8 to 12. First, go with faith and urgency Before explaining this point, there's another deja vu we need to discuss. And if you have your Bible, turn back to Luke chapter 9 and take a look at the first few verses. I'll read them for you. Then he called his twelve disciples together and gave them power and authority over all demons and to cure diseases. He sent them to preach the kingdom of God and to heal the sick, and he said to them, Take nothing for the journey, neither staffs nor bag, nor bread, nor money. And do not have two tunics apiece. Whatever house you enter, stay there, and from there depart. And whoever will not receive you, when you go out of that city, shake off the very dust from your feet as a testimony against them. So they departed and went through the towns preaching the gospel and healing everywhere. See how both Luke 9 and Luke ten begin with Jesus sending out his followers. He gave similar authority and instructions. He expected both sets of delegates to have faith. He prepared both groups of envoys for reception and rejection. An obvious difference is that earlier Jesus sent out the 12 apostles, and here he sends out seventy Some Bible translations have 72 instead of 70, but the lower number is supported by the majority of Greek manuscripts. It's not certain whether the 70 should include the 12 or be distinct. I think the 70 does not include the 12. So why did Jesus pick seventy? There's two major possibilities. One is that Jesus is acting as the new Moses. In the book of Numbers, chapter 11, God grants 70 elders, the same spirit that was on Moses. These men lighten the load of leadership. So perhaps Jesus is also lightening his own load of leadership and forming his own 70 to further his ministry. Another possibility is that Jesus is signaling his future ministry to the nations. Some commentators think that Jesus is making a connection with Genesis chapter 10. Their 70 names are listed in the table of nations Descendants of Noah populating the post-Deluvian world. Here are again 70, but this time for future evangelization of the world. For this end, they are getting some training now. Jesus focused on Israel during his ministry, but as his time on earth came to an end. He prepared more workers for the work to be done among the nations. After all, he is appointed to be a light to the Gentiles and salvation to the ends of the earth. So I prefer this second interpretation of the seventy. But unlike the names of Genesis ten These are unnamed. That's what Alex Chen pointed out for us. These unnamed followers of Jesus are known by him and given this awesome privilege to go and speak on his behalf. Like the twelve as seen in Mark 6:7, the seventy are sent two by two. They go in thirty-five pairs, so that none may despair alone. Also, they can corroborate their testimonies with multiple witnesses. But these guys need more than each other's company They need faith in God. And in verses one and two, we see reasons why they can have such faith. In verse 1, we read that they went where he himself was about to go. And here's Charles Spurgeon's commentary. Quote, what a mercy it is when the preacher knows that his master is coming after him. When he can hear the sound of his master's feet behind him, what courage it gives him. He knows that though it is very little that he can do. He is the thin end of the wedge, preparing the way for one who can do everything. End quote. And that's a great comfort to me. We go, but Jesus is coming behind us. Go with such faith In verse 2, Jesus uses an agricultural illustration to embolden the 70. He announces the harvest is truly great, but the laborers are few. Could you imagine if he said the opposite? The harvest truly is small, but the laborers are great. I mean what hope or encouragement would it be if only a few will respond to the gospel and there are too many messengers? Thankfully, the harvest truly is great. I believe this is still true today. You will never hear from me. There are too many laborers for the kingdom out there. Please don't enter ministry. There's plenty of work to do. You'll never be out of a job as a kingdom worker This is why the 70 prayed, and this verse is the reason that we pray. We pray to the Lord of harvests to send out laborers into his harvest. We're going out to collect what is rightfully his, what is already rightfully his, his harvest. Often soul winning is easy picking because all we need to do is be faithful witnesses, not some fierce debater or world-class apologist with a PhD. The harvest is plenty. Go with such faith The 70 must go with faith, and in verses 3 and 4, we see why they also need to go with urgency. They need to go with urgency because we read in verse 3 that they're sent out like lamb among wolves. I'm sure you've heard plenty of times that sheep are rather helpless creatures. As if that's not enough, the seventy are sent out as young sheep or lambs. We need to walk in faith and run with pace. We need to both trust our shepherd and distrust our foes. As Peter tells us, we must cast cares on God. And we must be careful of the devil. Sleep and rest in the Almighty, and be vigilant and resist the enemy. Go with such urgency. Verse 4 also combines urgency with faith. To carry neither money bag, knapsack, nor sandals requires faith. To greet no one along the road requires urgency. Now such haste may seem cold, but George Morrison observes In this commentary quote, In the East, greetings are so tedious, so full of flattery, so certain to lead on to wayside gossip That men who are out on a work of life and death must run the risk of seeming unsocial sometimes. They needed focus to be followers of Jesus and now they need focus to be laborers of Jesus. Go with such urgency. Even if they don't have time for chit-chat on the road, the somebody must invest in deeper relationships. Relationships with potential for discipleship. In verses 5 to 7, the 70 shifts, I'm sorry, the scenery shifts from outdoor road. To the indoor house. Just so you don't miss it, see how Jesus uses the word house five times in the span of three verses. In this setting, Jesus teaches us the second principle: rest with peaceful company. Besides the multiple occurrences of house, you see peace three times in verses five to six. A nice calm contrast to the wolves and frenetic pace outside. David Guzick Explains Jesus' instructions here. Quote, the customs of that time meant that they would likely stay in the home of hospitable people. Inns, if available, were often houses of prostitution and unsuitable for godly messengers. They were instructed to bring a blessing of peace to each house, if the home would receive it. But what kind of peace is this? Is it Hashalaom, the standard Israelite greeting, and wish for the well-being of others? Is it just people who are nice with calm demeanors? Commentator Joe B. Green thinks it's at minimum that, but far more. Green points to various passages of Luke that teaches us that true peace is rooted in Christ. We find it in chapter 1, 2, 1, 2, 7, 8, 19, 24. I can give you those passages later if you want. Green explains, quote, peace is portrayed not merely as something one might wish for another, but as an entity that can be transmitted and possessed or returned. Inasmuch as peace is the gift of Yahweh, the nature of Jesus' directive is to identify these sent ones as persons capable of extending the peace that is God's to others. Child of peace, that is one whose life is characterized by peace, then, is capable of more than one nuance. It can refer to one who has already begun to embody the wholeness these delegates of Jesus' mission will communicate. Or it can refer to those who are predisposed to welcome these messengers together with their message. So in other words, Green is saying that sons of peace not only accept the greeting of the 70, they are especially and particularly open to the message and the messengers of Christ. All the more reason to stay in their homes as long as possible and accrue relational capital instead of hopping from house to house In this way, Jesus is promoting long-term relational evangelism. I challenge you to be like the 70. Are there individuals, friends, family, neighbors, acquaintances, co-workers who are particularly open to the gospel? Are there sons of peace who may want to hear about the Prince of Peace While you may be busy in your schedule, can you rest with peaceful company in hopes that it will turn into a peaceful fellowship The world is grand, the people numerous, our calendars are full, and our to-do lists lengthy. But perhaps this autumn and winter, as our neighbors and friends are suffering from loneliness and even mental breakdowns, We might try to recreate the homey scene of verses five to seven. Yet the harvest is plenty enough and the world wide enough to evangelize town after town. In verses 8 to 10, we shift the scenery from an enclosed house to the cities where these homes reside. Note the multiple occurrences of the word city. You see it four times in five verses. Another repetition to note is the phrase, the kingdom of God has come near you in verses 9 and 11. It's the same exact phrase in the original Greek. This emphasis on the kingdom leads us to the third principle, proclaim with kingdom authority. This proclamation must be made at whatever city the seventh go and whatever way the citizens respond. One scenario is in verses 8 and 9. They welcome the messengers and show hospitality. With such reception, the members of the 70 are free to heal the sick there and preach the kingdom. Jesus grants power for physical healing in preparation for the spiritual healing. The miracles performed authenticate the message proclaimed. The kingdom of God has come near to you. The other scenario is in verses 10 to 12. They don't welcome the messengers and they don't show hospitality. With such rejection, the members of the 70 must go out into its streets, wipe off the dust off their feet, and preach the kingdom. These cities have rejected the most weighty message ever proclaimed. The kingdom of God has come near you. Now two questions. What does it mean for the kingdom of God to be near? And two, why is the same message presented twice? Now, first, how is it that the kingdom is near? During Jesus' ministry, he and his followers can genuinely say this Because the king and the Messiah was right there in the midst of Israel. And he had the authority to establish the kingdom. When the king's around, the kingdom is not far away. But what about the centuries that followed? Now almost 2,000 years later, can we still say God's kingdom is near? Back in May, while we were studying Revelation 1, 1 to 3, I cited a commentator named Alan Johnson. And he said, quote, the church in every age has always lived with the expectancy of the consummation of all things in its day. Iminency describes an event possible any day, impossible no day. Possible any day. Impossible no day. Even to us, the coming of the kingdom is near and imminent because it's an event possible any day, and impossible no day. So even if we're not sure when that day may be, we can assuredly proclaim today the kingdom of God has come near you. So proclaim this message with kingdom authority. The other question is: why is the same message presented twice? Shouldn't we change our message if they reject us? Shouldn't we try something different if they are indifferent? Absolutely not. We don't change the message because God doesn't change. Whether people accept the gospel or not, the kingdom is coming. This is good news for the saved, but bad news for the unsaved. The message of the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved, it is the power of God. There's one gospel, and we as Christ's followers spread his fragrance to two very different receptions To the one, we are the aroma of death leading to death, and to the other, the aroma of life leading to life. Though their reactions are two and different, our message must be one and the same. So proclaim this truth with kingdom authority. Individuals and cities who accept this truth have reasons to rejoice. When the prophesied day of judgment, the day of the Lord arrives. In that day the lofty looks of man shall be humble, the haltiness of men shall be bowed down, and the Lord alone shall be exalted In that day the branch of the Lord shall be beautiful and glorious, and the fruit of the earth shall be excellent and appealing for those of Israel who have escaped. In that day, every man shall throw away his idols of silver and his idols of gold, sin which your own hands have made for yourselves. What a glorious day for followers of Christ! But see how that same day looks so different to the unsaved. Individuals and cities who reject God's truth have reasons to mourn when the day of the Lord arrives. It will come as destruction from the Almighty. The day of the Lord is cruel, with both wrath and fierce anger, to lay the land desolate. And he will destroy his sinners from it. The day of the Lord is great and awesome and very terrible and dreadful. Darkness, not light, bitter noise. It is the day of the Lord's vengeance and anger. In that day the heavens will pass away with a great noise, and the elements will melt with fervent heat. Both the earth and the works that are in it will be burnt up. As Jesus says in verse 12, the fire that destroys Sodom and Gomorrah will seem like nothing compared to the fire of the day of the Lord. So will you face the stay with Christ or against Christ? Will you be born of the Spirit and enter the kingdom of God? Or be cast out into the outer darkness, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth? There's no middle ground. At any moment we can die and be carried away by angels into Abraham's bosom or be in torments and Hades. Either we will be celebrating with the bridegroom, shouting with joy, or be shut out in the dark, shouting in vain. Lord, Lord, open to us. The gospel has been proclaimed to you with kingdom authority. What is your response What will that future day of the Lord look like to you? Are you ready for it? It comes as a thief in the night. If you're not a Christian, please listen carefully. All of us, at one point or another, have resisted and rejected the message of Jesus By nature, we're not sons of peace who welcome God's messengers. We are sons of disobedience. We broke God's laws in our thoughts, words, and actions. So we deserve his wrath. But we can be sons of light and sons of day. Confess that you're a sinner. Repent from selfishness and self-righteousness. Place your confidence in Jesus the Son of God and his works. He came to earth, went to Jerusalem to die on the cross for our sins. Rose from the dead and ascended to heaven. And someday our Lord will return to judge all mankind Will that day be darkness and fire for you? Or will the Son of righteousness arise with healing in his wings? Place your faith in Jesus now before it's too late. You cannot earn the salvation. He gives it to us by grace as a gift. For those of you who have already placed your faith in Jesus Are you living for him as Jesus demanded from the 70? Do you heed the Great Commission and go with faith and urgency, whether it's far or close? Do you rest with peaceful company in hopes that these unsaved people will turn to Christ? Do you proclaim with kingdom authority or shrink under the authority of man? If these questions convict you, if these principles seem impossible, impossible to accomplish in your own strength. If these demands are met with our failures, we know that God gives us grace and the filling of His Spirit to try again If we have responded to the Great Commission with the Great Omission, or twisted it to be the great suggestion, let us repent. Let us be comforted by the great consolation of Jesus. I am with you always, even to the end of the age. Let's dream of worldwide evangelization in this generation. Let's pray Lord, for two thousand years We have seen your plan on display in this world in history as the fullness of Gentiles come in. As we attempt to reach every people, every people group, every tribe, every nation. As long as you tarry, we have work to do here on earth. Lord, there are times when we don't like this agenda. We like to be in our comfort zones Lord, sometimes we feel the temptation to just throw in the towel. I put in my time. I've done my share of ministry. I put in decades and I just like to live for myself now. Lord, is it possible that we are lukewarm? Is it possible that we have lost our first love? Is it possible that our devotions have grown cold? That as the great devotional writer Oswald Chambers said That our spiritual life looks like the Dead Sea, more than the Sea of Galilee, where we receive and receive, but do not give and give. In the waters of blessing that you've given us. Lord, we know that you've given us different relationships and different networks and different neighbors and different family members and all these things. We pray that we we would take your word and apply it, not just in this hour of Service or hour of Bible study or Sunday school. But help us to apply your word in our walks, in our journey, in our encounters with people. May you convict us and empower us by your Spirit. And we're thankful that you are with us. That you do not abandon us, even though like Peter, we may even deny you, or we fail you, and we are not bold in our witness. But we're thankful that you hold us and you protect us and you are patient with us. And we're thankful for your son, who never leaves us Pray all these things in his name. Amen.

sermons.title: The Woeful and the Joyful
sermons.speaker: Sung Cho
sermons.text: When I think about the Southern Gospel singer, songwriter, and comedian Mark Lorie at this time of the year. I usually think of the beautiful and solemn Christmas song that he helps write, Mary Did You Know But this week I was drawn to another song from him. It's called Jesus Laughing. Let me read you the first verse and the chorus. Quote, There's a picture on the wall that brings me comfort. My weary eyes rest on it from time to time. It's a sweet, unique depiction of the Savior. The only one I know, only one, the one I know, quite of its kind. It shows them laughing. Our Lord is laughing, his head thrown back with joy upon his loving face. And for a moment there something happens. I feel at peace just seeing Jesus laughing. Years back, I recall seeing a picture of Jesus laughing myself. Maybe it's the same one, same one that Mark Lorie is singing about. I thought myself that it was sweet and unique. But it was strange to me because I'm so used to picturing Jesus as a man of sorrows. And acquainted with grief. Yet he must have a sense of humor Remember what he said about the plank in your eye and the speck in your brother's eye? I mean, come on, the crowds must have been at least chuckling a little bit. I mean that's Dilbert and Calvin Hobbes level humor. Okay now moving on from laughter and humor, what about joy? Now we're on firmer ground. When asked why his disciples do not fast, Jesus replied, Can the friends of the bridegroom mourn as long as the bridegroom is with them? By implication, our Lord's time on earth with his followers was a happy occasion. Even as he was ready to depart, Jesus left them his teaching so that his joy may remain with them and that their joy may be full. And this is joy which can be taught and learned as we two strive to follow Jesus. I believe we get a glimpse of it in today's passage. Surprisingly, this joy is displayed on the way to the cross. Unexpectedly, this joy comes in the context of rejection. Supernaturally, this joy can be ours in the midst of our own struggles. Let's read Luke ten, thirteen to twenty-four together. Woe to you, Corazon. Woe to you, Baseda. For if the mighty works which were done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented long ago, sitting in sackcloth and ashes. But it will be more tolerable for Tyre and Sidon at the judgment than for you. And you, Capernaum, who are exalted to heaven, will be brought down to Hades He who hears you hears me. He who rejects you rejects me. And he who rejects me rejects him who sent me. Then the seventy returned with joy, saying, Lord, even the demons are subject to us in your name. And he said to them, I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven. Behold, I give you the authority to trample on serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy, and nothing shall by any means hurt you. Nevertheless, do not rejoice in this, that the spirits are subject to you, but rather rejoice because your names are written in heaven. In that hour, Jesus rejoiced in the Spirit and said, I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent. and reveal them to babes. Even so, Father, for so it seems good in your sight. All things have been delivered to me by my Father And no one knows who the Son is except the Father. And who the Father is except the Son. And the one to whom the Son wills to reveal him. Then he turned to his disciples and said privately, Blessed are the eyes which see the things you receive, for I tell you that many prophets and kings have desired to see what you see. and have not seen it, and to hear what you hear and have not heard it. How can we, as believers, have joy as we follow our Lord Jesus? How can we rejoice in the Spirit as He did? From this passage, I believe there are three principles for joy. One, handle rejection with heavenly perspective. That's verses thirteen to sixteen. 2. Rejoice in your salvation, not authority, verses 17 to 20. And three, appreciate the blessings of divine revelation, verses 21 to 24. First, handle rejection with heavenly perspective. When Jesus sent out The seventy and the twelve before that, he fully expected them to face rejection in various cities. Nevertheless, they were to remain steadfast in their kingdom message. They were to shake the dust off their feet to demonstrate their separation from them. Jesus told them in verse 12, it will be more tolerable in that day for Sodom than for that city. I'm guessing most of us do not want to face rejection. There's plenty to go around in this world. It might be rejection at the high school basketball team trial as your name's not listed among those invited back the following day. It might be rejection from your longtime crush as you see her date one of your friends instead. It might be rejection after your job interview As you receive that letter that reads something like, we regret to inform you. I might be using examples from my own life right now. Life is already full of rejections. And being a follower of Christ invites more. And all I want to do is hide away in my shell like a therapin. But as we see here and elsewhere, Jesus did not require of us what he himself did not face. He named specific cities where he performed great wonders, yet they did not receive him, save a few individuals. During Jesus' ministry, he concentrated most of his efforts on predominantly Jewish-populated cities and villages near the Sea of Galilee. On its northern side, he made Capernaum his base of operations. In this city, Jesus exercised an unclean spirit from a man in their synagogue. He healed Peter's mother-in-law, who had a fever, a paralytic, a centurion servant, and a nobleman's son from a distance. A few miles north of Capernaum was Corazon, and a few miles east of Corazon was Besseda. We don't have records of specific miracles from Khorazin, but in Bethsaida, we know that Jesus healed a blind man. He also fed the 5,000 near that city. I'm sure there are many other unrecorded miracles, as John says as he closes his gospel. You would think that with all these miracles, Jesus would have droves of Jews following him. But no, people of Khorazan and Beth Seda did not respond in faith. Even though they knew about the coming Messiah. If instead Tyre and Sidon, predominantly Gentile cities, filled with people who knew far less about the Messiah, saw the same miracles. They would have trusted Jesus. You would think that with Jesus making Capernaum his new home, it would be teleported straight into heaven. But no, they didn't convert to Christ in Mass, so instead it will be brought down to Hades. Again, Jesus did not require of us what he himself did not face. He understood rejection. Our Lord was the servant of Yahweh, who was despised and rejected by men of his generation. And he did not mince his words as he talked to his disciples about persecution. He did not promise them an easy and broad path to heaven. Narrow is the gate, and difficult is the way which leads to life. And there are few who find it. He warned them, if the world hates you, you know that it hated me before it hated you. Even now, the depraved world is not done persecuting Christ. Because he sits in heaven out of their reach, they will settle for his disciples on earth as their targets. Jesus does not sugarcoat the bitterness of rejections But God does want us to have a heavenly perspective on rejection. Jesus' disciples should know and rehearse the truth of verse 16. We shouldn't take rejections of the gospel so personally. It's not us the world rejects ultimately. Earthly perspective says, they reject me. Heavenly perspective says they reject God. When it comes to evangelism, I think having this perspective is really liberating. There's so much less pressure on you, on me, when we dissenter ourselves. After all, we're just humble ambassador of the great king. And we'll have a lot easier time if we see ourselves at the bottom of the organizational chart and not at the top of the hierarchy. Let God be the judge, and you be the faithful and obedient messenger. Let God the Son and God the Father take the credit for acceptance and the brunt of rejection. In this way, your joy and acceptance and your sorrow in rejection will have proper boundaries. This should be our heavenly perspective. The enemy would love to see you lose this heavenly focus, not only with obvious evil distractions, but get our attention on the gifts. Your eyes wandering away from the giver of those gifts. And that's the danger of the 70 faced as they return to Jesus from their mission. And that leads to the second point. Rejoice in your salvation, not authority. Arkans finds in verses seventeen to twenty two joys. One, a joy that needs moderating, that's in verses 17 to 19. And two, a joy that needs exalting, that's in verse 20. The joy that needs moderating is encapsulated in these words. Lord, even the demons are subject to us in your name See how Jesus celebrates their spiritual authority, but he also points them to the ultimate victory to come. When he says, I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven, he's not talking about some event that already took place. And he's not saying Satan has been vanquished permanently. The devil's power is active. He's going to keep himself busy for a while, oppressing a woman with the spirit. of infirmity, entering Judas and Iscariot, asking to take apart Peter, filling Ananias in Acts Manipulating Elimus, the sorcerer, equipping false teachers with the tricks of the trade, prowling like a roaring ravenous lion, throwing believers into prison. Just there's a lot more. She's very active. So really, when Jesus said, I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven, he's talking prophetically about what will happen later. Apostle John gave us this vision in vivid detail in Revelation 12, 7 to 9. Around the halfway point of the seven-year tribulation, here's what will happen. And war broke out in heaven. Michael and his angels fought with the dragon, and the dragon and his angels fought But they did not prevail, nor was a place found for them in heaven any longer. So the great dragon was cast down, that serpent of old, called the devil and Satan, who deceives the whole world. He was cast to the earth. And his angels were cast out with him. Now, this fall of Satan is still distant from Jesus' time, but even if this event is not immediate, but in the future, There were immediate implications in the present. Because Jesus is God, He has authority over demons, and He conferred that authority to the 70. At least temporarily they would be kept safe from supernatural and natural dangers like serpents and scorpions and even overcome them. Now, can you imagine this experience for these no names? Every day they use their hands for mundane use in their mundane jobs. Now their hands touch the sick and heal them. Every day their mouths spoke wishes and prayers with faint hope. Now their mouths uttered commands to subdue spirits. I can imagine that it would have been exhilarating, thrilling, and intoxicating If I was one of the 70, I would be drunk with this newfound power. With healing hands, I would be recognized as Dr. Cho in a new way With authoritative tongue, my dog will finally obey all my commands. You would hear my maniacal Disney villain laugh Jesus won't have that. In verse 20, Jesus uses the same word twice to prohibit and command. Do not rejoice in your spiritual authority. Do rejoice in your salvation. This is a joy that's underrated. This is a joy that needs exalting. Rejoice because your names are written in heaven. These unnamed unknowns are named and known by God Is your name written in heaven? Do you have reasons to rejoice in salvation? You can accrue all the power and authority in the world, but you'll never find lasting joy until you find the joy of salvation. Now concerning the names written in heaven, let me take you back to Revelation. According to Revelation 17, 8, the names of saints are written on the pages of the book of life, written from the foundation of the world. But how do we know our names are on that book? It's not like you can check out that book at the Howard County Library, take a pen and write your name on it if it's not in there. The book is not for checkout. It belongs to God. But Revelation 13, 8 gives us the information we need We learned there that the book of life is the book of life of the lamb slain. If we know what the lamb slain means, we can know how names are recorded in the book of life. If we grasp how somebody has died, then we can grasp how nobody can live This is the gospel I present to you. It has never been clearer than right now that human life is fragile and ephemeral. But God did not originally design and create us to suffer like this. Here is the source of our pain. All of us, like our first parents, Adam and Eve, sinned. That is, disobeyed God, turned away from him, and went our own way. It's the way of destruction. It's the way of death. It's the way of eternal damnation We stray down this path by our own volition, even though God is good to us God has every right to let us face our doom, but he didn't. We read in Isaiah 53, verse 6, all we like sheep. Have gone astray. We have turned everyone to his own way. And the Lord has laid on him the iniquity of us all. The Lord has laid the iniquity of us all, the wayward, sinful sheep, on whose the lamb thou wast slain. This lamb is none other than Jesus Christ. He's the Son of God who became the Son of Man. He lived a perfect obedient life as the spotless Lamb. And then he died a perfect sacrificial death. He took the penalty and consequence of our sin, the wrath of God, though he himself never sinned as our substitute Jesus came to earth and gave up the joy of his authority for the joy of our salvation. And for this joy that was set before him, he endured the cross, despising the shame, and sat down at the right hand of the throne of God. And now because he's in heaven, so are the names of the redeemed If you want to be saved, if you want to be known in heaven, you need to know the Savior, Jesus who is in heaven There's no way for you to earn your place there, no matter how much authority you possess. God saves us not because of the good works we have done. He saves us based on the good work of Jesus Christ. Salvation is God's gift of grace. Trust in Jesus alone, and you'll be saved. sermons.text: In nineteen fourteen, Robert Frost wrote a poem entitled Mending Wall. It's about a spring ritual shared between two neighbors. Every year they walk along the wall of rocks that divide them and they repair it. One of them, however, begins to wonder why they even need this wall. He has apple trees And his neighbor has pine. It's not like the apples will roll over and eat the pines. It's not like they have unruly cows that will trespass. But the other neighbor insists good fences make good neighbors What do you think? Do good fences really make good neighbors? Before we even talk about fences, it's most important to ask, what is a neighbor? What is a good neighbor? Thankfully, God provides answers in today's passage. Let's turn to Luke chapter 10, verse 25 to 37, and read it together. And behold, a certain lawyer stood up and tested him, saying, Teacher, what shall I do to inherit eternal life? He said to him, What is written in the law? What is your reading of it? So he answered and said, You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, with all your strength, and with all your mind, and your neighbor as yourself. And he said to him, You have answered rightly, do this and you will live. But he, wanting to justify himself, said to Jesus, And who is my neighbor? Then Jesus answered and said, A certain man went down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and fell among thieves, who stripped them of his clothing, wounded him, and departed, leaving him half dead. Now by chance a certain priest came down that road, and when he saw him, he passed by on the other side. Likewise a Levite, when he arrived at the place, came and looked, and passed by on the other side. But a certain Samaritan, as he journeyed, came where he was, and when he saw him, he had compassion. So he went to him and bandaged his wounds, pouring on oil and wine, and he set him on his own animal, brought him to an inn, and took care of him. On the next day when he departed, he took out two denarii, gave them to the innkeeper, and said to him, Take care of him, and whatever more you spend, when I come again, I will repay you. So which of these three do you think was neighbor to him who fell among the deeps? And he said, He who showed mercy on him. Then Jesus said to him, Go and do likewise. The main point of today's passage is that a good neighbor is one that loves you as him or herself. Three principles elaborate on this. One, love is God's demands fulfilled. Verses twenty-five to twenty-eight Two, love is divine opportunity missed. Verses twenty-nine to thirty-two And three, love is neighborly mercy revealed. Verses 33 to 37 First, love is God's demands fulfilled. It will be good for us to retrace our steps and connect verses 25 to 28. To what happened in verses 21 to 24, which we looked at last week. Recall how Jesus has just given thanks to the Father because he has hidden these things, kingdom truths, from the wise and prudent. And reveal them to babes. That's in verse 21. Jesus also told his disciples privately: many prophets and kings have desired to see what you see and have not seen it. And to hear what you hear and have not heard it, and that was in verse twenty four. These followers of Jesus were privileged beyond the scholars and the learned people of their day Right after he said these things, we have in verse 25, and behold, a certain lawyer. This one's the epitome of the wise and prudent. This one's closer to prophets and kings than fishermen and tax collectors. Now, lawyers are not jurisdoctors of today, but experts of the law of Moses. They're synonymous with scribes and probably the same as the teachers of the law. One way to look at lawyers in this passage is to see them as priests off duty. They served as legal experts when they weren't performing their temple duties. But all this knowledge would not do them good. We saw earlier in chapter 7, verse 30. That they, along with Pharisees, rejected the will of God for themselves, not having been baptized by John. They would also reject Jesus the Messiah, whom John the Baptist proclaimed. So reading today's passage in context, we shouldn't expect too much from our lawyer friend here, even if he stands tall and impressive. Behind this eloquence is an ulterior motive. The word for test in verse 25 is found three other times in the New Testament. And in each instance, there's a warning. Do not put God to test. Ironically, this Bible expert doesn't realize he's testing God. Jesus is no mere rabbi. He is Lord. He is the Son of God who reveals the Father It's likely that this man wanted to detect a mistake or expose some ambiguity in Jesus' words. But our Lord is too wise to fall for this trap. So he takes over the questioner role and has the man answer his own original question And without fanfare, the Q<unk>A session is over, and the discussion ended quicker and shorter than expected But let's slow down for our soul's sake. Even if the lawyer's motive was off. The question of eternal life is too important for us to speed tasted. Eternal life is tied up in God's demands. And all of God's demands are tied up in two commandments. One is in Deuteronomy 6. 5, You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, with all your strength, and with all your mind. The others in Leviticus 1918. Love your neighbor as yourself. Love your God above you. Love your fellow man near you. This twofold love is the fulfillment of God's demands. Jesus stressed the supremacy of these two loves at least two other times, once to a rich young ruler. and the other time to another lawyer in Jerusalem. This lesson was not lost on Jesus' followers like James and Paul, as you see in Romans, Galatians, and Seems simple Prioritizing love is simple, yet humbling. Is that really all that is? You might say to yourself Is love a concept that's difficult to grasp? No, it's found in childlike faith, not in ivory towers. Is love for the elite of the society? No, it's found among the lowly and the poor. Is love what most worldly career-driven types consider as a source of pride? No, it's sacrificial and takes the focus off of us. Love is God's demands fulfilled. God's demands are there so that we can enjoy a harmonious relationship with Him and our neighbors. But what happens when there are demands without love? They would be empty. Maybe you'll get a taste of this in this illustration. Uh a few years ago I read what Albert Einstein wrote to his first wife, Maleva. Sadly, it wasn't a love letter. His marriage was floundering, but for the sake of the children, he wanted to keep it going. So he wrote his wife a list of demands. Here it goes Quote, you will make sure that my clothes and laundry are kept in good order, that I will receive my three meals regularly in my room. That my bedroom and study are kept neat, and especially that my desk is empty for my use only. You will renounce all personal relations with me insofar as they are not completely necessary for social reasons Specifically, you will forego my sitting at home with you, my going out or traveling with you. You will obey the following points in your relations with me. You will not expect any intimacy from me Nor will you reproach me in any way. You will stop talking to me if I request it. You will leave my room, bedroom, or study immediately without protest if I request it. You will undertake not to belittle me in front of our children, either through words or behavior. End quote Here's a man who studied the laws of the universe, but not the laws of love. Here's a man who developed a theory of relativity, but not his relatability. Here's a man who wanted his demands devoid of love, but not God's demands fulfilled by love. A man brilliant in mind, but dull in heart. In his research, he changed the world far and wide. In his marriage, he destroyed his home, close and near. But let's not be so hasty to Judge Einstein or this lawyer in today's passage. Maybe we're like these two when it comes to knowledge, but could it be that we lost sight of love? Do we not also fail to love God with everything? Do we not find the knowledge of this command easy, but the obedience of it difficult? Do we not want to disjustify ourselves by thinking that we've done a good job with our neighbors?
