Whatever the excuse, love is divine opportunity missed Next, a Levite comes along. Our Canthus reminds us that Levites were not as widely recognized as priests, but they still played a uh still played key roles at the temple. They held privileged positions as liturgists and overseers. You could compare their office to the Christian office of deacons. The wording in verse 32 suggests that at least this one went up relatively closer to get a better look at the victim. But the end result is the same. He passed by the other side. Again, whatever the excuse, love is divine opportunity missed. Before we get to the climax of the parable, we should stop and ask whether we're like the priest and the Levite. When God gives us opportunity to show mercy, do we close our eyes, hold our nose, and pass by the other side? Are we asking in prayer, God use me as your instruments of mercy, but saying in secret, I don't want to get my hands dirty. Is love an opportunity you seize, or is love divine opportunity missed? We can talk about God's love all we want and recite John 3. 16 from memory. But do we know 1 John 3. 16? By this we know love, because he laid down his life for us. And we also ought to lay down our lives for the brethren. He continues in the next verse. But whoever has this world's goods and sees his brother in need and shuts up his heart from him, how does the love of God abide in him? We can have faith moving mountains, but is your faith moving to help others James 2, 14 to 17. It says, What does it profit, my brethren, if someone says he has faith but does not have works? Can faith save him? If a brother or sister is naked and destitute of daily food, and wannabe says to them, Depart in peace, be warmed and filled. But you do not give them the things which are needed for the body. What does it profit? Thus also faith by itself, if it does not have works, is dead. Of course, I'm not saying your good works of charity can save you and get you into heaven. Only Jesus and his finished work can save you. But God's children who genuinely trust in their father will bear good fruit and shine their light in the dark world. They will eventually repent from these sins of omission in due time if the scriptures convict them. They will not perpetually miss divine opportunities if the Holy Spirit is working in them. Vessels of mercy will become instruments of mercy. And that leads to the third point. Love is neighborly mercy revealed. Jesus is the author of this parable, so it's entirely up to him how to deliver the punchline. The third and the final man to encounter the victim could have been an Israelite layman, not Samaritan. He could have been an Israelite regular blue-collar worker. Then the point would be that religious elitism does not lead to mercy. Or Jesus could have said, but a certain tax collector or sinner It would make the same point, but more forcefully. It would still be scandalous. But nothing prepared for what followed But a certain Samaritan. Imagine the shock of the crowd I wonder if there were audible gasps, murmurs, heads lowered from awkwardness I wonder if there were teeth clenching, arms crossed, or even individuals getting up and leaving. Imagine the shock of James and John. Back in chapter 9. They wanted to call down fire from heaven to consume a whole lot of them. This was too much. A Samaritan? Really? Imagine the shock of the lawyer. He read of the Samaritans' syncretistic and mixed race origins from 2 Kings 17. He knew that they set up a rival religion with their own version of the Bible. Samaritan, really But the man was not in a position to refuse help. The Samaritans saw him and had compassion. Again, Jesus as the author of the parable could have shortened the story, just say the Samaritan helped the poor man at the end. No, Jesus will continue with details that are no doubt excruciating for the Jewish audience, the Samaritan. Based on what he had in his possession was most likely a merchant who had business in Jerusalem. Why else would he be in Jerusalem? Though hardly a holy man, he went and bandaged the wounds, probably ripping off his own garments to use as wraps. According to Joseph Fitzmeier, olive oil would cleanse and soothe the wounds, and the wine could work as an antiseptic. The lawyer could not bring himself to say the Samaritan, so he resorts to he who showed mercy on him Jesus dismisses him a second time, go and do likewise. Love is neighborly mercy revealed. A Samaritan. Really? The legal expert probably wished he left earlier. He was perfectly content with the narrow definition of neighbor. And judge him all you want. sermons.text: Christian author Kevin DeYoung shared in his book, Crazy Busy. I read an anecdote once about a woman from another culture. who came to the United States and began to introduce herself as busy. It was, after all, the first thing she heard when meeting any American. Hello, I'm busy. She figured it was part of our traditional greeting. I wonder if this immigrant came during this time of the year. A few decades ago I worked in retail at the family Christian store in Laurel, and I recall the late extended hours and the packed building. While back in Virginia, I went to Tyson's Corner one December day and turned right back when I saw a line of cars extending from the parking lot to the main road. I wonder how COVID restrictions will affect the shopping traffic this year. But here's a season in which I think we Christians have an opportunity to be distinct. Are we so busy that we don't have time for God and time for people? Have we lost our focus and messed up our priorities? Is our schedule full? And yet our souls empty. I believe today's passage can help us. So let's turn to the end of Luke 10. Luke 10, verses 38 to 42. Now it happened as they went that he entered a certain village And a certain woman named Martha welcomed him into her house. And she had a sister called Mary, who also sat at Jesus' feet and heard his word. But Martha was distracted with much serving, and she approached them and said, Lord, do you not care that my sister has left me to serve alone? Therefore tell her to help me And Jesus answered and said to her, Martha, Martha, you are worried and troubled about many things. But one thing is needed. And Mary has chosen that good part, which will not be taken away from her. We'll get to our sermon points soon, but before we explore this passage further, I wanted to address right away two misreadings of it One, some say Mary is better than Martha spiritually. Two, some say Mary represents a better spiritual life. I'll explain each. First, Mary is not really better spiritually. If we trace the storylines of Mary and Martha in the Gospels, We'll see that Martha is quite spiritual too. Granted, Martha did receive rebuke from Jesus here and later at the tomb of Lazarus. And whoever lives and believes in me shall never die. Do you believe this? She said to him, Yes, Lord, I believe that you are the Christ, the Son of God, who is to come into the world. That's in Matthew 16 and John 6 Martha expresses essentially the same profession of faith as Peter. That means she's been paying attention. That's impressive. So instead of saying one sister is better than the other, we should recognize Martha for her unique strengths, such as her initiative, hospitality, and leadership. Here's another misreading. To some, Mary represents the superior contemplative life. Living distraction-free as an ascetic, monk, or a nun at a monastery Martha represents the inferior active life, living distracted and divided in devotion between the secular and the spiritual. But I think this is reading too much into the text. And to introduce a distinction that was born only of later preoccupations. So then, what is going on in this passage? Preacher or layman, from the Word of God upon which all effective service rests. End quote. Charles Spurgeon is helpful and practical quote: The way to get the revival is to begin at the master's feet. You must go there with Mary, and afterwards you may work with Martha. End quote. So that's a good application by itself. Revival, you gotta go to Jesus' speech with Mary, and then afterwards you gotta go to work with Martha. But let me go further and offer a few more. Following Jesus entails three principles. One, follow Jesus by serving hospitably, verse 38. Two. Listen to Jesus undistractedly, verses 39 to 40, and 3. Cherish Jesus intimately, verses 41 to 42. First, follow Jesus by serving hospitably Allow me to reread verse 38. Now it happened as they went that he entered a certain village, and a certain woman named Martha welcomed him into her house. Now before we apply this principle, we have to unpack a lot of background info, so bear with me. We know from the Gospel of John, which we read earlier, that Martha lived in a town called Bethany, about two miles away from Jerusalem. It appears that Jesus' itinerary during his last months and days was not a straight V-line from Galilee to the cross. He was waiting for the right time, specifically just before Passover, before entering Jerusalem It appears Jesus regularly dropped by Bethany to visit his followers, like Martha and her family. I believe the 12 disciples were there too, but Luke's focus here is on Jesus, Martha, and Mary. And it looks like Jesus had a loving relationship with Martha's family for a while. Martha's father was Simon, and we know him as Simon the Leper. I'm willing to bet Jesus cured Simon of leprosy, but the name stuck, especially since it would help the early Christians differentiate him between other Simons. Simon the Zealot, Simon the Pharisee, Simon from Cyrene, Simon the Tanner, and of course Simon Peter. There's no mention of a wife, so I'm guessing he's a widower. Sometime earlier the family dynamics probably shifted because of the disabled father and likely deceased mother. I'm guessing Martha as the oldest took over as the matriarch of the house. And Martha had at least two siblings, one we see in today's passage, Mary. Lazarus, their brother, is not mentioned in Matthew, Mark, and Luke. You may find that strange because Jesus raised them from the dead, and one could argue that this is Jesus' greatest miracle besides the resurrection, of course. Why wouldn't Matthew, Mark, and Luke publicize such a wonderful event in Jesus' ministry and spread his fame? Well in John chapter twelve we learn why after they took Lazarus out of the rafts, they kept them under wraps, pun intended. At the time of the miracle, many Jews nearby knew Jesus was spending time with Lazarus and came to see them at Bethan. We read in John 12, 9-11. Now a great many of the Jews knew that he was there, but and they came, not for Jesus' sake only. but that they might also see Lazarus, whom he had raised from the dead. Who wouldn't want to see him, right? But the chief priests plotted to put Lazarus to death also, because on account of him many of the Jews went away and believed in Jesus. Jesus. Because Jesus was the number one target and Lazarus number two, it was necessary for the earliest believers to conceal Martha's brother's identity. Unlike Jesus, Lazarus can die again. So they probably moved him around and made no mention of him in the earliest three Gospels. After decades, once those antagonistics towards Lazarus died, andor Lazarus himself died, John felt that he could fully narrate the story. Until then it seemed prudent to make no mention of Lazarus and be very discreet about his siblings' location, as we see here, a certain village. With all that in mind, let's return to the main principle of verse 38. Follow Jesus by serving hospitably. Here, Martha demonstrates how to receive Christ just as earlier some received the 12 and the 70 sent out by Christ. This kind of hospitality would be crucial in the ongoing ministry of Jesus' followers. Christians must be givers of hospitable service and recipients of the same. This kind of welcome would be vital both in the early church and in the end times during the tribulation. And how about us in the present? Can we imitate Martha and follow Jesus by serving hospitably? You may not lead a victim on the road to an inn like the Good Samaritan, but you may lead someone to your home, like Martha. You are not Christ, so you cannot save sinners and bring them to the Lord's table, but you can imitate Christ and receive sinners and eat with them at your table. You may not revive the dead to life like Jesus, but you can refresh the hearts of the saints like Philemon. Now you may say to me, I don't have a nice spacious house or I'm too busy to host guests. I understand that everyone's application of this verse is not the same. Not everyone can show hospitality at home, but everyone can be hospitable. It's true that overseeing elders of the church should be especially hospitable as examples. But Peter tells all believers to be hospitable to one another in 1 Peter 4:9. And we can move beyond our church membership. Paul tells us in Romans 12. 13 that we should be distributing to the needs of the saints and given to hospitality. The original word for given is better translated as pursuing. Pursuing hospitality is not merely a tendency Or inclination, but literally active chasing after the love of strangers I think we're blessed with the resources to pursue the biblical goal of hospitable service. That means being hospitable to our church members and to guests of our Sunday services. It's a wonderful blessing for us to have live service in our building in this season Big enough to keep our distance and even though it's uncomfortable to keep our base coverings on, we're able to offer a meaningful alternative to the online experience. But once they're here, today experience our live hospitable service along with our live worship service. During worship, we may join the angels in heaven and be blessed as heirs of salvation. But would these same angels join us on earth and be entertained unawares as guests? Let's be worshipful and hospitable. Now, doing both is not easy. Doing both well, I mean. Just ask Martha, who was distracted, and that leads to the second point. Listen to Jesus undistractedly. In verses 39 and 40, we get a better understanding of the family dynamics. We got Mary sitting there at the feet of Jesus, soaking it all in, like a little child. There are two reasons this bothered Martha, one obvious and the one and the other less obvious. Obviously, because Mary is just sitting there and not helping with the food, what is less obvious, but nonetheless true, is that in first century Jewish context Men customarily sat at the foot of the rabbi as disciples, while women worked in the background to support them. But of course, Jesus is known to buck conventions. At this point, maybe Martha sent passive aggressive signals with loud pots clanging, audible sighs from the kitchen. She might tell you she's the only adult in the family. But when it comes to discipleship, being an adult does not always equate to spiritual maturity. We can be distracted with much serving and fail to listen to Jesus Now we need to be careful about how we talk to each other about serving, especially about Christian service. Essentially, service is a good thing, but excessively, service is a bad thing And what exactly is excessive? Personally, it could be different measures because one individual may have five talent, another have two, another one. If you can do many things well without distraction and listen to Jesus, more power to you. But when it comes to evaluating others' service, be slow to speak. If you're an empty nester and retired, don't judge someone busy with work and family and can't sign up for every ministry opportunity. If you're young and full of energy, don't look down on those slowing down because of age and can't chase around children anymore. Do a spiritual audit on yourself and see if you're not distracted with much serving. And what does distracted with much serving look like in a corporate church gathering? I know that this isn't an infallible measure, but when I visit churches, I try to count the number of minutes devoted to listening to God's Word, specifically the length of the sermon and the scripture readings. Last December, Pew Research Center published their analysis of 49,719 sermons delivered in April and May that were shared online by 6,431 churches. Here's a summary from Associated Press. Quote, according to Pugh, the median length of the sermons was 37 minutes. Catholic sermons were the shortest at a median of just 14 minutes, compared with 25 minutes for sermons in mainline Protestant congregations. And 39 minutes in evangelical Protestant congregations. End quote. We're not anywhere close to 14 minutes. We're way beyond that, so we're good. Often, short sermon length is symptomatic of distracting distraction in churches Sometimes distractions are found in music. I've been to modern style worship types where music portion lasts close to an hour and it's mostly music, not singing. And there's a lot of 7-Eleven songs, songs with seven words repeated eleven times. Now I might forgive them for that if the sermon lasts about the same length, but no, not even close. The sermon just becomes an add-on to the emotional concert experience. Lots of empty calories, if you ask me. Speaking of calories, some distractions could come from meal fellowships. I've also been to a church where some were so concerned about the potluck that followed the service that they missed the worship service entirely. I think they were in the kitchen finishing the food and heating it up. Perhaps in this case, it would be good to trim down the much service. And again, I want to reiterate, essentially service is a good thing, but excessively, service is a bad thing. If we're like Martha at all, being distracted with much serving is not just a surface issue. There could be self-centeredness underneath. Commentator Joel B. Green notes, quote, the nature of hospitality for which Jesus seeks is realized in attending to one's guest. Yet Martha's speech is centered on me talk three times. End quote. Lord, do you not care that my sister has left me to serve alone? Therefore, tell her to help me. That's my sister. She has left me. Tell her to help me. Green continues, quote, though she refers to Jesus as Lord, she is concerned to engage his assistance in her plans, not to learn from him his. Have we found ourselves in such self contradiction? You say it's not about you, but you say me, me, me. You claim you want God's way, but you rather have your way. You call Jesus Lord, but you act like you're the Lord. You call yourself a follower of Jesus, but you're the one barking orders. Has your voice triumphed over the voice of Jesus? We can be distracted with much serving and fail to listen to Jesus. The solution to our distraction is found in the last two verses of chapter 10. Hear the words of Jesus again. Marta, Martha. You are worried and troubled about many things, but one thing is needed. And Mary has chosen that good part, which will not be taken away from her. The third principle is this cherish Jesus intimately If I were to ask each of you whether you cherish Jesus, I'm sure you'd say yes. But Jesus is not an impersonal checkbox on your to-do list. He's your personal savior. He deserves your attention, your ear, your intimacy. Jesus gently reprimands Martha. He repeats her name in an authoritative and urgent yet intimate way. Just as God called Abraham and Samuel, just as David grieved for Absalom, and just as Jesus will humble Peter later Here, he humbles Martha because she worries and she is troubled. I find it interesting that in the original languages grammar, worry is in the active voice and trouble is in the passive voice. Martha has actively worried, and now she's the passive troubled victim of her distractions She has forgotten what Jesus has taught on the Sermon on the Mount. Do not worry about your life, what you will eat, or what you will drink, nor about your body, what you will put on. Is not light more than food and the body more than clothing Mary, on the other hand, has chosen the one thing needed, the good part, the sweet fellowship with Jesus, which will not be taken away I bet Mary would like the Fanny Crosby's line. Take the world but give me Jesus. She might repeat Will Thompson's lyrics. Jesus is all the world to me, my life, my joy, my all. I'm sure she would agree with Paul, who would count all things lost for the excellence of the knowledge of Christ Jesus his Lord, for whom he has suffered the loss of all things. And count them as rubbish, that he may gain Christ. These are testimonies of men and women who cherish Jesus intimately. For those who do not have a relationship with Jesus Those who do not cherish Jesus at all, let alone intimately, I want to ask you this. What is heaven, and how do you get there? Maybe you came here precisely because you want to know the answer. And I could turn to passages in Isaiah and Revelation to give you a glimpse of heaven. But I'm here to say to you, the sight of Mary with Jesus, there's a taste of heaven. Yes, heaven will be breathtaking. The pearly gates, the streets of gold, the pure river of water of life But what would he without Jesus, without the Lamb? John Piper once asked this poignant question, quote, The critical question for our generation and for every generation is this. If you could have heaven with no sickness and with all the friends you ever had on earth and all the food you ever liked, and all the leisure activities you ever enjoyed, and all the natural beauties you ever saw. All the physical pleasures you ever tasted, and no human conflict or any natural disasters. Could you be satisfied with heaven if Christ were not there? All those nice things are distractions compared to the one thing that is needed. Everything else pales in comparison to the good part Mary has chosen. Do not love the world or the things in the world. Feast and drink in the love of Jesus and the Father. Like we sang earlier. Oh, the deep, deep love of Jesus. 'Tis heaven of heavens to me. And it lifts me up to glory, for it lifts me up to thee. If you want to know this deep love of Jesus, you must know the gospel. God has created us in his image to enjoy him forever. But we've all sinned and turned away from him. The consequence of such decision is costly. Life away from God means eternal death. Wrath, damnation, loneliness. But God, our Creator, was merciful and sent his Son Jesus to earth Jesus lived a perfect life and paid for our sins with his life on the cross. He made a way for us to enjoy intimacy with God. He rose from the dead as proof that he indeed made a way to heaven and he ascended there. Now he awaits his return to earth so that we can be with him forever. To sit at the feet of Jesus and become his disciple, you must first repent and trust in him. You don't need to bring your much service to him to find acceptance. You can't earn God's gift of grace with good works. He will accept you as you are. Will you accept him as he is? Will you turn from your sins and self-reliance and trust in Him alone for eternal life? He loves you and wants an intimate relationship with you. Yes, it's sweet to trust in Jesus. Just from sin and self to cease, just from Jesus simply taking life and rest and joy and peace. Now to those who already have this relationship with Jesus. Have we served the saints too little? Failing in our hospitable service? Have we served the ministries too much? Failing to listen to Jesus. Without distraction. Have we cherished the Lord too little, failing to meet him intimately As we approach the Lord's table this morning, would you consider whether your heart resembles the humble posture of Mary or the frenetic pace of Martha? If we're honest with ourselves, I'm sure we've acted like Martha often. If that's true of you, join me in this prayer from the valley of vision. Entitled Vain Service. It's actually printed for you in the later pages. I'll pray this prayer as we close. Let's go to the Lord. O my Lord, forgive me for serving thee in simple ways. By glorying in my own strength, by forcing myself to minister through necessity, by accepting the applause of others by trusting in assumed grace and spiritual affection, by a faith that rests upon my hold on Christ, not on him alone. By having another foundation to stand upon besides thee. For thus I make flesh my arm. Help me to abhor myself in comparison of thee And keep me in a faith that works by love and serves by grace. Pray all these things in Jesus Christ's name. Amen.

sermons.title: Christian Prayer Life
sermons.speaker: Sung Cho
sermons.text: Teaching children to pray is a wonderful privilege one parents, grandparents, and teachers should take seriously. But we also need patience. It'll take time before they pray for the right things in the right way. Meanwhile, we should encourage them to continue, even if they say prayers like the ones I found online Dear God, my mom tells me you have a reason for everything on earth. I guess broccoli is one of your mysteries. Dear God, thank you for the baby brother, but what I prayed for was a puppy. Dear God, I need you to make my mom not allergic to cats. I really want a cat, and I really don't want to ask my mom to move out. Dear God, my grandpa says you were around when he was a little boy. How far back do you go? I might be sure laugh at them. As silly as these prayers sound to us, I wonder what God thinks Of our narrow, impatient, selfish prayers. Prayers said without sincerity, without earnestness, without repentance At least most of these children don't know better. Thankfully, God has given us instructions about prayer in His Word. As we grow in grace, I believe we will grow in our prayer life as well. Let's go to the word and learn how. We go to Luke chapter eleven, verses one to thirteen. Now it came to pass as he was praying in a certain place, when he ceased, that one of his disciples said to him, Lord, teach us to pray, as John also taught his disciples. So he said to them, When you pray, say, Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name, your kingdom come, your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven Give us day by day our daily bread, and forgive us our sins, for we also forgive everyone who is indebted to us. And do not lead us into temptation, but deliver us from the evil one. And he said to them, Which of you shall have a friend, and go to him at midnight, and say to him, Friend, lend me three loaves, for a friend of mine has come to me on his journey, and I have nothing to set before him. And he will answer from within and say, Do not trouble me, the door is now shut, and my children are with me in bed. I cannot rise and give to you. I say to you, though he will not rise and give to him because he is his friend, yet because of his persistence he will rise and give him as many as he needs. So I say to you, ask, and it will be given to you. Seek and you will find. Knock and it will be open to you. For everyone who asks receives. And he who seeks finds, and to him who knocks it will be opened. If a son asks for bread from any father among you Will he give him a stone? Or if he asks for a fish, will he give him a serpent instead of a fish? Or if he asks for an egg, will he offer him a scorpion? If you then, being evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him? I believe there are three principles here for the Christian prayer life. 1. Exalt God as our good Father above yourself, verses 1 to 4. Verse 2, approach God without shame and regard for others, verses 5 to 8. And three, expect God to give his best to his children. Verses 9 to 13. First, exalt God as our good father above yourself. When we compare this prayer with the one in Matthew, which we recited earlier during the service, you'll notice some differences. That fact in itself is a lesson. Jesus is more concerned about substance than exact wording, form than formula Verbal expression more than verbatim recitation. So we're not going to go into an in-depth compare and contrast study today. Instead, we'll just say this for now. In every prayer, Jesus first leads us to acknowledge someone greater, somewhere nicer. And something better. Our Father, His Kingdom, and His will, respectively. If only Martha followed this prayer's outline and order, she would not be worried and troubled about many things. If we follow the outline and order here, we would exalt God as our good Father above ourselves. The Lord's Prayer is occasioned by Jesus' example, and what an example it is. John A. Martin observes, quote, Jesus prayed at every major crisis point of his life. He prayed at the time of his baptism and at the time of the choosing of his disciples. He was often alone praying and also praying with others around. He prayed for Simon and he prayed in the garden before his betrayal. He even prayed on the cross. It's no wonder that disciple asked him for a prayer lesson. To be Christ-like is to pray consistently and often. Besides Jesus' example, the disciples, the disciples observed how John the Baptist left behind for his disciples a pattern of prayer. We know John's disciples basted while they prayed. And here's a safe bet that repentance is the main topic of those prayers. Another state bet is that Jesus' prayer is going to be different than John's. Based on his prayer later in Gethsemane and Paul's teachings later. We know that our Lord taught us to speak to God as Abba, a term of endearment, a child's word expressing intimacy. One of those first utterances in his or her life. Many suggest daddy as the modern English equivalent. But I agree with R. Kent Hughes' suggestion that ABBA is more reverent than that. So I like his suggestion to render it as dearest father. We may take for granted that we call God our Father, but this is revolutionary. This is not to say God is not referred to as Father in the Old Testament. He is. But in those various passages, God is father in a corporate, national, or covenantal sense. To address God as Father in individual prayers was unheard of. Furthermore, one would search in vain for parallels in rabbinic and ancient Palestinian Judaism. Take one example, a Jewish prayer called the Prayer of Eighteen Petitions, which has at its heading various forms of address. Lord God of Abraham, God of Isaac, God of Jacob, God most high, creator of heaven and earth, our shield and the shield of our fathers. In contrast, here's a prayer with a simple address. Abba The name of Father, though familiar and not ornate, must be hallowed God's name of Abba must be set apart, treated as sacred, and with the utmost respect and veneration. Simple humans often fail to set his name apart as holy. Christians are not so different than the house of Israel, who profane God's holy name among the nations. We as his children give our dearest father a bad name very often. So our only hope of exalting God is God Himself. That's why we pray. And God Himself will fulfill His purposes through His coming kingdom and His will when He restores Israel, rules the nations through Jesus His Son. Again, our Lord wants us to first acknowledge someone greater, somewhere nicer, and something better. Our Father, His Kingdom, and His will, respectively. As grandiose as all this sounds, the next line may seem like a downer. We just ask for his kingdom and now we turn to bread. Verse 2 is about extraordinary matters, while verse 3 is quite ordinary. Kingdom is high above and future, and bread is low below and present. This request for bread bothered later interpreters. They wanted this bread to be the bread of angels, according to Psalm 78. Or they connected the bread to the communion. But the earliest patristic readers simply saw this as this daily bread as the bread that sustains this life. What is suited to the essence, life, and constitution of our body. And I think this first instinct is correct. The bread we often take for granted, you must often ask God to grant it. We must request the God of heaven for the things of earth. We must ask our Father there to provide for his children here. But also at this ground level is the reality of sin and the need for forgiveness. We must be careful how we read the first sentence of verse 4 and avoid two unbiblical extremes. One danger is to make our forgiveness of others the basis for God's forgiveness of us. That's work-based salvation That conjunction for after the first comma does not mean we earn God's pardon by pardoning others, quit quo quo. We never deserve God's remission of our sins. It's always only by grace, through faith alone. But then the other danger is to completely disconnect our forgiveness of others With God's forgiveness of us. Our mercy towards others is not the root of our salvation, but it is still the fruit of our salvation. Our grace towards offenders does not save us, but it proves we're already saved. Only Jesus as God can truly forgive our sins to reconcile us to the Father. Now we are to forgive each other as God select, holy and beloved, because Christ forgave us. Our obedience on this matter is difficult, no doubt. I speak from my experience, my personal struggle, forgiving my late father. He left me and my mother. He was never there for my graduations and other crucial moments in life. For most of my life I lived with an underlying bitterness, like a low-grade pain There are times when it's filled over into bursts of anger. Like holidays, as I wonder why I can't have a normal family like others. Perhaps you too have a hard time forgiving for different reasons. You may tell me, you have no idea how much he owes me or how much he hurt me or what I've been through It's really hard to exalt God as our good Father above ourselves in times we are hurt by sin. But as God's children, we are graciously forgiven, so we can graciously forgive others. When we read verse 4 in context and start the prayer from the top, we recognize first someone greater than sin, someplace nicer than this broken world. And something better than our will to hold a grudge. I can recognize that God is a good father, though I had a bad father. We can exalt him above our deep pain. We do this without minimizing sin and without despairing either. Sin is real, but so is God And if forgiveness is necessary for sins that already happened, God's guidance is necessary for sins that could happen. We acknowledge God's sovereignty by asking him to lead us not into temptation. We also acknowledge God's power by asking him to deliver us from the evil one. Interestingly, the first word of the prayer is acceptance of God as our good Father. The final word of the prayer is the repudiation of Satan as the evil one. There's someone greater than the devil, somewhere nicer than his packs, and something better than his schemes In prayer, we exalt God as our good Father above ourselves. We turn in the next few verses to the attitude of prayer. Jesus tells us a short parable and we learn the second principle. Approach God without shame and regard for others. This principle hinges on the translation of a key word in verse eight. That word is persistence in the New King James Version. But the Greek word literally means shamelessness. The word with the opposite meaning is found in 1 Timothy 2 9. There, Paul instructs the women in the church to adorn themselves in modest apparel with propriety. So then it seems strange to suggest disciples should add impropriety to their prayer life. Isn't it good to be modest and conform to society's norms? Shouldn't we be less dramatic and care more about what others think of us? When it comes to prayer, Jesus is saying no. Impropriety is what gets this man to go to his friend at midnight. Shamelessness drives his man to knock on the door, stir up the children, and obtain what he needs to entertain his guest. He's so focused that he could care less what others think of him. Do you lose yourself in prayer like that to gain what you need? Do we approach God without shame or regard for others Two illustrations for your consideration. First, when it comes to shamelessness in prayer, sometimes the world puts us to shame. And here's what I mean. On one May weekend of 2017, we flew out to Montreal to enjoy their bagels, roam through the underground city. Visit the Center Bell where their hockey team plays. Another experience was visiting St. Joseph's Oratory, a Roman Catholic minor basilica. It's the tallest building in the city, more than 30 meters over Mount Royal summit. As you ascend, you will notice that between where you are and the parallel concrete steps, There's a central flight of wooden steps, 99 in all. On the day we visited, a devout Catholic was climbing them on her knees Stopping to pray at every step. On our way out, after an hour or so of touring, I recall she was still on her upward prayer journey. She didn't care what others thought of her, those near her, or those who can see her from Queen Mary Road. She was shameless. I tell you this story as a challenge from the lesser to the greater. Here is this woman. Whose religion is based on a false gospel of works-based salvation, willing to approach God without shame. How much more should we, who believe in the true gospel of justification by grace alone, through faith alone, approach God without shame? She has a fallible priest who is weak and tempted and prone to sin. We have a high priest who can sympathize with our weaknesses. In all points, tempted as we are, yet without sin. Let us therefore come boldly to the throne of grace. That we may obtain mercy and find grace to help in time of need. Are you boldly approaching God without shame and regard for others? Here's the second illustration. I never lived more than a state away from my mom, so I can easily visit her. The most I had to do was get on 495 and cross state boundaries. But I Re grew up as a third culture kid and she was often a continent away from her parents. She had to cross oceans and seas to visit her folks. So she called often and once three options came along, she learned to use apps and bones to stay in touch. Early in our marriage, we're sitting around in late evening, and she had to call her parents. Molly is five hours ahead of us, so it would have been 2 or 3 a. m. there. I wondered why she couldn't wait until the next day to call her folks, but Era just said something like, They're my parents. They will always pick up my phone call. I know my mom would do the same, but we don't have a time zone difference. Again, from the lesser to the greater. If the shameless persistence of an annoying neighbor gets you out of bed at midnight, how much more the shameless persistence of your child? Recall what we sang earlier. Arise, my soul, arise. The last verse. My God is reconciled. His pardoning voice I hear. He owns me for his child. I can no longer fear. With confidence, I now draw nigh. And Father, Abba, Father, cry. By God's grace, we are his children, and we need to feel no shame. Keep this in mind as we move on to verse 9 and the next point. Expect God to give his best to his children. Shamelessness and persistence are context sensitive A single man can ask out a girl, but she can say no. She doesn't have to give him her number. A college grad can seek a job from her dream company, but she may not find a position. You can knock on the door of the city hall, but it may not be open to you, sorry, by appointment only. But in the context of a father-child relationship. You will not only be heard, but you will receive. Now Jesus isn't saying that you'll get everything you ever wanted I mean, look at the examples used in verse eleven. Jesus is talking about bread and fish, not filet mignon, or a five-course meal. But when it comes to needs, yes, we can believe God will provide and give his best to his children If sinful human fathers know how to give good gifts, how much more the Holy Divine Father If men who can be capricious and cruelly dark one moment and bright the next know how to put food on the table, how much more our good father? He gives every good and perfect gift, the Father of lights, with whom there is no variation or shadow of turning. If you ever doubt God would give his best to his children, consider what he has already given. God gave his best because he gave us himself. Look again in verse 13. If you then being evil Know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your heavenly father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him? Before we talk about the spirit, the third person of the Trinity, let me back up and start with the first and the second persons. First, God the Father gave us God the Son. God so loved the world that he gave his only begotten Son. That whoever believes in him should not perish, but have everlasting life. For God did not send his son into the world to condemn the world, but that the world through him might be saved. You might say to me, I need to be saved. Yes, you need to be saved. God created us and loved us, but we turned away from him. We've send in thought, word, and deed. We've erred and went our own ways straight towards hell. If you die in your sins, you'll face eternal outer darkness, forever asking but never receiving. Seeking but never finding. Knocking, but never having the doors of heaven open to you The time to ask, seek, and knock on heaven's door is now. Jesus is the door. He's the way, the truth, and the life. He made a way for us to enjoy God forever by dying on the cross for our sins. There he took the punishment that we deserve. Rose from the dead to prove that he indeed made full payment for our mistakes. He ascended to heaven and now awaits his return. Now is the time to receive the greatest Christmas gift, Christ Himself. But the giving doesn't stop there. God the Father gives God the Holy Spirit to those who receive God the Son. In Acts, saints prayed and God sent the promised gift of the Holy Spirit, first to Jewish Christians, afterwards to Samaritan Christians, and then to all Gentile Christians like us. Now each believer receives the Spirit at the moment of salvation Do you want God as your gift? If so, turn from self-reliance and sin. Repent and let every one of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins. And you shall receive the gift of the Holy Spirit. Those are Peter's words. Turn to Jesus in faith before it's too late You don't have to be good enough, strong enough, rich enough to come to the Father. Jesus and his finished work on the cross are enough Through this gift of the Spirit, we prayerfully acknowledge the Giver, our dearest Father in heaven. Again from that hymn, Arise my soul, rise. We didn't sing this, but his spirit, it says, answers to the blood and tells me I am born of God. I find it interesting that as Paul and other early Jewish believers took the gospel to Greek speakers, they taught Gentiles the Aramaic word Abba. Keeping it intact, even transliterating it. Paul says in Romans, for as many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are sons of God. But you did not receive the spirit of bondage again to fear, but you received the spirit of adoption by whom we cry out, Abba Father. In Galatians, he wrote, and because you are sons, God has sent forth the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, crying out, Abba, Father. If we receive the gifts of Jesus and the Holy Spirit, there's no reason we should be timid in our prayers. We have every reason to exalt God as our good Father, he who did not spare his own son, but delivered him up for us all. How shall he not with him also freely give us all things? What will be your dear God prayer today? We can pray for God's will to be done through us by the power of the Holy Spirit within us. Until his kingdom comes, we can ask our sovereign God for the nations as we fulfill the Great Commission. In all our asking Let's make keep Green's words our prayer of gratitude. Thank you, O my Father, for giving us your Son. And leaving your spirit till the work on earth is done. Let's pray. Lord, we come to you as Father. We come to you as your children with childlike faith and humility. Admitting we are weak, that we need you. Admitting that we are small, and there's something greater than us, that you are greater than us. And we acknowledge you first, your kingdom and your will above our needs. Yet we come to you without shame. We come to you with expectation, full expectation that you are a good father, better than our earthly fathers. We thank you for your love. The deep love you've shown us by sending your son to die for us. Pray all these things in Jesus Christ's name. Amen.

sermons.title: Satan Hates Christmas
sermons.speaker: Sung Cho
sermons.text: It's getting close to Christmas, and maybe you'll pick up a book that begins like this. Quote, every Who down in Whoville like Christmas a lot. But the Grinch, who lived just north of Houville, did not. The Grinch hated Christmas, the whole Christmas season. Now please don't ask why. No one quite knows the reason. It could be his head wasn't screwed on just right. It could be perhaps that his shoes were too tight. But I think that the most likely reason of all may have been that his heart was two sizes too small. So today I'm taking a break from Luke and preaching one of those Christmas sermons. I thought about preaching from a famous Old Testament passage like the ones in Isaiah or Micah. The early chapters of Matthew and Luke are also natural places to look. But this year I wanted to look at Christmas from a different vantage point. Christmas from the last book of the Bible. Christmas in light of a cosmic struggle in heaven and earth. We want to see why, like Grinch, Satan hates Christmas, the whole Christmas season. Unlike Grinch, Satan's heart does not triple in size. Satan's demise is recounted in most dramatic fashion in the book of Revelation, the last book of the Bible. I'm going to turn to Revelation 12, but before we turn there, please let me give a quick outline of the book. A good verse to Mark is chapter 1, verse 19, in which Jesus commands John the Apostle. Write the things which you have seen and the things which are and the things which will take place after this. That's 119. And based on this verse, you can divide the book into three parts. Chapter 1, corresponding to the things John has already seen Chapters 2 and 3, things which are concerning the seven churches of Asia in his time, late first century. And things which will take place after this in the future, that's chapters four to twenty-two, the rest of the book. Digging deeper within chapters 4 to 22, we have seven seals, seven trumpets, and seven bowls. There are three groups of sevens connected in a dovetail fashion. In chapters four and five, the introductory scene in heaven, we learn that the lamb that was slain. is worthy to break the seven seals of the scroll. He literally unfolds the final stages of history in chapters six and seven. Now the seventh and the final seal initiate the seven trumpets. They are revealed one by one in chapters eight to eleven. At the end of chapter 11, the seventh trumpet in turn unleashes seven more judgments, the seven bull judgments that culminate with Jesus' second coming. But there's a gap between the close of chapter eleven and chapter sixteen between the seventh trumpet and the first bull. In chapters 12 to 15, focus turns from seven trumpets to seven representative figures. We are focusing on four of the seven. Personages today in chapter twelve, verse one through twelve. Israel, Satan, Christ, and Michael. I will not explain every detail or interpretation of these prophecies, but mainly consider this passage in relation to Christmas. Try to keep the big picture in mind. According to Daniel Akin, this chapter, quote, tells us in part and in summary fashion the grand redemptive story of the Bible. It is something of a panorama of salvation history. It tells us in fantastic imagery and vision the true story of the whole world. So now let's turn to chapter twelve, verse one through twelve, and read the passage together. Now a great sign appeared in heaven. A woman clothed with the sun, with the moon under her feet, and on her head a garland of twelve stars. Then being with child, she cried out in labor and in pain to give birth And another sign appeared in heaven. Behold, a great fiery red dragon, having seven heads and ten horns, and seven diadems on his head. His tail drew a third of the stars of heaven and threw them to the earth, and the dragon stood before the woman who was ready to give birth to devour her child as soon as it was born. She bore a male child who was to rule all nations with the rod of iron, and her child was caught up to God and his throne. Then the woman fled into the wilderness where she has a place prepared by God, that they should feed her there 1,260 days. And war broke out in heaven. Michael and his angels fought with the dragon, and the dragon and his angels fought, but they did not prevail, nor was a place found for them in heaven any longer. So the great dragon was cast out, that serpent of old, called the devil and Satan, who deceives the whole world. He was cast to the earth, and his angels were cast out with him. Then I heard a loud voice saying in heaven, Now salvation and strength, and the kingdom of our God and the power of his Christ have come. For the accuser of our brethren, who accused them before our God day and night, has been cast down. And they overcame him by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony, and they did not love their lives to the death. Therefore rejoice, O heavens, and you who dwell in them. Woe to the inhabitants of the earth and the sea. For the devil has come down to you having great wrath because he knows that he has a short time. So in line with the four representative key figures, we can divide these verses four sections and principles. And join in Israel's expectation of Christ. Verses 1 and 2. Two beware of Satan's hatred of God. Verses 3 and 4. 3. Worship Jesus as ruler of all, verses 5 and 6. And 4. Rejoice in the certain doom of the devil, verses 7 to 12. First, join in Israel's expectation of Christ You can tell in my wording of the principle that I take the woman of verse 1 as corporate Israel Of course, that isn't the only view out there. Catholics have identified her as Mary, the Queen of Heaven. Mary Baker Eddy, the founder of Christian Science, said she's this woman. Closer to my view is the view that the woman represents saved people throughout all of history. But I think the all-saints view is too general, and the one saint view is too specific. My main support for the corporate Israel view is from Joseph's dream in Genesis 37. In verses 9 to 11, there, Joseph relates the dream of the sun, the moon, and the stars, corresponding to Jacob, Rachel, and the sons of Israel. Israel enjoyed great privilege and position. To Israel were committed the oracles of God. And to them pertain the adoption, the glory, the covenants, the giving of the law, the service of God and the promises, of whom are the fathers, and from whom, according to the flesh, Christ came. Who is overall the eternally blessed God? Amen. That's from Romans nine, four to five. Messiah is the seed of Abraham, the lion of Judah, the root of Jesse, and the seed of David. The law of Moses contains the shadow of good things to come with the substance in Jesus. It was our tutor to bring us to Christ. The Israelites had all of these privileges through special revelation and election. But with such privileges came pain and trouble. God has often humbled his people under one bad king after another. Even under the domination of Gentile rule, according to their sinful plan and works, they have, as it were, brought forth wind. According to God's plan and works, Israel was sustained and brought forth the Messiah. For many centuries, Israel was expecting the Messiah and in this vision literally expecting the Messiah. We can join them, the faithful Israel, in their expectation of Christ. As most of you know already, my wife and I are expecting our first child in February. We're praying for a safe delivery, and we thank you for your prayers. During the last few months, I've realized that it's a challenge to sympathize with my wife. So she's been she's the one going through all the discomfort tests and of course ultimately the labor pains I can at least try to under read and try to understand all that's taking place inside of her and the child But sometimes the least we can do turns out to be the best we can do. In the same way I can't be a mother, we cannot be Israel We belong to the church. Israel already went through the pain, discomforts, tests, and ultimately the labor pains to bring forth the Messiah. But we can read and try to understand all that took place in her history and the child. We can turn to God's word, the holy scriptures, which are able to make you wise for salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus Given by inspiration of God and profitable for doctrine. I encourage you to look through the myriads of messianic prophecies in the Old Testament. Starting with the first prediction of Christ in Genesis 3. And that leads us to the next point. Beware of Satan's hatred of God. This hatred goes all the way back to the first chapters of the Bible, back to the Garden of Eden. To more accurately identify the great fiery red dragon of verse 3, we need to skip down to verses 9 and 10 for his other monikers. That serpent of old, called the devil and Satan, who deceives the whole world, the accuser of our brethren The dragon is the serpent of old, who for his part in humanity's fall was cursed. He was cursed above all beasts to be placed below all beasts. He caused the man to return to dust at the end of his life. The serpent would eat dust on his belly all the days of his life. As for the serpent's relationship with the woman, the Lord declared in Genesis 3:15, and I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your seed and her seed. And he shall bruise your head, and you shall bruise his heel. The enmity against this woman's seed has continued since Eden He got right to work with the second generation, with Cain and Abel. Our Lord exposes him in John 8. 44. As a diabolical murderer from the beginning, who does not stand in truth, because there is no truth in him. When he speaks a lie, he speaks from his own resources. For he is a liar and the father of it. He rightly deserves the name of the devil, which comes from the verb diaballo. Meaning defame, slander, accuse falsely. The devil, the murderous father of lies, hates That the word became flesh and dwelt among us, full of grace and truth. While Jesus came to save the world, the devil comes to deceive the world. The ancient serpent, the murderer from the beginning, the father of lies, the devil is also Satan, which is a transliteration of the Hebrew word for the enemy, adversary. In the Old Testament, we see Satan most frequently in the book of Job 11 times in the short span of the first two chapters. Elsewhere he incites King David to number Israel in First Chronicles 21. In the post-exilic period, Satan stands to oppose Joshua the high priest in Zechariah 3 Satan has earned the title over the millenniums as the accuser of our brethren Returning to Revelation 12, 3, Satan appears without subtlety as the great dragon with seven heads and ten horns. I'm not going to spend too much time giving various views on the numbers here, but based on Daniel 7 and 8, I believe that the many heads represent a worldwide confederate kingdom of New Babylon under multiple kings. There's a relationship with the beast, which I will not explore right now. Just know that the authority he wields is counterfeit and ephemeral. He has also at his disposal the fallen angels who have rebelled with him We don't know exactly when this revolt took place. It's likely the short time frame after the sixth day of creation When God saw everything that he has made, and indeed it was very good, and before man's fall in chapter 3. We do know for certain that the majority of angels stay loyal to God. Though he could have sent his angels to do this task, the dragon positioned himself to destroy Jesus as soon as he was born. That was quite evident in Herod's actions in committing the massacre of children two years and younger in Bethlehem region. Herod's son Archelaus would probably have done something similar. Satan tried to directly tempt Christ to cause them to fall like the first Adam. Desperate the dragon sent the religious leaders after Jesus? He may have thought that he won at the crucifixion, but he didn't realize that even as Herod And Pontius Pilate, with the Gentiles and the people of Israel, were gathered together against Christ. They could only do whatever God's hand and his purpose determined before to be done. Everything Satan and his minions did was futile. They were not dealing with the mere mortal. That leads to the third principle: worship Jesus as ruler of all. The long anticipation of Israel finally led up to this moment. the birth of her Messiah, the male child who was to rule all nations with the rod of iron. The rod of iron harkens back to Psalm 2, 9. And we saw the reference earlier in the message to the church of Diatira in chapter 2, verse 27 in Revelation. The iron rod first and foremost belongs to Jesus Christ. It signifies his authority, superior even to the authority of the dragon. Even with the seven heads, ten horns, and seven diadems. We see the same rod later in the book as Jesus fulfills his destiny in his second advent in chapter 19. Verse 5 does not delve into all the details of Jesus' ministry, just his birth, destiny, and ascension. As a child was caught up to God and his throne. Again, Daniel Atkin is helpful, quote: The reason the ascension is highlighted rather than the crucifixion and resurrection is twofold. One The crucifixion and resurrection were beautifully expounded in chapter 5. And two, the ascension is the unquestionable proof. That Satan was defeated in that he could not prevent Christ from rising from the dead and ascending back to his Father, where he now is seated at the right hand of the throne of God. Perhaps the very place that Satan coveted when he fell. Unable to drag Christ down from heaven, the dragon persecutes Israel in verse 6 This verse looks forward to the second half of the seven-year tribulation when the Antichrist breaks the covenant with many. That's the Christ that restored Jerusalem temple, and there will be a great tribulation. For the faithful remnant of Israel, the time of Jacob's trouble. But at the end of that 1,260 days, they can look upward. Behold, he is coming with clouds, and every eye will see him, even they who pierced him And all the tribes of the earth will mourn because of him. Even so. Amen Frustrated at every turn the dragon will rally the troops and make a desperate assault on heaven, with the end approaching and Israel facing great danger. It's no wonder Michael, their watcher, stands up as Daniel predicted in Daniel 12. Michael is the fourth great representative figure, and his appearance leads to The fourth point, rejoice in the certain doom of the devil. In verses 7 to 9, the devil and his angels fail in their attempts to invade heaven. Outnumbered and outpowered, they fall again. Unlike the first ball, they are barred, shut out, no longer able to come before the Lord, like they have done in the past, like in the book of Job. I believe that Jesus our Lord prophetically saw this final fall in Luke 10, 18, when he said, I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven. Without this access, Satan will lose his title as the accuser of our brethren, who accuse them before our God day and night. In verses 10 to 12, we have a spontaneous outburst of praise, a frequent and delightful sound throughout Revelation. Robert Thomas observes that this praise falls into three stanzas: the arrival of God's kingdom and Christ's authority in verse 10. The earthly victory of the saints who identify with Christ in his witness and death. Verse 11. And the celebration over the expulsion of the dragon. and warning to earth because of the devil's ejection from heaven. Verse 12. End quote Just a paraphrase, all three verses speak of the dragon's disgrace, but verse 10 emphasizes God and Christ. Verse eleven, Christ and the Saints. And verse twelve, heaven and earth All three verses amount to our joy, not just in the future, but now. All three verses give us reasons to rejoice in the certain doom of the devil. You can see why Satan hates Christmas. Jesus' birth sets into motion verse four and all that follows. And every turn the dragon is denied his ultimate evil desires. The devil's condemnation and strengthened kingdom and the power of his antichrist will meet their end. Now, salvation and strength in the kingdom of our God and the power of his Christ have come. That's reason to rejoice. Though hellish beasts overcome the witnesses of God, though Babylon the Great, the mother of Harlots, is drunk with the blood of the saints and with the blood of the martyrs of Jesus. Though worshippers of the beast's image kill those who refuse to bow, saints overcome the dragon by the blood of the lamb and by the word of their testimony. And they do not love their lives to the death. That's reason to rejoice. Look at verse 12. Our citizenship is in heaven. In our father's house are many mansions. We are sojourners and pilgrims desiring a better, that is, a heavenly country. We will dwell in a city which has foundations, whose builder and maker is God. This fallen world will become hell under the dragon and his antichrist, who will reign for a little while. We rejoice because soon the kingdoms of this world will become the kingdoms of our Lord and of his Christ, and he shall reign forever and ever. That's reason to rejoice. We're not sure the exact source of the loud heavenly voice in verse ten. But could you echo those words? If Satan hates Christmas because it sets into motion his demise Would you love Christmas because it sets into motion your salvation? If you'd like to join in this chorus of praise, Look no further than the male child in verse 5 and his blood in verse 11. Jesus is the Lamb that was slain. He is the lamb without blemish and without spot. But then why was he slain? He died because all we like sheep have gone astray. We have turned everyone to his own way. And the Lord has laid on him the iniquity of us all. The Son of God shared in our flesh and blood, so that through death he might destroy him who had the power of death. That is the devil. How bidding that Jesus defeated Satan with the power of death by his humble obedience to the point of death, even the death of the cross. He rose from the grave and ascended to heaven. That is caught up to God and his throne. Someday the Lamb who was slain will overcome forces of evil. For he is Lord of Lords and King of Kings, and those who are with him are called, chosen, and faithful If you want to be among those called, chosen and faithful, hear God's call. Know his merciful and compassionate choice of sinners. And come to him in faith God gives you victory and joy over sin and evil by grace alone, through faith alone, in Christ alone You cannot earn eternal life. You must receive it as a gift by trusting in Jesus for your hope of heaven If you are born again, you will enter the kingdom above. And one born of God overcomes the world. And this is the victory that has overcome the world. Our fate. The blood of the Lamb is the outward object of our faith The word of our testimony is a subjective experience of our faith. Will you trust in Jesus today and forever? Even as we'll have tribulation in this world, we can love God more than our lives to the point of death. We can be of good cheer because Jesus has overcome the world. This Christmas we can sing and rejoice in the certain doom of the devil Like we sang earlier, Jesus came to save us all from Satan's power when we were gone astray. Tidings of comfort and joy. What will be your place in the grand redemptive story of the Bible? The panorama of salvation history, the true story of the whole world. Perhaps you feel like you have nothing to look forward to. Open up the Bible and join in Israel's expectation of Christ. Perhaps you've grown complacent in your spiritual walk. Be sober and vigilant and beware of Satan's hatred of God. Perhaps you lost your way and feel as if the world is spinning out of control. Worship Jesus as ruler of all. He sits at the right hand of God the Father. Perhaps you're depressed and sorrowful as you watch the world grow more decadent day by day. Rejoice in the certain doom of the devil. Satan hates Christmas because it spells the end of his rule. We love Christmas because it's the new beginning. As Christ is born, so is our hope of being reborn. I pray you'll be filled with Christmas joy, and your heart triples in size. Let's pray. Lord, we just thank you and we praise you, and we glorify you. Because we know the the ending already. We know that in the end we win. But not because we're such special people, not because you're saints, even the greatest of saints can change the world as we like to say often. But Lord, because of what your son has done when he became flesh and lived the perfect life, and went to the cross obediently and willingly to die for our sins. As the Lamb that was slain now has victory over the world, where we too can join in triumph as we trust in him. Lord, we know that the world is a scary place. And the world is a fallen place. But we look forward to that kingdom that will come when your son comes back. When you send your son come back on earth to establish that kingdom. Lord, until that day, help us to be faithful Lord, encourage us through your word. May we worship you with our hearts and our lips. We thank you and we pray all these things in Jesus Christ's name. Amen.

sermons.title: Divine Saviors and Good Tidings
sermons.speaker: Sung Cho
sermons.text: Thank you again for joining us on Christmas Eve in one of the last days of twenty twenty. We all need to give ourselves a pat on the back for surviving. Then take a deep breath and brace yourselves for 2021. I think you'd agree that twenty twenty will go down in infamy, not only because of COVID-19, but because of the US election. Officials at each other's throats, vitriol in the news, diatrives on Twitter, maybe even arguments at dinner tables. Disagreements about the presidential office. Some do not like the one leaving the White House. Others do not like the one entering the White House Some do not like either of them. Maybe you're sick of promises made and promises broken Yet, like rubber neckers near a car wreck, we can't look away But political angst, exaggerations, and empty promises are nothing new. Let me take you back two millenniums, a few years before Jesus' birth. In modern-day Turkey, near the Aegean Sea, are ruins of a city named Preene. If you were to visit there, you'd see high-quality Hellenistic art and architecture, the temple, Batina. a sanctuary for Zeus, a theater, an agora. Though relatively a small city, you'd also find re remnants of political districts where the local government operated. And if you're a real political history nerd, you'd look closer and locate what's known as the preenne calendar inscription. Written in honor of Caesar Augustus. It's called calendar inscription because it justified the Roman decree to start a nude calendar based on the emperor's birthday. I've included a translated portion in the bulletin. Please follow along as I read it. Since Providence, which has ordered all things and is deeply interested in our life, has set in most perfect order by giving us Augustus whom she filled with virtue that he might benefit humankind, sending him as a savior, both for us and for our descendants That he might end war and arrange all things, and since he, Caesar, by his appearance, excelled even our anticipations, surpassing all previous benefactors And not even leaving to posterity any hope of surpassing what he has done. And since the birthday of the god Augustus was the beginning of the good tidings for the world that came by reason of him, and on and on. A scholar named Craig Evans has noted the similarities between the contents of this inscription with the words that begin the Gospel of Mark. I'll get to the word Savior in a minute. But first look at the words towards the end of the quote. God. Was the beginning of good tidings. And now look at Mark 1. 1, the beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God. Italics and underlines indicate general agreement in meaning. Bold print indicates even closer agreement down to the part of speech and number. What's the point here? Evans believes Mark is inviting his readers to compare Jesus with the most powerful ruler of the day The Roman Emperor Caesar Augustus. He wants all to see that Jesus is better than the best that the world offers. But while Mark begins with Jesus' adult life, we can dial back the clock further. As I read Luke 2, 8-13, pay attention to the parallels between it and the inscription Now there were in the same country shepherds living out in the fields, keeping watch over their flock by night And behold, an angel of the Lord stood before them, and the glory of the Lord shone around them, and they were greatly afraid. Then the angel said to them, Do not be afraid, for behold, I bring you good tidings of great joy, which will be to all people. For there is born to you this day in the city of David a Savior who is Christ the Lord. And this will be the sign to you You will find a babe wrapped in swaddling cloths, lying in a manger. And suddenly there was with the angel a multitude of the heavenly host, praising God and saying, Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, goodwill toward men. Again Italics and underlines indicate general agreement and meaning. Bold print indicates even closer agreement down to the part of speech and number. Between the Prien inscription, Mark and Luke, there's the overlapping mention of good tidings or news, Evangelion, or the Gospel. But uniquely between the inscription and Luke, there is a mention of Soter, Savior. In the former, Providence sent Augustus as Savior. In the latter, God sent Jesus as Savior. The citizens of Prienne are told Caesar would benefit humankind. The shepherds near Bethlehem are told Christ would bring good will toward men. Politicians wish that an emperor would end war and arrange all things. Christians know that our Lord will finally bring peace on earth. This is what we believe. The Bible takes our eyes off of the fallible leaders of today. Our eyes are on Jesus, and upon his shoulder is the everlasting government. He has already surpassed what Augustus has done. Whereas the earthly kingdoms are rooted out and pulled down, destroyed and thrown down. We are looking forward to a kingdom that cannot be shaken. It's okay to feel homeless here, politically speaking. As pilgrims heading to heaven, we can wholeheartedly say, This world is not my home. I'm just passing through. Do you want the assurance that no matter what happens, our place in heaven is secure? Here are the good tidings Jesus our Savior brings. God loves us and created us to enjoy a relationship with Him. But each of us has turned our backs on him. We refuse to submit to his kinship, and that's the beginning of our troubles. That's sin. He has every right to exclude us from his kingdom because he sets the standard for entrance We chose willingly hell on earth to die while living. And it's just a prelude of what's to come. But God who loves us and created us is the same God who saves us. He sent his son Jesus on earth to live a perfect life. Unlike benefactors who are all talk, Jesus laid down his life on the cross. There he took the consequences of our sins and paid for them in full. To prove that he has truly accomplished salvation, he rose from the dead, prove he was truly alive and ascended to heaven Any day now he'll return and establish that eternal kingdom of heaven on earth. Jesus lovingly invites you, enemies of the state, to become citizens of his kingdom. Come and receive eternal life freely by grace. Turn from yourself self-gratification, self-righteousness. And trust in Jesus, the Savior. I urge you, begin this relationship with Him before it's too late. You'll regret forever if you breed your last without securing your entrance into heaven Perhaps this sounds like too much right now. You just came to sing some Christmas carols and hear music. But if you want to talk more later, please use the QR code or link on the bulletin cover to get in touch with us. We offer six to seven-week classes to introduce you to Christianity. We also have free Bibles and Christian literature in the lobby. Please take as many as you wish. As we close, please know this is the story of Christmas. Caesar Augustus was born to royalty in Palatine Hill of Rome, where one historian calls the first nucleus of the Roman Empire. Jesus was born in obscurity in the little town of Bethlehem, not afforded even a room in an inn. But our humble King will return someday, crowned with many crowns. Jesus, he truly is Lord at his birth. Lord, we come before you and very often disappointed by what's happening. Politically, in the society, and in our personal lives. People leave us, people disappoint us People exalt themselves only to be dragged down, caught in their own words. And Lord, your word is very clear that we are fallible. And even the best of us, even the best of us like Adam, fell With the perfect environment around him. But we're thankful for your son, the second Adam, who came, who is the King of Kings and Lord of Lords. He truly is the Savior. And his coming, first coming and second coming really is The good tidings to come. And we're thankful for those of us who believe in that good news. And we pray for those who do not understand or refuse to believe. That you will open up their hearts to see the love of Christ. Lord, we're thankful for this evening that we can be reminded of what you have done. by sending your son to us. And we pray in your son's name. Amen.

sermons.title: Proclamations Against Neutrality
sermons.speaker: Sung Cho
sermons.text: Compromise, tolerance, middle ground. In certain contexts, these words sound good. In marriage, there needs to be some kind of compromise. In a local church congregation, we need some tolerance of diversity In, I would say, third-tier theological convictions. In politics, there needs to be some meeting of opposites in the middle ground to move forward. I admit that compromise, tolerance, and middle ground in certain contexts make sense But in other situations, neutrality does not make sense. Take, for example, the ecumenical document from about 25 years ago entitled. Evangelicals and Catholics together. It was designed to support a cooperative movement between two major traditions based on some commonalities Including the Trinitarian Doctrine and the Nicene Creed. The seeds of this movement were planted in the 70s with earlier collaborations Like the moral majority led by Jerry Falwell. Now, I respect Catholics for social causes that they have thoughtfully championed. I think it's fine to join them in the march for life. I think they're key partners in the fight for religious liberty. I believe most of them will help in the preservation of Judeo-Christian values But the problem with the document, specifically evangelical and Catholics together, is more theological than ethical. Take, for example, this one sentence from it. Quote, we affirm together that we are justified by grace through faith because of Christ. Let me read that again. We affirm together that we are justified by grace through faith because of Christ. Now it's not that Catholics do not believe in justification, grace, and faith. They do, but they don't believe that justification is imputed righteousness. They say it's infused righteousness. They don't believe that justification is by grace alone, through faith alone. That word alone is why faithful Protestants died. Why they were burned at the stake. Why they were sent to exile. Let's not pretend like the Reformation didn't happen. And then the next paragraph begins like this. Quote: All who accept Christ as Lord and Savior are brothers and sisters in Christ. Evangelicals and Catholics are brothers and sisters in Christ. Even if prominent names like Chuck Colson And Bill Bright and J. I. Packer and Pat Robertson endorsed or signed this document.
