This present inheritance of life is how a Christian can have joy in this life on earth. We can walk without stumbling around because Jesus is the light of the world. He who follows him shall not walk in darkness, but have the light of life, according to John 8 and verse 12. What calmed the light? What joy Christians have because we can clearly see our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. Without Christ, a person stumbles around in darkness Because as Jesus says in John 11 and verse 10, there is no light in him. Without Christ, a person cannot see clearly the way to perform that which is good and right. Without Christ, a person has no present inheritance in the light, nor do they have a real hope for a future glory. A person may think they are good enough, but their understanding of good enough is clouded by the darkness they walk in. Because without Christ, there is no light. How does one qualify to be a child of light? After the prayer in Colossians 1:12, Paul begins to describe how a Christian is qualified to be a partaker of this inheritance of light. And as I read verse 13, you'll notice right away that a person's qualification has nothing to do with their self. Rather, verse 13 tells us, he, as God the Father, has delivered us from the power of darkness and conveyed us into the the kingdom of the Son of His love, in whom we have redemption through his blood. That's Jesus' blood, the forgiveness of sins. Christians are qualified to inherit light because God the Father has rescued us from the power of darkness and carried us away to Jesus' kingdom, and he did so through the blood of Jesus. Lightfoot says, we were slaves in the land of darkness. God rescued us from this thraldom. He transplanted us thence and settled us as free colonists in the kingdom of his son in the realms of light. A Christian's qualification does not rest in doing good works. Though good works will still be present. It does not rest there. It rests in Christ The question then is, are you qualified to be a child of light? Does the description we read about in Paul and Timothy's prayer describe you and your desire? Are you increasing in the knowledge of God's will? Are you living a life that is in the light? One that produces good works that are both pleasing and fruitful? Are you trusting on God's strength? Or are you living life your way, trusting in your own knowledge and in your own strength to deal with the circumstances and people in your life Are you doing good for goodness' sake and not Christ? This is the pivot point that separates a Christian from a person who tries to do good. It is the person of Jesus Christ. And this is where the letter to the Christians in Colossus pretty much stays focused throughout the remaining chapters It is Christ that makes a Christian a Christian. Without Christ, the works that anyone does, even if they are good in everyone else's eyes, without Christ, they are considered wicked. Paul makes this point clear to the church in Colossae as we will read when we discuss the second thing I wanted to look at this morning, and that is a description of works. This description of works is first provided in a high-level statement of fact. That I think provides a clear dividing line between the works of a Christian and the works of a person trying to do good. Once this dividing line has been defined, Paul gives several examples of works that fall on either side of this dividing line. So what is the dividing line between a Christian's works and the works of a person who is trying to do good. Let's read together in Colossians chapter 1, verses 19 to 22. For it pleased the Father that in him all the fullness should dwell, and by him to reconcile all things to himself. by him, whether things on earth or things in heaven, having made peace through the blood of his cross. And you who are once alienated and enemies in your mind by wicked word Yet now he is reconciled in the body of his flesh through death to present you holy and blameless and above reproach in his sight In these verses, we read of a person without Christ, before Christ, and after Christ, the effect that Christ has on that person's world. Works. The person without Christ is compared to the Christian who is only so because of Christ. We see that a person without Christ is really an alien, an enemy of God by wicked works. Whereas the Christian is considered holy, blameless, above reproach in God's sight. This is something that only God can do Because both a person that tries to do good and a Christian are sinners deserving hell. Romans 3. 23 tells us: for all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God. In Galatians chapter 3 and verse 10, we learn, For as many as are of the works of the law are under the curse, for it is written, Cursed is everyone who does not contend you in all things which are written in the book of the law, to do them. And even James, who strongly teaches that genuine faith requires works, says in chapter 2 and verse 10 of his letter. For whoever shall keep the whole law, and yet stumble in one point, he is guilty of all. These verses prove the point made by the author in Ecclesiastes seven and verse twenty. For there is not a just man on earth. Who does good and does not sin. But though the Christian is deserving of hell, because Christ is the Christian's Lord and Savior, Christ works a work that only God can do and reconciled us to Him. This is the dividing line between the works of a Christian and the works of a person trying to do good. It's not the individual's works. It's the reconciling work of Jesus. The idea of reconciling may appear difficult to grasp, but Charles Ryrie simplifies this idea for us. He says, to reconcile means to change. Pretty simple, right? However, he goes on to say, it is important to observe that in reconciliation only man is changed. God is not. And this truth that God does not change is consistent with Scripture. We are told in Malachi 3 and verse 6, for I am the Lord, I do not change. And so with reconciliation, a change happens in man as a result of Jesus' work. We read of Jesus' reconciling work in verse 20, where all things are reconciled to him. John MacArthur notes that this text does not teach that all will believe. Rather, it teaches that all will ultimately submit. And I think this truth that all will not believe is reinforced by the very next verse, verse 21, where we see that some do not accept the reconciling work of Jesus We have both the person without Christ having their wicked works, and then the person with Christ, the Christian, having a life described in verse 22 as holy, blameless, and above reproach. Thus, not all will believe. Some will remain enemies with God. But in the end, even the enemies of God will submit to Him. Philippians 2 verses 10 to 11 solidifies this truth that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow with those in heaven and those on earth and of those under the earth, and that every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord to the glory of God the Father. Jesus' work is of reconciliation. We're also given the details of how Jesus performed his work of reconciliation. In these verses that we read. In verse 20, he made peace through the blood of his cross. And in verse 22, he gave the body of his flesh through death. This reconciling work was accomplished when Jesus died on the cross for the sins of the whole world. Jesus made a way for the sinner to change from an enemy of God to a friend of God. By shedding his own blood on the cross, by dying in the place of us guilty sinners, and then rising again on the third day. This is the good news, the gospel that's revealed to us in the Bible. The good deeds that people do will not help them to cross the dividing line of works. Their deeds will still be wicked to God. Only the finished work of Jesus on the cross will cause a person to have a change in their works, where their works are no longer wicked, but acceptable. Paul reminds Timothy or Titus of this in Titus 3, in verses 3 to 5, when he says, For we ourselves were once foolish, disobedient, deceived, serving various lusts and pleasures. living in malice and envy, hateful and hating one another. But when the kindness and the love of God our Saviour toward man appeared, not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to his mercy, He saved us. God, in his mercy, provided a way of reconciliation through the work of Jesus Christ. To cross this dividing line, a person has to accept the work of Jesus accomplished when he died and rose again. Romans 5. 10 tells us, for if when we were enemies we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son, much more having been reconciled, we shall be saved by His life. Have you been saved or rescued from a life of wicked works in the eyes of God? From a life of enity with God? If so, if you have faith in Jesus, then we are told in Colossians 1 and verse 23 to continue in it, to not be moved away from the hope of the gospel which you heard. As believers in Jesus Christ, we are to show that we belong to Christ by being steadfast and grounded in the truth that we have been taught through Scripture. When the world tries to make us doubt the hope that we have, or when we fail to live up to what we know is right and feel like we are worthless because we can't do the smallest thing for Christ. We should stand on the promises that we know that are complete through Christ's work of reconciliation. If you don't know if you've been rescued from your wicked works, the Bible tells us how. How we sinful people can be holy, blameless, and above reproach in his sight. It is by grace through faith in Jesus Christ. Ephesians 2, verses 8 and 9 tells us: For by grace you have been saved through faith. And that not of yourselves, it is the gift of God. Not of works, lest anyone should boast. Your good works won't save you. Because as we saw in verse 21 of Colossians 1, an enemy's works are wicked, and you are an enemy of God. until you cross that dividing line. Trusting in Christ's work of reconciliation, the work that was accomplished through the shedding of his blood on the cross, through the death, burial, and resurrection of Jesus. Jesus. What are you waiting for? Lift up your voice and follow the advice of Romans ten, verses nine and ten. That if you confess with your mouth the Lord Jesus and believe in your heart That God has raised him from the dead, you will be saved. For with the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation The dividing line between the works of a Christian and the works of other people are not the works of the individuals, but the reconciling work of Jesus. With this understanding, we are now ready to look at the third thing in our discussion this morning, and that is a response to works. The result of crossing this dividing line is made evident in Colossians 3, where we're given a list that describes some works that are done both by those without Christ and those that are Christians. Let's briefly look at this list together in Colossians three, verses five to nine. Therefore, put to death your members which are on the earth fornication, uncleanliness, passion, evil desire, and covetousness. Which is idolatry. Because of these things, the wrath of God is coming upon the sons of disobedience, in which you yourselves once walked when you lived in them. But now you yourselves are to put off all these anger, wrath, malice, blasphemy, filthy language out of your mouth. Do not lie to one another In the first portion of these verses, we have works that are eliciting a response from God, works that bring God's wrath These works are summed up as idolatry and described in blunt terms such as fornication, which is illicit sexual intercourse in general Uncleanliness, which is the impurity of lustful, luxurious, wasteful living. Passion, which is a depraved affection of the mind or emotion. Evil desire, which is a desire for what is forbidden or lust, and covetousness, which is a greedy desire to have more Without Christ, these are the works that manifest themselves in many people. They see nothing wrong with sex outside of marriage With affections and desires for those of the same sex as them, with living life only to bring themselves pleasure and always wanting more. Without Christ, people are bringing God's wrath by the works they do. These are works that Christians used to do also before we accepted the reconciling work of Jesus. In place of our own works. After crossing that dividing line, the Christian no longer has to live their life in these ways, as we have the power of Jesus working in our lives. To put to death these wrath-bringing works, including the power to put off the works that are described in verses 8 and 9. These words that a Christian is able to put off or to strip away include anger, which is an abiding, settled, and habitual anger that includes in its scope. The purpose of revenge, wrath, which is the boiling agitation of the feelings, malice, which is ill will or desire to injure. Blasphemy, which is speech injurious to another's good name, filthy language, which is foul speaking, or low and obscene speech, like dirty jokes. And lying, which is not telling the truth. Without Christ, these types of works will stain a person trying to do good. A stain that ruins any good work that they may attempt to do. A stain that will not come out by the will of the person alone. A stain that causes their works to be sin. This is why a person without Christ cannot have acceptable works before God. Their works are permeated with sin. A Christian, though, has had the stain removed. A Christian has cried out to God, as David did after his sin with Bathsheba in Psalm 51:7, saying, Wash me and I shall be whiter than snow. For the Christian, the stain of sin has been removed, and our works can be acceptable before God. As such, all these works listed in verses 5 to 9 of Colossians 3, a Christian is able to put to death or able to put off because Christ is our strength. Ultimately, a Christian is not yet perfect. And so if you're like me, then as I read this list, you thought to yourself, hmm, many of these works are works that I find myself still doing, if not in my flesh, then at least in my mind. And then you groan, as Paul groaned In Romans 7. 24, O wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from this body of death? In these words, I think we have the proper response to works. This kind of response to works is the difference between a person without Christ and the Christian. The Christian responds by struggling to be free from this body of death. A struggle that occurs between the flesh and the Holy Spirit in Galatians 5. 17 says The flesh lust against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh. And these are contrary to one another, so that you do not do the things that you wish. A person without Christ, though, does not have the Holy Spirit warring against the flesh. Rather, they are living according to their flesh Which Romans 8, verses 5 to 7 says, is setting their mind on the things of the flesh, to which we're told to be carnally or fleshly minded is death. Because the carnal mind is enmity against God. The person without Christ does not struggle against their body of death because they do not have the spirit of Christ to cause a conflict. I'm reminded of a story I once read in the Our Daily Bread booklet that really struck me as a young adult struggling with sin in my own life. The story goes that two men went duck hunting. And on the way to the hunting location, their wagon wheel broke. And while the Christian got out and changed the will, the will fell down and smashed his thumb. The Christian let out a swear word, but he immediately dropped on his knees and prayed out loud to God for forgiveness. His friend saw this and said, I don't see why you struggle with such a little thing, such as swearing. It's nothing to me. The Christian did not have a response at this time. But later that day, while hunting, they shot some ducks, and they were retrieving the ducks. They saw one duck that was still struggling to get away from the hunters. The Christian looked at his friend and said, You asked me earlier why I struggle in my Christian life You see that duck? The one struggling? That's me. You, my friend, are that dead duck over there Without Christ, a person does not struggle with the works of their flesh. Works that go against God's command because they do not have the Spirit of Christ in them. Whereas a Christian struggles to put off these works that go against our Lord and Savior, because we are alive. Christ is in us. And since a Christian is alive in Jesus, we are able to do as Colossians 3 and verse 17 commands, that in whatever we do, in word or deed, Do all in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father through him. Once again, we see Jesus playing a role in the Christian's life Earlier, we saw the person of Jesus as the pivot point between the Christian and the person trying to do good without Christ. We then saw Jesus' work of reconciliation or change as the dividing line between wicked and acceptable works. And now we see Jesus being the reason a Christian struggles against their flesh. And so that we can serve Jesus in whatever we do. Or say, Jesus is the Christian's Lord, which means he is our master. And our response to works is to obey our master no matter what the cost. And while we're at it, we are to give thanks to God the Father. As the lyrics to the worship song goes: give thanks with a grateful heart. Give thanks to the Holy One. Give thanks because he's given Jesus Christ, his son. Without Christ, we can do nothing good. As we live here today and go about our daily routines, may we be bold to make known to those around us that a Christian is more than someone who does good things. May we remember the description of a Christian as a person who acts on what they know is the truth in God's word is not tossed around by the world's thinking of God. right and wrong. A grounding that is made possible because a Christian has the light of Christ showing the way in this dark world May we remember that works are really wicked in God's sight if you are an enemy of God. If you have not trusted the changing work of Jesus accomplished on the cross. Cross. May we remember that a Christian responds to words in a daily struggle to serve the Lord Jesus. Knowing that this struggling to please Jesus shows that we are truly alive in Him. May our words and deeds show the difference. Between a Christian and other people that are watching. Amen. Let's go ahead and pray. Father, thank you for the truth of your word. Thank you for making a way for sinful man to come before you. Thank you for the finished work of Christ. On the cross, for the hope of eternal life through Christ. Thank you for making us holy, blameless, and above reproach in your sight. Thank you for your mercy. In Christ we praise you. Amen. Children can be dismissed for children's church.

sermons.title: A World of Worries
sermons.speaker: Sung Cho
sermons.text: Are you happy, content, satisfied here in United States? Around this time last year, Forrest magazine produced a piece entitled, Ranked, the Twenty Happiest Countries in the World. It was an odd time to read it because the pandemic was just beginning to sweep the globe and travel restrictions were enforced. At any rate, the article cites from the World Happiness Report, an annual survey by the Sustainable Development Solutions Network for the United Nations. It looks at the state of global happiness in 156 countries, ranking countries using the Gallup World poll, and six factors, including life expectancy. Generosity, social support. For our third year in a row, Finland topped the list with Helsinki as the happiest city in the world as well Denmark and Switzerland follow. US came in at 18. I was disappointed to see South Korea at 61, barely beating Japan at 62. Mali was at one hundred fourteen at the very bottom of the ranking. Any guesses Afghanistan, Kabul as the unhappiest city as well. Now I didn't look deep into the complexity of this happiness formula or algorithm, but the editors of the report said something that caught my eye Looking at, quote, earlier studies of earthquakes, floods, storms, tsunamis, and even economic crises, they observed, quote, surprising increases in happiness. In the wake of what might otherwise seem to be unmitigated disasters. End quote. Increases in happiness in unmitigated disasters. That means even fallen humanity understands that happiness is not entirely determined by happy circumstances. Here's my from the lesser to the greater argument here. If we belong to God's kingdom, If we rejoice in the hope of the glory of God and even glory in tribulations. If we believe godliness with contentment is great gain. For we brought nothing into this world, and it is certain we can carry nothing out, then how much more shall we be happy, content, and satisfied? What is the opposite of joy and hope, glory and tribulations and godliness with contentment? You recall Dr. Bill priest on Luke 12, 13-21, which is a warning against foolish living and covetousness. We can deceive ourselves into thinking we have many goods laid off for many years and we can take our ease, eat, drink, and be merry. Our souls may be required of us perhaps this very night. Then who will take possession of our treasures? We do not want to be laying up treasures for ourselves and fail to be rich toward God. But even if we do not covet and idolize money, worry and anxiety may beset us at times, even us Christians. Even if we've been following the Lord for many years, unbelief and fear may plague us. Perhaps in 2020 some of you suffered greatly in your finances. Personally, I'm a planner. It doesn't take too long before my outlook of the future turns into a downward spiral of despair Whether we're rich or poor, young or old, there's the danger of caring too much about secondary matters. As F. F. Bruce observed, quote, you can be as unfaithful to God through care as well as through covetousness. You can be as unfaithful to God through care as well as through covetousness. And so we talked about covetousness. In Luke 12, 13 to 21. So now let's talk about care in verses 22 to 34. So follow along with me as I read it. Then he said to his disciples, Therefore I say to you, do not worry about your life. what you will eat, nor about the body, what you will put on. Life is more than food, and the body is more than clothing. Consider the ravens, for they neither sow nor reap, which have neither storehouse nor barn, and God feeds them. Of how much more value are you than the birds? And which of you by worrying can add one cubit to his stature? If you then are not able to do the least, why are you anxious for the rest? Consider the lilies, how they grow. They neither toil nor spin. And yet I say to you, Even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these. If then God so closed the grass, which today is in the field and tomorrow is thrown into the oven. How much more will he clothe you, O you of little faith? And do not seek what you should eat or what you should drink, nor have an anxious mind For all these things the nations of the world seek after, and your father knows that you need these things. But seek the kingdom of God, and all these things shall be added to you. Do not fear, little flock, for it is your father's good pleasure to give you the kingdom. Sell what you have and give alms. Provide yourselves money bags which do not grow old A treasure in the heavens that does not fail, where no thief approaches nor moth destroys, for where your treasure is, there your heart will be also. To guard ourselves from cares of life, obey the teachings of Jesus I derive four principles from this passage. One, value your life essentials, verses twenty-two to twenty-four. Two, trust in God, not your mortal inability, verses twenty-five to twenty-eight. Three, seek God's everlasting kingdom, verses twenty-nine to thirty-one. And four, give to obtain heavenly treasure and peace. Verses thirty-two to thirty-four First, value your life essentials. After addressing the complaint of the man disputing with his brother and the crowds Jesus turns to his disciples. He sets forth before them the principle in verse 22. Unlike the fools and the covetous, the followers of Jesus must not worry about life, or at least the lesser things of life. Like food, less important matters of body such as clothes. I think verses 23 and 24 support this basic idea By challenging our hierarchy of values. Note how verse 23 employs the formula blank is more than blank, and verse 24 is a comparison of humans to birds. But you would think that it'd be easy to grasp that life is more than food and the body is more than clothing. We may know these truths, but we don't always act like it. Consider how people lose their minds over food. The children of Israel said some insane things to Moses as they left Egypt. They've been enslaved by Egyptians for Centuries. They left behind that iron furnace about a month ago. They witnessed Pharaoh's army drawn in the Red Sea days ago And now what do they say to Moses and Aaron in the wilderness? Oh, that we have died by the hand of the Lord in the land of Egypt. When we sat by the pots of meat, and when we ate bread to the full, for you have brought us out into this wilderness to kill this whole assembly with hunger. Exodus 16, 3. They did not value freedom as a life essential. They did not believe life was more than food. Let's fast forward, closer to our time. Consider how the culture values our looks more than our health. While I was growing up as a teen, having the latest pairs of basketball shoes, the brand new Nike sneakers, endorsed by Michael Jordan, it was all the craze. Now don't get me wrong, I enjoy comfortable and good looking shoes as much as the next person, except unlike the next person, I'll probably wear them until they're threadbare and the soles are detached. And I'm not against sneakerheads who collect shoes as a hobby or appreciate fashion. But if it becomes an unhealthy obsession, perhaps you're valuing apparel over the body. In your estimation, is the body more important than clothing? So we show how food and clothing um are commonly overestimated and Dustin versus You know, twenty-three there, right? In verse twenty-four, we see how human worth is underestimated. Jesus uses a simple illustration from nature to expose our faulty value systems. Ravens do not store up like farmers or hoard like the rich man in the earlier parable. Yet God feeds them The argument from the lesser to the greater is that if God sees these birds, how much more will he provide for us? It's notable how earlier in the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus essentially said the same thing, but spoke of generally the birds of the air. Here he specifically identifies ravens classified as unclean according to the law of Moses. That's in Leviticus 11 and Deuteronomy 14. Again, the argument from the lesser to the greater. If God feeds birds regarded as abominations, how much more will he provide for us regarded as his children? We must value life essentials, even if the world doesn't There's a lot of talk out there about self-love and believing in yourself. Let me tell you, that God's Word tells you the truth about your word and things While the world gives you half truths and lies. Popular culture may tell you that fancy eating and clothing are hashtag life goals. I don't understand what the hashtag is for. Someone can explain it to me. Modern science may teach you that you're just an evolved version of the animals The Bible teaches us the opposite: to value ourselves, our families, our friends, our neighbors, even our enemies, as those made in God's image. Even if we're disappointed in humanity, we never give up on humans. And if we align ourselves with Jesus here We find the proper motivation for our ministries, mercy ministries, outreach, evangelism, and ultimately the Great Commission. It is urgent that we ask the Lord to properly realign our values. It is a priority to esteem what's essential in life. Why? Because we're finite beings with real limitations. Accepting that truth is quite liberating and guards us from the cares of life And that leads to the next point, trusting God, not your mortal inability. It's helpful in many ways to know we're helpless in many ways. We'll never be God, even if we try to play God. Jesus shows us the futility of our ways. Our anxiety accomplishes nothing, gets us nowhere, helps none around us. As you see in other Bible translations, the word for stature in verse 25 can also mean lifespan. I agree with them so that Jesus' argument relates to time, not space. The question is better translated as, and which of you by Warring can add one qubit to his lifespan? A qubit is about 18 inches, and that would actually be a significant growth spur physically. But what is 18 inches in the timeline of our lives, which stretches for meters and meters? Hours of worrying won't buy you a second. If you can't affect the smallest thing in the world, why worry about things beyond your control? Commentator Walter Lightfield summarizes, quote, The point here is that if it is futile to worry about small matters we cannot control, it is even more futile to worry about the larger matters that lie even farther beyond our control. So just sit pretty. Sit pretty like the lilies. Jesus again uses a simple illustration from nature to stress our need to rest in God. The argument from the lesser to the greater is that if lilies grow without effort and display their beauty, If these flowers are resplendent with glory greater than that of Solomon, that God close the grass that way, that will be thrown into fire. How much more will he clothe us? Whether it's valuable life essentials or our mortal inability. Our failure to see these truths, big truths, come from our little faith. We must stop trusting in ourselves and begin to trust in God. Now, before I move on to the third point of this sermon, I want to speak to those who have never established a relationship with God through faith. The two truths we covered, human dignity and human inability, are important gospel principles. As I mentioned earlier, God granted us the ultimate status and privilege of being his image bearers. According to Psalm 8, our Creator made us a little lower than angels, crowned us with glory and honor, caused us to have dominion over all his creatures, and put all things underneath our feet. Now the obvious question to ask is this, what in the world happened? I don't have a crown on my head. I have a headache I don't have dominion over animals. I can't even control my dog. I don't feel like I have all things underneath my feet. I feel like all things are crushing me under its weight. What happened? At the turn of the twentieth century, British newspaper The Times sent out an inquiry to famous authors. What's wrong with the world today? One author replied, Dear sir, I am. What went wrong? We did. That truth still holds today. To be more specific, we have sinned. We have broken God's laws. We have turned away from Him. Instead of worshiping God, the Father, the Giver, we bow down to the gifts. We've changed the glory of the incorruptible God into an image made like corruptible man, and birds and four-footed animals and creeping things. Our end is destruction. Our God is our belly. Our glory is in our shame. We've set our mind on earthly things. We do not properly value life essentials because we do not properly value the life giver Instead of trusting the provider, we've deluded ourselves into thinking we are self-sufficient. We think we can add miles to our lifeline. We can't save our bodies though, let alone our souls. Our Lord has warned, what profit is it to a man if he gains the whole world and is himself destroyed or lost? Our best plans for tomorrow supply us with the worst worries for today. We say with evil boasting and arrogance, today or tomorrow we'll go to such and such a city, spend a year there, buy and sell and make a profit. Refuse to admit our weakness and speak properly. If the Lord wills, we shall live and do this or that. We do not trust in God, but we lean on our mortal inability. None of us would value our life essentials and exercise faith left to our own. God took the initiative He sent this Jesus, his son Jesus on earth. He showed us what it means to live with proper perspective on life, valuing life and body over food and clothing. He God himself walked among us and showed us perfectly what it means to be a human. He trusted the father moment by moment, joyfully fulfilling his role in the form of a bondservant But God did not just send his own son in the likeness of sinful flesh. He condemned sin in the flesh. We could not extricate, separate, and cleanse the sin that resides in us. Jesus solved the sin problem by taking upon himself our sins at the cross. All our sinful worries of the mind, our careless words of the mouth, our wicked deeds of the hands, Jesus paid for them as if he himself committed them. After finishing his work on the cross, Jesus rose from the dead and ascended to heaven. He will return one day to judge the world. Now is the time to repent. Turn away from your moral ineptitude and mortal inability. Believe, trust, place your hope of heaven in Jesus. He shows us the love of God, rich and pure, measureless and strong, to those who are poor and impure, limited and weak. Bring your faith, even your little faith, before the Lord, and He'll accept you Now, God does not want our just faith to stay small, right? He wants our minimal faith for salvation to grow maximally. For sanctification. Though entering God's kingdom requires no work, living for God's kingdom requires hard work. Again, we must take care to not care for the things of the world. That leads to the third principle, seek God's everlasting kingdom Verse 29 communicates the same basic idea as verse 22 that began this passage But I do want to highlight the word behind the phrase have an anxious mind. The word in the original language is hard to translate, but saying it may give you a better idea of its meaning. Is meteorizal and it sounds like meteor, something suspended in midair. Again, Walter Lightfield is helpful in describing the metaphor Worry means someone is in suspense or up in the air. Even if our earthly circumstances are in suspense Even if our uncertain future is up in the air, we have this command from the Lord to avoid an anxious mind. Now this verb root does sound interesting, but what weaves verses 29, 30, and 31 together is the verb root for seek. The simple word for seek is in verse 29 and 31, and a compound word for seek after in verse 30. Altogether, we see that there are things we should not seek, and there are things we should seek. We should not seek what we should eat or drink and be anxious about them. Now it's not that these things are bad in themselves. You see in verse 30 how it says our Father knows that we need them But we're easily drawn to the world through these things. And they're baits, they're like baits on a fish fly Soon, possessions become obsessions, content becomes discontent, want becomes need. To resist the allures of this lustful world, we must look beyond it. Seek the kingdom of God, not what the nations of the world seek after. This must be our highest priority. As Jesus already said in the Sermon on the Mount: seek first the kingdom of God, and all these things shall be added to you. But what does this kingdom living look like day to day? If we trust the Lord to add all these things to us, we must be willing to subtract certain things. If God is going to multiply our blessings, we must divide up our bounty. That leads to the fourth principle for carefree life, give to obtain heavenly treasure and peace. There's a saying attributed to Martin Luther. I'm still trying to find the source. And it goes, There are three conversions necessary. The conversion of the heart, the conversion of the mind, and the conversion of the purse. The heart, the mind, and the purse all connected. Your heavenly account and your bank account linked, your faith and your works of charity attached. So much of giving is motivation, and finding the right motivation is the key. And the first of the two motivations in this passage is trust. Trusting God the Son and trusting God the Father. We trust Jesus the way sheep trust their protective shepherd. We trust our heavenly father the way children trust their earthly fathers. It's not fear, it's not guilt, it's faith in God and his liberality, his good pleasure to give us the kingdom. Giving, motivated by faith, brings glory to God. But faithful giving is not only for God's glory, it's also for our good. That's the second motivation. It's for our good to give away our goods. Verse 33 begins with a simple command to liquidate our hoardings and give to the needy, but then we are told to give now so that we may receive later. Randy Alcorn has some memorable principles for application. You can't take it with you, but you can send it ahead Financial giving stores up eternal treasures in heaven. Here's a quote that sounds like Jim Elliott meets Dave Ramsey. We can trade temporal possessions we can't keep. To gain eternal possessions we can't lose. Trade in your Gucci and Louis Vuittons for money bags for eternity. Your fading trinkets for lasting treasures This is for God's glory, and this is for our good. One more quote from Elkhorn, a illustration. Imagine you're alive at the end of the Civil War, you're living in the South, but you're a northerner. You plan to move home as soon as the war is over. While in the South, you've accumulated lots of Confederate currency. Now suppose you know for a fact the North's going to win the war and the end is imminent. What will you do with your Confederate money? If you're smart, there's only one answer. You should immediately cash in your Confederate currency for U. S. currency. The only money that will have value once the war is over. Keep only enough confederate currency to meet your short-term needs See, that's the happy predicament we find ourselves in. We do not belong to this world, and our ultimate happiness Is not in Finland, Denmark, or even the United States. The kingdoms of this world are fading. But God's kingdom is righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit, and there will be no end. And if home is where the heart is, then heaven is where our treasure should be. For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also. Make moves to cash in for the future. Keep only enough for the short term Now, how you actually and specifically apply this principle, to whom, to where you should give our decisions, you must carefully and prayerfully consider. As a representative of this church, I do want to remind you of recent suggestions made by the Budget Committee. They contacted all of our supported missionaries and inquired of their needs. Valerie's needs are now met through our approved 2021 budget. We also have in that budget special missions fund. But if the Lord is moving you to give, please prayerfully consider the causes of three ministries. One, assist church expansion with Bill and Beth Bryant. Two, without reservation, Kent and Kim Frazier. And three, team in Spain, we prayed for them earlier, Carrie and Sharon Owen. These three have tangible, practical, and urgent needs, and they could use our timely assistance. The council has decided to designate our Easter offering to these three ministries. So prayerfully consider if the Lord is leading you to give you By your giving, you're learning to apply the word, demolish idols, experience blessings of obedience. You're learning to be biblically happy, leaving behind a world of worries for the world to come. But remember, you'll never outgive our Father. That's what we'll see as we prepare for the Lord's Supper. Let's meditate on the Father's gift of Jesus. He who did not spare his own son, but delivered him up for us all. How shall he not with him also freely give us all things? Let's pray Lord, we thank you for your daily provisions. We praise you because you richly provide for us. And Lord We're sorry for many times that we have not responded in faith and joy and gratefulness. But Lord, we complain like the Israelites in the wilderness. Not being satisfied with your daily provision which you have ordained. But we're thankful in your bounty, your goodness, your greatness. Your loving kindness, your mercies that are new every morning. We pray that we will remember these truths as we Going before your table to the Lord's Supper. Pray all these things in Jesus Christ's name. Amen.

sermons.title: Housekeeping Matters
sermons.speaker: Sung Cho
sermons.text: In ancient Greek literature, there is an important motif or theme of nostos, which means arrival or homecoming. It appears most dramatically in Homer's Odyssey. Odysseus's goal of reaching home to his family is threatened over and over again for many years. Meanwhile, his wife Penelope, son Telemachus, and the servants are forced into a tough choice. Will they stay loyal to their husband, father, and master? Or will they turn aside to the suitors who seek to replace them? When I first read this epic, there was something compelling and admirable about those loyal to Odysseus. Something that rang true even in this fiction. That's because we're waiting for our master to arrive and take his rightful place as king. But we're not just part of a cool story. This is reality. Jesus is really returning. And until he does, we as his servants have some housekeeping to do. Last week from Luke 12, 22 to 34, we discussed the carefree life. It means not worrying about food or clothes. It means trusting in God. We must look beyond what the world seeks after and seek God's kingdom. Give away our goods and store up for heaven the world to come. In today's passage, we have more exhortations from Jesus. Verses 35 to 48 teaches us the proper posture to maintain as we wait for our master. Here we'll find principles for living now in light of Jesus' return. How to awake out of sleep. To set our minds on things above. To avoid entangling ourselves with affairs of this life. To hold fast what we have. Let's turn to Luke twelve, thirty-five to forty-eight. Let your waist be girded, and your lamps burning, and you yourselves be like men who wait for their master when he will return from the wedding That when he comes and knocks, they may open to him immediately. Blessed are those servants whom the Master, when he comes, will find watching. Assuredly, I say to you, that he will gird himself and have them sit down to eat, and will come and serve them And if he should come in the second watch or come in the third watch and find them so, blessed are those servants. But know this, that if the master of the house had known what hour the thief would come, he would have watched and not allowed his house to be broken into. Therefore, you also be ready, for the Son of Man is coming at an hour you do not expect. Then Peter said to him, Lord, do you speak this parable only to us or to all people? And the Lord said, Who then is that faithful and wise steward, whom his master will make ruler over his household, to give them their portion of food in due season? Blessed is that servant whom his master will find so doing when he comes. Truly I say to you that he will make him ruler over all that he has. But if that servant says in his heart, My master is delaying his coming, and begins to beat the male and female servants, and to eat and drink and be drunk. The master of that servant will come on a day when he is not looking for him, and at an hour when he is not aware, and will cut him in two and appoint him his portion with the unbelievers And that servant who knew his master's will and did not prepare himself or do according to his will shall be beaten with many stripes. But he who did not know yet committed things deserving of strife shall be beaten with few. For everyone to whom much is given, from him much will be required. And to whom much has been committed, of him they will ask the more. Two overarching truths govern the passage, according to one commentator, Joel Green, the certainty of his coming and the uncertainty. of his timing. We know he's coming back. We just don't know when Christ's return is heaven's business, while obedience is our business. From our end, as God's servants, we can strive to follow three house rules. 1. Be constantly watchful, verses 35 to 41. 2. Be godly in your duties, verses 42 to 41 forty four and three beware of selfish living verses forty five to forty eight First, be constantly watchful. Way before Era went into labor with Nathaniel, we were advised to make what's called a hospital bag. We packed a small luggage with clothes, snacks, chargers, and other stuff we'd need for an extended stay at the hospital. Of course, we didn't know when the baby would come exactly. Similarly, verse 35 shows us someone who is ready at any given moment. Girding of yourself means you got your belt on and you're able to work immediately God required that kind of urgency at the first Passover meal. God told the Israelites to be ready to go, go, go. With the belt on your waist, your sandal on your feet, and your staff in your hand. So you shall eat it in haste. It is the Lord's Passover. That's Exodus 12. 11. Be constantly watchful. As for the lamps, Jesus speaks to us from the days before light bulbs and before kerosene oil was used. Wicks have to be trimmed with care and oil, olive oil kept in good supply. In Jesus' parable of the wise and foolish virgins, the ones unprepared ran out of oil. So they had to go out for a midnight run for more as their lamps were failing. They missed on the coming of the bridegroom and they were shut out of the wedding. Without the aid of the light, they could not be constantly watchful Now the woman in that parable desire to attend the wedding, but the men in verse 36 here are waiting for their master to return from a wedding. They were to be alert for that knock on the door, ready at any time to attend to him. What's amazing is the reward promised in verse 37. See Marvin Pate explains, quote, those servants who are alert to their master's return will be blessed. So blessed are they, in fact, that the Lord will reverse the roles and serve them by burning up his loins and seating them at the table and serving them. Servants will be served, the attendants attended to, waiters waited on Later, on the night Jesus was betrayed, he did just that. He reversed the rules and served his disciples. John 13, 4 to 5 says, we see there, we read how our Lord rose from suffer and laid aside his garments, took a towel and girded himself. After that, he poured water into a basin and began to wash the disciples' feet and to wipe them with the towel with which he was girded. That's our Savior, the humble King. Though we don't deserve anything but wrath, He shows us grace. Though we're like dogs who eat crumbs that fall from the table. Though we're like that poor Lazarus out of reach of that rich food Jesus treats us like the way David treated Mephibosheth. He shall eat at my table like one of the king's sons. What an amazing grace. That's the blessing awaiting the servants, those who wait for our master. So be constantly watchful. Verse 38 tells us that we must be ready at all times, even in those times we're tempted to relax. The Romans would post sentries during the watches of the night from sunset to sunrise, about 6 p. m. to 6 a. m. They divided the night into four equal periods of three hours, six to nine, nine to twelve, twelve to three, three to six. The Hellenistic and Jewish custom, on the other hand, cut up the night into three equal periods of four hours, six to ten, ten to two, two to six. An example of this three-period scheme is in Judges 7. 19. I think Jesus too is speaking of three watches of the night. So then we must be vigilant all through the darkness, dusk to dawn, when eyes get heavy, lamps grow dim, bodies are weary. Then we'll be the blessed servants of the Lord. Be constantly watchful In verses 39 and 40, the metaphor shifts from the servants of the house to the master of the house, from the imminent welcome of the master to the imminent danger of the thief. But the main point is the same. Be constantly watchful. Again, there's the certainty of his coming and the uncertainty of his timing. So like these housekeepers, therefore you also be ready, for the Son of Man is coming at an hour you do not expect. Before Jesus continues, we have an interruption from Peter. He wanted to know whether this parable relates to the disciples only or to everyone, including unbelievers. We have no record of Jesus' direct answer here, but we know that Jesus regularly speaks truths that elicit response from everybody. Whether that response is belief or unbelief, enlightenment or blindness, gain or loss, We learn from Matthew 13 that Jesus spoke in parables both to reveal and to conceal heavenly secrets. Only God's chosen will grasp God's truths. Only those whose spiritual eyes and ears the Spirit has opened will see and hear to understand. Yet the Lord has always been generous and liberal in dispensing his mercies and truth. And the certainty of his coming and the uncertainty of his timing Demand response from both Christians and non-Christians. Let's begin with the non-Christians first. Since Jesus is coming back for certain, but we don't know when, it's imperative that you repent and believe in the gospel. All have sinned, and we all deserve God's wrath. But Jesus died on the cross for your sins, rose from the dead, and ascended to heaven Until he returns, we have an opportunity to find mercy It's too dangerous, actually insane, to come back to this decision later or go another second without Jesus. It is appointed for men to die once, but after this the judgment. I warn you, there is but a step between you and death Because the day of judgment is coming, now is the time to repent. Hear these urgent exhortations. Behold, the day of the Lord comes cruel with both wrath and fierce anger to lay the land desolate, and he will destroy its sinners from it. That's Isaiah 13, 9. Truly these pines of ignorance God overlooked, but now commands all men everywhere to repent, because he has appointed a day on which he will judge the world. in righteousness by the man whom he has ordained. He has given assurance of this to all by raising him from the dead. That's Acts 17, 30 to 31. God says also in 2 Corinthians, in an acceptable time I have heard you, and in the day of salvation I have helped you. Behold, now is the accepted time. Behold, now is the day of salvation. Now you don't need to do anything to deserve salvation. Find acceptance by putting your hope of heaven in Jesus alone. He paid for it all on the cross. Receive the gift of eternal life by grace through faith alone, not by works. Do so today. Now is the accepted time to be accepted. And if you're already a Christian, be grateful. Humble yourselves and be faithful until death. Not only be a good servant, but be a good steward. Now, what's the difference between servants in verses 35 to 38 and the steward in verses 39 to 40? I don't think the shift in focus from the servants of the house to the master of the house is arbitrary. I think it's quite an effective teaching strategy. Jesus transitions from general servanthood to a more specific concept of stewardship By doing so, our Lord gives us a greater awareness of our duties here and now. That leads to the second house rule: be godly in your duties. When we speak of godly stewardship, we should be thinking of two qualities based on this passage. faithful and wise. We may possess different gifts, hold different offices, have available different ministry opportunities, but we must be faithful and wise in all that we do. Now, what does it mean to be faithful in your duties? To be faithful, first of all, means being confident in God and his faithfulness. In saving and preserving us. To be faithful means being Christ-like. It means being faithful over what's been given, even if it's small or insignificant. To be faithful means being like Tychicus, who cared for the saints and comforted them. To be faithful means being like Epacras, who ministered on behalf of the saints. Fervently pray for their maturity and suffering together with those in trouble. To be faithful means being exemplary leaders. To be faithful means helping the brethren and strangers and serving God through suffering. Be godly and faithful in your duties. And what does it mean to be wise in your duties? To be wise means to be wise in Christ and His Word, not in your own opinion. To be wise means to hear the words of Jesus and put them to practice and be like that man who built his house on the rock, not on the sand. To be wise means being vulnerable as sheep and harmless as doves, yet like snakes, skillfully navigating through life's dangers. As stated earlier, to be wise means to be prepared for Jesus' coming, like the five virgins who had enough oil for the night. As we will see later in Luke, to be wise means sharing material resources with those who will share eternity with you. Be godly and wise in your duties. Faithfulness and wisdom can be difficult to maintain. Recently I learned that Max Lucato, the famous evangelical author. Wrote a letter to apologize to the LGBTQ community. He was sorry that a 2004 sermon he preached was, quote, disrespectful, hurtful. He also claimed, quote, faithful people may disagree about what the Bible says about homosexuality, but we agree that God's holy word must never be used as a weapon to wound others. End quote. Now I haven't read or heard that 2004 sermon, so I won't make any judgments yet. I'm not here to overreact and proclaim that Max Ocato is no longer a Christian. I won't define his entire ministry career based on one weak moment. But can faithful people really disagree about what the Bible says about homosexuality, as Lucato claims? Was it really wise for a pastor of his status to write a letter like this? Against the pressures of the world, we all fall short of being faithful and wise consistently. We need God's grace. We're thankful that his divine power has given us all things that pertain to life and godliness. We have the Holy Spirit for personal faithfulness. And when we fail from time to time, we have God who shows us mercy. Even when our faithfulness is like the morning cloud, and like the early dew it goes away. His faithfulness, his faithfulness he shall establish in the very heavens. Even though sometimes we foolishly try to be made perfect by the flesh, he grants us wisdom from above. We're given grace and mercy to be godly, faithful, and wise in our duties And fulfilling those duties in God's power in the present will have God's reward in the future. So be godly in your duties. Sadly, there are those who know that Jesus is coming to judge, those who heard these exhortations to be faithful and wise, and yet they refuse to follow God's will. The words of Christ go in one ear and off the other. The delusions they say in their heart suppresses suppress the truth. That leads to the third house rule, beware of selfish living. Beginning in verse 45, we have a different scenario with the same servant who was introduced in verses 42 to 44. In the previous scenario, he chooses the path of faithfulness. In verses 45 to 48, in another scenario, he chooses the path of wickedness. There are two ways to live in light of the certainty of Jesus' coming and the uncertainty of his timing. So that means we're looking at an unbeliever in verses forty-five to forty-eight. I think that two supporting arguments for this interpretation are one, the mention of unbelievers directly in verse forty-six. And two, in a parallel passage in Matthew 24, 45 to 51, 24, 45 to 51, the evil servant is punished with the hypocrites, and there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth. This is clearly a chilling description of hell, the eternal outer darkness. Now remember that those who are saved will never have to worry about facing God's wrath. There's now no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus. So then, how is this passage relevant to Christians? The answer is this: God has given us his word so that we would know about the degrees of punishment in hell. And by extension, the degrees of rewards in heaven. First, we should know that the Bible clearly teaches degrees of punishment in hell. There's an essay on this very topic on the Gospel Coalition website by Albert N. Martin and Fred Zaspel. It's a good read. There has to be degrees of punishment for sinners because God's righteous judgment is exact and based on every word, deed, thought, and motive. And this degree of punishment is based on three major factors. One, how much a person abandoned him or herself to sin. Two, how much a person led others to sin. And three, how much a person had abused his or her privilege in light of knowledge. That third factor of privilege and light is key. The servant in verse 47, who knew his master's will and did not prepare himself or do according to his will. Would receive greater punishment because he had abused his privilege and light of knowledge. An example of this case today might be those who grew up In a Christian family, attend church, hear God's call many times, yet still refuse to believe. They'll receive greater degree of punishment in hell than those who have fewer privileges. By extension, we may discuss the degree of rewards in heaven. While we're looking at two types of hellbound sinners here, that second sentence in verse 48 has application for saints as well. Let me read it again. For everyone to whom much is given from him, much will be required, and to whom much has been committed of him, they will ask the more. Just as there are degrees of punishment in hell, there are degrees of rewards in heaven. For example, Jesus tells us the parable of the talents. in which the man entrusts one servant with five talents, another with two, and yet another with one Each received their lot according to his own ability. Now the one with five talents who earned five more, and the second one with two talents who earn two more are both in heaven. But obviously rewarded differently. Apostle Paul also believed that there are saints who suffer greater loss of heavenly rewards than others. While all of us have Christ as our foundation, not all of us wisely build upon that foundation. How do we know whether our ministries had lasting quality? 1 Corinthians 3:13 to 15 tells us that the day will declare it. Because it will be revealed by fire. And the fire will test each one's work of what sort it is. If anyone's work which he has built on it endures, he will receive a reward. If anyone's work is burned, he will suffer loss, but he himself will be saved, yet so as through fire. So even if we don't have to worry about hellfire, we do have to be concerned about the refiner's fire. And all this to say, beware of selfish living. Selfishness leads the sinner to the judges condemning hell And the saint to the Father's correcting discipline. To maximize our talents and minimize our losses, live for the Master's glory, not vainglory. At times we may be tempted to live for the moment instead of living for Jesus, thinking, my master is delaying his coming. We may have wars and fights among us, biting and devouring each other. We sometimes forget how much we've been given and how much we've been committed. So we lose sight of how much will be required of us and how much we are asked to do. We're thankful for mercy. We're thankful that we won't receive stripes and beating in eternal judgment. Because Jesus took them in our place for us at the cross. He was wounded for our transgressions. He was bruised for our iniquities. The chastisement for our peace was upon him. And by his stripes we are healed. So out of this gratitude, let us live for the Lord. As his coming is certain, but his timing is uncertain. Let's serve our master by faith until he comes. We will stand as children of the promise. We will fix our eyes on him, our soul's reward. Till the race is finished and the work is done. We'll walk by faith and not by sight. Let's pray Lord, we're thankful that you are in control of all the affairs of the universe and you know That exact year, month, day, and time, hour, minute, the time you have ordained for the return of your son. Lord, until then, help us at this time to be ready and watchful, to be faithful and wise. Lord, to avoid selfish and carnal living. We pray that at every moment that we would seek you in your word to be filled with your goodness as we think about you. As we pray to you, as you open our mouths to preach the gospel to others, as we share our hearts and your word, with our students, with our fellow brothers and sisters. Pray that you would find us ready. And we're thankful for this wake-up call. Lord, through your word. Pray that we will live such lives this week. Pray all these things in Jesus Christ's name. Amen.

sermons.title: Crisis Response
sermons.speaker: Sung Cho
sermons.text: The word crisis has an interesting range of meanings. Today, when we use the word crisis, we may think of an economic downturn. environmental problems, or some unrest during midlife from ages 40 to 65. The word crisis was also used in a medical context in the past. Merriam Webster defines the word as the turning point for better or worse in an acute disease or fever. The English word crisis can be traced back through Latin all the way back to the Greek word Chrysus, which appears more in legal and judicial contexts. That's certainly the case in the New Testament. And it appears that with every true crisis, there's an important decision to be made. Whether that decision comes from individuals, governors, doctors, or judges The same goes for the believer in his or her crisis of faith. When individuals in the US decide to follow Christ, there are often celebrations at home and baptisms at churches. But now consider what awaited Chu, a Laotian man in his twenties, and a convert to Christianity from Buddhism. Here's what happened to Chu in his own words. Quote: One day my brother and uncle came to me and lied to me. They invited me to go to their house, which I agreed to without hesitation. Little did I know that when we arrived at my uncle's house, they would beat me and tie me up with the rope. They told me I need to return to my old faith. They would continue to beat me. They bound me with the rope with my hands behind my back. My brother, an average-sized man, but with a solid build, used the side of his palms to hit my neck and face over and over again I was tied from seven in the morning until seven at night. Eventually Chu escaped, and he was able to get his pregnant wife safe to her parents. They found a church family to help them in the long run. What will be your response to such crisis? Consider also the story of Yaren, a young Christian. He shared a gospel with a close friend who Betrayed his trust by reporting Yaron's newfound faith to his family. As traditional conservative Muslims, Yaron's family could not tolerate his conversion. They threatened him multiple times and insisted that he return to Islam, despite their demands and knowing that he might be killed. Yaren remained steadfast in his faith. He refused to deny Christ as his Savior. For that his cousins dragged them to the top of a four-story building and There are countless stories like this one Some report that more Christians have died for their faith in the 20th century than all other centuries of church history combined. What will be your response to such crisis? In today's passage we'll find biblical principles for our own crises of faith. In reality, all throughout Luke 12, and we'll see in the first part of Luke chapter 13, there are plenty of good principles. Commentator Joe B. Green observes the unity of thought from 12. 1 to 139 and entitles the section as Vigilance in the Face of Eschatological Crisis. Vigilance in the face of eschatological crisis, that sounds like a mouthful. But simply put, as the kingdom is approaching In the face of eschatological crisis, be ready for its coming. Vigilance And such spiritual readiness demands much from us. We have present imperatives because of God's future indicatives We must, because he will. And if we're ready for that end-time crisis of judgment, we'll be ready for the present crisis of faith. Let's see what else we need to do from verses 49 to 59. Luke 12, 49 to 59. I came to send fire on the earth, and how I wish it were already kindled. But I have a baptism to be baptized with, and how distressed I am till it is accomplished. Do you suppose that I came to give peace on earth? I tell you, not at all, but rather division. For from now on five in one house will be divided, three against two, and two against three. Father will be divided against son and son against father, mother against daughter, and daughter against mother, mother-in-law against her daughter-in-law, and daughter-in-law against Her mother-in-law Then he also said to the multitudes, Whenever you see a cloud rising out of the west, immediately you say, A shower is coming, and so it is. And when you see the south wind blow, you say there will be hot weather, and there is. Hypocrites, you can discern the face of the sky and of the earth But how is it you do not discern this time? Yes, and why even of yourselves do you not judge what is right? When you go with your adversary to the magistrate, make every effort along the way to settle with him, lest he drag you to the judge, the judge deliver you to the officer, and the officer throw you into prison. I tell you, you shall not depart from there till you have paid the very last might This passage neatly divides into three units with three questions and three distinct images. of family strife, weather patterns, and legal court. That corresponds to three responses to crisis to Come. One, expect division, not peace in the world. Verses 49 to 53. And two, discern now as the time to repent. Verses 55. four to fifty six and three, judge whether you are right with God. Verses fifty seven to fifty nine First, expect division, not peace in the world. Reading these verses, some may be shocked about Christ's mission on earth. What's all this talk of fire and even wishing it were already kindled? Shouldn't we be inclusive of all? Isn't the mission of Jesus in John 3:16, which we read earlier? For God so loved the world that he gave his only begotten Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish but have everlasting life. Don't we read earlier in Luke 1 that Jesus is the dayspring from on high who has visited us To guide our feet into the way of peace. Didn't the heavenly host announce to the shepherds on that first Christmas? Glory to God in the highest, and on earth, peace, goodwill toward men. The simple answer is that Jesus brings both peace and division. Two things can be true at once, and in fact, you can't have one without the other. For true peace to even be possible, sinners and saints must be divided. And it's Jesus who both unites and divides. Heals and hurts, warms and burns. It depends on where you stand with him. When Simeon held that infant Jesus and looked into his face, he not only saw a light to bring the glory of God's people Israel. He saw a child destined for the fall and rising of many in Israel, and for a sign which will be spoken against. A sword to pierce, a sword that'll cut and divide. Jesus is not only the dayspring who rises as the Son of righteousness with heat. Healing in his wings. He also inaugurates the day of the Lord, burning like an oven, and all the proud, yes, all who do wickedly will be stubble. Our Lord not only leads the sheep to still waters with the shepherd's staff in his hand, he'll also stand with winnowing fan in his hand. He'll thoroughly clean out the threshing floor and gather his wheat into the barn, but he will burn up the chap with unquenchable fire. So, yes, Jesus divides humanity into two irreconcilable categories: either your wheat or chaff, the just or the wicked, sheep or goat. And only after such division can there be peace. For now, those uh though these two categories are clearly distinct in God's eyes, there's a mixed multitude. in the present. The unsaved and the saved grow together in the field of the world. sermons.title: Buried Treasure
sermons.speaker: Sung Cho
sermons.text: As I was reflecting on the closing events of Jesus' earthly ministry, I thought about the burial of Jesus. The Bible does speak of Jesus' burial, and each of the four gospel writers records the event. Paul delivered to the Corinthians what he himself received. As good news, that Christ died for our sins according to the scriptures, and that he was buried, and that he rose again the third day according to the scriptures. For much of church history, believers recited creeds and confessions. You may recall this line of the Apostles' Creed. He suffered under Pontius Pilate, was crucified, died, and was buried. And not only were the earliest church members taught verbally that Jesus was buried, they learned of it by association with immersion baptism Paul reminds believers, even congregations he has not met yet, that they were buried with Jesus through baptism into death. But even if the scriptures teach us about Jesus' burial, we probably give it less attention than other events. It's like the middle child, sandwiched between Jesus' death and resurrection. And yes, I must say it, his burial is buried in the middle. Yet, there is something valuable in this doctrine of Christ's burial. So tonight let's unearth this treasure as we consider what Jesus did for us. First, Jesus was buried openly by men who had followed secretly. The man who took the initiative in giving Jesus a proper resting place was Joseph from Arimathea, a city of the Jews. Here's all we know. According to Matthew 27, he's rich and could afford to have his own tomb. More on this later. According to Mark 15, 43 and Luke 23, 50, he was a prominent council member, that is, a member of the Sanhedrin. Which is like the first century Jewish Supreme Court of Religion. They were the ones ultimately responsible for the crucifixion of Jesus and the later persecution of the early church. That's why it took courage for Joseph to bury Jesus. He was a disciple of Jesus, but secretly for the fear of Jews. Yet somewhere along the way he grew brave. He did not consent to the decision and the deed of the Sanhedrin, which unjustly condemned and killed Jesus. Mark tells us in chapter 15, verse 43, that coming and taking courage, he asked Pilate for the body of Jesus. Where does such courage come from? It was his faith in Jesus growing over time. That faith made him a good and just man. Luke says Joseph was good, the same description used for Barnabas in Acts 11, 24. Again, because of his faith, Luke also says Joseph was a just man. He was just, like his namesake, Joseph, the husband of Mary. So then, a righteous Joseph was there when Jesus came out of the womb as a helpless babe, and another righteous Joseph was there to bury him in the tomb as a helpless corpse. Joseph also resembles Simeon in Luke 2, who was waiting for the consolation of Israel Like Simeon, Joseph was himself waiting for the kingdom of God. We know considerably less about the fate of Nicodemus. We have to infer from his actions As John tells us in chapter 19, verse 39, he at first came to Jesus by night. And that takes us back to chapter 3, where he's introduced as a man of the Pharisees, a ruler of the Jews. Yet he had much to learn about God's kingdom, rebirth, Christ's mission, and the condemnation of the world. Next, we see him towards the end of chapter 7. We see him among the unbelieving leaders of Jerusalem, the Sanhedrin who wanted to arrest Jesus during the Feast of the Tabernacles. Even unlawfully. In response, Nicodemus speaks up in protest in verse 50. There, does our law judge a man before it hears him and knows what he is doing? And now back to John 19. The final word on Nicodemus is that he's at the burial of Jesus Because he brought an abundance of myrrh and aloes, he too was rich, like Joseph. Again, more on this later. But for now, let's focus on the fact that every time we hear of Nicodemus, we're reminded that he visited Jesus by night. Like Joseph, his ally, he was a secret disciple. What we learn about Joseph and Nicodemus together is that they should have and could have been bolder in their faith before this crucifixion. Both could have followed Jesus in full daylight, not in fearful darkness, but that opportunity was lost. Yet they did not lose this opportunity to display their affection publicly at last. Joseph uses his privileged position to secure the body of Jesus. It was a position he most likely lost eventually. That's because the narrative implies that these two buried Jesus themselves instead of paying hired hands to do it. I guess they could have because they were rich. That means they were secret disciples no more. It would have been difficult to approach Pilate secretly. They could not have buried Jesus without crowds of pilgrims and citizens noticing two rich prominent Jews of the Sanhedrin. I'm quite confident that Joseph was a believer, and I'm pretty sure Nicodemus was one too. Their faith is on display before all. That's something to imitate. But let's return to their weakness. Do you ever feel regret for following Jesus later than you should have? So I knew the gospel from an early age. So I could have given myself to Christ completely as a teenager. It was not until late in my high school years that I devoted myself fully to the Lord. I also consider how I could have been more vocal and open about my faith in my twenties and thirties. Like Joseph and Nicodemus, I was often a secret believer in the cover of darkness. Do we not fail like them? Do we not lament our fear of men? What I would do to go back and give more of myself to my Savior Yes, better late than never, but even better early than late. Perhaps you sympathize with Augustine, who came to faith later in life and mourned in his confessions. Late have I loved you, beauty so old and so new, late have I loved you And see you were within, and I was in the external world and sought you there. And in my unlovely state, I plunged into those lovely created things which you have made. You were with me, and I was not with you. The lovely things kept me far from you. So if they did not have their existence in you, they had no existence at all. You called and cried out loud and shattered my deafness. You were radiant and resplendent. You put to flight my blindness. You are fragrant, and I drew in my breath, and now pant after you. I tasted you, and I feel but hunger and thirst for you. You touch me, and I am set on fire to attain the peace which is yours. There's nothing Joseph could do, Nicodemus could do, Augustine could do, and we can do to take back the time lost. The strips of linen, the spices, and the stones to seal the tomb all played a part. Nicodemus's lavish gift of myrrh and aloes would preserve the body until the resurrection. God allowed these rich men to care for that holy body, to fulfill their piety. That way, God would not allow his holy one to see corruption, to fulfill his prophecy. In Psalm sixteen. Let's also think about the honor due to Jesus. In Isaiah 53, verse 9, we read concerning the suffering servant, and they made his grave with the wicked, but with the rich at his death, because He had done no violence, nor was any deceit in his mouth. Christ's resting place in Joseph's tomb Was a sign to the world that God's servant has done no wrong and spoke no wrong. On one hand, Jesus died on the cruel cross like a hated criminal On the other hand, Jesus was buried in the rich tomb like a beloved champion. Contrast this with the fate of Judas Iscariot. Jesus was buried as a single grain for our great gain. In John 1941, we're given some details concerning Joseph's tomb, which became Jesus' tomb. Let me read it again. Now twice in chapter 19, and even twice in one verse for emphasis, we learn that Jesus was buried in a garden. What's the significance? Here's what I believe. Just as Jesus was buried with the rich to signal the integrity of his sinless life. He was buried in the garden to signal the vitality of his endless life Matthew Henry has some good devotional insights concerning this quote, That in a sepulchre in a garden, Christ's body was laid. In the Garden of Eden, death and grave first received their power, and now in a garden they are conquered, disarmed, and triumphed over. In a garden Christ began his passion, and from a garden he would rise and begin his exaltation. Christ fell to the ground as a corn of wheat, and therefore was sown in a garden among the seeds, for his dew is as the dew of herbs. He is the fountain of gardens. I find Henry's reference to John 12, 24 interesting. Let me read it. These are words of Jesus. Most assuredly I say to you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the ground and dies, it remains alone. But if it dies, it produces much grain. Just perhaps to stress this truth, God arranged for Jesus' burial in the garden. And see how great is the result. If there is no sorrowful sowing of the single grain, there is no joyous weeping of the many harvest Christ must sleep the sleep of death as wheat and become the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep. See how from one came many, as by one man's disobedience many were made sinners So also by one man's obedience, many will be made righteous. The only begotten Son was brought into shame So that he might bring many sons into glory. Tonight we remember that one act of obedience, Look at the cross. Christ Himself bore our sins in his own body on the tree, that we, having died to sins, might live for righteousness, by whose stripes you were healed. Look at the grave. Our Lord proved that the weakness of God is stronger than men. Because He was buried in the grave to ransom us from the power of the grave. Look at the empty tomb. Jesus was raised from the dead by the glory of the Father. So we also should walk in the newness of life. Let's remember now during the Lord's Suffer, what great price was paid by our Lord and Savior Jesus And let us respond to his sacrifice as the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world. Let us devote our lives to Christ, our time, energy, wealth, to bring him glory. Crown him with many crowns, the lamb upon his throne. Crown him the Lord of life, who triumph over the grave. Let's pray. Lord, we come before you and want to make this our prayer. Were the whole realm of nature mine, That were a present far too small, love so amazing, so divine, Demands my soul, my life, my all. For you accepted us. You gave this great treasure, the gospel, the most precious gift of your Son Jesus Christ. Die on the cross for us, for our sins. We who are so undeserving of this grace. And now we come to you with hearts of gratitude. We want to offer you our lives. And even if we were to give everything, the whole realm of universe, it would be too small in comparison to what you have done for us. The gift that you've given us through your Son Jesus Christ. We thank you and we pray all these things in Jesus Christ's name. Amen.
