Both in our individual walks and our journey together as a local congregation. This road is not easy. It is the narrow gate and a difficult path. But his divine power has given to us all things that pertain to life and godliness. And we need Christ-like courage and compassion. And even when we falter in our steps, we can find comfort in Jesus. Let's sing our final song. Whatever my God ordains is right. His holy will abideth. I will be still, whatever he does And follow where he guided. He is my God, so dark my road. He holds me that I shall not fall, and so to him I leave. At all. Let's pray. So there are many questions in life. Why was I born to this family? In this country, in this era of history? Why is my path filled with this combination of darkness and light? Joy and suffering. Why have you ordained my path to be like this? And Lord, at times we lose heart. At times we'll come we complain before you and we're perplexed. And then we look to your son. We see how he has obediently followed the path you have given him. For the joy set before him, endured the cross, fulfilled his role as prophet, gave himself as a sacrificial king. As our high priest. And we are inspired and we are thankful because of what your son has done. And because of that, we can live for you in gratitude. And we pray that you give us strength each and every day to be courageous and compassionate as your son is. Yes. Fail these things that Jesus Christ me. Amen.

sermons.title: Kingdom Table Manners
sermons.speaker: Sung Cho
sermons.text: We are blessed by the unlikeliest of people. Their testimonies, examples, and legacies have touched us We're enriched by the faith of the least among us. Has God not chosen the poor of this world to be rich in faith and heirs of the kingdom? Which he promised to those who love him. God has chosen the foolish things of the world to put to shame the wise, and God has chosen the weak things of the world To put to shame the things which are mighty and the base things of the world and the things which are despised, God has chosen. And the things which are not to bring to nothing the things that are, that no flesh should glory in his presence. These are not just theories and abstract concepts. We can put flesh and bones on these verses and come up with A heroic saint from Baltimore like Johnny Erickson Tata, a quadriplegic who lives a fruitful life for God. Then there are stories of God's miraculous provision in the life of George Mueller. Just reading about that in Matthew's devotional the other day. Earlier we sang hymns written by individuals who suffer greatly in their lives. Charlotte Ellis, who wrote those famous words, just as I am. Was respected by the likes of Charles Spurgeon and Billy Graham. She was educated and gifted in the arts, but at age 33, she began to suffer from a crippling fatigue. Even leaving her bed, lifting her pen, or composing letters became difficult, but she looked beyond her troubles to glorify Christ and comfort others. Another woman of Victorian England, Frances Ridley Havergale, faced similar struggles, yet lived a fruitful life, and wrote songs like Like a River Glorious. Across the Atlantic, God used the blind woman in United States At six weeks old, Fanny Crosby developed a minor eye inflammation, and the doctor carelessly treated her and left her blind for the rest of her life. Yet she did not wallow in bitterness. Here's the first poem she wrote as an eight-year-old. Oh, what a happy child I am! Although I cannot see I am resolved that in this world contented I will be. How many blessings I enjoy that other people don't. So weep or sigh because I'm blind, I cannot, or I won't. Through her life, Crosby wrote more than 8,000 songs, many of them forgotten, but some gems are left for us, just such as Blessed Assurance, to God be the glory, who sang that. Deaned, and pass me not, O gentle Savior. Church music expert Donald Husted recognized her as, quote, the most prolific and significant writer of gospel songs in American history. While not nearly as prolific or gifted, Crosby reminded me of the Scottish blind preacher, George Madison. He wrote that classic, Oh Love That Will Not Let Me Go. We just sang that too. He wrote the lyrics in five minutes on the evening of his sister's marriage. It was a happy occasion for her, but it was a sad time for the forty-year-old Bachelor George, as he had to say goodbye to his longtime caretaker and companion. That night he was reminded how twenty years before, because he was going completely blind, his fiance broke his heart and left him. Though he lived in darkness and never married, he traced the rainbow through the rain, and felt the promises not vain, that morn shall tearless be. We could go on and on. But the core reason we have such testimonies is because The heavenly banquet is open to such people. From Luke 13, 10 onward, we've been considering the big question: who will participate in the kingdom? We saw in verses 10 through 17 that the kingdom doors are open to a woman with a spiritual and spine problem, but close to adversaries of Jesus. In verses 18-30, we saw that the kingdom is great, yet the entrance narrow, and the demographics surprisingly diverse with many Gentiles. We close chapter 13 with the shocking news that Jerusalem of all cities would not be in, at least not until later when Jesus returns. Now as we begin chapter fourteen, we continue to ask who will participate in the kingdom? And we're surprised again by the answers. The kingdom is open to the sick, the humble, the poor, the mean, the lame, the blind. And because the kingdom belongs to such people, our love, hospitality, and social life should include them as well. Let's take a closer look at Luke fourteen, one to fourteen Now it happened as he went into the house of one of the rulers of the synagogue of the Pharisees to eat bread on the Sabbath, that they watched him closely And behold, there was a certain man before him who had tropsy. And Jesus answering spoke to the lawyers and Pharisees, saying, Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath? But they kept silent And he took him and healed him and let him go. Then he answered them, saying, Which of you, having a donkey or an ox that has fallen into a pit, will not immediately pull him out on the Sabbath day? And they could not answer him regarding these things. So he told a parable to those who were invited when he noted how they chose the best places, saying to them, When you are invited by any one to a wedding feast, do not sit down in the best place, lest one more honorable than you be invited by him. And he who invited you and him come and say to you, Give place to this man. And then you begin with shame to take the lowest place. When you are invited, go down, go and sit down in the lowest place, so that when he who invited you comes, he may say to you, Friend, go up higher, and you will have glory in the presence of those who sit at the table with you. For whoever humble exalts himself will be humbled And he who humbles himself will be exalted. Then he also said to him who invited him, When you give a dinner or a supper, do not ask your friends, your brothers, your relatives, nor rich neighbors. Lest they also invite you back, and you be repaid. But when you give a feast, invite the poor, the maimed, the lame, the blind, and you will be blessed, because they cannot repay you. For you shall be repaid at the resurrection of the just In this passage, I perceive three kingdom rules of etiquette or table manners, quite practical and applicable in our outreach efforts. They are one, love your neighbor. 24-7. Verses 1 to 6. 2. Humble yourself to be exalted. Verses seven to eleven and three, seek God's ultimate blessings, verses twelve to fourteen The first kingdom table rule is to love your neighbor 24-7. The first event in this chapter is one another one of those Sabbath controversies We've seen this before. Jesus heals someone on Saturday. The religious leaders see it and accuse them of breaking number four in the Ten Commandments. In the Gospel of Luke, we first read of a Sabbath healing in Capernaum in chapter 4, verses 31 to 37. There was no opposition at that point. In chapter 6, however, things change. Jesus and his disciples went to the grain fields, tucked the heads of grain, and ate them, rubbing them in their hands. Some of the Pharisees said to them, Why are you doing what is not lawful to do on the Sabbath? In response, Jesus declared himself to be the Lord of the Sabbath. Just after this incident, Luke relates another Sabbath healing in the same chapter. Jesus heals a man with the withered right hand, but not before asking. Is it lawful on the Sabbath to do good or to do evil, to save life or to destroy? In that chapter 6, Sabbath controversy, in verse 7, so chapter 6, verse 7, we see the same verb used there, used in chapter 14, verse 1. Watched closely. Just like the scribes and the Pharisees back in chapter 6, the lawyers and the Pharisees and Chapter 14, watch them closely. Trying to catch Jesus in his words or actions to see if he slips up on something We see the same verb later in chapter 20, verse 20. There the chief priests and the scribes of Jerusalem watched him and sent spies who pretended to be righteous. that they might seize on his words, in order to deliver him to the power and the authority of the governor, and thus Pilate Luke uses this verb one more time in Acts chapter 9, verse 24. As the Jews of Damascus watched the city gates day and night, They intended to kill Paul, or Saul at that time, who betrayed him and began there to preach the faith which he once tried to destroy. So back to Luke 14, I think that there was an ulterior motive behind the leader's invitation in verse 1. After the community synagogue meeting, they arranged for one of the rulers of the Pharisees to invite Jesus to his home for a meal along with others. Perhaps these religious leaders heard about what happened to the woman back in chapter 13, verses 10 to 17. Perhaps they wanted to inspect Jesus themselves in a less public place. It's very likely that they arranged for the man suffering from dropsy to stop by during the meal. Jesus saw right through the ruse, yet at the same time, he saw the need of this man. He was suffering from edema, swelling caused by excess fluid trapped in the body's tissues. To their shame, the lawyers and the Pharisees remained silent when Jesus asked, Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath? Their answer should have been a resounding yes. Their motto should have been Love Your Neighbor, twenty-four-seven Jesus asked the further question in verse 5: Which of you having a donkey or an ox that has fallen into a pit? Will not immediately pull them, pull him out on the Sabbath day. It's a rhetorical question in two ways. First, it's rhetorical because the answer is obvious. Any man in his right mind would immediately pull out his donkey or ox out of a pit, even on a Sabbath day. Why it was a source of living How could they get by without their beast of burden? The question is also rhetorical in another more poetic way. The word for pit in verse 5 could be translated as a well, that is a well of water, and we see that translation of the same word In John chapter 4, verses 11 to 12. Now we go back to the word for dropsy in verse 2, which in the original language is hydropicos, which that is literally looking watery. Recall that dropsy is edema, access fluid in the body. Putting the two together, here's what we got. These Pharisees and lawyers cared more about an animal suffering and trapped in water than a human being suffering from water trapped in his body. Their motto should have been Love Your Neighbor 247 But now how about us? Do we have traditions and habits in place that prevent us from loving our neighbor 24-7? If so, we may be lacking kingdom table manners. Are we vigilantly and actively seizing opportunities to do good to all? What chances have slipped away because we're preoccupied with our ox or donkey, our work or automobile, our nine-to-five and our ride. Love your neighbor 24-7. That way, our invitations to enter God's kingdom is that much sweeter And consistent with the love of Christ But there's something else we need besides love. If we're going to have kingdom table manners, we must also display humility. That leads to the second kingdom table rule. Humble yourself to be exalted. Because this episode took place at a home and not a synagogue, the conversation naturally turns to other matters of social customs. Jesus noticed how the invitees chose the best places, seats closest to the host Recall that the host of this party was not just some guy. He wasn't even just one of the religious leaders. He was one of the rulers of the Pharisees. Sitting next to him would get you places in life, and everyone would recognize you That's why they weren't interested in humbling themselves to be exalted. Rather, they wanted to exalt themselves to be exalted In response, Jesus told them a parable to teach them a lesson. The setting of the parable is familiar to the hearers. It's not hard to imagine being invited to a wedding. In first century wedding receptions, you're not going to see a seating chart poster at the entrance. You're not going to find tableplace cards with your name written in pretty cursive Ordered in bulk from etc. com. So you stand before empty seats in this scenario and you're left to your presumptions. Presumptions about your status and relationship with the host. And this is an opportunity to humble yourself to be exalted. Two scenarios are given. One, you make a beeline to the best seat, right next to where the host would sit. You get a tap on the shoulder and the host tells you give place to this man. You go down to the lowest place, and everyone watches your humiliation. Verses 8 and 9 correspond to the first part of verse 11. Whoever exalts himself will be humbled. Here's the second scenario. You enter the feast and see everyone clamoring for the best seats, but you decide to take the spot no one wants. Get a tap on the shoulder and the host tells you, friend, go up higher. Go up to a better place and everyone watches your exaltation. Verse ten corresponds to the second part of verse eleven: He who humbles himself will be exalted. Now, Jesus' parable is so close to real life and practical that it's not hard to come up with an application. Next time you go to a party, don't assume that you should get the best spot. But let's dig deeper and start with our hearts. Humility is not merely outward behavior, but a mindset. And to change our mindset, we need to know the mind of God revealed in the Word. Meditate on Philippians 2. Verses 5 to 11. I'll read it for you. Let this mind be in you, which was also in Christ Jesus. who being in the form of God did not consider it robbery to be equal with God, but made himself of no reputation, taking the form of a bond servant, and coming in the likeness of men. And being found in appearance as a man, he humbled himself and became obedient to the point of death, even the death of the cross. Therefore, God also has highly exalted him and given him the name which is above every name, that at the name of Jesus Every knee should bow of those in heaven and of those on earth and of those under the earth, and that every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord. To the glory of God the Father. It's good to be humble, but I tell you what No matter how much you humble yourself to be exalted, you will never outhumble Jesus, and you will never be exalted higher than Jesus. Sure, you might give up your social rank or climb down the hierarchy. But you'll never be able to say, I was exalted in heavenly status with God, and I made myself of no reputation on earth. You'll never be able to say, I committed no sin and no deceit was found in my mouth. I deserve no punishment from God. You'll never be able to say, I humble myself to die on the cross for the sins of the world. The Father raised me as first fruits of resurrection. And exalted me to have the name which is above every name, and someday every knee will bow at my name. Jesus humbled himself to be exalted, not for vain glory, but for divine glory. He descended so that we may ascend with him. He sat with us in earthly places to make us sit with him in the heavenly places. Let to ourselves we're proud sinners who sin in thought, word, and actions. We are among those who dwell on the earth. Without Christ were objects of wrath, the vengeance is the Lord's and recompense. We may climb to heights in this life But our foot shall slip in due time. For the day of our calamity is at hand, and the things to come hasten upon us We will be humbled in the end. So instead of being humbled in hell forever, why not humble yourself before God now? As James tells us, humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord and he will lift you up. Humble yourself in repentance and faith. Repent, that is, turn away from those sins that condemn you. Lament and mourn and weep. Let your laughter be turned to mourning and your joy to gloom. Then believe, that is, turn to Christ, trust in Him for eternal life, to exalt and lift you out of the horrible pit of damnation Out of the miry clay. He will set your feet on upon a rock and establish your steps. And if the Lord exalts you, you never have to feel insecure in humbling yourself. You have the audience of one. God is the only one you need to impress. But if you love others and humble yourself, you're liberated to seek His approval above all else. And that leads us to the third kingdom table rule: seek God's ultimate blessings. In verse 12, Jesus turns his attention to the ruler of the Pharisees who invited him. What Jesus is about to do is quite bold. He rebuked his Pharisee friends, told them to get over themselves, and now he's about to tell the host whom he should invite. I'm sure the host thought, It's my house, my feast, and my table. What right does this Galilean guy have to tell me what to do? Well, we all know him as the Son of God. That's why he has that right. To get a better understanding of how shocking this would have been, we need some background info. Commentator Joel B. Green is helpful here. Quote, the powerful and privileged would not ordinarily think to invite the poor to their meals, for this would one Possibly endanger the social status of the host, to be a wasted invitation Since the self-interest of the elite could never be served by an invitation that could not be reciprocated. And three, Ensues an embarrassment for the poor who could not reciprocate and therefore would be required by social protocols to decline the invitation. Against all norms and customs, Jesus introduces his own brand of kingdom table manners. I'll read it again. When you give a dinner or a supper, do not ask your friends, your brothers, your relatives, nor rich neighbors, lest they also invite you back and you be repaid. But when you give a feast, invite the poor, the main, the lame, the blind, and you will be blessed, because they cannot repay you, for you shall be repaid at the resurrection of the just Joseph Fitzmayer keenly observes, quote, four affluent types of human beings able to recompense are contrasted with the four unfortunate types unable to do so. Are we able to look beyond immediate blessings from men to seek ultimate blessings from God? I would like to discuss two possible applications, one individual and one corporate. They're my suggestions, so take them for what they're worth. First individually, let's talk about the blessing of verse 14. Perhaps today or tomorrow or sometime this week. You can open up your bank account, budget, your busy calendar, and ask yourself, how much time, how much of my time, money, and resources resources, have I spent for those who cannot repay me back? The question I'm going to try asking myself Secondly, corporally, let's talk about the kinds of people who belong to our church or visit our church. Are we accommodating to the poor, the mean, the lame, the blind? As for the poor, I think our church is faithful in giving and generosity. But as for the main, the lame, and the blind, I think we could make some improvements. I must say until I fractured my hip over ten years ago, I didn't care for automatic doors and elevators What boy were they useful during those months of recovery when I was in crutches. Fast forward to 2021. Former elder Kerry has suggested that we install automatic doors at the wheelchair access. The council is working on that with the help of the deacons. Also, I was thinking about the luncheon we had last week. Maybe we should install an elevator so that some of our elderly and frail saints can go up and down the stairs without trouble. Or maybe we could create some space at this level so that we can all fellowship together instead of being separated. Whatever we decide to do, we should look to help those who can't pay us back. That includes even those who do not appreciate us. Our Lord commanded: love your enemies, do good and lend, hoping for nothing in return. And your reward will be great, and you will be sons of the Most High, for He is kind to the unthankful and evil And this kind Father has given us his son, loving even his enemies, humbling himself to death To be exalted to receive God's ultimate blessings. In gratitude we come to the Lord's table. With that same gratitude, we're motivated to preach good news and love the sick, the poor, the maim, the lame, and the blind. We're glad to share tables with them as brothers and sisters in the kingdom of God. Let's pray Lord, we come before you and we're thankful and humbled because we see ourselves And we see nothing of significance that merits heaven. You owe nothing to us, as if we have done something great to be invited into the kingdom hall, the banquet that is to come in the kingdom. We're thankful for the sacrifice of your son. Who called us, who perfectly loved his neighbors, who was perfectly humble, who sought your approval above all else. And Lord, we want to be like your son. As we think about his sacrifice this at this service during the Lord's Supper. May we be more and more conformed to your image. To be more Christ-like. Pray all these things in Jesus Christ's name. Amen.

sermons.title: Unexcused Absences
sermons.speaker: Sung Cho
sermons.text: The COVID restrictions, shrinking church attendance numbers, and the formation of the growth committee Have got me reflecting and thinking about reasons people don't go to church, whether it's our specific church or churches in general. I found one website where they collected a variety of excuses for missing church. There were 186 entries on one page, but I'll just name a few excuses that I found interesting. Some of them run together. I'll go to church when I stop smoking, drinking, cussing. I listen to church on radio. I attend church by watching it on TV. Three words. Church online. Actually, that's two words. I went to that other church two years ago and I wouldn't want them to get jealous. The whole service is catered to old people. The whole service caters to young people. There are too many hypocrites in the church. There are too many sinners in the church. It's too cold in there. Why don't they turn off the heat? It's too hot. Why don't they get air conditioning? What more? I don't go to church because I might get saved and have to go all the time Now this wasn't a formal survey or a statistical study, just a blog page with people sending in possible excuses. I don't know how many are genuine excuses or They were genuinely sharing these or but I'm sure you've heard some of these or at least something similar to them. Maybe you made them yourselves Now there's a lot that's going on beneath these words. Excuses can reveal much. And if we're good listeners and discerners, we can dig deeper. Remember Proverbs 20 verse 5, counseling the heart of a man is like deep water. But a man of understanding will draw it out Missing church is a major problem, no doubt, but the most serious problem Is that people we know and love are going to miss the kingdom of God. Sure, there will be excuses. Hundreds and thousands of them. But there's nothing humorous or laughable about that. Just because we make excuses, that doesn't mean they're excusable. God has been loving, gracious, and patient, and yet we've turned away from his invitations to be with him. But there's the good news of our Lord, our loving Lord, still pursuing and drawing us into his heavenly banquet. That's the gospel that's pres uh uh present in um parable format in today's passage. So let's read Luke 14. fourteen verses fifteen to twenty four now Now, when one of those who sat at the table with him heard these things, he said to him, Blessed is he who shall eat bread in the kingdom of God. Then he said to him, A certain man gave a great supper, and invited many, and sent his servant at supper time to say to those who were invited, Come, for all things are now ready. But they all with one accord began to make excuses. The first said to him, I have bought a piece of ground, and I must go and see it. Ask you to have me excused. And another said, I have bought five yoke of oxen and I am going to test them. I ask you to have me excused. Still another said, I have married a wife, and therefore I cannot come. So that servant came and reported these things to his master Then the master of the house, being angry, said to his servant, Go out quickly into the streets and lanes of the city, and bring in here the poor and the maimed, and the lame and the blind And the servant said, Master, it is done as you commanded, and still there is room. Then the master said to the servant, Go out into the highways and hedges and compel them to come in, that my house may Though we make excuses all the time, our absence in heaven will be marked as unexcused. And here are three reasons why. One, God is gracious in his kingdom invitations. Verses 15 to 17. 2. Mankind is resistant to God's call, verses 18 to 20. And three, God is determined to fill his kingdom. Verses 21 to 24 First, God is gracious in his kingdom invitations. We begin with verse 15, but it's connected to the previous passage. Recall that Jesus has been invited to the house of a certain unnamed ruler of the Pharisees. It was Sabbath and our Lord has caused quite a stir by healing a man suffering from edema He advised those who took the best places at the feast to humble themselves. He then had the goal to tell the host to invite those who cannot repay him. No doubt both Jesus' actions and words have met made this an unforgettable Saturday. One of the men at the table with Jesus, who heard these things, said, Blessed is he who shall eat bread in the kingdom of God. We're not sure why he said this. Perhaps he wanted to ease the building tensions in the room. Perhaps he just wanted to say something everyone can agree on. Jesus doesn't rebuke the man or his statement. Yes, it is blessed to be eating bread in the kingdom of God. Heaven is a festive celebration, and it behooves us to be there. But perhaps there was a false presumption Perhaps people assumed that everyone sitting and eating bread in that house would be sitting and eating bread in heaven. To correct this error, Jesus takes this opportunity to teach using a parable. It's similar to the parable of the wedding feast in Matthew 22, verses 1 to 13. I encourage you to check that out, Matthew 22. But keep in mind this chapter, Luke 14, takes place on the way to Jerusalem, while Matthew 22 takes place at Jerusalem. So just a quick question, why does Jesus use similar stories at different settings? There's no need to overthink the reason for this Jesus was a skillful teacher who used common themes and images to teach multiple lessons. As one commentator observes, quote, use the same parabolic theme to teach different truths. Is frequent in rabbinical writings. Jesus is simply doing what any teacher of his day would do. The parable begins with a magnanimous invitation. See in verse 16: the suffer is great, and the man invited many. And this was no potluck. There was nothing that the guests had to do except come and enjoy the bounty. From the host's point of view, we can infer that there is a double invitation format. And Joel B. Green explains: quote, Jesus' story assumes the extension of double invitations. A practice rooted in pragmatic needs of more than one sort. First, preparation for the feast required a count of the number of invitations accepted With the number of anticipated guests determined, the host is able to determine what animal is to be killed and cooked. Guests also needed time to prepare themselves. And there's something similar to this today. During our wedding planning, we first sent out Save the Date cards and then formal invitations later. There was something similar before Jesus' day too. Perhaps as Esther did with Haman and the king. The man first called the guests to a smaller supper to invite them to a later, greater supper. That's in Esther 5 to 7. Recall that when it was time for the banquet, the eunuchs came to escort Haman to the location So correspondingly, in this parable, the servant came to lead the guests to the house at supper time. And we know what happens next. But before I go on to that, but for now, let's appreciate how God is gracious in his kingdom invitations. Just want to reflect on how gracious God is. And all through the scriptures, we see how our triune God desires to be with us, and he extends his grace. See how God the Father is gracious. He is long-suffering, abundant in loving kindness, rich in mercy and truth. Yeah, our God the Son is gracious. Jesus came so that we may have life and that we may have it more abundantly. Though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, that you through his poverty might become rich. He became a servant and gave his life as a ransom for many to become the author of eternal salvation. In Him we have redemption through His blood, forgiveness of sins, according to the riches of His grace. And let's not forget finally how God the Spirit is gracious. And we spent some time praying this morning about the works of the Holy Spirit. The Holy Spirit has been given to us in our hearts as a guarantee and as a seal. What are we guaranteed? We're guaranteed new heavenly bodies, an eternal house, a building from God not made with hands, to someday replace this earthly house and the tent of our frail bodies. Our perishing outward man. The indwelling spirit is the Father's down payment for the heavenly residence and real estate. He's given to us as proof that He's going to keep His promise. He's the guarantee of our inheritance as God's children. We've been sealed until the day of redemption when he claims his purchased possessions. I'll talk about how we can claim these riches of glory and grace as our own later, but for now let's move on to the second point. Mankind is resistant to God's call. What happens next in verse 18 is nothing short of an unmitigated disaster. They all with one accord began to make excuses. All of them with one accord. This is that one type of unity we don't want. Yet the fallen world, as diverse as it is, is one on this point. That's why Paul can say confidently There is none righteous, no not one. There is none who understands. There is none who seeks after God. They have all turned aside. They have together become unprofitable There is none who does good. No, not one. Though there are many excuses, God has revealed Himself so that the world is without excuse. Mankind is resistant to God's call. But let's hear some of those poor excuses anyway. Jesus gives us a sample of three in verses 18, 19, and 20. I think there's somewhat of a progression from least valuable to most. Perhaps there's even a progression of man's blessings we find in Genesis chapter two land, animals, and marriage with women. A piece of ground is good, but it's not like a living breeding animal. Five yolks or pairs of oxen are good, but they do not compare the covenant of marriage with a human companion. A woman. Now to be clear, none of these are bad in themselves. They're gifts from God, what theologians call common grace. Blessings universally bestowed upon all. Classic proof texts for common grace include Matthew 5:45, Acts 14:17, and Romans 1:18-23 I'm not gonna go through all of them, but just know that Father in heaven makes his son rise on the evil and on the good. And sends rain on the just and on the unjust. Common grace is a witness to our benevolent God, filling our hearts with food and gladness. To lead us to bow to our sovereign Creator. Common grace was supposed to be like an aroma of a meal drawing us into the banquet. Common grace was not meant to furnish excuses to stay at home. But mankind is resistant to God's call. We often make God's gifts excuses to not enter his kingdom. This is foolishness. Even the best in the world cannot compare to the least in the kingdom. I'd rather be a doorkeeper in God's house than the king of my royal dwelling Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things shall be added to you. God has given us the ultimate. But we've settled for the penultimate. I think of what C. S. Lewis has observed in Mankind. When we think of unbelievers, we may initially believe they spurn God because their ambitions and desires are too strong. Lewis disagrees, quote, our desires are not too strong, but too weak. We are half-hearted creatures, fooling about with drink and sex and ambition when infinite joy is offered us. Like an ignorant child who wants to go on making mud pies in a slum because he cannot imagine what is meant by the offer of a holiday at the sea. We are far too easily pleased. That's the best in our world are mud pies in a slum. And the least in God's kingdom is holiday at the sea. Paul discovered this in that Damascus experience He count on all things lost for the excellence of the knowledge of Christ Jesus his Lord, for whom he has suffered the loss of all things, and count them as rubbish. That he may gain Christ. But not many are like Paul. So God is gracious in his kingdom invitation Mankind is resistant to God's call. sermons.text: What does it mean to have a heart for the lost? How can we live for the spread of the gospel? Or it could be That the extraordinary work of evangelism looks quite ordinary Edward Kimball was a dry goods salesman. He was no pastor or evangelist. He belonged to Mount Vernon Church in Boston as a layman, who volunteered his time as a Sunday school class teacher of teenage boys. But he wasn't content with meeting these kids once a week. He was determined to get to know them better individually throughout the week. Their interests, backgrounds. One day he felt burdened for one young man in particular, named Dwight, and decided to visit him Now, Kimball had his doubts and fears about this idea, but he concluded that the Holy Spirit was leading him to go visit Dwight at his workplace. So on April twenty-first, eighteen fifty-five, Kimball visited the Holton Shoe Store where Dwight worked. Found them in a stock room in the back, and there spoke to him of Christ's love. Shortly thereafter, the young man accepted the love of God and devoted his life to serving him. Now this Dwight is better known as D. L. Moody. We know very well what he went on to do. We may celebrate his life more than Edward Kimball's, but listen to Moody's later recollection of that encounter with Kimball at the back of the shoe store. When I was in Boston, I used to attend a school Sunday school class, and one day I recollect my teacher came around behind the counter of the shop I was at work in and put his hand upon my shoulder. And talk to me about Christ and my soul. I had not felt that I had a soul till then. I said to myself, this is a very strange thing. There is a man who never saw me till lately, and he is weeping over my sins, and I never shed a tear about him. But I understand it now and know what it is to have a passion for men's souls and weep over their sins. I don't remember what he said, but I can still feel the power of that man's hand on my shoulder tonight. How does the story of D. L. Moody, who went up and touched millions of lives all over the world, with the gospel message begin? It begins with Kimball, one obscure man who visited him at a shoe store, touched his life with the gospel message. We're thankful for Edward Kimball's and D. L. Moody's of the world. I'm sure you can speak of people like them who've touched your life personally. I have a feeling there are more Edwards and Dwight's in the world, but what's most important is that we too, like them, must have a heart for the lost. But there's someone even more qualified to speak about having a heart for the lost. Let's turn to Luke fifteen, one to ten, and see what Jesus has to say. Then all the tax collectors and the sinners drew near to him to hear him. And the Pharisees and scribes complained, saying, This man receives sinners and eats with them. So he spoke this parable to them, saying, What man of you, having a hundred sheep? If he loses one of them, does not leave the ninety nine in the wilderness, and go after the one which is lost, until he finds it? And when he found it, when he has found it, he lays it on his shoulders, rejoicing. And when he comes home, he calls together his friends and neighbors, saying to them, Rejoice with me, for I have found my sheep, which was lost. I say to you that likewise there will be more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine just persons who need no repentance. Or what woman, having ten silver coins, if she loses one coin, does not light a lamp, sweep the house, and search carefully until she finds it? And when she has found it, she calls her friends and neighbors together, saying, Rejoice with me, for I have found the peace which I lost. Likewise I say to you, there is joy in the presence of the angels of God over one sinner who repents. To have a heart for the lost, we need to heed two principles from this passage 1. Receive sinners who listen to Jesus, verses 1 and 2. And 2. Rejoice when sinners repent. Verses 3 to 10. First received sinners who listen to Jesus. Last year, Dave Shive spoke at our church on August 16th. on the same passage and began by establishing the connection between this passage and what came before it In other words, as we begin chapter 15, it's helpful to look back at what just happened at the close of chapter fourteen. Recall in our study of chapter 14, 25 to 35, how Jesus explained the cost of following him. His disciples must deny themselves, forsake all things, and rely on him. Our Lord issued this challenge to the great multitude that went with him He who has ears to hear, let him hear. So who has those ears to hear? Who would rise to the occasion? As Jesus looked with his penetrating prophetic gaze into the mass of the people Who will emerge out of obscurity and out of nominalism? I think of that hymn from Francis Ridley Havergale. Which captures the gravitas of the moment? Who is on the Lord's side? Who will serve the king? Who will be his helpers? Other lives to bring Who will lead the world's side? Who will face the foe? Who is on the Lord's side? Who for him will go? We have the answers right at the beginning of this chapter. You might read these verses and think there was some kind of mistake. Luke, are you sure it wasn't the Pharisees? And scribes who drew near to listen. No mistake here. Indeed, it was the tax collectors and sinners who had ears to hear. Now, the category of sinners was of two main types. One, Jews who fell short of the law of Moses and its demands. And two, Gentiles who were without the law and thus without God. Tax collectors were of the first type, Jews who worked for the hated and oppressive Roman Empire. Many of them fleecing their customers by taking much more than required for their own pockets. No wonder they were classified alongside heathens, harlots. Extortioners, unjust, and adulterers But when tax collectors and sinners came to Christ in repentance and faith, Jesus would demand that they turn away from their dishonest practices. Though Jesus loves sinners as they are, he did not allow them to remain as they are. But even if they repented genuinely and left their past behind, Their reputation stuck with them. But that's why the religious elites could not believe that Jesus would receive sinners who listened to him. But as followers of Christ, we should not be surprised by this. If we've been reading Luke carefully, we'd be properly prepared for this incident. Earlier, Luke records specifically that tax collectors went to the Jordan to be baptized by John the Baptist. The forerunner of Jesus' ministry. That's in chapter 3. Later in chapter 5, Luke records the conversion of Levi or Matthew, the tax collector. Now, this event is not unique to the third gospel. But Luke highlights the greatness of the feast that he threw for his friends and associates. Luke showcases the tax collectors' charity and hospitality. And just as they were present in chapter 15, Pharisees were there in chapter 5, turned off by Jesus' reception of sinners Our Lord responded in chapter 5, verses 31 to 32. Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick. I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance. Jesus received sinners who listened to him. One more event to prepare us for chapter 15. In chapter 7, John the Baptist sends messengers to ask whether Jesus is the prophesied Christ. He sends back an affirmative answer and then turns to the crowds to confirm John's ministry. Right then, Luke records the following in verses 29 to 30, chapter 7. And when all the people heard him, even the tax collectors justified God, having been baptized with the baptism of John. But the Pharisees And lawyers rejected the will of God for themselves, not having been baptized by Him. As Jesus spoke good things about John the Baptist, those baptized by him spoke good things about God, declaring God to be righteous. Among them were tax collectors we saw earlier in chapter 3. Again, Jesus received sinners. So listen to it. But the religious leaders will not listen. They rejected God's will revealed through the Messiah and his forerunner. Now here we are again in chapter 15, with crowds of people listening to Jesus. But the crowds have split between those deemed unworthy of God's kingdom and those deemed worthy. It's as if the tax collectors and sinners heard and followed the words of that hymn: Let not conscience make you linger, nor of fitness fondly dream. All the fitness he required is to feel your need of him. These rejects and outcasts certainly felt their need for Christ. But the Pharisees and the scribes, though outwardly wise and mighty, they did not feel that desperation for Jesus. They're willing to share tables with Jesus Himself, but not with those tax collectors and sinners. We will see Jesus' reaction to them next. But before we go on, in application of the first principle I want to ask you whether you'd receive sinners who listen to Jesus. Would the proud religious hypocrites complain about you as they did with Jesus? This Christian man or woman receives sinners and eats with them. What our neighbors complain about us, those folks at Faith Bible Church receive the worst people and eat with them. Again, I'm not saying we should be lax on repentance or preach grace Remember, this gracious call to discipleship at the beginning of Luke 15 comes on the heels of the costly call to discipleship at the end of Luke 14. But we must stop looking at outward appearances. We must learn to receive sinners who listen to Jesus Okay, you may say to me, I'm ready to receive sinners, any of them who listen to Jesus. But where do I find them? In Evangelism Explosion, we have this process of finding and securing prospects. When I was part of EE in college, we were trained to look for prospects among visitors to our campus ministry meetings, dorm roommates, classmates, and friends from other student organizations. We'd get into panic mode if we couldn't find someone to meet for our weekly OJT, which is on-the-job training. Even if you don't know EE, you're not part of E, or you were never part of it, we all should be looking for prospects And a prospect is someone who we believe might want to draw near and listen to Jesus Once we identify them, we need to get them, whether it's our unbelieving family, friends, neighbors, in the earshot of Bible teaching Obviously, one way is to invite them out to our regular Sunday services or Bible studies. If they come, you can ask afterwards: what did you think about the lesson or the sermon? What are your thoughts about the good news that the pastor shared? Or if they're not ready to go to church. You can ask them whether they'd be interested in reading a book of the Bible together with you. You could use Christianity Explained or a basic introduction to our faith. You can teach that material at your home or at a cafe. I find that the phrase reading a book together is less condescending than and more welcoming. Then do you want me to teach you the Bible? That's just me. Whatever approach we follow or questions we ask, we need the Lord to help us. We need him to help us discern whether our prospects are genuinely seeking Jesus or not. They may have some reservations and questions for you. When they ask these, we must discern and figure out whether those inquiries are sincere questions or what E. E. calls smokescreens Smoke screens as in they're hiding their lifestyle of sin behind a barrage of questions. There are those out there because they're not ready to repent. Remember, unbelievers not only disbelieve from ignorance and lack of knowledge, but they also disbelieve because of moral corruption. John 3:19 says, And this is the condemnation: that the light has come into the world, and men loved darkness rather than light, because their deeds were evil. But if they are drawn to the light of Christ, willing to leave behind the darkness and be ready to forsake their evil deeds We have reasons to celebrate. That leads to the second point. Rejoice when sinners repent. From verse 3 until the end of the chapter, we have three parables that communicate the same basic message. They are the parable of the lost sheep, the parable of the lost coin, and the parable of the lost son, better known as the parable of the prodigal son. John A. Martin summarizes the common idea God is vitally concerned with the repentance of sinners. All three speak of things or a person being lost and then found, and of rejoicing when the lost is found. There are commonalities even in details. Joe B. Green observes, quote, the three parables of Luke fifteen, through common structure and subject matter And repetition of key terms and phrases presents a cumulative response to the indictment of the Pharisees and legal experts in verse two. This fellow welcomes sinners and eats with them. You can see the repetition of key terms and phrases yourself woven throughout the three parables. There are the repeated mentions of friends, neighbors, and call together. More importantly, there are repetitions of lost eight times and find again eight times. Most importantly, nine times there are words related to joy and mirth. What connects the first two parables together is the introductory formula of what man or woman having, but if he or she loses one And then there are some common words at the end of the two parables, I say to you, likewise, over one sinner who repents. Putting it all together, we should rejoice when sinners repent. Yet, in spite of these observable parallels, there are some differences between the three stories. Again, Joel Green is helpful, quote: one may observe an escalation from one parable to the next. A shepherd suffers the loss of one sheep from a flock of one hundred, whereas the woman suffers the loss of one coin out of ten. This escalation will continue in the next parable with the loss of one of only two sons. So we will see how the two parables covered today builds up to the final one, which we'll cover next week, Lord willing. Today we just focus on the first two parables. Because these two are more like short anecdotes and less like lengthy novels. There's a limit of inferences we can draw from them. For example, we can't assume that the man in the first story doesn't care about the 99 sheep and left them exposed to predators and thieves. If danger equates to needing repentance, then we can conclude from verse 7 that the majority of the flock is safe throughout the story. But here are some inferences we can draw. The rhetorical questions in verses four and eight Reveal that while the parables are fictional, they are relatable, everyday concerns of everyday individuals. Jesus asks those questions as if the response will be, of course he leaves the 99 in the wilderness and goes after the one. And of course she lights a lamp, sweeps the house, and searches carefully. We also infer that the motif of losing and finding is well known among all social classes. Some commentators note how owning a hundred sheep implies the first man is pretty well off, but the woman who owns ten silver coins is relatively poor. But they both know the value of that lost one and seek it. Their joy in finding the lost is so great that they must invite others. They can't contain their excitement. The man invites his guy friends and neighbors, while the woman invites her lady friends and neighbors. One says, Rejoice with me, for I have found my sheep which was lost. The other says, Rejoice with me, for I have found the peace which I was which I lost. Such rejoicing In the earthly realm is a small reflection of the heavenly joy. We see at the end of both parables that the joy is celestial In heaven and in the presence of the angels of God. Now who exactly is celebrating here? Well, yes, I'm sure the saints in heaven are happy. Yes, the angels are also rejoicing. But heaven is joyful mainly because our God the Father is joyful. Now, if you don't believe me that our Father in heaven rejoices over the repentant, let me invite you to look at some passages. Zephaniah three sixteen to seventeen And it says concerning the restored Israel in the future In that day it shall be said to Jerusalem, Do not fear Zion, let not your hands be weak. The Lord your God in your midst, the mighty one, will save. He will rejoice over you with gladness. He will quiet you with his love. He will rejoice over you with singing. We saw earlier in Luke 12. 32. Jesus himself assuring his disciples, do not fear little flock, for it is your father's good pleasure to give you the kingdom. Paul wrote concerning his own conversion in Galatians 1:15-16. It pleased God who separated me from my mother's womb and called me through his grace. To reveal his son in me, that I might preach him among the Gentiles. God rejoices, He has a good pleasure, and it pleases him. To see sinners turn to Him. In the household of God, how we understand our Heavenly Father is crucial. Do we see him as an angry, disappointed being, distant and cold? That was sort of my default, fleshly view of him. Because my earthly father was absent for most of my life. Of course, we know that God is loving and caring, even if our parents did not reflect His authority well. But we don't want to go to the other extreme and view him as light on sin either. C. S. Lewis lamented once, quote, We want in fact not so much a father in heaven as how a Grandfather in Heaven, a Sina benevolence who, as they say, like to see young people enjoying themselves, and whose plan for the universe was simply that it might be said at the end of the day A good time was had by all. This is a mistaken view of God. God who rejoices when sinners repent is perfect in power, in love, and purity. He will by no means clear the guilty, but he also justifies the ungodly. How? Look no further than the gospel of Christ, for it is the power of God to salvation for everyone who believes. You may not believe that you're in need of salvation, but let me tell you that you are that one lost sheep and that one lost coin. You ought to follow the example of tax collectors and sinners who drew near to Jesus to hear him Do not be, like the Pharisees and scribes, too proud to have fellowship with Jesus and those who don't meet their standards. The fact is, all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God. But we can be justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus. Now we cannot be declared righteous before God by doing good works of the law. We inevitably fail. But there is the promise that the just shall live by faith, live forever in the presence of God. The way to be found is to repent. You must admit that you turned away, every one of us, to our own way. You must return to the shepherd and overseer of your souls. You must be laid on his shoulders to return to safety You must repent. We repent by turning away from ourselves, our self-indulgence and our self-righteousness. The tax collectors and sinners had to repent of their self-indulgence. The Pharisees and the scribes had to repent of their self-righteousness. Either way, we turn from ourselves and trust in the finished work of Jesus. Be the perfect God and perfect man at the same time, live the perfect life. Yet he suffered and died on the cross for our sins. He was punished for our sins of evil thought, word, and actions, sins of omission and commission. He then rose again from the dead and ascended to heaven. Someday he'll return to establish the promised kingdom on earth. Will you trust in Christ alone for your hope of salvation? It is all by grace, not works Every time a sinner repents and believes in the good news of Jesus, our Father in heaven rejoices. The fact that he knows in advance all who would believe does not at all dampen that joy. That may be a mystery to us, but here's what we know for sure. We can rejoice with the heavenly host at each conversion. We can rejoice when sinners repent. If God rejoices in the presence of angels in heaven, so should we in the presence of saints on earth I believe one way we celebrate together an individual's repentance is through the baptismal service. The believer's baptism is a joyful and festive occasion. But many can see that someone has given his or her life for Christ. Originally, these initiation events were out and open in rivers and other public places. In the days before baptismal pools and church buildings. Today I'm praying for growth in evangelism, conversions, and baptisms. That we would have many opportunities as a local church to rejoice when sinners repent. Please join the Group Committee and the Council in prayer for that joy of salvation to be a normal part of our church. That we will receive sinners who listen to Jesus and rejoice when they repent. Let's join heaven in celebration as our God says. Rejoice with me, for I have found that which was lost. Wouldn't that be a festive occasion? A wonderful sound in our church? Amazing grace, how sweet the sound, that saved a wretch like me. I once was lost, but now I'm found Was blind, but now I see. Let's pray. Lord, we thank you that you receive us Lord, help us to remember our calling. Not many of us were wise. Not many of us were mighty in the eyes of the world. You show us amazing grace because we are like the tax collectors and sinners. We thank you for the convicting work of the Spirit that opened our eyes to the depth of our sin. How we need your son. And we're thankful for the grace and mercy that receives us as sinners And now that we are part of the fold, now that we are destined for the kingdom of God, now that we are citizens of heaven. Help us to rejoice every time we see new believers, new converts, new commitments to be disciples of your Son. May we continually sing. Of your amazing grace. Pray all these things in Jesus Christ's name. Amen.

sermons.speaker: Sung Cho

sermons.text: Sometimes you see an imitation and then appreciate the original so much more, as I was preparing this week. I encounter a something in the literature of Mahayana Buddhism, and this was written a century after Jesus. It is a story of a young man who leaves his father's house and is gone for many years. His father searches for him, even moving to another country and becomes wealthy on the way, the son, meanwhile, becomes a beggar. One day the son happens to come to the town where his father lives. He doesn't recognize his father, but the father recognized his son at first sight and sends his servants after him. After failing to force him to stay, the father sends servants dressed in street clothes to recruit him to work for him. He works at the lowliest of tasks, shoveling manure. The son works faithfully, but lives in a shack nearby. Many years later, the father declares that he will treat this poor man as a son and make him his heir, but the son is indifferent to the inheritance. He continues to live in his shack and works. Now the householder perceives that his son is mature and mentally developed And before he dies, the Father declares before all, This man is really my natural son, the heir of all that I possess. Now, how does this story of the lost son compare with the parable we know so well? If you're like me, you prefer Jesus' version in Luke 15. Why? Because Jesus Christ shows us God's amazing grace to sinners. Sure, we may like the Buddhist version because we see someone starting at the bottom and working hard on his way to the top. But that's not grace. Let's read Luke fifteen, eleven to thirty-two, for a better understanding of God's amazing grace. Then he said, A certain man had two sons. And the younger of them said to his father, Father, give me the portion of goods that falls to me. So he divided to them his livelihood. And not many days after the younger son gathered all together, journeyed to a far country, and there wasted his possessions with prodigal living. But when he had spent all, there arose a severe famine in all that land, and he began to be in want. Then he went and joined himself to a citizen of that country, and he sent him into his fields to feed swine. And he would gladly have filled his stomach with the pots that the swine ate, and no one gave him anything But when he came to himself he said, How many of my father's hired servants have bread enough and to spare? And I perish with hunger. I will arise and go to my father and will say to him, Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you, and I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Make me like one of your hired servants. And he arose and came to his father. But when he was still a great way off, his father saw him and had compassion. And ran and fell on his neck and kissed him. And the son said to him, Father, I have sinned against heaven and in your sight, and am no longer worthy to be called your son. But the father said to his servant, Bring out the best robe and put it on him, and put a ring on his hand, and sandals on his feet. And bring the fatted calf here, and kill it, and let us eat and be merry. For this my son was dead, and is alive again. He was lost and is found. And they began to be merry. Now his older son was in the field, and as he came and drew Near to the house, he heard music and dancing. So he called one of the servants and asked what these things meant. And he said to him, Your brother has come, and because he has received Him safe and sound, your father has killed the fatted calf. But he was angry and would not go in. Therefore his father came out and pleaded with him Him. So he answered and said to his father, Lo, these many years I have been serving you, I never transgressed your commandment at any time, and yet you never gave me a young goat that I might make merry with my friends. But as soon as this son of yours came, who has devoured your livelihood with harlots, you killed a fat of calf for him. And he said to him, Son, you are always with me, and all that I have is yours. It was right that we should make merry and be glad, for your brother was dead and is alive again. And what's lost and is found. When we behold God's amazing grace, what should our response be? I see three responses here. One, repent and return to the Father. That's verses eleven to twenty, the first part of verse twenty. Two, make Mary because of God's mercy. From second half of verse twenty to verse twenty twenty four and three leave behind simple legalism. That's verses twenty five to verse thirty two First, repent and return to the Father In verse 11, the third parable begins basically the same way the first and the second ones began. A certain man had two sons, like the way a certain woman had ten coins, and a certain man had 100 sheep. But unlike the earlier two parables, Jesus doesn't set up the story in one verse and ask a rhetorical question. Unlike the first two parables, Jesus is going to speak elaborately on how one of the sons is lost. Verses twelve to sixteen show us how he was dead and so lost. There's a lot packed into verse twelve We can assume that he's in a Jewish family and as the younger one, he's destined to d inherit a third of the property. But for him to ask his father first for his portion is brazen, ungodly, disrespectful. According to one commentary, a father could arrange to grant the inheritance either before or after his death, but it was usually done after. Against such customs, the younger one took the initiative, and the father granted it. It's as if the sun said, that I can't wait until you're dead. I need my money now This young man rejected his family and turned his back on God. The father, no doubt heartbroken, accounted for all his wealth, no small feat, as he appears to be quite wealthy, and gave the younger the portion due to him. All that Paul warned about, the last days and perilous times, in Second Timothy three, verse two Came true in this household. Lovers of money, boasters, proud, blasphemers, disobedient to parents, unthankful, unholy. In verse thirteen, the lost son becomes the prodigal son In the flurry of events, before the rumors spread far and wide, and before his conscience catches up with him, the younger son's out of the house The phrase gathered all together, Fitzmeier explains, means converting everything to cash. You left to spend it all at a faraway place A Gentile region, where he doesn't have to deal with the reminders of God. Whoever keeps the law is a discerning son, but a companion of gluttons. Shames his father. This shameful son lived a lavish lifestyle that left them broke. In verse 14, we see that once a severe famine hit the land, nothing could sustain him. His companions turned out to be fairweathered friends. Verse 15: He has nowhere to turn except the citizen of that country who hired him to feed pigs in his fields. This young man was once a Jewish citizen above his servants in his land. Now he is a slave below a Gentile in a foreign country. Once honorable among his peers, now among swine, he adds to his moral filth ceremonial uncleanness. He was once the envy of the poor, stomach constantly filled as his family gave him everything. Now we see in verse 16 That he would gladly have filled his stomach with the pots, the carrot, that the swine ate, and no one gave him anything And then in verse 17, we have a pivotal moment, an epiphany. Jesus tells us that he came to himself. And we see a similar expression in Acts chapter 12, verse 11. Like Peter, who snapped out of it and realized he was safe. This prodigal son came to himself and realized something. Better to be his father's hired servant. Now William Barclay explains how quote the Ordinary slave was in some sense a member of the family, but the hired servant could be dismissed at a day's notice. He was not one of the family at all But still, status low was better than the status quo. Better to eat the bread and crumbs there than to envy the pigs and their pods here. Better to live with humility than perish with hunger. This is true repentance. This is returning to the Father. Is echoing what the sons of Korah said, A day in your courts is better than a thousand. I would rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God than dwell in the tents of wickedness. It's having the lowly posture of the Syrophoenician woman. Yes, Lord, yet even the little dogs under the table eat from the children's crumbs Is approaching with the godly sorrow of David, who knew for certain, a broken and a contrite heart. Diesel God, you will not despise. In verses eighteen and nineteen, the younger son, though lost and dead, displays true repentance, which makes him found and alive. He invokes that familiar name again: Father. He understands the height of his sin. He has sinned against heaven, the Heavenly Father, as well as his earthly Father He understands the consequence of his sin. He is no longer worthy to be called a son. But he also understands the possible mercy for his sin. And because he understood and believed in the goodness of the Father, he arose and went to him. That leads us to the next point. Make merry because of God's mercy Though this prodigal son emptied his pocket of every penny, he could not empty the rich reserves of God's mercy. And at the first sight, faint sight of his son, the father had compassion. He ran and fell on his neck and kissed him. This was quite a sight. A wealthy landowner pulling up his robes, a man of stature casting away his dignity That's not something the people saw every day, but the father was so eager to see his son again One Christian author Trevan Wax considers another possibility for this haste. The father knew that if someone else were to meet the son first, they might beat him, send him away, or publicly humiliate. Him for shaming the family. The community had nothing but disgust for such a scoundrel But now the community would know for sure that the prodigal is restored as the son. We can bet the son was not ready for such a warm reception. Perhaps he had to pull his goading father off of him to say the lines he rehearsed. Father, I've sinned against heaven and in your sight, and I'm no longer worthy to be called your son But the least of God's compassions overwhelms the best of our confessions. As C. Marvin Pate writes, quote, The depth of the Son's repentance is matched only by the depth of the Father's love. Nothing in our hands we bring, but he makes the riches of his grace abound to us. In every way, the father restores his dead and lost son to his previous position of glory. He is treated as the guest of honor with the best robe, a ring, and sandals. His return home is an occasion for a feast to kill the bat and calf for the meal. Theologian Kenneth Bailey, who spent much of his life in ministry in biblical lands, Estimates that the meat would have been enough to feed 35 to 75 persons. This was not going to be a small quiet dinner just with family. Remember the shepherd who found that lost one out of hundred sheep. Remember the woman who found that lost one out of ten coins. They called their friends and neighbors and said, Rejoice with me. So how much more is the father who found his lost son? He went from the deep sadness of David weeping over Absalom to the joy of Jacob who learned Joseph was still alive. He can't contain his joy, keep his happiness to himself. So they began to be merry. Now, Jesus, the storyteller, could have ended this parable right here at verse 24, and it would have been perfectly symmetrical with the previous two parables. Or he could have wrapped it up nicely with a conclusion like verses 7 and 10, perhaps something along the lines of: Likewise, there is joy with our Heavenly Father over one sinner who repents. But that's not how this parable or this chapter ends. We have to reckon with verses twenty-five to thirty-two. That leads us to the third point. Leave behind simple legalism. As Jesus narrates the response of the older son, the symmetry with the other two parables is broken. But at the same time, there's a nice book end to this chapter. Remember how Luke 15 began. If you have your Bible with you, go back to verses 1 and 2. And I'll reread it for you. Then all the tax collectors and the sinners drew near to him to hear him as Jesus And the Pharisees and scribes complained, saying, This man receives sinners and eats with them. I made the point last week that we should receive sinners and live who listen to Jesus. Well we know in this context who would not receive sinners who listen to Jesus Jesus, the Pharisees, and the scribes, they were like this older son in the parable As a typical, responsible, hardworking firstborn, the older one worked in the field. and came home for the day. In verses 29 and 30, look at the way the elder son refers to himself, and then listen to the way he refers to the father and the younger brother. When he refers to himself, it's about how much he has done, how perfect he is, how he deserves a party with his friends. When he refers to his father, it's about how stingy he is. I shared a sermon from Edmund Clowney this week, and he has some good insights on the heart of the older brother. He has no conception of his father's love for his brother or for him. He has no love for his brother either He will not call him my brother, but only this son of yours. He calls him son, but this is not the same word for son we see in the previous one. verses. There's tenderness. There's grace and warmth in that word and his voice Even in the face of such strident, hostile, and cold legalism, son, you are always with me, and all that I have is yours, he says The patient and compassionate Father basically repeats what he said earlier in verse 24. The son was dead and is alive again. He was lost and is found. The father tries to reconcile the younger son to the older son. Though the legalistic one calls the prodigal this son of yours, the father reminds them he's your brother. It was right that they should make merry and be glad. To do what's right, you must leave behind simple legalism. The original word for it was right in verse 32 is seen frequently throughout the Gospels and Acts to communicate God's purposes that must be accomplished. For example, it was right that Elijah must come before the Messiah. It is right that tribulation comes before God's kingdom arrives. And it was right for the Pharisees and the scribes to be merry and be glad when they saw the tax collectors and sinners come to Jesus. Come in repentance and faith. Turn away from the prodigal ways of the tax collectors and sinners, the prideful ways of the Pharisees and scribes. Turn to Jesus. For when we look at each other We can say we were dead and are alive again, and we're lost and are found How deep the Father's love for us, how vast beyond all measure, that he should give his only son to make a wretch his Treasure. Or we know that this parable Has inspired many, many artworks, paintings, poems, songs. And Lord, we pray that it would have influence in our lives. It would touch us. For those of us who have never come to you, the merciful Father. For those of us who don't really understand what a loving father is like, that this word would touch Us. May we revisit it over and over again. May we understand the sacrifice of your son that brought us near to this loving Father. For those of us who have walked with you for many years, remind us of our destiny where we're going. But we're not home yet, but we pray that our hearts will be warmed and encouraged. Lord help us to be more like the younger son and be less like the older son. We know that legalism and pride, we still have to fight those things in this walk with you, in this sanctification.
