sermons.speaker: Sung Cho
sermons.text: I looked at my age demographics this week because I was thinking about charitable giving across generations. My birthday is very late in 1980. I teeter between the categories of Generation X and Millennial. But I clearly and fondly remember owning and listening to a Walkman playing Mario on the 8-bit Nintendo Entertainment System. Chatting online with friends with dial-up internet and gas prices closer to a dollar. So I'm going to align myself with Gen X According to one ranking about eight years ago, the greatest generation born before 1945 had the highest percentage of its population giving at 88%. So while their numbers are shrinking, many of them give. Not surprisingly, baby boomers born between 1946 and We're second in percentage of givers at 72%, and boomers contribute most to the sum of all charitable giving As for the Gen Xers and Millennials, the older contributes more, but only 59% of us give, and we make up a smaller percentage of the population. I'm looking at all this and I wonder in general whether the baton's been dropped, a message lost in transit. And I'm talking about I'm applying this to Christianity here. Between the older believers and younger Christians. Will substantial charitable giving start to fade over time? My parents never taught me budgeting per se, but they were definitely frugal and that was impressive. Most I've learned about biblical finances was from a fanatic Dave Ramsey disciple, and I don't know too many of them. Thankfully, God has much to say about earning, saving, and spending money. Today's passage in Luke 16, 1 to 13, is a crucial. Let's read it now. He also said to his disciples, There was a certain rich man who had a steward, and an accusation was brought to him that this man was wasting his goods. So he called him and said to him, What is this I hear about you? Give an account of your stewardship, for you can no longer be steward. Then the steward said within himself, What shall I do? For my master is taking the stewardship away from me. I cannot dig, I am ashamed to beg. I resolved what to do, that when I am put out of the stewardship, they may receive me into their houses. So he called every one of his master's debtors to him, and said to the first, How much do you owe my master? And he and he said a hundred measures of oil. So he said to him, Take your bill and sit down quickly and write fifty Then he said to another, And how much do you owe? So he said, hundred measures of wheat And he said to him, Take your bill and write eight. So the master commended the unjust steward, because he had dealt shrewdly. For the sons of this world are more shrewd in their generation than the sons of light. And I say to you, make friends for yourselves by unrighteous mammon, that when you fail, they may receive you. into an everlasting home. He who is faithful in what is least is faithful also in much And he who is unjust in what is least is unjust also in much. Therefore, if you have not been faithful in the unrighteous mammon, who will commit to your trust The true riches. And if you have not been faithful in what is another man's, who will give you what is your own? No servant can worship uh can serve two masters. For either he will hate the one and love the other, or else he will be loyal to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve God and mammon Handling money is no easy matter. We must know its potentials and risks, both temporal and eternal consequences. In this particular passage, as disciples of Jesus, we must understand money in context of three major areas of life. Friendship, stewardship, and worship. I derive three money principles, one Use fating funds to make eternal friends one to nine. Two, be a faithful steward to receive much reward verses ten to twelve And three, holy worship God, not money. Verse thirteen First, let's talk about friendship and how we can use fading funds to make eternal friends. This is the first and main principle that Jesus derives from the parable. The point seems obvious, but commentators have struggled with some of the details of the parable and the structure of this passage. For example, structurally speaking, where does Jesus' story end exactly? I take the view that it ends in the middle of verse 8, and then our Lord begins the explanation there. Comparing the sons of this world with sons of light. Jesus' proposition in verse 9 wraps up the section nicely. It parallels the steward's thought in verse 4 with words and phrases that when they may receive into As for the details of the story itself, it helps to compare this parable with the preceding one. Both are realistic fiction, featuring wealthy men, and both suffer loss because of a prodigal. Whether it's the prodigal son or the prodigal servant, both prodigals had to own up to their mistakes and come face to face with their respective authorities. Both engage in monologues and come to some kind of plan to preserve themselves in the future. But there are of course some key differences, whereas repentance is a theme of the prodigal son parable. Shrewdness is the theme of the prodigal steward parable. At the end of the story, here there is no substantial character transformation from lost and dead to found and alive. The steward's just as unjust as he was at the beginning. He's still one of the sons of this world, not one of the sons of light. So we need to be careful to pick out what's commendable in this steward, which is just one quality, and discard all others And that one quality to be emulated is only and namely shrewdness. And here's what shrewness looks like. Backed into a corner. This man knows for sure he's getting fired. He can't dig himself out of this mess, figuratively and literally. He's been at this white-collar job for so long, manual labor is not an option. He was about to take a free fall from a lofty position. To be a resource manager for a wealthy man was to be envied by all. Such employment was so coveted that some sold themselves as slaves to wealthy individuals for such a status. Now he's afraid he'll end up in the streets begging. The steward's plan is not given in detail, but it is executed in verses 5 to 7. The goal is to ingratiate himself to his master's borrowers so that they'll welcome him. into their homes once he's let go. Make his bosses' debtors indebted to him. They'll show hospitality later for his kindness shown now. Time's taken away so he gets right to work, and the two transactions recorded are typical of many he conducted between then and the termination of his employment. The first transaction reduces a hundred measures or a tuce of olive oil. Batos in Greek relates to bot in Hebrew. In our terms, we're talking about eight or nine gallons per measure. That means this customer owes 900 gallons of oil As for the second client, he owed a hundred measures of or chorus of wheat. Chorus in Greek relates to kor in Hebrew, and in our terms, we're talking about 10 to 11 bushels per measure. That means this customer owes one thousand bushels of wheat. And these are large sums Amounts exchanged between aristocrats, lords, and nobles. For one reference, look at Ezra chapter seven, verse twenty-one to twenty-three. How much Artacirces, the king of Persia, granted Ezra as limits, up to one hundred cores of wheat, one hundred baths of wine, one hundred baths of oil The steward's not playing around with pocket change. He's wheeling and dealing with the rich owners of olive groves and wealthy patrons with acres of land. So also these reductions are not small discounts. That much is certain. Now, some commentators, like Joseph Bitzmayr, have attempted to delve deeper into details. Some think that the amounts deducted, specifically 50 measures of oil and 20 measures of wheat, Are not part of the principal owed to the master, rather the discounted amounts are the extra interest or the commission owed to the manager Now to charge that much for handling fees seems ridiculous, but remember this guy is no paragon of virtue. It's not hard to imagine him filling his own pockets at the expense of his boss and his debtors. Whether the discount is from the principal or the interest, we're not sure. But we see that the steward's employer is impressed. He was forward thinking. He was using his position in the present to position himself in the future. He was operating within the bounds of unstable rules to stabilize himself. Again, we're not talking about sound business ethics here. We're not praising the steward's dishonesty, mismanagement, and underhandedness We're praising his shrewdness. We have something when we something similar when we think about Rahat We don't praise her past sexual immorality or even her deception of her fellow citizens. We just praise her for her faith and works. In the same way, there's a kind of shrewdness in worldly scoundrels that can be learned by godly saints. This should not surprise us. Jesus compares those who hear and obey him to the wise and shrewd man who built his house on a rock. He told his disciples as they went out to be shrewd as serpents. In another parable, the five virgins who were prepared for the coming of the bridegroom were shrewd. Earlier in Luke 12, 42, we saw how faithfulness goes hand in hand with shrewdness. Jesus and his disciples, his apostles, wanted us to be shrewd. According to God's will, not wise in our own opinion. If we're going to be shrewder and wiser, we first need to accept that the sons of this world do a better job preparing for the next phase of their lives than the sons of light preparing for heaven. Unbelievers recognize the power of money, and even in their corrupt ways, value friendships that last a lifetime. Can we do better with friendships that last eternity? I have to ask myself, honestly, if I were to die right now, how many saints would invite me over to their celestial mansions to hang out? Some of you know that 1988 Christian song by Ray Boltz that goes, Thank you for giving to the Lord. I am a life that was changed. Thank you for giving to the Lord. I am so glad you gave. The third verse goes like this. One by one they came, far as the eyes could see. Each life somehow touched by your generosity. Little things that you have done, sacrifices made, unnoticed on the earth, in heaven now proclaimed. They always play the song when missionaries came over. But anyway, um I don't think it's going to play out like that exactly. But I agree with the sentiment. And for better guidance on how to use money to make eternal friends, I encourage you to read and meditate on these passages. I'm not going to read them right now, I'll just give you the references. Matthew ten, forty to forty-three, Matthew twenty-five, thirty-one to forty-six Luke twelve, thirty-two to thirty-four, Romans fifteen, twenty-five to twenty-seven, Galatians six, six First Timothy six, seventeen to nineteen. There are actually many more, but that's just a start. But whether it's someone sent out by Jesus, the poor individuals among us, other churches in poverty, or faithful ministers who depend on your generosity. We can build eternal friendships with our wealth. If the Lord has blessed you materially, think of ways to use your money To help siblings in Christ and build relationships with them. It could be formal monthly donations or just a tasty lunch on you. One more thought before I go on to verse 10, and it has to do with the peculiar phrase, unrighteous mammon. Let's look at it one word at a time. The word mammon comes from the Hebrew verb which means to be firm or put trust in. It's not that hard to go from that word root to money, wealth, and possessions. It's also not difficult to see how mammon could be an idol, a rival to God. More on that later. As for unrighteous, Jesus did not mean that money is intrinsically evil But we've been warned sufficiently that often our relationship to money is sinful. Jesus taught that the cares of this world, the deceitfulness of riches, and the desires for other things entering in, choke the word of the kingdom. Those who desire to be rich fall into temptation and a snare, this is Paul now, and into many foolish and harmful lusts, which drown men in destruction and perdition. For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil, for which some have strayed from the faith in their greediness, and pierced themselves through with many sorrows. So money may not be the root of all evil, but the love of money definitely is. He who loses love I'm sorry, he who loves silver will not be satisfied with silver. Low he who loves abundance with increase. This also is vanity. Says that in Ecclesiastes five ten Well then the best approach to unrighteous mammon is to make sure it doesn't make you unrighteous. I read a piece from Paul Tripp, a biblical counselor, warning against five dangers of money. See if you can relate to them. One, money can cause you to forget God. Two, money can change the way you think about you. Three, money can cause you to look down on others. Four, money can weaken your resolve to fight temptation. And five, money can finance your allegiance to the kingdom of self Well boy these pitfalls, if in whatever state we're in, we learn godliness with contentment. Riches sprout wings and fly away like an eagle, to be eager to give to the weak and the poor, especially fellow believers. Make friends with them as they will be strong and rich in heaven. But even more important than our friends in heaven is our Master in Heaven, and that leads to the second point about stewardship. Be a faithful steward to receive much. Here are two features of these verses that stand out. First, in verses 10 to 12, we have the constant theme of faithfulness. I think that it was in God's wisdom that these verses immediately follow the preceding parable. Verses 10 to 12 are there to make sure we only follow the unjust steward in his shrewdness. Not his untrustworthiness. In his desperation, the steward in the parable did only one thing that was commendable. As a general rule, we should not be like him. We need to strive at all times to be faithful stewards to receive much reward. The other feature, so secondly, we observe the parallelism that runs through these verses. What is least corresponds to the unrighteous mammon and what is another man's. Much corresponds to true riches and what is your own. We need to understand that worldly currency is not what counts most. But it counts least. While unrighteous mamma is corruptible, true riches are not. Our material blessings on earth belong to this world, which will fade away. What we have in heaven will truly be ours. Now, from verses 10 to 11, we go from general to specific. Generally speaking, how you manage frivolous matters says a lot about how you manage weightier matters. We'll either be faithful or unjust with what's been entrusted to us. Now in verse 11, Jesus teaches specifically about money, referring to it once again as unrighteous mammon. How we balance our budget, donate to those in need, use wealth for God's glory. Says a lot about how we'll manage heavenly riches. Consider the money in your account as an audition, a tryout, an evaluation. You're being tested now for the future management of your own riches. I encourage you to go home and consider your spending thus far in 2021. Five months have passed. How much have you stored up for eternity? Have you been a faithful steward? If we were to do something like a kingdom audit, what would be the total invested in helping fellow saints and furthering the spread of the gospel? A few cents, a few dollars, tens, hundreds, thousands Will we receive much reward as individuals? And how about as a church? I don't have much to say here except I feel that God will reward us for our faithful giving. But if we were to model ourselves continually after a specific church, We could look to the church of Philippi. From the first day of their founding, they distinguish themselves by their giving and enjoy fellowship in the gospel with Apostle Paul. They stood out from other churches as he departed from Macedonia. Paul writes, No church share with me concerning giving and receiving. But you only. For even in Thessalonica you sent aid once and again for my necessities. Here's a church filled with faithful stewards who receive much reward. Let me tell you as a transitional statement that faithful stewardship requires a worshipful attitude In some church services, the offering time becomes a sort of an intermission from worship. A time to chat with those sitting next to us, check our smartphones, stretch, run out for a drink, etc. But thankfully, I was taught that offering time is still worship time. I think that's true. If I go back to Philippians chapter four and read what Paul said about their generous donation And I see it in verse seventeen to twenty. Not that I seek the gift, but I seek the fruit that abounds to your account. Indeed I have all and abound. I am full, having received from Epaproditus the things sent from you. A sweet smelling aroma, an acceptable sacrifice, well pleasing to God And my God shall supply all your need according to his riches and glory by Christ Jesus. Now to our God and Father be glory forever and ever. Amen. We are best as faithful stewards when we see giving is for God's glory. We're supplied in our needs as we give to others' needs. Our offering is a sweet-smelling aroma, an acceptable sacrifice, well pleasing to God. Our gifts can be the fruit that abounds to our accounts. But what happens when money meant to be sacrificed on the altar becomes the object of our worship? When we become consumers and no longer see God as a consuming fire. What happens when we care less about being well-pleasing to God and more about well-pleasing to ourselves when our heavenly accounts run empty, but our earthly accounts Abound. That leads us to the third money principle of worship. Holy worship God, not money A philosopher once said, Money is a great servant, but a bad master. I think this is true and relevant here. We've already seen how money can serve us in making friends for eternity. We've also seen how faithful stewardship of temporal possessions pays off in eternal dividends. But all throughout we've been dealing and calling money as unrighteous mammon for a reason Because of our evil hearts, it tends to corrupt, lead us to greed, covetous, and idolatry. Yes, money is a great servant, but a bad master. We must gain mastery over money lest we become its slave. To do that, we must learn to hate and despise money and instead love, be loyal, and serve God. We must wholly worship God, not money. Ultimately, this struggle with love of money is a battle for our hearts. Here are some diagnostic questions to see if Mammon is your idol. Is this world your home? Or is heaven your home? For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also. When we think of paradise, who or what comes to mind? Do we worship the creature and creation rather than the creator? Is God Himself your exceedingly great reward? The critical question for our generation and for every generation is this. If you could have heaven with no sickness, And with all the friends you ever had on earth, and all the food you ever liked, and all the leisure activities you ever enjoyed, And all the natural beauties you ever saw, all the physical pleasures you ever tasted, and no human conflict or any natural disasters Could you be satisfied with heaven if Christ were not there? I hope your answer is no. What would heaven be without Christ? Without our wholehearted worship of the one and only triune God. If you desire true friendship, stewardship, and worship, and never heard of the gospel before, the good news. I ask you, come to the Father through Jesus. He's been good to us. Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above. And comes down from the Father of Lights, with whom there is no variation or shadow of turning. But we've been ungrateful and foolishly worshiping the gifts rather than the giver of those gifts. We've used what God has given us for our selfish purposes. We've turned away from Him But our Father is kind to the unthankful and evil. When we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his son. Christ, though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, that you through his poverty might become rich. So God's Son never sinned, he humbled himself even to the death of the cross for our sake. There at the crucifixion, Jesus paid for sins we'd committed, took the penalty of hell we deserved. He then rose from the dead, proved many times over that he's alive and ascended to heaven. Someday he'll return to judge the world. Before it's too late, come to Christ in repentance and faith. Turn away from self-indulgence and self-reliance Turn to Jesus and place your hope of eternal life in Him alone. All the money in this world, and even if we were to add it all up through history, He cannot buy you a ticket to heaven. Per save to the finished work on the cross, the greatest gift of all Eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord. Trust in Him alone for salvation. It is by grace alone, through faith alone, in Christ alone. And we're saved so that we might worship God alone. And this morning let's remember the cost that we was paid as we observe the Lord's Supper. Let's pray. Lord, we're thankful each and every day for the roof over our heads, clothes on our back, food on our table. Lord, those things were meant to point to you. And how many times have we taken you for Granted, that we've been ungrateful, that we complained and forgotten all the good things you provide for us. We do not count your blessings one by one. We dismiss them altogether. We forget about them. In our comforts. Or it's sad to say some of us need your discipline to be reminded that we need you. And it's not about the gifts. Help us to loosen our grip on the things of this world, see it as vanity, and come to you Renouncing all. We rather have your son than the things of this world. Take all that we have Where all these things are sinking sand, we put our feet on the gospel, and we want to build on the foundations of that gospel. Help us to make friendships that last for eternity. Help us to be good stewards with our time and possessions. May we worship you and you alone. We thank you and we pray all these things in Jesus Christ's name. Amen.

sermons.title: Wrong on the Money
sermons.speaker: Sung Cho
sermons.text: In 2011, a man from California named Larry was facing various hardships. His daughter was seriously ill, and his scoliosis was beginning to twist his spine. His construction business was failing. His van and car broke down. Completely. He was a recovering drug addict, but still faced plenty of trouble ahead. But then during these rough times, Larry remembered a man he saw on TV. A televangelist by the name of Todd Koontz. These are his words. I understand the laws that govern ensure Stocks and bonds, and all that is involved with Wall Street, he once said, looking directly into the camera. God has called me as a financial deliverer. He wore a suit, carried a Bible, and urged viewers to give money to him as seeds. If they plant these seeds in faith, the amount will return to them, multiplied. Donors can choose from various types of seeds, including the $500 Favor Seed, the $88 Double Blessing Seed, and the $360 Turnaround Seed. Fast forward about ten years, and the wisdom of Jesus still rings true. You will know them by their fruits. Now Larry lives in a small Alabama town. On the wall of their living room hangs a small-framed Bible verse. Be anxious for nothing. Philippians 4:6. Thankfully, Larry's faith is still intact. He says, Life is not easy, but we're blessed. We have food in the refrigerator, we have two cats that love us. My wife got part-time work in a store and I get disability benefits In Tatkunst, he was convicted of tax fraud and evasion and sentenced to five years in prison. His attorneys took the case all the way up to Supreme Court, but his appeal was denied. Serving his time in Pensacola federal prison camp and scheduled for release. on june third, twenty twenty five. It's sad to see men masquerading as Christian ministers. Stealing money by means of false doctrines. But this has been a problem since Old Testament times. Moses warned against counterfeit prophets in Deuteronomy 13. In New Testament times, Paul struggled against false apostles, deceitful workers, transforming themselves into apostles of Christ. It's still a problem today. And often what drives these despicable televangelists and prosperity gospel preachers Is the love of money. Today's passage has something to say about those religious leaders who hide their idolatry of money. And endanger themselves and their followers. Let's turn to Luke sixteen, fourteen to seventeen. Now the Pharisees, who were lovers of money, also heard all these things, and they derided him. And he said to them, You are those who justify yourselves before men But God knows your hearts, for what is highly esteemed among men is an abomination in the sight of God. The law and the prophets were until John. Since that time the kingdom of God has been preached, and everyone is pressing into it. And it is easier for heaven and earth to pass away than for one tittle of the law to fail. The challenge of today's passage is not understanding the various separate statements. The real challenge is understanding how they fit together. These things appear disjointed and without flow. What's the unifying theme here? At least verse 14 is connected with the previous passage about idolatry of Mammon and the story of the rich man and Lazarus coming up in verse 19. But in verse fifteen, how do the Pharisees exactly justify themselves before men? And what does that have to do with the loving you know loving money? Verse 16, what do the law of the prophets, John the Baptist, and God's kingdom have to do with all this? Finally, in verse 17, how does the eternality of the law Relate to this discussion. My proposal is that these religious leaders Driven by their avarice, have made other grave errors. One sin leads to another Verse fourteen tells us the fatal diagnosis that lead to all other sin diseases addressed in verses fifteen. 16 and 17. The love of money is the gateway drug that leads us down to worse problems. Greed is the sick root that produces rotten fruit. Paul, an apostle of Christ, a Pharisee himself, puts it in a nutshell. sermons.text: Strange convergences, odd coincidences, weird alignments I read about some this week. A couple find themselves in the same childhood photo taken at a beach vacation 11 years ago, so they lived 300 miles apart at the time. Stephen Hawking shares the same dates of birth and death with Galileo and Einstein, respectively. Don Will Spoot's brother saved Abraham Lincoln's son from death. We read of these and find them amusing. But the coincidence I want to talk about now has to do with the convergence of even more disparate elements. 2021, this year when a strong pro-LGBTQ plus president was elected. June, this month's designation as the Pride Month. June 20th, this day, as we celebrate Father's Day, in this hour, 11 a. m. service, as we look at Luke 16, 18. So we have here politics, LGBTQ plus, a traditional holiday of Father's Day, Jesus' teaching on divorce. How do these pieces fit together? What helped me to fit these pieces together was a book by the Presbyterian scholar Carl Truman, entitled The Rise and Triumph of the Modern Self. Cultural Amnesia, Expressive Individualism, and the Road to Sexual Revolution. I've been recommending this book, both formally and informally If you decide to get it, do digest this slowly. I think many of the arguments will help you understand how we got here. Now I don't have time to go through all of the book's details, but for today I revisited two quotes that might help us understand how in one month of June 2021, we have this odd hodgepodge, celebrations of both traditional marriage and gay marriage, Adam and Eve and Adam and Steve. Here's the first quote from Truman. Individuals who disagree about gay marriage might think they are disagreeing merely about the limits of the legitimate identity of the country. Attracting parties, but their actual differences go much deeper than that. They disagree on nothing less than the very definition of marriage relative to its ends. Simply put, people disagree about the purpose of marriage, so they disagree about the spouses or the partakers of marriage, what it means. If marriage is for my pleasure or convenience, then the partners are consumers. If marriage is not a holy matrimony from God, then it's up to us to draft his terms and agreements. Now, to be more specific, something Truman wrote later was remarkable and condemning. It seems that gay marriage as an institution is here to stay. Whether it has opened the door to a general collapse in marriage as a two-person arrangement remains to be seen. Certainly, in terms of its underlying philosophy, there's nothing to stop such an eventuality, but The basic redefinition of marriage did not take place with Obergefell versus Hodges in twenty fifteen. But when Governor Ronald Reagan signed no-fault divorce into law in California in nineteen seventy. I'll repeat that. The basic redefinition of marriage did not take place with O'Burgefeld versus Hodges in 2015. But when Governor Ronald Reagan signed no-fault divorce into law in California in nineteen seventy. Some of you lived through that decision in nineteen seventy and experienced its impact. But just as a review, no fault divorce means divorce without grounds. That is a legally accepted reason. In Maryland, all you need to do for a divorce is either a twelve-month separation or even easier, a simple mutual Mutual consent. As for the 2015 Supreme Court case, Jim O'Burgefell fought for legal recognition as his late same-sex partner's surviving spouse, and he won. And here we are now in 2021, during the Pride month of June. Could the Baltimore Pride 2021 that took place this past week and is ending today be traced back not only to DC six years ago? But to California about half a century ago, in other words Is the current homosexual craze at least partly due to the heterosexual abandonment of traditional marriage Is it important to repudiate false ideas like no false divorce to be effective witnesses for Christ? I believe so. But to be properly equipped for a cultural battle, we must know God's word. Go back not only to the last decade or last Century, but millenniums, first to Jesus' time and first century, then even further back to Moses, and then even further back to the sixth day of the creation week Let's start by reading Luke sixteen, eighteen. Whoever divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery, and whoever marries her who is divorced from her husband commits adultery Now I dislike topical sermons but and because preparing them is hard and even listening to them, but And technically speaking, today's message is not topical since we're moving right along in the current series on the travel narratives of Luke, the middle chapters of the third gospel. But we're going to dig deep into one subject, and Luke 16, 18 is just a springboard into it. There's much to cover and I got a lot of notes for you there in the bulletin, so you might as well call it a topical sermon But I'm still going to contextualize verse 18 with the rest of Luke 16. That's a tough task in itself Remember that most of this chapter deals with money. Verses 1 to 13 was about money as it relates to our friendship, stewardship, and worship. Verses 14 to 17 expand on verse 13 as Jesus exposes the Pharisees and their love of money. Their greed has led them to self-righteousness Exclusion from God's kingdom and neglect of God's eternal truth. We'll see once more in this chapter the grave consequences of loving money In verses 19 to 31. But back to verse 18 and why the prohibition of divorce is there where it is I think that verse 18 is not as closely connected to the love of money as the other parts of Luke. Instead, I think it's better connected to the verses before it, verses 15 and 17. There are two specific key words in those verses: one, abomination, and two, law, that help us contextualize verse 18. First, let's talk about abomination in verse 15. You recall Jesus said, You are those who justify yourselves before men, but God knows your hearts. For what is highly esteemed among men is an abomination in the sight of God. How is divorce related to abomination Joe B. Green has a good explanation. Just read along with me. I included the quotes there. In Israel's scriptures, the term abomination can be used to denote, among other things, idolatrous activity in general, but also immoral financial dealings. And the act of remarrying a woman who has been divorced. That was an abomination in the sight of God, along with their love and idolatry of money. As a quick application, I wonder, do we as a church have proper discernment concerning Christian leaders Can we see beyond the surface? Sure, they may be highly esteemed among men because of their charisma, their oratory skills. Winsome personality, strong leadership skills. But can we see at least partly as God sees into their hearts? What if that charismatic leader has a terrible marriage and sex addiction problems? What if the celebrity pastor has no accountability when it comes to his personal finances and his home life? That's it to say these are real problems today, and it's hurting our witness to the world I'm not saying we need to know every detail, but we should know at least a little bit about their personal lives, especially at home and their marriage. Again, they may justify themselves before men, but God knows their hearts. What is highly esteemed among men is the abomination in the sight of God. Now let's talk about the law in verse 17 and related to verse 18. What does law have to do with divorce? And we'll look at Deuteronomy in a second, but we must first understand this. Not surprisingly, high in ranking was infidelity, and number two. There are others. Number three, too much conflict and arguing. Four, getting married too young. And five, financial problems. There are many illegitimate divorces out there, and for many that get married again. Illegitimate remarriages. Now you may ask Does Jesus have anything specific to say about the uncleanness in Deuteronomy 24, verse 1? Is there any fault that could make the first divorce legitimate I believe so, though it's worth repeating that permission is not promotion. We should do all we can to save a marriage, even if there's immense amounts of hurt and suffering. But I believe there are legitimate reasons to end marriage with the divorce, what I list as three exceptions, and they all start with A. One of the thornier issues in the New Testament studies is the reconciliation of Matthew passages about divorce. With the parallel passages in Mark and Luke. If you only read Mark 10, 11 to 12 and Luke 16, 18 today's passage, you would think that Jesus never ever permits divorce. But Matthew 5, 31 to 32 and 19:9 include the famous Matthew Exception Clause. I'll read Matthew 5:31 to 32 and then 19:9. So, Matthew 5, this is the Sermon on the Mount, verse 31 to 32. Furthermore, it has been said: whoever divorces his wife, let him give her a certificate of divorce. But I say to you that whoever divorces his wife for any reason except sexual immorality causes her to commit adultery. And whoever marries a woman who is divorced commits adultery. And I say to you, whoever divorces his wife, except for sexual immorality, and marries another, commits adultery. And whoever marries her who is divorced commits adultery. Again, we need to note that Jesus is much stricter than his peers, who took the permission of divorce as a promotion of it. But here in Matthew, we see an exception clause except for sexual immorality. So there's a fault that could legitimize divorce. The word for sexual immorality there is pornea, and it's a general and context context-sensitive word. It could mean various things: premarital sex, adultery, incest, bestiality, homosexuality, depending on the context. My view is that contextually speaking, the exception clause primarily has to do with adultery. In other words, adultery is a legitimate reason for divorce. Of course, there are some arguments against my view. One is that there's another more specific word for adultery that Jesus knew and could have used: boikea. Also, since adultery was punishable by death, according to Leviticus twenty and Deuteronomy twenty-two, allowance for divorce appears to be a moot point. My response is this. I think it was in Jesus' amazing foresight that he used a general word, sexual immorality, punea, rather than a specific one. We see today that there is an exponential increase in sexual sins that defy easy categories. Not only are there many ways to commit adultery, there's also the rise of bisexuality and transgenderism I think if a married woman decides to become a lesbian, the husband has reasons to divorce her. This isn't just what happened to a fictional character of the famous TV sitcom Friends. It's happening as we speak. Did Jesus not anticipate such a scenario? Yes, he did, not by spelling out every possible divorce and remarriage scenario, but with his wise choice of the word Punea, sexual immorality. As for the capital punishment passages, Leviticus 20, verse 10, and Deuteronomy 22, 20. Those are cases where both the adulterer and the adulteress are caught in the act or proven guilty. During those thousands of years before genetic tests, it would have been difficult to condemn all the secret affairs that went on. sermons.text: Last time I preached on this passage, we're about to look at it was late May of 2016 I was dressed in African traditional clothing, speaking through an interpreter to a group of young students in my in-laws Christian school in Bamako Mali. sermons.text: Well, one of the benefits of growing older is seeing predictions of a dark future come to nothing. I'm sure people were relieved that as 1984 arrived, George Orwell's dystopian future vision was not realized. The so-called Mayan prophecies predicting that the world would end in 2012 were not true. Some of these are entertaining, some are silly, while still others are eerily coming to fruition. There is one more I want to mention. In 1992, English writer Phyllis D. James wrote a book entitled The Children of Men. It depicts a dystopian future set in, you guessed it, 2021. What's most interesting about this future is this. Mankind is reeling from mass infertility and is on the brink of extinction. In mid-90s, sperm count dropped to zero, and the last people to be born were marked as omegas, and they enjoy many special privileges. In the span of about twenty-five years, these omegas are spoiled and act-entitled. Newborn animals are idolized in place of newborn babies. Except for a privileged few, the elderly and the infirmed are forced into suicide. Thankfully none of this is happening. But like many dystopian novels, readers are motivated to keep the fiction from moving into reality. I hope you don't need much convincing that we'd be impoverished in a world without children, with our babies and infants. We deserve rather to be left outside in the outer darkness under his wrath. But our Heavenly Father did not leave us in our pitiful state. He sent His Son Jesus Christ, and as we sang earlier. He who was rich beyond all splendor, all for love's sake became poor. Jesus humbled himself and died a horrible death on the cross. Though he was wholly innocent and sinless, he suffered for our sake, as a substitute for sins we've committed in thought, word, and deed. He died, he was buried, he rose again on the third day and ascended to heaven. Christ did all this so that you through his poverty might become rich. Rich in heaven. Now the price has been paid and the way has been paved. The question is: do you want to inherit eternal life by following Jesus? Again, he may not be asking you to relinquish all your cash, but he's definitely asking you to relinquish your hope of salvation in cash or anything you might trust to enter heaven. There's nothing you can do in your power to enter God's kingdom. It's all in his power. It's all a gift of grace. So repent. Turn from trusting in yourself and place your faith in Jesus and his finished work. Now, even as we stand upon Christ's finished work with confidence, even as we no longer trust in gold, silver, and precious stones. We can still store up heavenly treasures and build on the foundation of Christ, Jesus, with gold, silver, and precious stone, as 1 Corinthians 3 tells us And that leads to the third point, be assured of God's reward. There are disciples called to leave house, parents, brothers, wives, and children for the kingdom's sake. If the Lord has given you a family and all of them believe, praise the Lord. Really thank God every day for that. That's not my case. The same Jesus who prayed for unity among believers declared that he came to bring division. Five and one house will be divided, three against two, and two against three Father will be divided against son and son against father, mother against daughter, and daughter against mother, mother-in-law against her daughter-in-law, and daughter-in-law against Mother-in-law Concerning wives, we understand from 1 Corinthians 7 that Christ can cause a rift in a marriage. I have a friend who followed Jesus this way, not only emptying his savings to go to seminary, but also being abandoned by his unbelieving wife. We must be prepared for this kind of sacrifice. In contrast to the rich young ruler, certain disciples of Jesus have left all to follow him, but there are promises of reward. For Peter and others who occupy the office of apostleship, though lowly on earth, they will be exalted in twelve thrones over twelve tribes of Israel in the kingdom. There are also rewards for disciples in general, like you and me. We read in verses 29 and 30: assurance of rewards for all who leave the world to follow Jesus. Note how the rewards are not only promised for the future, as we normally expect, but it says in verse 30, also. In this present time. Are you assured not only of treasures in heaven, but blessings of following Christ in this life too? Jesus isn't saying you'll be rich here on earth. He already ruled that out in verse 22. He's talking about new relationships that you gain in God's family. In this world, we may lose the family of birth, but in the church, we gain the family of rebirth. We gain fathers, brothers, mothers, and sisters. We have this local church. Fellow believers as family of Christ. Of course, none of these rewards would be possible without Jesus. Even if we suffer, we're encouraged as there is consolation in Christ, comfort of love, fellowship of the Spirit, affection and mercy. Even if we lack, we can give and serve. God is able to make all grace abound toward you. That you always having all sufficiency in all things. May have an abundance for every good work. Let's always remember that Christ is our all. Hallelujah. All I have is Christ. Hallelujah. Jesus is my life. Let's pray Lord, we thank you for your word, how you make it clear to us that we must follow you through your Son Jesus Christ to enter the kingdom of heaven. But Lord, because of our sinful and covetous hearts, Lord, we cannot easily wrest ourselves from the grip that we have on this world. Lord, may you reveal to us this week what idols we have harbored in our hearts. Lord, may we believe that you are the one who provides for us. You are the one who saves. You are the one who rewards. May we forsake all idols. May we believe in your power to save. May we believe that you reward us richly when we follow you. Maybe not in this lifetime, but in the future. We thank you and we pray all these things in Jesus Christ's name. Amen.

sermons.text: About a half a century before Jesus was born, a Roman governor stood before a river called Rubicon. His official term was about to expire and the Senate gave him clear instructions to disband his army and return to Rome. If he were to bring his army across the river, the northern boundary of Italy, he would be in effect leading his soldiers in an insurrection. Committing treason and declaring war against the Roman Senate. The rest is, as they say, history. On January 10, 49 BC, Julius Caesar took his 13th Legion across the shallows of Rubicon. The die has been cast. Today we say crossing the Rubicon. to describe any revolutionary act. A point of no return, a risky venture. Go big or go home. Have you had such moments recently? One could argue if you haven't had any significant risks, if you haven't taken any of them, you haven't really lived a worthwhile life. Besides my decision to follow Christ, my personal crossing the Rubicon moments include pursuing vocational ministry, and crossing the Atlantic to Africa to ask E-Ray's parents permission to marry their daughter. Now, those were some intense times of much prayer. And it's a good thing I prayed because Jesus understands. The weight of difficult decisions. At this point in Luke, our Lord was inching closer to Jerusalem by the day. And in fact, his stop at Jericho, in the case, he's not far. But unlike Julius Caesar, who came as a dictator, Jesus came to die as the servant king. That was his destiny. If I was Jesus, I would I would have moped, asking God, why me? Or despairing because no one really understands the trials I'm about to face. What's amazing about my Lord is how he's walking toward his own death. And it's business as usual, teaching and ministering. Each day he draws closer to Jerusalem, and each day he casts out demons and performs cures In today's passage, we'll learn how Jesus stood at a crossroad and marched forward, and what it means to follow Him ourselves. Let's read Luke eighteen, thirty-one to forty-three Then he took the twelve aside and said to them, Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem, and all things that are written by the prophets concerning the Son of Man will be accomplished. For he will be delivered to the Gentiles and will be mocked and insulted and spit upon. They will scourge him and kill him. And the third day he will rise again. But they understood none of these things. The same was hidden from them, and they did not know the things which were spoken. Then it happened as he was coming near Jericho that a certain blind man sat by the road begging, and hearing a multitude passing by, he asked what it meant. So they told him that Jesus of Nazareth was passing by. And he cried out, saying, Jesus, son of David, have mercy on me. Then those who went before warned them that he should be quiet, but he cried out all the more, Son of David, have mercy on me So Jesus stood still and commanded him to be brought to him. And when he had come near, he asked him, saying, What do you want me to do for you? He said, Lord, that I may receive my sight. Then Jesus said to him, Receive your sight. Your faith has made you well And immediately he received his sight and followed him, glorifying God. And all the people, when they saw it, gave praise to God. I find here in today's passage two principles for following Jesus 1. Understand Jesus' mission to fulfill the scriptures, verses 31 to 34. 2. Imitate the blind man's faith to glorify God. Verses 35. First, understand Jesus' mission to fulfill the scriptures Verses 31 to 34 is one of three major predictions of Christ's suffering directed to his disciples. Matthew and Mark present the three in more rapid succession, one after another. Matthew has one in chapter sixteen, second in chapter seventeen. And the third in chapter 20 in the span of five chapters. Mark is even more swift. The three predictions are in three consecutive chapters. 8, 9, and 10. Luke differs from them as he presents the first two in chapter 9, but the third one is here way later in chapter 18. With a lot of mini predictions in between. And here's a quick recap. Prediction one was in Caesarea Philippi. About 150 miles away from Jerusalem. Recall that Peter has just made his famous confession in reply to Jesus' question: Who do you say that I am? The Christ of God. We read next that Jesus strictly warned and commanded them to tell this to no one, saying, The Son of Man must suffer many things. and be rejected by the elders and chief priests and scribes and be killed and be raised the third day Later coming down south from Caesarea Philippi to Galilee, Jesus predicted his upcoming death again. He closed the gap from 150 to 75 miles from Jerusalem. It's been about 10 days, and two major events took place. Jesus was transfigured before Peter, James, and John. And two, Jesus freed and restored the demon-possessed boy to his father. Luke tells us in 9. 43, the reaction of the crowds. And they were all amazed at the majesty of God. But then Luke continues. But while everyone marveled at all the things which Jesus did, he said to his disciples, Let these words sink down into your ears. For the Son of Man is about to be betrayed into the hands of men. But they did not understand this thing, and it was hidden from them, so that they did not perceive it, and they were afraid to ask him about this thing. Like I said already, we don't hear that third final official prediction of Jesus' suffering at Jerusalem until chapter 18 That's about nine chapters in between prediction two and three. Along the way, there were hints like the sign of Jonah in 1130. Then Jesus remarked in passing in 1333, it cannot be that a prophet should perish outside of Jerusalem. Seventeen twenty-five. First he must suffer many things and be rejected by this generation. But these small predictions were not standalone teachings, but in context of conflict with Herod and in-time prophecies. Now as they near Jericho and are only about fifteen miles from Jerusalem, Jesus must have spoken the words of 1831-33 with great solemnity and conviction, looking at them straight in the eyes Let me read those words again. Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem, and all things that are written by the prophets concerning the Son of Man will be accomplished. For he will be delivered to the Gentiles and will be mocked and insulted and spit upon. They will scourge him and kill him. And the third day he will rise again. What's unique about the third prediction is not the destination of Jerusalem, it's not the prediction of death, it's not the prediction of the resurrection. In each verse here in Luke, there's some noteworthy detail Jesus stresses. In verse 31, there's the mention of the prophetic scriptures that must be fulfilled. I can't stress how important this is for our Lord. You pick up the New Testament, and from the earliest pages, you see many cross-references back to the Old Testament. You could say that Jesus lived a fulfilling life because he lived to fulfill the scriptures. But even in his death, Jesus would accomplish what's written. As Paul would write later to the Corinthians, Christ died for our sins, according to the scriptures. He was buried, he rose again the third day, according to the scriptures. From conception to virgin birth, to infancy, to adulthood, to his public ministry, to death, to burial, to resurrection, to ascension, to his return, to the kingdom. Jesus accomplishes all things that are written by the prophets concerning himself In the first half of verse 32, there's the mention of the Gentiles. We already knew from the first prediction and elsewhere that the elders, chief priests. Scribes and this generation would reject Jesus. We already knew from the second prediction and elsewhere that our Lord would be betrayed into the hands of men. Now we know from the third prediction that Christ will be delivered to the Gentiles. But how do all these pieces fit together? We must bear in mind that all these details are complementary, not contradictory. We know from Acts 4, 25 to 28, the Herod, Antiphus, Pontius Pilate, the Gentiles, and the people of Israel were all united against Christ. And yet each was responsible for the sinful part played in the killing of Jesus. To be precise, Israelites and their rulers manipulated and used Gentile power to kill Jesus. They delivered Jesus up, denying him, and asked Pilate to do the dirty deed. Though the Roman governor did not want to shed innocent blood, the unbelieving Jews forced his hand, as they could not execute anyone in their own authority. They formed a mob and demanded the one and only outcome, the crucifixion of Jesus. That's how the Gentiles and the Jewish leaders work together. Next, in the second half of verse 32, and in the first half of verse 33, we have more details of Jesus' suffering. Our Lord will be mocked, insulted, and spit upon. They will scourge him and kill him. Now, what is scourging? According to one Roman poet named Horace, is torture using a tool literally called the horrible whip. Here's one description. It consisted of a handle to which several cords or leather thongs were affixed, which were weighted with jagged pieces of bone or metal, to make the blow more painful and effective. It is comparable in its horrid effects only with the Russian naut. The victim was tied to a post, and the blows were applied to the back and loins, sometimes even in the wanton cruelty of the executioner, to the face and the bowels. So hideous was the punishment that the victim usually fainted and not rarely died under it. The number of blows was not usually fixed, the severity of the punishment depending entirely on the commanding officer. By its application, secrets and confessions were wrung from the victim. It usually preceded capital punishment. It was illegal to apply to a Roman citizen. Because the Romans scourged Jesus, they were not bound to follow the limit of 40 lashes prescribed in Deuteronomy 25. The rest of the details we read fulfilled in Mark 15, 16 to 20. Then the soldiers led him away into the hall called Praetorium, and they called together the whole garrison, and they clothed him with purple. And they twisted a crown of thorns, put it on his head, and began to salute him. Hail, King of the Jews! Then they struck him on the head with the reed and spat on him. And bowing the knee, they worshipped him. And when they had mocked him, they took the purple off him, and put his own clothes on him, and led him out to crucify him. The Gospel writers recorded these details to remind themselves and prove to others. That Jesus fulfilled God's word. It's not that they were sadists or enjoyed cruelty or violence. All that Christ suffered specifically pointed to his mission. That mission can be summarized in the following passages spoken by Jesus and others. Behold, I have come to do your will, O God. The Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve and to give his life, a ransom for many. Surely he has borne our griefs and carried our sorrows, yet we esteemed him stricken, smitten by God and afflicted But he was wounded for our transgressions. He was bruised for our iniquities. The chastisement for our peace was upon him. And by his stripes we are healed. All we like sheep have gone astray. We have turned everyone to his own way. And the Lord has laid on him the iniquity of us all. Jesus suffered, died, and rose from the dead on the third day. All for our sakes. As our substitute. That means we are the ones who deserve the deliverance to the Gentiles, the mockery, the insults, the spitting, the scourging, the crucifixion. Why? Because we've all sinned and turned away from God. Now we deserve his wrath. God created us and it's written in the scriptures that he saw everything that he had made and indeed it was very good Yet, like Adam, we've broken God's law and contradicted his word. In fact, the only thing we've accomplished with regard to the scriptures is the verdict on mankind, writ large. There is none righteous, no, not one. There's none who understands, there's none who seeks after God. They have all turned aside. They have together become unprofitable. There's none who does good. No, not one. But God sent his son Jesus. He lived a perfect life. He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth. The Word of God who became flesh, in perfect harmony with the Word of God Yet he died, the death of the worst criminal and lawbreaker, even though he is deserving of every blessing of obedience. Even as he continued in all things which are written in the book of the law to do them, he died, cursed upon a tree. He suffered all these things, and rose from the dead, so that you may be blessed. But the only way to claim these blessings as your own is by personal repentance and faith. We must repent of our so-called good and flat out bad attempts to live without Christ. We repent of self-righteousness because the fact that no one is justified by the law in the sight of God is evident, for the just shall live by faith. We repent of self-indulgence because we must turn to God from idols and our wicked ways. We must place our hope of eternal life in Jesus Christ. His life, death, resurrection, ascension, and his judgment to come. There's nothing we can do to earn a place in heaven. That's what the Bible says And as we read every month on Communion Sundays, Titus 3:5, not by works of righteousness, which we have done, but according to his mercy, he saved us. Trust in Jesus alone and accept God's mercy as a gift of grace. This may sound elementary to you because you've heard the gospel presented many times in many ways. But the way that Luke phrases verse 34, you think he's trying to emphasize the disciples' lack of understanding. He says the same thing in three different ways. They understood none of these things. This saying was hidden from them. They did not know the thing which were spoken. But the story is not over. Later, after Jesus rises from the dead, he opened their understanding that they might comprehend the scriptures. For now the twelve are in the dark. But once the disciples of Jesus Understand the gospel message. The response is simple. Ask God for mercy. And if you're ever in need of an example of how to ask God to be merciful to you, we have that in the Bible too. And that leads to the next point. Imitate the blind man's faith to glorify God. This passage has parallels in Matthew 20 and Mark 10, just like the previous passage. The main discrepancy between the three Gospels is the exact location of the healing relative to Jericho and the number of blind men. Matthew records that two blind men sat alongside the road and they were healed as Jesus left the city. Mark also records that Jesus was leaving the city when he performed the miracle, but only one man is mentioned. We even learn that his name is Bartimaeus. Luke, as we see here, in contrast to both Matthew and Mark, says that Jesus was coming near, approaching Jericho when he healed a blind man. There's no need to overthink this. It's not that the three writers are contradicting each other Rather, we should simply consider three factors. One, Jesus performed many signs and more specifically gave sight to many blind men during his ministry. Two, beggars would dwell in the margins of the cities, so travelers would see them whether they are arriving or departing. 3. It is likely then that Jesus healed one blind man while entering Jericho and then healed two more while leaving the city, one of them being Bartimaeus. There are then three healings of blind men around Jericho The similarities and circumstances, words and actions are not out of the ordinary, considering the various repetitions in Jesus' ministry. So these critical issues are not problematic. So now let's focus more on the actual exchange between Jesus and the blind man. And there's a lot packed in his prayer. Son of David, have mercy on me. Son of David is an important title of Jesus It recognizes our Lord's physical lineage and royal pedigree to rule over Israel. Remember how God has promised David in a covenant. that he will establish his kingdom and the throne of his seed forever. The signs Jesus performed convinced at least some that he was indeed the promised Savior King from David's line. Yet not all believe this. Though Jesus was born in Bethlehem, the fact that he grew up in Nazareth of Galilee was a hindrance to their faith. But evidently, this was not a hindrance to this blind man. He believed that Jesus of Nazareth is the son of David who could help him. There are only a select few in the Gospels who both recognize Jesus as David's son and ask for his mercy. There are the two blind men in Galilee, Matthew chapter 9, verse 27. There's the woman of Canaan who interceded for her daughter in Matthew 15, verse 22. There are the three blind men of Jericho, including this one in today's passage. All of these individuals were outsiders, away from the society of Israel. Beggars, helpless, desperate. Yet with persistent faith, they covered that distance and drew near to Jesus. They refused to remain silent when others tried to hush them. The blind man, though helped by others, literally walked by faith, not by sight. Once considered in the margins of the nation, they have obtained mercy as God's people. There is great reward in such faith. The most obvious and personal is the recovery of sight for this man But as this man began to see, he sees the light in more ways than one. He has been called out of darkness into his marvelous light He saw Jesus his Lord and his Savior. Like that old man Simeon in the temple. This man on the road saw his salvation with his eyes. And his faith is proved sincere by its fruits. The fruit of lifts, the sacrifice of praise to God. Like the Samaritan leper, we saw in chapter 11. His faith made him well, and he glorified God. His worship was contagious as others joined in and gave praise to God as well. What would it mean for you to imitate this man? Perhaps you already have faith in Jesus like him, but you'd like to grow. Well, I think there's at least two applications for us. One, and I've been saying this pretty frequently, prepare a testimony. And two, find an audience. First, this man has a unique story of encountering Jesus as his Savior, but not everyone will have their failing eyes cured like him. But everyone can glorify God. Every saint can share how Jesus has personally changed him or her. The goal of every testimony should be glory to God and causing others to praise God. Do you have a testimony ready to share? Secondly, a testimony needs an audience. Now, the audiences are of two types. First, we have our church family During our prayer meetings, Sunday schools, men's groups, ladies' events, accountability groups, we share struggles and prayer requests. But another thing we should do is regularly share what Jesus has done for us. Also, another type of audience consists of our unsaved family, friends, and neighbors. Can you testify to God's mercy? Not only in the confines of our church building, but also out on the road. Perhaps that's what it means for you to cross the Rubicon. Faith is not merely a private matter between you and God. God wants us to proclaim as the psalmist did in 111, verse 1. Praise the Lord. I will praise the Lord with my whole heart in the assembly of the upright and in the congregation. We also read in Mark 16, verse 15, Go into all the world and preach the gospel to every creature. In a day like today, as we remember the sacrificial death of Jesus, as we imitate the bold faith of this man of Jericho, I see no better way to end our time together than observing the Holy Communion. For as often as you eat this bread and drink this cup, you proclaim the Lord's death till he comes. That's great. Lord, we thank you that though we were once blind spiritually, though we were dead spiritually, You beckoned us, you called us, you made us alive. You made us alive through the death of your Son Jesus Christ. A shameful, scornful death Lord, the punishment that we deserve was laid on him. And for that we're thankful And we praise you. And we want to live in a grateful way to glorify your name. To cause others to praise your name. Pray all these things in Jesus Christ's name Amen. Please rise and we'll sing O Christ, what burdens, bow thy head. We'll sing verses one, two, and three for now.

sermons.text: Someday I hope that my boy will read the classic novels of J. R. R. Tolkien. And what parent wouldn't? The author created a complex and rich fictional universe with no less complex and rich characters And one of Tolkien's genius moves was to place at the forefront of the storyline the race of hobbits. Short, childlike people with furry legs. Fantasy novels have typically featured humans, elves, dwarfs, dragons, orcs, and wizards. Oh my. Those are not new. But to have Bilbo Frodo and his hapling friends as unexpected heroes who save the world, that was unheard of. Diminutive, not built to be warriors, peaceful and often overlooked. Hobbit became protagonist in Tolkien's most famous stories. Some say it wasn't a premeditated move, but it turned out to be a good one in his writing career. But generally speaking, why do stories that feature little people make such a huge impact? Some surmise that they're more relatable. Like these little ones of Middle Earth, people in the 20th century felt small, insignificant, and powerless in a big, intimidating world. Such fictional characters are memorable for the way they tap into something deep in us. But so are non-fictional characters. In today's passage in Luke, we see a true story of a man who met Jesus, and though he was small, marginalized, and unimportant in the eyes of the world. Our Lord calls him by name. We can relate with him because in these uncertain times in the dark world. We like him can follow Jesus and make an impact for eternity. Let's turn to Luke 19, 1 to 10. Luke nineteen, one to ten Then Jesus entered and passed through Jericho. Now behold, there was a man named Zacchaeus, who was a cheap tax collector. And he was rich. And he sought to see who Jesus was, but could not because of the crowd, for he was of short stature. So he ran ahead and climbed up into a sycamore tree to see him, for he was going to pass that way And when Jesus came to the place, he looked up and saw him and said to him, Zacchaeus, make haste and come down, for today I must stay at your house. So he made haste and came down and received him joyfully. But when they saw it, they all complained, saying, He has gone to be a guest with the man who is a sinner. Then Zacchaeus stood and said to the Lord, Look, Lord, I give half of my goods to the poor. And if I have taken anything from anyone by false accusation, I restore fourfold. And Jesus said to him, Today salvation has come to this house, because he also is a son of Abraham. For the Son of Man has come to seek and save that which was lost. How can we relate to Zacchaeus and learn from him here in this passage? I observe three principles. One, seek Christ with a childlike faith. That's verses one to four. Two, receive Jesus with eager joy. Verses five to six. And three, prove your salvation with genuine fruit. Verses 7 to 10. And I'll repeat these later. First. Seek Christ with a childlike faith. Verse 1 picks up where we left off last time towards the end of chapter 18. Jesus was approaching the city of Jericho, which tells us he was close to Jerusalem. Still outside Jericho, he healed a certain blind man. Now inside the city in chapter 19 and passing through it, our Lord encounters another person, a man named Zacchaeus. Now there are many ways to introduce this guy. We could sing together the children's song. Zacchaeus was a wee little man. A wee little man was he. He climbed up in a sycamore tree for the Lord he wanted to see and on and on. Well that song presents only the bare outline of the story There's much more in the scriptures. I think a good way to understand this man is to ask some questions about his status. Consider this a pop quiz for you, a word problem to solve. Is Zacchaeus the type of person God would save or not? Let me put it another way. We've been exploring the theme of responding to the kingdom in the last major portion of the travel narrative from chapter 1711 to 1927. Would Zacchaeus be the type of person to respond to the offer of the kingdom positively or negatively? Now we could skip down to verses 9 and 10, and it's kind of like the answer sheet at the back of the textbook. The answer is yes, God did save Zacchaeus and he did respond positively to the kingdom. But we need to show the work on this problem. Let me do that with you and go back with me to verse 2. There we learn that he's a cheap tax collector. Those three words, chief, tax collector, are actually one in the original language. A compound word with the prefix arch and the normal Greek word for tax collector. Let me start with tax collector. If you lived as a devout Jew in first century You might think that being a tax collector would disqualify Zacchaeus from the kingdom. People view them as the worst sinners, as we see that in verse 7, traitors of Israel. Working for the enemy, the Roman Empire. But if you read Luke carefully thus far, you'd see that some tax collectors are welcomed by God. Some followed John the Baptist. In line with his forerunner, Jesus called one of them, Matthew, to be his disciple. He also called Matthew's colleagues to repentance. Ironically, tax collectors were closer to the kingdom than religious leaders. Though branded as outsiders, they accepted God's will as spoken by John and Jesus. While Pharisees and lawyers did not. As we see in that famous chapter, Luke 15, they were dead and alive again. Lost, but now found. There were cause for joy in heaven. Finally, Jesus in a parable pointed to a tax collector, not a Pharisee, as a model of humility. And righteousness that comes through faith in Christ. So, based on Jesus' treatment, we can say that being a tax collector and sinner does not block you from being a kingdom participant. But we must remember that Zacchaeus was not just any tax collector. He was, in a sense, a ruler. We don't know how many, but he was an arch tax collector over lesser of his kind. In the same way, Michael the Archangel is over angels, and Justin Welby, the Archbishop of Canterbury, is over the Church of England. I bring this up because the title of ruler, from which we get the prefix arch, does not help your position in relation to the kingdom. The data in Luke supports this. Besides one exception among Jewish leaders, Jairus, the ruler of the synagogue Consider how later most rulers demanded Jesus to be crucified and sneered at him. Earlier in chapter 14, Jesus stopped at the house of one of the rulers of the Pharisees. Yet what were they doing? They were watching him closely to see if he would violate their Sabbath customs. Most recently in the previous chapter, chapter 18, a certain ruler asked Jesus, Good teacher, what shall I do to inherit eternal life? We learned in the subsequent exchange, he was far from the kingdom of God. He loved his riches as his idol above all else. He walked away from Christ in the end. And like this young ruler, we're told in chapter 19, verse 2 that Zacchaeus was. Rich. Remember what Jesus said about those wealthy like him. How hard it is for those who have riches to enter the kingdom of God. For it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God. The Gospel of Luke contains a lot more than that in the previous chapters. Mary sang in chapter 1, verse 53, how God sends the rich away empty. Later, Jesus warned, Woe to you who are rich, for you have received your consolation. He told his followers, Don't invite your rich neighbors who will repay you. In parables, he taught that riches are thorns that choke the seed and render it fruitless. He who lays up treasure for himself is not rich toward God. Money is unrighteous mammon that must be handled carefully. It was the rich man who in his lifetime received his good things, and likewise Lazarus evil things. Then their fortunes were reversed in eternity. He realized his folly too late, the rich man. And even when rich people show piety, they give out of their abundance, unlike the widow who gives out of her poverty her two mights, as you'll see in chapter 21. Zacchaeus' rich status is a hindrance to the kingdom So let's tally up the score here. On the positive column, Zacchaeus is a tax collector and a sinner. Christ welcomes such ones. sermons.text: So it's good to be back home. And for those who thought of us and prayed for us, thank you. And I had a good time with family and a few friends in Korea. And as some of you know, I've spent the first nine years of my life there before immigrating here. I visited once back in the summer of 2004, so it's been a while. Now, I spent the majority of my life in the States. I've been a citizen of the US more than twice as long as I've been a citizen of the Republic of Korea. I know the streets of Laurel better than the streets of Daigu. So during this trip, I felt as if my identity was split between two communities. Two very different cultures. But there's a third and perhaps the most, not perhaps actually the most important factor in my identity. It relates to a place that you can find on a map. The closest parallel is found here. This morning, as we worship God, remember His Son, and fellowship together. As a Christian, what we do here as a church should have the most impact on my self-understanding. As our Lord taught us, our spiritual family is formed by those who do the will of the Heavenly Father. As Peter reminds us, we are a holy nation. Paul tells the Philippians, our citizenship is in heaven. One of my favorite reminders of our group identity from outside of the Bible comes from The second century apologetic work entitled the Epistle to Dionytus. Quote Christians are indistinguishable from other men either by nationality, language, or customs. They do not inhabit separate cities of their own, or speak a strange dialect, or follow some outlandish way of life. Their teaching is not based upon reveries inspired by the curiosity of men. Unlike some other people, they champion no purely human doctrine With regard to dress, food, and manner of life in general, they follow the customs of whatever city they happen to be living in, whether it's Greek or foreign. And yet there is something extraordinary about their lives. They live in their own countries as though they were only passing through. They play their full role as citizens but labor under all the disabilities of aliens. Any country can their can be their homeland, but for them their homeland, wherever it may be, is a foreign country. Like others, they marry and have children, but they do not expose them. They share their meals, but not their wives. They live in the flesh, but they are not governed by the desires of the flesh. They pass their days upon earth, but they are citizens of heaven. Obedient to the laws, they yet live on a level that transcends the law. Christians love all men, but all men persecute them. Condemned because they are not understood, they are put to death, but raised to life again. They live in poverty, but enrich many. They are totally destitute, but possess an abundance of everything. They suffer dishonor, but that is their glory. They are defamed, but vindicated. A blessing is their answer to abuse, deference, their response to insult. For the good they do receive, the punishment of malefactors, but even then they rejoice, as though receiving the gift of life They are attacked by the Jews as aliens, they are persecuted by the Greeks, yet no one can explain the reason for this hatred. It's a good reminder of our identity. Now, unfortunately, churches then and churches today forgot and forget to live according to their true identity. Like ancient Israel, we falter between two opinions. We set our minds on things below and not on things above. As a result, many so-called Christians do not look distinct from the world.
